en: Oṃ,
the Chāndogya Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmaveda.
Now begins the first chapter:
May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, as well as strength and all my senses, be nourished.
May everything pertaining to Brahman and the Upaniṣads not reject me, and may I not reject Brahman; may there be no rejection, may there be for me no rejection.
Whatever qualities are contained in the Upanishads for one who is devoted to the Self—may those be in me; may they be in me.
Om. Peace, peace, peace.
The Commentary composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. Introduction:
The *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* consists of eight chapters beginning with the words, "Om! This very syllable... and so forth.

For those desiring to know its meaning in brief, this *Ṛjuvivaraṇa*, a commentary on the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad-bhāṣya* composed by the venerable Narendrapurī Yatīndra in a concise form, is now commenced.

Regarding the connection [of this work]: all ritual action (*karman*), when accompanied by the knowledge of deities such as Prāṇa, is the cause for attaining the world of Brahman via the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*);
whereas pure [action] is the cause for attaining the world of the moon via the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādi-mārga*).
For those who follow their own nature and have fallen away from both paths, a miserable downward course is described;

yet, in neither of these two paths is there an ultimate attainment of the human goal. Therefore, the Upaniṣad is commenced to set forth the knowledge of the non-dual Self, independent of karma, which destroys the causes of the three courses of transmigratory existence.
Furthermore, the attainment of absolute supreme bliss does not occur apart from the realization of the non-dual Self;
for it will be said: “Now, those who know otherwise than this, having other rulers, belong to perishable worlds,” and in the case of the opposite, “He becomes his own ruler.”

Thus, having stated that for one who falsely identifies with the realm of duality, there is bondage—just as a thief experiences binding and burning upon grasping a heated axe—and the attainment of the suffering of saṃsāra; it follows that for one who truly identifies with the non-dual Self, just like a non-thief, there is an absence of binding and burning upon grasping the heated axe, as well as the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra, which is liberation (mokṣa).
Therefore, the vision of the non-dual Self does not coexist with ritual action (karman).

Because there can be no subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) toward such statements as "Being is one only, without a second" and "All this is indeed the Self," which arise from the dissolution of the distinctions between action, its factors, and their results;
[if you argue] that there is a cognition of injunctions regarding ritual action (*karma-vidhi-pratyaya*), we say no,

because the injunctions for ritual action are intended for one who possesses the notion of being an agent and an enjoyer, and who is possessed of defects such as passion and aversion toward the fruits of action produced thereby.
If it is argued that ritual action (*karman*) is prescribed even for one who has understood the entire meaning of the Vedas and possesses the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*), we say no.

This is because the innate cognition of being an agent, an enjoyer, and so forth—which constitutes the domain of eligibility for ritual action—is sublated by such [Vedic] statements as "Being is one only, without a second" and "The Self alone is all this.
Therefore, ritual actions are prescribed only for those who possess defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
This does not apply to one who possesses the knowledge of non-duality (advaita).
For this very reason, he will say: "All these [practitioners] attain worlds of merit;
but he who is established in Brahman attains immortality."

In this context of the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita-vidyā*), meditations (*upāsanā*) that are means to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) are described—meditations whose fruits are closely proximate to absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

These include those whose objects are Brahman slightly modified by non-duality and so forth, as well as those whose fruit is the success of ritual action (*karma-samṛddhi*) and which are connected to the constituent parts of rituals.

Because of their commonality of being secret and their commonality of being mental modifications (*manovṛtti*), just as the knowledge of non-duality is merely a mental modification, so too are the other meditations of the nature of mental modifications; for such is indeed their commonality.
What, then, is the distinction between the knowledge of non-duality (advaitajñāna) and the various forms of meditative worship (upāsanā)?
It is said:

the knowledge of non-duality is that which sublates the innate cognition of distinctions among the agents and other factors of action, as well as actions and their results, which have been superimposed upon the actionless Self.
Just as in the case of a rope and so forth, the ascertainment of the true nature of the rope—which is characterized by the cognition that superimposes a snake and the like—is caused by illumination;

however, meditation (*upāsana*) consists in producing a continuous flow of identical mental modifications (*cittavṛtti-santāna*) directed toward some object presented according to the scriptures, uninterrupted by cognitions of a different nature—this is the distinction.

These meditations are presented first because they purify the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*), thereby illuminating the reality of things and thus assisting in the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita-jñāna*); furthermore, since they have an objective support (*ālambana-viṣayatva*), they are easy to accomplish.

In this regard, because the practice of ritual action has been firmly established, the surrender of the mind to meditation alone is difficult while abandoning action; therefore, for the time being, meditation is first introduced as having the constituent parts of ritual action as its object:
"Om—let one meditate on this syllable as the Udgītha."
"Om"—with these words he sings the Udgītha. This is its further explanation. 1.1.1.
ChUpBh_1,1.1: The introductory commentary states: "One should meditate upon this syllable *om* as the *udgītha*.
This syllable *om* is the most proximate designation of the Supreme Self;
for when it is employed, He becomes pleased, just as a person in the world is pleased when his own dear name is uttered."
When the word "that" (*tad*) is employed as something else [than itself], the mere form of the word is perceived once its denotative function has been set aside;
thus, it becomes a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self, like an image (*arcā*) and so forth.

In this way, it is understood in all the Vedāntas that the means for the meditation on the Supreme Self is most excellent both by virtue of being a Name (*nāman*) and by virtue of being a Symbol (*pratīka*).
Its preeminence is well known from its frequent application at the beginning and end of recitations (*japa*), ritual acts (*karman*), and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
Therefore, one should meditate upon this very syllable—which consists of phonemes (*varṇa*)—as being denoted by the word *udgītha* because it is a constituent part of the *udgītha* chant.

One should maintain a firm, one-pointed concentration (*aikāgrya*) upon the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the ritual act and serves as a symbol (*pratīka*) for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The scripture itself states the reason why the syllable *oṃ* is denoted by the word *udgītha*: "For one sings [the Udgītha] with 'Om'.
Since one begins the singing with "Om," therefore the syllable *oṃ* is the *udgītha*; this is the meaning.

Its "explanation" (*upavyākhyāna*)—that is, the detailed exposition of that syllable stating that its meditation is such-and-such, its power is such-and-such, its fruit is such-and-such, and so forth—is the explanation.
"It proceeds"— this is the completion of the sentence.
//1// Of these beings, the earth is the essence.
Water is the essence of the earth;
plants are the essence of water;
man is the essence of plants.
The essence of the person is speech;
the essence of speech is the Ṛgveda;
the essence of the Ṛgveda is the Sāmaveda.
The Udgītha is the essence of the Sāman.
Of these beings, both moving and stationary, the earth is the essence, the goal, the final resort, and the support.

Of the earth, water is the essence; for the earth is woven like warp and woof in water, and therefore water is the essence of the earth. Of water, plants are the essence, because plants are a transformation of water.
Of these, man is the essence, because man is a transformation of food.
Of that man, too, speech is the essence;
for among the limbs of a person, speech is the most excellent.
Therefore, the essence of speech is said to be the person;
of that speech, too, the *ṛc* is the more essential essence;
of the *ṛc*, the *sāman* is the more essential essence.
Of that Sāman as well, the Udgītha—being the subject under discussion—is the syllable Om, which is the most essential.
This very Udgītha is the essence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.3)
Thus, this very syllable *oṃ*, known as the Udgītha, is the "most excellent essence" (*rasatama*), being the essence beyond all subsequent essences beginning with the elements;
it is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is the symbol of the Supreme Self; and it is "the highest goal" (*parārdhya*), meaning its station is the ultimate state.

"Parārdhya" means that which deserves the "parārdha," which is twice the highest number (para); the intention is that it is worthy of the station of the Supreme Self because it is to be meditated upon like the Supreme Self.
It is the eighth in the enumeration of the essences beginning with earth; it is the Udgītha, that which is the Udgītha. //3//
"What is the Ṛk? What is the Sāman? What is the Udgītha?"—thus it is investigated. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.4)
It has been stated that speech is the essence of the *ṛc*. Which is that *ṛc*, which is that *sāman*, and which is that *udgītha*?
The repetition "which... which" (*katamā katamā*) is for the sake of showing respect.
But surely, according to the rule “the suffix *ḍatamac* is used when many members of a class are questioned,” since there is no plurality of *ṛc*-classes here, how can there be the use of *ḍatamac*?
This is not a fault.
In the analysis *jātau paripraśnaḥ* (an inquiry regarding a genus), the term *jāti* (genus) refers to individual instances (*vyakti*) such as the *Ṛgveda*, which can logically be plural;
however, it is not analyzed as *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ* (an inquiry of a genus).
Now, one might object: "If the analysis were *jāteḥ paripraśnaḥ*, then examples such as 'Which Kaṭha? would be appropriate, but they are not suitable for the analysis *jātau paripraśnaḥ*."
Even in that case, there is no fault, because the question is intended with reference to the plurality of individual instances within the very class [of persons] such as the Kaṭhas and so forth.

If the question were directed at the genus (*jāti*), then an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) would have to be formulated for cases such as "which one? (*katamā katamā*); thus, it is thoroughly considered—that is, a full deliberation has been made. //4//
Speech indeed is the Ṛg;
breath is the Sāman.
The syllable "Om" is the Udgītha.
This, indeed, is a couple: speech and breath, and the Ṛk and the Sāman.
For when an inquiry has been made, it is appropriate for a reply to be given: "Speech is the Ṛk, breath is the Sāman.

Although speech and the Ṛk are one, there is no contradiction regarding their being the eighth, because this is a separate sentence from the preceding one, intended to establish the quality of attainment (āpti) in the passage, "The syllable 'Om' is the Udgītha.
Since speech and breath are the sources of the Ṛk and the Sāman, it is said that "speech is the Ṛk, breath is the Sāman."

For, by grasping speech and breath—the sources of the Ṛg and Sāman verses respectively—all Ṛg verses and all Sāmans would be encompassed; and when all Ṛg and Sāmans are encompassed, all rites accomplished by means of the Ṛg and Sāmans would be encompassed;
and when those are encompassed, all desires would be encompassed.
The doubt that the syllable "Om" is merely the Udgītha by way of figurative identification is dispelled.
By the words "That indeed is this," the couple is indicated.
To the question "What is that couple? he replies: it is speech and breath, which, being the causes of all Ṛk and Sāman, constitute the couple.
The phrase "the Ṛk and the Sāman" means that the words "Ṛk" and "Sāman" denote the causes of the Ṛk and the Sāman;
it does not mean that the Ṛk and the Sāman themselves constitute an independent couple.
For otherwise, there would be two couples: one consisting of speech and breath, and another consisting of the Ṛk and the Sāman.
Furthermore, the designation in the singular as "this pair" would be untenable [if it referred to the Ṛg and Sāman].
Therefore, the state of being a pair belongs only to speech and breath, which are the sources of the Ṛk and the Sāman. //5//
This couple is united in this syllable "Om. Indeed,
when a couple comes together, they fulfill each other's desire.
This very couple, characterized in this manner, is merged in this syllable *oṃ*.

Thus, the couple—distinguished by the quality of attaining all desires—is found to be merged in the syllable *oṃ*; therefore, the possession of the quality of attaining all desires by the syllable *oṃ* is well-established.

Since it is well-known that the syllable *oṃ* consists of speech (*vāṅmaya*), is produced by breath (*prāṇa*), and is merged with the couple, and since it is well-known that the couple is the fulfiller of desires, an illustration is stated.

Just as in the world, when a couple—a male and a female—come together and unite through sexual intercourse, they then fulfill or attain each other's desire; in the same way, the fact that the syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of fulfilling all desires is established by means of the couple who have entered into its own self. This is the intended meaning. //6//
He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha, truly becomes a fulfiller of desires. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7)

The commentator states that the Udgātṛ priest who worships it also comes to possess its qualities: "He indeed becomes the fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer, he who thus worships this syllable as the Udgītha endowed with the quality of attainment.
The meaning is that such is the fruit for him as previously described, according to the Vedic text: "In whatever way one worships it, that very thing one becomes. //7//
Now,
this very syllable is the syllable of assent; for whatever one assents to, one says "Om" to that.
This indeed is prosperity: that which is permission.
Truly, he becomes a fulfiller of desires who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.8)
The syllable *oṃ* is also endowed with the quality of prosperity.

How so? This very subject under discussion is the syllable of permission (*anujñākṣara*), and it is both permission and a syllable. "Permission" means consent; that is to say, it is the syllable *oṃ*.
How is "assent" (anujñā) defined? Scripture itself explains it:
whatever knowledge or wealth a wise man or a wealthy man grants permission for in this world, he expresses his consent by saying simply "Om.
Thus it is stated in the Veda: "Thirty-three [gods]—'Om,' he said," and so forth.
And likewise in common worldly usage, when someone says, "I take this wealth of yours," the other replies, "Om.
Therefore, this very thing—namely, permission—is prosperity; that which is permission is prosperity, because permission has its root in prosperity.
For one who is prosperous gives permission by saying "Om"; thus, the meaning is that the syllable *oṃ* possesses the quality of prosperity.

"Because he is a worshipper of the qualities of prosperity, being possessed of those qualities, he indeed becomes a fulfiller of the desires of the sacrificer— he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha," and so forth, as before. By means of that, this threefold knowledge proceeds.
With "Om," he causes [the Hotṛ] to announce; with "Om," he recites the Śastra; with "Om," he sings the Udgītha.
For the sake of honoring this very syllable, by means of its greatness and its essence.
Now, the syllable is praised for the purpose of inspiring devotion because it is to be meditated upon.

How so? By means of that aforementioned syllable, this triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*)—characterized by the Ṛgveda and the others—and the ritual action prescribed by that triple knowledge [are sustained]; such is the meaning.
For it is well known that it is not the triple knowledge itself that proceeds through the acts of recitation and so forth, but rather the ritual action that proceeds in that manner.
Furthermore, it is understood from the indicative mark—"He utters 'Om' as the *āśrāva*, he recites 'Om' as the *praśaṃsā*, and he chants 'Om' as the *udgītha*"—that this refers to the Soma sacrifice.
And that ritual is for the sake of honoring—that is, for the purpose of worshiping—this very syllable;
for it is indeed a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self.
That worship is indeed directed toward the Supreme Self alone, according to the Smṛti: "By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.
[This is done] by means of majesty and essence.
Furthermore, it is by the majesty— that is, the greatness— of this very syllable, meaning by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the officiating priests and the sacrificer;
likewise, it is by the essence (*rasa*) of this very syllable, meaning by the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) produced from the essence of rice,
barley, and so forth, that sacrifice, oblation, and other rites are performed through the syllable.
And that [offering] reaches the sun;
from there, through the sequence beginning with rain, vital breath and food are produced;
and by means of the vital breaths and food, the sacrifice is performed.
Therefore it is said: "They rejoice through the greatness of the Imperishable. (9)
Therefore, both perform [the ritual]:
he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different.
Whatever one performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upaniṣad—that alone becomes more powerful. This, indeed, is the further explanation of this very syllable.

In this regard, it is established that one who possesses knowledge of the Imperishable must perform ritual action; with this in mind, the text says: "By means of that Imperishable, both perform the work—both he who knows this Imperishable as it has been explained here, and he who knows merely the ritual action but does not know the true nature of the Imperishable.
Both of them perform the ritual action.
And since the fruit would arise from the power of the two actions alone, what is the use of knowing the true nature of the syllables therein?
For it is observed in the world that when two people eat *harītakī*, purgation occurs for both, whether they are familiar with its taste or not.
This is not so.
But because knowledge and ignorance are indeed different—for knowledge and ignorance are distinct—the word "but" (tu) serves to exclude the [previous] position.

It is not merely the knowledge that the syllable *oṃ* is a constituent part of ritual action that constitutes the knowledge possessing the qualities of being the most flavorful, the attainment, and the prosperity; rather, it is something superior to that.
Therefore, the intention is that an increase in the result is logical due to the addition of those auxiliary factors.
For it is observed in the world that between a merchant and a Śabara in the sale of gems such as rubies, the merchant obtains a greater result because of his superior knowledge.

Therefore, whatever action one performs while endowed with *vidyā*—that is, with specialized knowledge—and with faith—that is, being full of faith—and with the *upaniṣad*, meaning joined with yoga; this is the sense.

That very same action becomes more powerful—that is, it yields a greater fruit than the action of the ignorant—because of the statement that the action of the knower is more powerful; the intention is that even the action of the ignorant is indeed powerful. Furthermore, there is no lack of qualification for the ignorant person regarding action.
In the section concerning Uṣasti, because the performance of priestly duties is seen even for those who are ignorant,
there is one single meditation on the Imperishable (akṣara) as possessing the qualities of being the most flavorful, the attainment [of all], and abundance;
for no other effort is observed between these attributes.
Indeed, because this very syllable under discussion, known as the Udgītha, is to be meditated upon in many ways through numerous attributes, there follows this detailed exposition. //10//
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
It is said that once the gods and the asuras contended with one another.
Both were the offspring of Prajāpati; then the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By this we shall overcome them. (ChU 1.2.1)
"Devas and Asuras":
the *devas* are the functions of the senses illuminated by the scriptures, derived from the root *div*, meaning "to shine.

The *asuras* are those opposed to them; they are the natural functions of the senses consisting of darkness (*tamas*), so called because they delight (*ramanāt*) in their own vital breaths (*asu*)—the various activities of living directed toward sense objects.
The two particles *ha* and *vā* are used here as indicators of a preceding narrative event.

In that [situation], which was characterized by the mutual seizure of each other's domains as the cause, they "contended" (*saṃyetire*). Since the root *yat* preceded by the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "battle," the meaning is that they engaged in battle.
The "asuras" are the natural functions of the senses, consisting of the nature of darkness (*tamas*), which operate to suppress the functions of light (*prakāśa*) prescribed by the scriptures.

Likewise, the "gods" are their opposites, whose essence is the light of discernment regarding the objects of scriptural meaning; they operate to suppress the asuras, which consist of natural darkness.
Thus, like a battle characterized by mutual suppression and emergence, there occurs within every body among all living beings a battle between gods and asuras.
The intention is that [this conflict] has been proceeding for a time without beginning.

Here, it is narrated by means of a scriptural story (*ākhyāyikā*) for the sake of discerning knowledge regarding the origin and distinction between merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), with the purpose of teaching the method for the purification of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, both the gods and the asuras are called "progeny of Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyāḥ*), as they are the offspring of Prajāpati.

Prajāpati is the person (puruṣa) who is qualified for ritual action and knowledge, according to another Vedic scripture which states: "The Puruṣa alone is the Uktha; he himself is the great Prajāpati. For his functions of the organs—both those prescribed by the scriptures and those innate—are like offspring, because they arise from him.

On account of the specific cause characterized by the excellence or deficiency of those respective [qualities], the gods took—that is, they brought forth—the ritual function of the Udgātṛ, which is indicated by its constituent part, the Udgītha.
Since it is impossible to bring forth that alone in isolation, the intention is that they brought forth the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices.
To the question "For what purpose did they bring it?", it is said: they did so with the intention, "By means of this ritual, we shall overcome these Asuras. //1//
They meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one smells both the fragrant and the foul-smelling;
for this [organ] has been pierced by evil.

And when they desired to take up that Udgītha rite, then those gods meditated upon the nasal breath—the conscious sense of smell located in the nose—as the performer of the Udgītha; that is to say, they performed meditation by means of the Udgītha-portion [of the rite].
The meaning is that they meditated upon the syllable *oṃ*, known as the Udgītha, by viewing it as the nasal breath.
For in this way, there would be neither the abandonment of the relevant subject matter nor the introduction of an irrelevant subject matter.
Indeed, the meaning is that they meditated upon the syllable *om* as belonging to this very [syllable].
For in this way, there would be neither the abandonment of the relevant subject matter nor the introduction of an irrelevant subject matter.
Indeed, it is of this very syllable that [the text says], "of this syllable," for the syllable *oṃ* has been introduced as the object of meditation.
But was it not just stated that they took up the ritual action characterized by the *udgītha*;
how then do you say that they meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* through the vision of the nasal breath?
This is not a fault.

For it is intended that the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha* chant, is to be meditated upon as the deity Prāṇa through the vision of the agent of that action; it is not independent. Therefore, it is rightly said that they brought forward the ritual action for the sake of that meditation.

When the Udgātṛ had been thus chosen by the gods, the Asuras—whose nature is darkness—pierced that very deity, the Prāṇa in the nose who is of the form of light, with their own inherent evil consisting of attachment to unrighteousness;
the meaning is that they brought about contact with it.
For that nasal Prāṇa became one whose discriminative knowledge was overcome by the attachment and conceit arising from the perception of pleasant odors.

By that defect, he became associated with evil; thus it has been said: "The Asuras pierced him with evil. Because he was pierced by the evil of the Asuras, therefore, impelled by that evil, the olfactory breath (*ghrāṇa-prāṇa*) of living beings perceives foul odors.
Therefore, the world perceives both— the fragrant and the foul—
because it has been pierced by evil.
The mention of "both" is not intended to be restrictive.

It is just as in the case of the scriptural passage, "Whose two oblations both meet with disaster," because of the scriptural statement in the same context: "Whatever here is unseemly, that he smells. //2//
Then, indeed, they meditated upon speech as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, it speaks both the true and the false;
for it is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the eye as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly.
For this is pierced by evil. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.4)
Then, they meditated upon the ear as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one hears both that which is worth hearing and that which is not worth hearing.
For this is pierced by evil.
Then they venerated the mind as the Udgītha.
The Asuras pierced it with evil.
Therefore, by means of it, one forms both kinds of intentions: that which is to be intended and that which is not.
For this is pierced by evil.
This inquiry was initiated by the Śruti for the purpose of experiencing the purity of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) so that it may become an object of meditation.
Therefore, the deities of the eye and other senses are examined in succession and excluded, as they were pierced by the evil Asura; the rest is the same.
Then [the text says], "Speech, sight, hearing, mind," and so forth.
Other deities, such as those presiding over the skin, the sense of taste, and others, though not explicitly mentioned here, are also to be understood;
for there is another scriptural passage stating, "In this very way, these deities are indeed afflicted by evils. (3-6)

Then, they meditated upon that very breath which is the principal one as the Udgītha. When the Asuras attacked it, they perished; just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a solid stone, so did they perish. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.7)
Because they were pierced by the Asura [weapon], the deities of the sense of smell and the others were set aside;

then, immediately thereafter, they meditated upon that which is well-known as the "chief" (mukhya) breath located in the mouth as the Udgītha. When the Asuras reached it, just as before, they shattered it—that is, they destroyed it—by mere intention alone.

Without having done anything at all to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), how were they destroyed? To this, he provides an illustration: just as in the world a stone that is "unbreakable" (*ākhaṇa*) cannot be dug up, nor can it be split even with spades and other tools—it is called "unbreakable" precisely because it cannot be broken—having reached such a stone, by implication, a clod of earth (*loṣṭa*), a lump of dust, [is likewise destroyed].

And from another Vedic text: "Just as a stone thrown at another stone with the intention of splitting it might, without doing anything at all to that stone, itself shatter and break apart—so do they perish. This is the meaning. //7//
Just as a clod of earth, having struck a stone, crumbles away, even so does he crumble who desires evil against one who knows this, and he who seeks to harm him.
He is indeed like that clod of earth.

Thus, because he has been purified by not being overcome by the Asuras, he is called "Prāṇa. For one who knows this and has become the self that is Prāṇa, the scripture declares this result: "Just as [a clod of earth] against a stone...
This is the very illustration.
In this very way, he is shattered and perishes.
Who is this person? He says: "He who desires—that is, wishes—to do evil, which is unworthy, toward one who knows thus, namely one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) as described;
and he who also seeks to harm him—that is, injures the knower of the vital breath by employing abuse, beating, and so forth—he too is destroyed in exactly the same way. This is the meaning.

Because this knower of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), being of the nature of the vital breath itself, is like a "stone-cleft" (*aśmākhaṇa*)—meaning he is unassailable. Now, an objection might be raised: "Is not the nasal breath also of the nature of air, just like the principal (*mukhya*) breath? In that case, how is it that the nasal breath was pierced by evil while still being the vital breath itself, yet not the principal one?
This is not a fault.

But as for the nasal [breath], although it is of the nature of air, it is pierced due to the defectiveness of its place and organ; yet it is logical that it is not pierced because the deity presiding over its place is more powerful.

Just as axes and other tools perform their specific functions when held by a skilled person but not when in the hands of another, so too, because it is accompanied by the defective nose, the deity of the nose is pierced and is not the primary [breath].
By this [breath], one perceives neither fragrance nor foul odor,
for it is free from evil.
Whatever it eats and whatever it drinks, by that it sustains the other vital breaths.
Indeed, it is only after failing to find this [Self] at the end that one departs;
for at the end, one simply opens [the mouth]. Thus ends the section. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.9)

Because the principal [breath] was not pierced by the Asuras, therefore one does not perceive either fragrance or foul odor by means of that [breath] itself; rather, the world perceives both of these by means of the sense of smell alone.

And because the effects of evil are not seen in it, it is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*); that is, evil has been struck away, destroyed, or removed from it—this is the meaning of "free from evil," for it is pure.

Furthermore, while the sense of smell and the others are "self-serving" due to their attachment to pleasant things and so forth, the principal [breath] is not like that; rather, it serves the purpose of all.
How so? It is said: by that which is eaten and drunk by the principal [breath], the world protects and sustains the other [senses] such as the nose;
for by it their stability is maintained—this is the meaning. Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) sustains everything, and for this reason it is pure.
But how is it understood that their subsistence is primarily through what is eaten and drunk?
It is said: "This very primary breath" means that food and drink are the functions (*vṛtti*) of the primary breath.
"Finally," that is, at the end, at the time of death, "having not found"—meaning not having obtained—it departs;
the meaning is that the collection of vital breaths (prāṇa) such as the sense of smell and so forth [departs].
For one who is without vital breath is indeed unable to eat or drink.
Therefore, the departure of the aggregate beginning with the sense of smell is well-established;
for at the time of departure, a desire to eat is observed in the vital breath (prāṇa).
Hence, "he opens his mouth" means that he performs the act of opening the mouth.
For that [desire for food] is the sign of one who has departed [from the body] when food is not obtained. //9//
Aṅgiras meditated upon him as the Udgītha.
It is he indeed whom they consider to be Aṅgirasa, because he is the essence of the limbs (aṅga).
Regarding this, some have established the connection as follows: "Aṅgiras—that is, the principal breath (mukhya-prāṇa), characterized by such qualities—performed the Udgītha; Baka [did so] as well.
This is because of the statement: "They consider this very Aṅgirasa to be Bṛhaspati and Ayāsya, the breath.
This is indeed the case when the literal sense of the text is impossible.
However, it is possible that even in the case of the injunction regarding the seers (*ṛṣi*), it may be taken according to the literal text, as in other scriptural passages (*śruti*).
Therefore, they call him "the Seer of the Hundred Verses" (*śatarcin*) while he is actually [the vital breath] itself;
likewise, the scripture brings about the vital breath by means of the seers themselves, such as Mādhyma, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, and so forth.

In the same way, he makes these sages—the Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, and Ayāsya—who were practitioners of the meditation on Prāṇa, into Prāṇa itself for the sake of realizing their non-difference, just as in such passages as "Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is the mother.
Therefore, the sage named Aṅgiras, being Prāṇa himself, meditated upon himself as the Aṅgirasa-Prāṇa Udgītha; this is what is meant.
Since he is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the limbs and their essence (*rasa*), therefore he is *Āṅgirasa*. //10//
With that, Bṛhaspati meditated upon him as the Udgītha;
indeed, they consider this very one to be Bṛhaspati.
For speech is indeed the Bṛhatī; he is its lord.
Therefore, he meditated upon that Udgītha as Ayāsya;
for they consider this very one to be Ayāsya,
because he goes forth from the mouth (āsya).
Likewise, because he is the lord (*pati*) of speech (*vāc*), which is the *bṛhatī* meter, he is Bṛhaspati.

Because he issues forth (*ayate*) from the mouth (*āsya*), he is the seer Āyāsya; the meaning is that he is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Similarly, another worshipper should also meditate upon the self as the vital breath, endowed with qualities such as being Aṅgiras and so forth, as the Udgītha; this is the meaning.
By means of this, Baka Dālbhya came to know it;
he became the Udgātṛ priest for the people of Naimiṣa,
and he used to obtain desires for them by singing.
It was not only Aṅgiras and the others who performed this meditation.
Baka by name, the son of Dalbhya—Dālbhya—also came to know that Prāṇa exactly as it had been shown;
and having known it, he became the Udgātṛ priest for the performers of the sacrificial session (sattra) at Naimiṣa.
And by the power of his knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa), he sang forth the objects of desire for these people of Naimiṣa; "ha" is used in the sense that he indeed sang them. //13//
"He indeed becomes an attainer of his desires, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the syllable as the Udgītha. This is with reference to the self (ādhyātmam). ChUp 1.2.14.

Likewise, another Udgātṛ priest who knows this becomes a fulfiller of desires—he who, knowing thus, meditates upon the syllable *udgītha* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) endowed with the aforementioned qualities. The visible fruit for him has been stated; as for the invisible fruit, the intention is that it is established by another scriptural passage: "Having become a god, he goes to the gods," which speaks of becoming one with the Self of Prāṇa.

This concludes the meditation on the *udgītha* concerning the self (*adhyātma*), intended to focus the mind for the meditation on the *udgītha* regarding the deities (*adhidaivata*) which is about to be described. //14//
Thus ends the second section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, with regard to the deities.
One should meditate upon that very one who shines as the Udgītha.
Rising indeed, he sings the Udgītha for the sake of all creatures;
rising, he drives away darkness and fear.
He who knows this indeed becomes a dispeller of fear and darkness. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.1)

Now, immediately following this, the meditation on the Udgītha concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*) is introduced for the purpose of showing that the Udgītha is to be meditated upon in many ways. "That which is yonder sun that shines—one should meditate upon it as the Udgītha"; the meaning is that one should meditate upon the Udgītha by means of the vision of the sun. As for the objection: "Since the word *udgītha* denotes a syllable, how can it apply to the sun?"—it is replied: ChUpBh_1,3.2 The sun is the *udgītha*. Because it rises (*udeti*), therefore it is called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon this [sun] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for the sun indeed bestows food upon all beings. Through this, one obtains food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.2) The sun is the *udgītha*. Because it rises (*udeti*), therefore it is called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon this [sun] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for the sun indeed bestows food upon all beings. Through this, one obtains food. Because it is expanded (*udita*), therefore it is called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon this [ether] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for in the ether, one eats food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.7) ChUpBh_1,3.8 The *udgītha* is also the quarters of space (*diśaḥ*). Because they extend upward (*udayaṃti*), therefore they are called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon these [quarters] as the *udgītha*. They are the bestowers of food; for in the quarters of space, one eats food. Through this, one obtains food. One should meditate upon this [lightning] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for through lightning, one eats food. Through this, one obtains food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.10) The *udgītha* is also the lightning. Because it flashes upward (*udyotate*), therefore it is called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon this [lightning] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for through lightning, one eats food. Through this, one obtains food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.10) ChUpBh_1,3.11 The *udgītha* is also the sound (*svanaḥ*). Because it sounds forth (*unnati*), therefore it is called *udgītha*. One should meditate upon this [sound] as the *udgītha*. It is the bestower of food; for through sound, one eats food. Through this, one obtains food.
Rising or ascending, he indeed sings the Udgītha for the sake of creatures—that is, for the purpose of producing food for creatures.
For if he did not rise, there would be no ripening of rice and other grains; therefore, he "sings the Udgītha," as it were.
Just as the Udgātṛ priest sings for the sake of food, so too is the Sun the Udgītha; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he who knows the Sun— who dispels the nocturnal darkness and the fear born from it for living beings—
indeed becomes a dispeller, a destroyer, of fear characterized by birth and death, as well as of the darkness that is its cause, namely ignorance. 1.
This one here and that one yonder are indeed the same;
this one is warm, and that one is warm.
They call this one "Svara" (Sound), and they call that one "Pratyaśvara" (Response). Therefore, one should meditate upon both this and that as the Udgītha.
ChUpBh_1,3.2: Although the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sun appear as if distinct due to the difference in their locations, nevertheless, there is no difference in their essential nature (tattva).
How so? Because the vital breath is indeed the same—that is, equal—to the sun in its qualities, and the sun is the same to the vital breath;
for this vital breath is warm, and that sun is also warm.
Moreover, they call this breath "svara," that is, they speak of it as "svara";
and they call that sun "pratyāsvara.
This is because the breath indeed "sounds forth" (svarati), but once dead, it does not return.
Savitṛ, having set, returns again day after day;

therefore, on account of this quality as well as their name, Prāṇa and Āditya are identical with one another. Thus, because there is no difference in their essential nature, one should meditate upon this Prāṇa and that Āditya as the Udgītha. //2//
Now,
indeed, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* itself as the *udgītha*.
That which one breathes out is the *prāṇa*.
That which one breathes out is the *apāna*; now, that which is the junction of the *prāṇa* and the *apāna* is the *vyāna*;
that which is the *vyāna* is speech.
Therefore, without breathing in or breathing out, one utters speech.

Now, indeed, by means of another method, the meditation on the *udgītha* is being stated: one should meditate upon the *vyāna*—which is a specific function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) characterized as will be described later—as the *udgītha*.

Now its true nature is defined: that which a person breathes out—that is, expels air through the mouth and nostrils—is the specific function of the wind called *prāṇa*; and that which he breathes in—that is, draws air inward through those same two—is [the function called *apāna*]. This...
"Breathing" (prāṇa) is the function designated as inhalation (apāna).
To the question "What follows from that?", it is said: Now, that specific function which exists between those two—prāṇa and apāna—which have been described by their characteristics, is vyāna.
The intention is that what is well-known in the Sāṅkhya and other scriptures is not this [Vedic] Vyāna, because its specific nature is defined by the Śruti.

But why, setting aside Prāṇa and Apāna, is the meditation on Vyāna alone enjoined with such great effort? He states the reason: "Because it is the cause of efficacious action"—namely, "That which is Vyāna is speech."
Because speech is the effect of the vyāna breath:

since speech is brought about by the vyāna, people utter—that is, pronounce—speech while neither breathing out nor breathing in, that is, without performing the functions of the prāṇa and apāna breaths. //3//
That which is speech is the *ṛc*.
Therefore, even without breathing in or breathing out, one utters the *ṛc*.
That which is *sāman* is that;
therefore, one sings the *sāman* without breathing in or breathing out.
That which is *sāman* is the *udgītha*.
Therefore, he sings the Udgītha without inhaling and without exhaling.

Similarly, the intention is that one performs a specific speech-unit, namely a Ṛc, as well as the Sāman situated within that Ṛc, and the Udgītha which is a constituent part of the Sāman, by means of the vyāna breath alone, while neither inhaling nor exhaling. //4//
Therefore, whatever other vigorous actions there are— such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a firm bow— one performs them without breathing out or breathing in.
For this reason, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* breath itself as the *udgītha*.

Not only does one perform the utterance of speech and so forth from this [breath], but also other powerful actions that must be accomplished through an excess of effort— such as the churning of fire, running across a race-course, and the drawing of a firm bow— he performs these while neither breathing in nor breathing out.
Therefore, the vyāna is superior to the functions of prāṇa and the others.
Meditation upon that which is superior is better because it is fruitful, like the worship of a king.
For this reason and for this cause, one should meditate on the vyāna alone as the udgītha, and not on any other function.
The fruit is the state of possessing more intense vigor in action. //5//
Now, indeed, one should meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*: namely, *ut*, *gī*, and *tha*. The breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed *ut*.
For by means of the vital breath one rises up;
speech is song;
for they call songs "speech."
Food is the support; for upon food all this is established. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.6)
Now, one should indeed meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*, lest they be regarded merely as the syllables of a word. Therefore, he specifies them as "the *udgītha*.

This means the syllables of the name *udgītha*; for even when meditating on the syllables of a name, the meditation is effectively performed upon the bearer of that name, just as in the case of saying "Amuka-miśra.
Prāṇa alone is "ut"; one should contemplate Prāṇa in this syllable "ut."

How is the *prāṇa* superior? He says: for everyone rises by means of *prāṇa*, since one sees the collapse of that which is without *prāṇa*; therefore, there is a commonality between rising (*ud*) and *prāṇa*.
Speech (*vāk*) is song (*gīḥ*);
for the learned call speech "songs" (*giraḥ*).
Likewise, all this is established upon food; therefore, there is a commonality between food and the syllable *thā*. //6//
Heaven indeed is the *ut*;
the intermediate space is the *gī*.
Earth is *tham*;
the sun is *ut*;
the wind is *gīḥ*.
Agni is the *tham*;
the Sāmaveda is the *ut*;
the Yajurveda is the *gīḥ*.
The *Ṛgveda* is its udder. Speech yields for him the milk that is the yield of speech;
he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food.
He who, knowing them thus, meditates upon these syllables of the Udgītha—namely, *ud*, *gī*, and *tha*—[attains the aforementioned rewards]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.7)

The commonalities among the three [worlds] as stated in the Śruti are to be seen by that same correspondence even in the remaining [elements]. The sky (*dyu*) alone is [the *udgītha*], because it is situated high up; the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is [the *pratihāra*], O Gārgi, because it is the middle of the worlds.
The earth is [the syllable] *tha*, because it is the support for living beings;
the sun is *u*, because of its upwardness;
and the wind is *gīḥ*, because it swallows fire and the other elements.
The Agniṣṭoma is so called because it is the locus for sacrificial rites;
the Sāmaveda alone is "heaven" because it is praised as heaven;
and the Yajurveda is "swallowing" because the deities swallow the oblation offered with the *yajuṣ* formulas.

Because the Sāman is supported upon the Ṛk which resides in the Ṛgveda, the fruit of the meditation on the syllables of the Udgītha is now stated: "It milks [or] milks for this practitioner. Which is that speech? What is the milk?
What is this milking? He says: it is the milking of speech.
The intention is that it is the fruit accomplished by the words of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; that milking of speech milks itself—it milks its own self.
Furthermore, one becomes possessed of food, having abundant food, and an eater of food, with a kindled digestive fire.
He who, knowing these syllables of the Udgītha to possess exactly the qualities described above, meditates upon them as "Udgītha"—[he obtains the aforementioned rewards]. //7//
Now,
indeed, there is the fulfillment of one's wishes;
one should worship [the fires] as "approaches."
One should meditate upon that Sāman with which one intends to chant the praise.
Now, therefore, the fulfillment of blessings—that is, the fulfillment of desires—is being explained; this is the remainder of the sentence.
"Approaches" (upasaraṇāni) means those which are to be approached, to be resorted to, or meditated upon. How so? One should meditate thus.

One should meditate in this manner: for instance, with whatever *sāman* or specific *sāman* the Udgātṛ priest is about to praise—that is, perform a hymn of praise—he should approach that *sāman*, draw near to it, and reflect upon it through its origin and other such characteristics. //8//
In which *ṛc* [he recites], that *ṛc*; from which seer it originated, that seer;
One should run toward whichever deity one intends to praise.

One should meditate upon that Ṛc in which the Sāman occurs by means of its deity and other attributes; one should meditate upon that Ṛṣi to whom the Sāman belongs; and one should meditate upon that deity whom one intends to praise. //9//
With whatever *chandas* one is about to chant, one should meditate upon that *chandas*; with whatever *stoma* one is about to chant, one should meditate upon that *stoma*. (ChUp 1.3.10)
One should meditate upon that *chandas* (meter), such as the *gāyatrī* and others, with which one intends to praise;
and upon that *stoma* (hymn-form) with which one will be praising.
The use of the middle voice in "stoṣyamāṇa" is because the fruit of the constituent parts of the *stoma* accrues to the agent.
One should pursue that hymn of praise. //10//
In whichever direction he intends to praise, let him run toward that direction.
In whichever direction one intends to praise, one should run toward that direction with the presiding deities and the others. //11//

Having approached the Self at the end, let him praise it, meditating on his desire and remaining vigilant. For that desire for which he praises will surely be fulfilled for him—whatever desire he may have when he praises, whatever desire he may have when he praises. Thus ends ChUp 1.3.12.

The Udgātṛ priest should praise himself—his own form—with his lineage, name, and so forth, reciting the Sāman verses and others in sequence; finally, having approached himself at the very end, he should praise while meditating on his desired object, remaining vigilant and not making any error regarding the vowels, sibilants, consonants, and other elements of the chant. Consequently, it is near—that is, very quickly—indeed, that the desired object for one who knows thus will be fulfilled, that is, it will reach fulfillment.
Who is this person? He is one who possesses a desire; being one who possesses such a desire, he should praise.
The repetition is for the sake of showing respect. //12//
Thus ends the third section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Om! One should meditate upon this syllable as the Udgītha.
"Om"—thus indeed one sings the Udgītha. This is its further explanation. 1.4.1.

The repetition of the syllable *akṣara* introduced at the beginning with "Om, this... and so forth is for the purpose of ensuring that the subject does not shift elsewhere due to being interrupted by other meditations on the syllables of the *udgītha* and so on.
This section begins because the meditation on the very same *akṣara* under discussion, characterized by the qualities of immortality and fearlessness, is now to be enjoined.
The passage beginning with "Om" has already been explained. //1//
The gods, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge;
they covered themselves with the meters.
Because they covered [themselves] with these, that is the reason for the "metrical nature" (chandastva) of the meters.
It is now stated what the gods did when they were afraid of death, the destroyer:
"They entered the threefold knowledge"—that is, the ritual action prescribed by the three Vedas; the meaning is that they commenced Vedic rites.
They did so considering that [the Vedic rites] to be a protection (*trāṇa*) from death.
Furthermore, by performing recitations, oblations, and so forth with those meters and mantras not employed for specific ritual acts, they concealed themselves within other rites;
because they concealed [themselves] with these mantras, the nature of the meters and mantras as "chandas" (concealers) is indeed well-established. //2//
Thereupon, death beheld them there— just as one might look for a fish in water— in the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*.
But having discovered them, they rose above the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus* and entered into the tone (*svara*) itself.

There, Death beheld those gods who were devoted to ritual action, just as in the world a fisherman might see a fish in water that is not very deep, considering it capable of being caught by means of a hook and a net; in this way, Death perceived—that is, saw—the gods as beings who could be overcome by the means of the exhaustion of their karma. This is the meaning.
It is asked, "Where did he see those gods? It is replied: "In the Ṛg, the Sāman, and the Yajus"—meaning, in the ritual acts associated with the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman.
Those gods, having been purified by Vedic ritual and being of cleansed soul, came to know what Death intended to do.

Having understood this, they turned away from ritual acts—from the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus, meaning from the ritual acts connected with the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman. Having risen above those rituals, being hopeless regarding the removal of the fear of death through such action, they cast that aside and entered the Imperishable (akṣara), which possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness and is designated by the word "Svara"; that is, they entered it.
They became devoted to the meditation upon the syllable Om.
The word *eva* has the sense of restriction, serving here to exclude the notion of conjunction;
the meaning is that they became intent upon the meditation on that [Self]. //3//
When one encounters a *ṛc*, one utters "Om" as a high-pitched tone; likewise for a *sāman* and likewise for a *yajus*. This syllable is indeed that tone; it is immortal and fearless.
Having entered that, the gods became immortal.

But how, again, is it said that the Imperishable (akṣara) is denoted by the word "svara" (sound)? When one encounters a *ṛc* verse, one utters "Om" as its response; likewise for the Sāman and the Yajus. This indeed is the "svara. What is that? It is this very syllable, which is immortal and fearless. Having entered into that, the gods became, according to their respective qualities, immortal and fearless. //4//

He who, knowing it thus, utters this syllable, enters this very syllable—the sound, the immortal, the fearless. Having entered it, he becomes immortal, even as the gods are immortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.4.5)
Furthermore, whoever else, like the gods, knowing this syllable to have such qualities as immortality and fearlessness, praises it— that is,
offers worship to it (for here "praise" is intended to mean "meditative worship")—
he likewise enters into this very same syllable, which is sound, immortal, and fearless.

And having entered that royal palace, he does not become immortal in a manner distinguished by the distinction between inner and outer circles of the king—as if he had merely entered—nor is there any deficiency or excess in his immortality; this is the meaning. //5//
Thus ends the fourth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; and that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
That sun, indeed, is the Udgītha; it is the Praṇava.
For it goes along sounding "Om."

Having restated the meditation on the *udgītha* as qualified by the vision of it being Prāṇa and Āditya, and having established the identity of the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, the following section is now commenced to explain the meditation on the syllable (*akṣara*)—qualified by the attributes of the distinction between Prāṇa and its rays—which yields the fruit of many sons:
"Now, indeed, that which is the *udgītha* is the *praṇava* of the Bahvṛcas; and that which is the *praṇava* for them [is the *udgītha*]."
That very same [deity] is what is denoted by the word *udgītha* in the *Chāndogya*:
"Verily, that sun is the *udgītha*. He is also what is denoted by the word *praṇava* for the followers of the Ṛgveda, and none other.
How is it that the sun is the *udgītha*?
The syllable *om*, known as the *udgītha*, is indeed this [Savitṛ], because he utters it while chanting—since roots have multiple meanings—or else, because he goes (*svaran*) while moving;
therefore, this Savitṛ is the *udgītha*. //1//
"It was indeed this very one that I praised; therefore, you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"You must tend the rays of light."
"Indeed, they will become many.
Thus with reference to the deities. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.5.2)
"I have indeed chanted toward him"—that is to say, having made no distinction between the rays of the sun and [the Self], I have performed meditation upon him.
For that reason, "you are my only son," thus said Kauṣītaki—the offspring of Kuṣītaka—to his son.
Therefore, "you must turn around the rays and the sun separately," that is to say, you must distinguish them.
"By virtue of you, thus indeed shall many be your sons"—this is with reference to the deity. //2//
Now,
with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that which is this principal vital breath (prāṇa) as the Udgītha.
Saying "Om," he indeed goes forth chanting.
Now, immediately following this, the internal [aspect] is described:
"One should meditate upon that which is this principal breath (prāṇa) as the Udgītha," and so forth, as before.
Likewise, this breath also goes along sounding "Om"; for it is as if granting permission by saying "Om" for the sake of the functioning of speech and the other organs—this is the meaning.
For indeed, those standing near a person about to die do not hear the utterance of "Om" by the departing breath;
on account of this similarity, the utterance of "Om" in the case of the sun should be regarded as a mere formal acknowledgment. //3//
"It was indeed this one whom I sang to; therefore you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son.
"Sing to the breaths as the Plurality, for then many sons shall be mine."
"Upon him alone have I meditated," and so forth, as before.

Therefore, perceiving speech and the other organs, as well as the principal breath (prāṇa), as the Udgītha distinguished by its various qualities, one should sing with the mind to that Plurality (bhūman).
The meaning is: "Repeat [the meditation] as before."
The meaning is that he had the intention, "Indeed, many sons shall be mine.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha.
For even from the Hotṛ’s seat, one may rectify a poorly performed Udgītha—yes, one may rectify it.
Now, indeed, the vision of the identity between the *praṇava* and the *udgītha*, beginning with the words "That which is the *udgītha*," has been explained; it is possible to bring forth its fruit.

What is that? Even if the *udgītha* is badly sung—that is, if the singing (*udgāna*) performed by the *udgātṛ* priest in his own ritual duty is defective, meaning it has been marred—then he rectifies it;
that is to say, he joins it back together.
Just as medical treatment brings about the restoration of equilibrium when there is an imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātus). //5//
Thus ends the fifth section of the first chapter in the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. This [earth] indeed is the Ṛg-veda.
Agni is the Sāman.
This Sāman is thus supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc.
This very [earth] is that; fire is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. 1.6.1.
Now, in order to attain the perfection of all fruits, another meditation on the *udgītha* is prescribed: "This earth itself is the *ṛc*;
one should perceive the earth as the *ṛc*.
Likewise, fire is the *sāman*."
The view of fire upon the *sāman*:
how is it that earth and fire possess the nature of *ṛc* and *sāman*? It is said in reply:

This very thing, this Sāman called "Agni," is situated upon this earth as its *ṛc*; that is to say, it is established above it, just as the Sāman rests upon the *ṛc*. For this reason, even now, the Sāman is chanted by the chanters of the Sāman as being supported by the *ṛc*.
And just as the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are not absolutely distinct from one another, so too these two—the earth and fire—have attained the status of being denoted by the single term "Sāman.
Therefore, the pair of earth and fire is not distinct from one another, being eternally conjoined like the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*.
And for that reason, the meaning is that the earth and fire possess the nature of the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*.

Some maintain that this very [verse], "This indeed is she; Agni is he," is intended for the purpose of enjoining the visualization of the earth and fire upon the *sāman* and its syllables, respectively. 1.
The intermediate space itself is the Ṛg;
the wind is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. The intermediate space itself is that Sāman.
The wind is *ama*;
that is the *sāman*. ChUp 1.6.2.
The sky is indeed the Ṛc;
the sun is the Sāman.
Thus, this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. The sky is indeed the Sāman;
the sun is the Āma.
That is the Sāman. ChUp 1.6.3.
"The intermediate space is indeed the Ṛg, the wind is the Sāman," and so forth, as before. 2–3.
The stars indeed are the Ṛg;
the moon is the Sāman.
Thus, this Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. The stars themselves are the Sāman.
The moon is the *ama*;
that is the *sāman*. ChUp 1.6.4.
The moon is the lord of the stars; therefore, it is Sāman. 4.4.4.
Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *Ṛc*;
and that which is the blue, exceedingly dark [light] is the *Sāman*.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc.
Now, that which is the white light, the white radiance of the sun, is the *Ṛk*.
And that which is the blue, the exceedingly black—that is, the extreme darkness—within the sun, is the *Sāman*;
for it is seen by one whose vision is perfectly concentrated. 5.
Now, that which is the white light of this sun is indeed *sā*;
and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is *amā*.
That is Sāman.
Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, golden even to the tips of his nails, entirely consisting of gold—[that is Sāman].
These two are indeed light and darkness; that is *sā* and this is *ama*, hence *sāma*.
Now, that which is within the sun—within the midst of the sun—is golden, as it were; it is "golden" because it resembles gold, for it is not possible for the Divine to be a modification of gold.
Because [the qualities of] being the source of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur-veda, and having evil removed, are impossible [in that case];

for there is no possibility of the attainment of evil and so forth in a golden [image], which is insentient, such that it would need to be prohibited; and because [these qualities] are not perceived in the visual [image].

Therefore, the word *hiraṇmaya* is indeed an elided simile (luptopamā), meaning "consisting of light" (*jyotirmaya*). The same application [of this principle] holds for the subsequent [terms] as well. [The term] *puruṣa* is so called because he dwells in the city (*puri śayanāt*) or because he fills (*pūrayati*) the world with his own self.
He is seen by those whose eyes have turned away [from sense objects] and whose minds are concentrated, depending on such means as celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Since even the facial hair and hair of a radiant being might be black, he specifies: "golden-bearded, golden-haired.
The meaning is that his beard and hair consist of light itself.
From the very tips of the nails—meaning including the nails and the tips of the nails—the whole [body] is like gold; that is to say, its nature is light. //6//
As a lotus flower is reddish-yellow like a monkey's buttocks, so are his eyes;
his name is "Ut."
He has risen above all evils;
indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils.
Of that [person], who is thus golden-colored in every respect, there is this particularity regarding the eyes.
How so? His "kapyāsa" (monkey-buttock) refers to the buttock (*āsa*) of a monkey (*kapi*);
the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the instrument for the action of sitting (*ās*, to sit).
The end of the monkey’s back is where he sits;
his two eyes are like a lotus that has blossomed on a monkey’s back, exceedingly radiant.
Because it is a comparison using a comparison, it is not a "deficient simile" (hīnopamā).
This is the secondary name of that very [Self] distinguished by such qualities.
How is it secondary?
This deity is "free from all evils"—that is to say, together with evil and its effects.
That which he will describe as "the Self free from evil" and so forth is "udita," meaning risen or emerged; therefore, its name is "Ud."
Whoever knows this very Uddālaka, endowed with such qualities, in the manner described, he too indeed rises up—goes forth—from all evils.
The two particles *ha* and *vā* are used for emphasis;
the meaning is "he certainly rises up. //7//
The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are its two shoulders;
therefore, it is called the *udgītha*.
Therefore, he alone is the Udgātṛ;
for he is the singer of this [Sāman].
He is the ruler of those worlds that are beyond yonder sun, and of the desires of the gods.
Thus with reference to the deities. ChU 1.6.8.

Regarding his status as the *udgītha*, since it is intended [to show] that he is like Āditya and the others, the text says: "The *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are his two joints (*geṣṇau*)," meaning the two sections characterized as the earth and so forth.
For the deity is the self of all;
because he is the lord of the desires of both the higher and lower worlds, his having the earth, fire, *Ṛk*, and *Sāman* as his joints is appropriate.
And because it is the source of all;

since it is thus named and has the *ṛk* and *sāman* as its essence (*geṣṇa*), therefore the state of being the *udgītha*—which follows from having the *ṛk* and *sāman* as its essence—is stated by means of a cryptic expression (*parokṣa*), because the God loves what is cryptic; hence it is called the *udgītha*.
For that very reason, he is the *udgātṛ* (the chanter), because he sings forth (*ud-gāyati*) the *udam*.
Because he is the singer (*gātṛ*) of this aforementioned "High Name" (*unnāman*), it is fitting that the name *udgātṛ* (the Udgātṛ priest) is well-established for him.

This very deity, the High Name, rules over those worlds which are beyond and above this Āditya—that is, the worlds that go upward—and not merely as their ruler, but by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), he also sustains them, as stated in the Vedic mantra:
"He supported the earth and this heaven," and so forth.
Furthermore, "he desires the objects of the gods"—this has been stated as the *adhidaivata*, the nature of the deity, namely the Udgītha, with reference to the divine realm. //8//
Thus ends the sixth section of the first chapter in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now, with respect to the self (ādhyātmam).
Speech is indeed the *ṛc*,
and breath is the *sāman*.
This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*.
Therefore, the Sāman is sung as resting upon the Ṛc. Speech indeed is the Sāman;
breath is the Āma.
That is Sāman. ChUp 1.7.1.
Now, the internal [correspondence] is stated:
Speech is the *ṛc* and breath is the *sāman*,
because of the commonality of their being situated below and above respectively.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the wind (*vāyu*), is called the sense of smell; speech itself is that *prāṇa*, "I am" (*ama*), and so forth, as before. //1//
The eye itself is the Ṛk;
the self is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. The eye itself is that Sāman.
The Self is the syllable *ām*.
That is the *sāman*. ChUp 1.7.2.
The eye itself is the Ṛg; the Sāman is the Self.
Here, "Self" refers to the shadow-self, for it is the Sāman because it resides therein. //2//
The ear itself is the Ṛg;
the mind is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc. The ear itself is the Sāman.
The mind is the *am* sound;
that is the *sāman*. 1.7.3.
The ear is indeed the Ṛg and the mind is the Sāman; because the ear is the presiding principle, the mind possesses the nature of the Sāman. //3//
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the Ṛg;
and that which is the dark, deep-black is the Sāman.
This Sāman is supported upon this Ṛc;
therefore, the Sāman is sung as being supported upon the Ṛc.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is indeed that [Sāman].
Now, that which is blue-black—that is *Ama*;
that is *Sāman*.
Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *Ṛg*. And that which is the dark blue, deeper than black, like the sun—the locus of the power of sight—that is the *Sāman*. 4.
Now, that person who is seen within the eye— he is indeed the Ṛg,
he is the Sāman.
That is the hymn; that is the sacrificial formula; that is the sacred word.
Of this [person], that very form is what the form of yonder [sun] is;
whatever are its two joints, those are his two joints;
and what its name is, that is his name.
Now, that person who is seen within the eye is as described before. That same [set of deities],
consisting of speech and so forth with respect to the self (adhyātma), and earth and so forth with respect to the divine (adhidaivata), is the Ṛc.
Moreover, it is well known that the *ṛc* consists of syllables bound into quarters;
likewise is the *sāman*.
Or, by association with the *uktha*, the *stotra* is the *sāman* and the *uktha* is the *śastra*.
Other than the *uktha*, likewise the *yajus*—including *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and so forth—all that is the sacrifice of speech (*vāgyajus*), and that is He alone.
For we have already stated that this is because He is the self of all and the source of all. Because it occurs in the context of the *ṛc* and other [Vedic meters], that Brahman is the three Vedas.
The very same form of that person in the eye is extended [to the other];
what is that? It is that which belongs to "that" person in the sun—namely, "golden" and so forth, as was described with reference to the divine realm (adhidaivata).
Whatever are the two *geṣṇas* (places of rest) and the two joints (*parvan*) of that [Āditya], those very same are the two *geṣṇas* of this [Cākṣuṣa] as well;
and whatever is its name, "Nāda" and "Udgītha," that very same is its name.

If it be argued that there is a distinction between Āditya and Cākṣuṣa because of the difference in location, the transfer of form, qualities, and name, and because of the designation of a difference in their spheres of lordship (*īśitṛtva*), we say: no.
Because it is impossible for a single entity to attain both natures simultaneously—either by means of this [one] or that [other].
If it is argued that this is possible through a twofold manifestation, [we reply: No;
for he will state later, "He becomes onefold, he becomes threefold," and so forth. It is not so.
Because a single conscious entity, being partless, cannot logically undergo division;
therefore, there is indeed identity between the internal and the divine.
As for what you said—that the extension of form and other qualities is a cause for distinction—that is not intended to establish a difference.
Rather, it is for this purpose: so that no suspicion of difference [between them] arises due to their difference in location. //5//
He is the one who rules over those worlds that are on this side of him, and over the desires of men. Therefore,
when these people sing to the lute, they sing of him.
Therefore, they are winners of wealth.
This very person in the eye (the *cākṣuṣa-puruṣa*) rules over those worlds that are below this internal self and have gone downward, as well as over the desires related to human beings.

Therefore, when these singers sing upon the lute, they sing of him alone. Because they sing of the Lord, they are "winners of wealth"—meaning they are endowed with the acquisition of wealth, that is, they become wealthy. //6//
Now, he who, knowing it thus, sings this Sāman— verily he sings both.
By means of that [sun] alone, he attains those worlds which are beyond it, as well as the desires of the gods.
Now, he who, knowing this thus, knowing the god Udgītha as described, sings the Sāman—he sings of both the one in the eye and the one in the sun.

The fruit for such a knower is stated: by means of that very sun, he attains those worlds which are beyond it; the meaning is that, having become the deity residing within the sun, he attains them as well as the desires of the gods. (ChUpBh 1.7.7–8)
Moreover, by this very means he attains those worlds that are on this side of it, as well as the desires of human beings.
Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows this should say: [ChU 1.7.8]
"What desire shall I obtain for you by singing? For he who, knowing this, sings the Sāman, is indeed master of obtaining desires—he who sings the Sāman, sings the Sāman.
Furthermore, by means of this very [sun] as the ocular one, he attains those worlds which are below this one, as well as human desires; the meaning is that he becomes the ocular one.

Therefore, an Udgātṛ who knows thus should say to the sacrificer: "Which desire of yours shall I bring forth by singing? For this reason, since this Udgātṛ is capable—meaning he is able—to accomplish a desire through his singing, he is the master of the fulfillment of desires by means of the Udgītha.
Who is he? He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*—he sings the *sāman*.
The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation (*upāsana*). //8-9//
Thus ends the seventh section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, there were three who were skilled in the Udgītha: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali.
They said, "We are indeed skilled in the Udgītha; come, let us have a discussion on the Udgītha."

Because the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be meditated upon in many ways, [the author] introduces another meditation with the fruit of the quality of being "higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) by means of a different method.
The historical narrative (itihāsa), however, is for the purpose of easy comprehension.
"Three" means having the number three.
"Ha"—this is the meaning of the traditional narrative (aitihya). They became skilled and proficient in the Udgītha, that is, in the knowledge of the Udgītha.
The intention is that they had gathered together at a certain place, time, or on account of a certain occasion.
For it is not the case that in the entire world only three possess skill in the knowledge of the *udgītha* and so forth;
indeed, we hear of those such as Uṣasti, Jānaśruti, and Kaikeya who are nearly omniscient. He asks, "Who are these three? and says: Śālāvatya is by name Śilaka, the descendant of Śalāvat.
Caikitāyana is the descendant of Cikitāyana;
Dālbhya belongs to the lineage of Dalbha or is a *dvaimātura* (born of two fathers);
Pravāhaṇa by name is the descendant of Jīvala—these three said to one another, "We are indeed renowned as being skilled and proficient in the *udgītha*."

Therefore, "well then, if you have permission, let us discuss the Udgītha"—meaning let us engage in a formal debate (*vāda*) consisting of the presentation of arguments and counter-arguments based on knowledge of the Udgītha. For in such a discussion with one who possesses that knowledge, there occurs the destruction of misconceptions, the arising of new understanding, and the removal of doubt; thus, association with those possessing such knowledge must be undertaken—this is the purpose of the traditional narrative (*itihāsa*).
For it is indeed seen in the case of Śilaka and others. //1//
"So be it," they replied, and sat down together.
Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said:
"Let the two venerable ones speak first;
I shall listen to the words of the two wandering mendicants as they speak. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.2)
Having said, "So be it," they sat down together; it is said that they sat there.
Then, because of the king's boldness, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to the other two: "May the two venerable ones speak first.
From the indicative mark [in the word] "brāhmaṇayoḥ" (of the two Brahmins), it is clear that this person was a king.
"I shall listen to the speech of you two Brahmins as you speak"—others [interpret this] as "speech devoid of meaning," because of the specific qualification "speech. //2//
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come now, let me ask you a question.
"Ask," he replied.
Regarding those two who had spoken, Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "Come now; if you will permit me, I shall question you. Being thus addressed, the other said, "Ask. [Śilaka asked:
"What is the goal of the Sāman?"
"Voice," he said. "What is the goal of voice?
"Breath," he said.
"What is the goal of food?
"Food," he said.
"What is the goal of food?"
"Water," he said. ChU 1.8.4.
Having received permission, he said: "Which is the *sāman*?"—because the *udgītha* is the subject under discussion;
for it is the *udgītha* that is introduced here as the object of meditation.
And he will later say, "the udgītha that is higher than the high. "Gati" means support or ultimate resort.
Being thus questioned, Dālbhya said: "The tone (svara)."

Because the Sāman has sound as its essence, it is logical that whatever has a certain essence has that [essence] as its course and that as its support—just as a jar and other such objects have clay as their support.
[The question follows: "What is the course of sound?"
"It is breath," he said.
"For the tone is produced by breath; therefore, breath is the goal of the tone.
"What is the goal of breath? "It is food," he said.
For life-force (prāṇa) has food as its support;
for the Śruti says, "Life-force indeed withers without food," and also, "Food is the bond."
"What is the destination of food? "Water," he said, "because food originates from water. //4//
"What is the goal of water?
"That world," he said.
"What is the destination of that world?
"One should not lead it beyond the heavenly world," he said.
"We establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world."
For this Sāman is called "the Praise of Heaven."
"What is the goal of water? "That world," he replied.
"From that world, rain comes into being.
When asked, "What is the goal of that world?", Dālbhya said: "No one should lead the Sāman beyond that heavenly world to any other support; so he said."
Therefore, we also establish the *sāman* upon the heavenly world;
the meaning is that we know the *sāman* as being established in the heavenly world.
