It is the *sāman* whose praise (*saṃstāva*)—that is, its glorification as being the heaven—is the "heavenly praise" (*svargasaṃstāva*). For there is a Vedic revelation stating: "The heavenly world is indeed the Sāmaveda. (5)
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation.
If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off."

The other, Śilaka Śālāvatya, said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "It is unestablished and unsteady"—the meaning is that the *sāman* has not reached its ultimate goal by way of being higher than the high (*parovarīyas*). The word "vā" recalls the traditional authority, and "kila" indicates tradition; [he says], "O Dālbhya, this is your *sāman*."

But if someone who is intolerant and ignorant of the Sāman should now say at this time, "The Sāman is not established; it is established"—thus speaking erroneously—[the teacher would say]: "Your head shall fall off;
it will clearly fall off.
If such an offender were addressed thus, his head would indeed fall off without a doubt; however, the intention is that I am not saying this [of you].

Now, if one has committed an offense deserving of having one's head fall off, then one's head would fall even if not told by another; if one has not committed an offense, it does not fall even if told.
Otherwise, there would be the arrival of what was not done and the destruction of what was done.
This is not a fault;
for the attainment of the fruit of a performed action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, depends upon place, time, and causal conditions.
This being so, even ignorance—which is the cause for the downfall from the "summit" stage—depends upon the condition of another's speech. //6//
"Come,
let me learn this from your reverence," [Nārada said].
"Learn it," he replied.
"What is the goal of that world?
"This world," he said.
"What is the goal of this world?"
"One must not lead the world beyond its foundation," he said.
"We establish the Sāman upon the world as its foundation,
for the Sāman has its praise grounded in the foundation."

Thus addressed, Dālbhya said: "Come now, let me learn from your reverence this: on what is the Sāman established? Being thus addressed, Śālāvatya replied: "Know it. When asked by Dālbhya, "What is the goal of that world? Śālāvatya said: "This world.
For this world nourishes that world through sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth.
"The gods subsist upon what is given from here"—so indeed say the Vedas.
For it is directly perceived that the earth is the support of all beings;
therefore, it is logical that this world is likewise the support of the Sāman.
When asked, "What is the goal of this world? Śālāvatya replied:
"No one can lead the *sāman* beyond this world, which is its foundation;
therefore, we establish the *sāman* upon the world as its foundation."
The meaning is that because the *pratiṣṭhā-saṃstava*—the praise as a foundation—is praised as being the foundation, it is the *Sāman*;
for there is the scriptural text: "This [earth] indeed is the *Rathantara*. //7//
Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him:
"O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite."
"But if someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' or 'Your head will fall off,' and you were to say, 'Come,
let me learn this from your reverence,' [the teacher] said,
'Learn it.'"
When he had spoken thus, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him, "O Śālāvatya, your Sāman indeed has an end," and so on as before.
Thereupon Śālāvatya said, "Come now, let me learn this from your reverence. The other replied, "Know it," and being permitted, he spoke. 8.
Thus ends the eighth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"What is the goal of this world? [he asked].
"It is space," he said.
"Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone;
they dissolve back into space."
For space indeed is greater than these;
space is the ultimate resort.
“What is the goal of this world?
“Space,” said Pravāhaṇa;
for space is the supreme Self, according to the Vedic scripture: “Space, indeed, is its name.”
For its function is the production of all elements,
and within it alone is the dissolution of the elements.
It emitted that light.
For it will later state, "The fire [is merged] in the highest deity.
Indeed, all these beings, both stationary and moving, arise from space alone through the sequence of fire, water, food, and so forth, by implication.

At the time of dissolution, they merge back into space by that very same reverse process; for since space alone is greater than and more vast than all these elements, it is therefore the supreme resort, the ultimate goal, and the foundation of all beings throughout the three periods of time—this is the meaning. //1//
This very Udgītha is higher than the high;
it is infinite.
For him it becomes higher and better, and he wins worlds that are higher and better, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as the higher and better. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2)

Because he is higher than the high (*paraḥ paraḥ*), more excellent even than the excellent (*varīyaso 'py eṣa varaḥ*), and both supreme (*paraḥ*) and more excellent (*varīyān*), this Udgītha has become the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); such is the meaning. Therefore, he is infinite (*anantaḥ*), having no end. One who knows him thus as the infinite, having become the Supreme Self, and as the most excellent Udgītha, meditates upon that very Udgītha. Regarding his reward, the text says: "For this knower, there shall be a life that is more excellent, higher than the high, and increasingly distinguished."

There is a visible fruit and an invisible one: he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha, conquers worlds that are progressively more excellent, reaching as far as the world of Brahman-ether. //2//
Atidhanvā Śaunaka, having taught this very Udgītha to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said to him:
"As long as they shall know this Udgītha among their offspring, so long will there be a superior life for them in this world."
Furthermore, having taught this Udgītha to his disciple Udara-Śāḍilya, Atidhanvan by name— the descendant of Śunaka (Śaunaka)— said: "As long as they shall know this Udgītha in your lineage—
that is, in the continuity of your progeny—
for that long their life will be *parovarīyaḥ*, meaning successively more distinguished than these well-known worldly modes of living."
Life shall come from them. //3//
"Likewise, there will be a world for him in yonder world.
He who, knowing this, meditates upon it, his life in yonder world becomes indeed higher and more excellent, and likewise there will be a world for him in yonder world— yes, a world in yonder world.
Likewise, regarding that unseen world beyond, Atidhanvan Śaunaka said to Śāṇḍilya, "There will be for you a world even higher than the high.

One might suspect that such a result belongs only to those of great fortune in former ages and not to people of the present age; to dispel this doubt, he says: "Whoever, knowing it thus, now meditates upon this Udgītha—for him too, in this very world, there shall be a world even higher than the high."
In that same way, there is life in this world and in the world beyond; thus it is called "the world" (loka). //4 //

Thus ends the ninth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. While the Kurus were being devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa, together with his wife Āṭikī, lived as a wanderer in the village of Ibhyagrāma.
In connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, it must also be explained that there is a meditation concerning the *prastāva* and the *pratihāra*; therefore, this [section] is commenced.
The narrative is for the sake of easy understanding.
"When the Kurus were struck by hailstones"—*maṭacī* means hailstones; "struck" means destroyed; "the Kurus" refers to the crops of the Kurus.

Then, when a famine had arisen, Uṣasti by name—the son of Cakra (Cākrāyaṇa)—was wandering about in the village of the wealthy (ibhyagrāma) due to the lack of food; [the village] belonging to one who is fit for an elephant (ibhya), that is, a lord of elephants or an elephant-keeper. [The word *ibhya* is derived from *ibha*, meaning "elephant," with the suffix *yat* indicating fitness. The root *drā* is used in the sense of contemptuous movement. He was accompanied by his wife, an Āṭikī woman whose female characteristics such as breasts had not yet developed.
"Having gone to a miserable state" means having reached the final stage; "he dwelt" means he lived, having taken refuge in someone's house. //1//
He begged from him as he was eating some boiled pulse;
he said to him:
"There are no others besides these; and those whom I have brought here [are they]. // ChUp 1.10.2 //
Wandering for the sake of food, he happened upon a man at a threshing floor eating—i.e., consuming—some *kulmāṣas*, which are contemptible beans; having found him by chance, he begged from him.
That man said to Uṣasti:
"From this heap of leavings being eaten by me, there are no other *kulmāṣas* besides these."
And when he was asked, "What shall I do with these which have been placed and deposited by you in this heap? Uṣasti replied: //2//
"Give these to me," he said;
he gave them to him.
"Come, let there be a drink," [the father said].
"Then my drink would indeed be left-over," he replied. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.3)
"These [are] these," is the meaning.
"Give them to me," he said.
That Ibha gave them to him, to Uṣasti; he bestowed them.
When told, "Come, take this water nearby as a drink," he replied, "This water of mine would indeed become defiled if I were to drink it. To him who had spoken thus, the other replied: 3.
"Are not these also leavings? "Indeed,
I would not have lived if I had not eaten them," he said.
"Kāma is my well," he said. ChUp 1.10.4.
"What? Are these beans not even leavings? When he was thus addressed, Uṣasti said, "No, I would not have lived—I would not have lived—if I had not eaten these beans.
The meaning is: "I could obtain water for drinking at my own will.

And the intention is this: that even for one who has reached such a state, who possesses knowledge, virtue, and fame, who is capable of helping himself and others, there is no touch of sin even while performing such an act.
Even for him, when there exists another means of livelihood that is not contemptible, this contemptible act leads to fault;
the intention is that for one who performs it out of pride in his own knowledge, a fall into hell will certainly occur, as indicated by the mention of the word "perishing" (pradrāṇaka). //4//
Having eaten, he brought the leftovers to his wife;
even before they were consumed, she became well-supplied with food.
Having accepted them, he set them aside.

Having eaten those [beans], he compassionately gave the remainder—the leftovers—to his wife. Because she had obtained excellent alms (*subhikṣā*) even before the beans were brought, she was already well-fed. Nevertheless, out of her feminine nature, she did not despise them; having received those beans from her husband's hand, she set them aside. //5//
In the morning, as he was rising, he said:
"Alas! If we could obtain some food, we might obtain a measure of wealth."
"This king is about to perform a sacrifice;
let him choose me for all the priestly offices. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.10.6)

Knowing her deed, as he was rising at the time of dawn—abandoning his bed or sleep—he said while his wife was listening: "If only we could obtain even a little food! Having eaten that food, we would be able to go out and obtain some measure of wealth—a small amount of wealth."
"Then our livelihood will be secured.
And he states the reason for obtaining wealth: "That king is going to perform a sacrifice at a place not far from here.
Because he is the one performing the sacrifice (*yajamāna*), the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) is used.
And that king, having recognized me as a worthy recipient, might choose me for all the duties of the officiating priests—that is, for the purpose of performing the priestly rites. //6//
His wife said to him,
"Come, husband, here are these very beans."
Having devoured them, he went to that sacrifice which had been spread out.
When he had spoken thus, Jāyā said to him: "Come, my lord, take these very beans which were placed in my hand by you.
Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice of the king which had been spread out and extended by the officiating priests.

There, he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the Stotra. He then said to the Prastotṛ: ChUp 1.10.8: "Prastotṛ, when you chant the Prastāva, to what do you chant the Prastāva? The Prastotṛ replied: "To the *prāṇa* (the vital breath), sir. He said: "The *prāṇa* indeed is the Prastāva. Therefore, should anyone seek to harm you, you should say: 'I take away your *prāṇa*!'—and thus you will surely take away his *prāṇa*. ChUp 1.10.9: "Pratihartṛ, when you chant the Pratihāra, to what do you chant the Pratihāra? The Pratihartṛ replied: "To the *apāna* (the downward-breathing), sir. He said: "The *apāna* indeed is the Pratihāra. Therefore, should anyone seek to harm you, you should say: 'I take away your *apāna*!'—and thus you will surely take away his *apāna*. ChUp 1.10.10: "Udgātṛ, when you chant the Udgītha, to what do you chant the Udgītha? The Udgātṛ replied: "To the *āditya* (the sun), sir. He said: "The *āditya* indeed is the Udgītha. Therefore, should anyone seek to harm you, you should say: 'I take away your *āditya*!'—and thus you will surely take away his *āditya*. ChUp 1.10.11: Then he said to them: "If you have [thus] understood this, then who among you is a chanter? But if you have not understood this, then you are merely chanters of the Sāman. ChUp 1.10.12: Thereupon, they approached him with fuel in their hands, saying: "Let us choose you as our Udgātṛ. He said: "What [benefit] shall I provide for you? They replied: "Whatever one might obtain through the office of an Udgātṛ. He said: "Then let it be so. They said: "So be it. ChUp 1.10.13: Therefore, when one knows this, even if many [people] are chanting, one should say: "I am the one who chants over you. And indeed, he becomes the one who chants over them. ChUp 1.10.14: Now, concerning the syllables: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. These are the three *vyāhṛti*s. This is the triple-footed Gāyatrī. Its feet are these worlds. Its essence is the self (*ātman*). The fourth is its head; the fifth is its trunk; the sixth is its tail, the support. ChUp 1.10.15: When one meditates upon it as sixfold, the *Ṛc* becomes sixfold, the *Sāman* becomes sixfold, and the *Yajus* becomes sixfold. The *Ṛc* is sixfold; the *Sāman* is sixfold; the *Yajus* is sixfold. All this that exists here is sixfold. One attains all this. ChUp 1.10.16: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The Gāyatrī, which has the foot consisting of beings, protects the person from the third death—that which is other than the known and the unknown. ChUp 1.10.17: What is the known is the mortal. What is the unknown is the immortal. What is the measured is the mortal. What is the unmeasured is the immortal. Both of these, being supported by the breath (*prāṇa*), are contained within the breath. Therefore, one should meditate upon the breath alone. ChUp 1.10.18: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The breath is the Gāyatrī. The breath protects all this that exists here. One should worship it as the life-span, as immortality. Life is the breath. Immortality is the breath. ChUp 1.10.19: As for the statement, "One should worship it as the life-span": because as long as the breath dwells in this body, so long does one live. Therefore, one should worship it as the life-span. ChUp 1.10.20: As for the statement, "One should worship it as immortality": when, upon departing, the breath departs from this body, then one becomes immortal in the world of heaven. Therefore, one should worship it as immortality. ChUp 1.10.21: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The wise man, knowing the Gāyatrī as such, places the self in the self. Having become immortal, he attains the immortal Brahman in the world of heaven. ChUp 1.10.22: As for the statement, "Having become immortal, he attains the immortal Brahman": the mortal element in him is the breath. By means of that breath, he attains the immortal Brahman in the world of heaven. Thus far with respect to the body. ChUp 1.10.23: Now, with respect to the deities: That world is the *bhūḥ*; the sky is the *bhuvaḥ*; and *svar* is the sun. This is the triple-footed Gāyatrī. Its feet are these deities. Its essence is the self (*ātman*). The fourth is its head; the fifth is its trunk; the sixth is its tail, the support. ChUp 1.10.24: When one meditates upon it as sixfold, the *Ṛc* becomes sixfold, the *Sāman* becomes sixfold, and the *Yajus* becomes sixfold. The *Ṛc* is sixfold; the *Sāman* is sixfold; the *Yajus* is sixfold. All these deities are sixfold. One attains all these deities. ChUp 1.10.25: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The Gāyatrī, which has the foot consisting of the gods, protects the person from the third death—that which is other than the known and the unknown. ChUp 1.10.26: What is the known is the mortal. What is the unknown is the immortal. What is the measured is the mortal. What is the unmeasured is the immortal. Both of these, being supported by the *āditya*, are contained within the *āditya*. Therefore, one should meditate upon the *āditya* alone. ChUp 1.10.27: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The *āditya* is the Gāyatrī. The *āditya* protects all this that exists here. One should worship it as splendor, as glory, as fame, as power, as nourishment, and as everything. ChUp 1.10.28: As for the statement, "One should worship it as splendor": because the *āditya* shines with splendor in this world, therefore one should worship it as splendor. ChUp 1.10.29: As for the statement, "One should worship it as glory": because the *āditya* is glorious in this world, therefore one should worship it as glory. ChUp 1.10.30: As for the statement, "One should worship it as fame": because the *āditya* is famous in this world, therefore one should worship it as fame. ChUp 1.10.31: As for the statement, "One should worship it as power": because the *āditya* is powerful in this world, therefore one should worship it as power. ChUp 1.10.32: As for the statement, "One should worship it as nourishment": because the *āditya* bestows nourishment upon this world, therefore one should worship it as nourishment. ChUp 1.10.33: As for the statement, "One should worship it as everything": because the *āditya* is everything in this world, therefore one should worship it as everything. ChUp 1.10.34: Regarding this, there is this verse: "The wise man, knowing the Gāyatrī as such, places the self in the self. Having become immortal, he attains the immortal Brahman in the world of heaven. ChUp 1.10.35: As for the statement, "Having become immortal, he attains the immortal Brahman": the
Having gone there and approached the Udgātṛs—the persons who chant the Udgītha—he sat down near them in the place of chanting (*āstāva*), meaning he sat down in their vicinity.
Having sat down, he spoke to the Prastotṛ. (8)
"O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off. (ChU 1.10.9)
"O Prastotṛ!"—thus he addresses him to draw his attention.

"If you, being ignorant of that deity which follows and is inherent in the *prastāva* (the introductory chant), should chant the *prastāva* in my presence—that is, even in the absence of one who knows it—then your head shall fall off. This implies that there is indeed no qualification for ritual action for those who know only the mere performance of the rite.
And that is undesirable, because even those who lack knowledge are seen to perform ritual actions,
and because the scripture speaks of a southern path;
furthermore, if they were ineligible [for the northern path], only the northern path would be heard of for those lacking knowledge.
Furthermore, the southern path is not caused by *smārta* (traditionally prescribed) actions alone,
because of scriptural statements such as "by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth;

and because of the qualification "spoken by me," there is no lack of eligibility for action only in the presence of the wise, but rather [it applies] everywhere, including the *agnihotra*, *smārta* rites, study, and so on.
Since authorization is seen in various instances, it is established that even those who know only the ritual action have the right to perform the rite;
thus [it is said]: "Your head shall fall off. (9)
In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ priest:
"O Udgātṛ, if you perform the Udgītha chant without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter apart. (ChUp 1.10.10)
In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ priest:
"O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will shatter apart.
Terrified, they remained silent.
In the same way, he spoke to the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ; the rest is the same as before.

Having desisted—that is, ceased—from their ritual duties out of fear that their heads would fall off, those [singers] beginning with the Prastotṛ remained silent and did nothing else, because they were still in need [of protection]. 10–11.
Thus ends the tenth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, the sacrificer said to him:
"I wish to know the Blessed One," he said.
"I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa," he replied.

Then, immediately after that, the royal sacrificer said to Uṣasti: "I wish to know—that is, I desire to understand—the venerable one, the one worthy of honor. Thus addressed, Uṣasti replied: "I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa; have you heard my name before? he said.
He said:
"I have indeed sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly offices."
Or rather, out of ignorance of the Blessed One, I chose others.

The sacrificer said: "It is true that I have heard of you, venerable sir, as one possessed of many virtues; I sought you out for the office of officiating priest through all the duties of the *ṛtvij* priests, and having searched, because I did not find you, venerable sir, I chose these other seers."
"But let the venerable one himself perform all the priestly offices for me.
"So be it," [the other replied].
"In that case, let these very ones whom you have granted be the ones to praise;
however, you must give me as much wealth as you would give them.
"So be it," the sacrificer replied.
"Even now, let the venerable one indeed perform for me all the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)"; being thus addressed, Uṣasti said, "So be it.
However, in that case, let these very priests whom you previously chose—now fully authorized and permitted by me, being well-pleased—perform the praise;
as for this [remaining] task, it must be done by you.
When he was told, "As much wealth as you would give to all these others, such as the Prastotṛ and the rest, so much should you give to me," the sacrificer replied, "So be it. //3//
Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off.'"
"Which is that deity? ChU 1.11.4.
Then, having heard these words from Auṣastya, the Prastotṛ approached him; he came to Auṣastya with humility and said:
"O Prastotṛ, that deity concerning whom the venerable one previously spoke to me—'Which is that deity who is dependent upon the Prastāva portion?'—who is that deity? (ChU 1.11.4)
"Breath," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings enter into breath alone."
They rise up after the vital breath (prāṇa).
This deity is dependent upon the Prastāva.
If you had chanted the Prastāva without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, as I have told you.
When asked, he said, "The vital breath (prāṇa).
It is appropriate that the vital breath is the deity of the *prastāva*.

How so? Because all beings, both stationary and moving, enter into the vital breath alone at the time of dissolution; having aimed toward the vital breath, they emerge with the very nature of the vital breath. The meaning is that they rise up from the vital breath alone.

At the time of its origination; therefore, this very deity is inherent in the *prastāva*. If you had chanted it without knowing her—had performed the *prastāvana*, the *prastāva* section—you would have had your head fall off, your skull would have fallen away, had you been told so by me at that time.
"Your head would have fallen off.
Therefore, you have acted rightly; the intention is that you have done well because you desisted from the action even though I forbade you. //5//
Then he approached the Udgātṛ priest, saying:
"O Udgātṛ, the venerable one said to me, 'If you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will shatter.'"
"Which deity is that? ChU 1.11.6.
Likewise, the Udgātṛ asked: "Which deity follows and is inherent in the udgītha portion?"
"The sun," he said,
"for indeed all these beings sing to the sun as it stands on high."
This very deity is connected with the Udgītha.
Had you sung the Udgītha without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, as I had told you.
When asked, he said, "The Sun.

The meaning is that all these beings indeed sing to, utter sounds toward, and praise the Sun as it is high above. Because of the commonality of the word *uccha-* (high/shining) and the commonality of the word *pra-śabda-* (sound/utterance), [the Sun] is like the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "This deity," and so forth, is to be understood as before. //7//
Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said:
"Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you perform the Pratihāra chant without knowing the deity that is associated with the Pratihāra, your head will shatter apart.'"
"Which is that deity? (ChU 1.11.8)
In the very same way, the Pratihartṛ priest then approached him and asked, "Which deity is associated with the Pratihāra?"
"Food," he said.
"For indeed, all these beings live by taking food unto themselves."
This very deity is connected with the Pratihāra.

If you had sung the Pratihāra without knowing it, your head would have fallen off—just as it was said by me, "as it was said by me. Thus it was said by me. Thus it was said by me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.9)
When asked, he said, "Food. Indeed, all these beings live by bringing food toward themselves from every side as their very self.
This deity, because of its commonality with the word *prati* (toward), is associated with the *pratihāra* division of the Sāman.
"The rest is the same as what was stated by me.
The collective meaning is that one should meditate upon the sections of the *prastāva*, *udgītha*, and *pratihāra* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the sun (*āditya*), and food (*anna*).
The fruit is either the attainment of the state of the vital breath and so forth, or the success of the ritual action. //9//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, therefore, follows the "Canine Udgītha."
Now, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to recite his Vedic study.
In the preceding section, a miserable state caused by the lack of food was described, characterized by the eating of leftovers and stale food.

Lest that state should occur, the following section concerning the dogs (*śauva*) is now introduced for the sake of obtaining food; it concerns the *udgītha*, the chanting of the Sāman, as perceived by dogs.
Therein, there were indeed two persons: one named Baka Dālbhya, the son of Dalbha, and the other named Glāva Maitreya, the son of Mitrā.
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "ca" (and);
for he is indeed a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (a son belonging to two lineages),
since an option is untenable regarding a real entity (*vastu*), just as it is with respect to actions.
For there are Smṛti texts stating, "one who has two names" or "one who belongs to two gotras," and the partaking of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) from both sides is also observed;
this may be due to the sage's mind being fixed on the Udgītha or because of his disregard for [worldly] seers.
The word *vā* is used for the sake of *svādhyāya* (private recitation).
He went out from the village—that is, he departed—to a secluded place near water in order to perform *svādhyāya*.
From the indicative mark of the singular verb "he went out" (*udvavrāja*) and "he waited" (*pratipālayāñcakāra*), it follows that this seer was one.
The intention is that the sage’s performance of his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) out of a desire for food is indicated by his waiting for the time of the *udgītha*. //1//
To him there appeared a white dog;
other dogs approached it and said:
"May the Blessed One sing for us food;
we are hungry," they said.

ChUpBh_1,12.2: Satisfied by his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), either a deity or a seer (*ṛṣi*), having assumed the form of a dog—a white dog—manifested himself and appeared before that seer for the sake of bestowing grace upon him. Other smaller dogs approached that white dog and said: "May the Blessed One procure food for us by means of singing; that is to say, may he produce it through song. It is entirely reasonable to understand this as follows: the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) or the senses such as speech and the rest, who subsist on food and were satisfied by his private recitation, took on this form and showed favor to him.
"We are indeed hungry; we are hungry," they said. //2//
He said to them, "Come to me right here early in the morning.
Then Baka Dālbhya— or Glāva Maitreya, as some say— waited there.
When this had been said, the white dog spoke to those small dogs: "Let them not come near me here, in this very place, every morning at the time of dawn.
The lengthening [of the vowel] is for metrical reasons;
or it may be a scribal error.
The fixing of the time for the morning [offering] must be performed at that very time in order to avoid being without firewood.
Or else, because the Sun, the giver of food, would not be facing him in the afternoon;
therefore, Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya, according to some—waited right there, meaning he remained in expectation. //3//
Just as here [in the ritual], when they are about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna, they run forward holding onto one another, so did they run forward.
Having sat down together, they made the sound "hiṃ."

Those dogs, having come right there into the presence of the sage, just as here in this world the Udgātṛ priests, when about to chant the Bahiṣpavamāna hymn, stand closely joined together, each grasping the tail of the other with his mouth; so they moved about, meaning they performed a circumambulation. Having thus moved about and sat down together, they uttered the sound "hiṃ," that is, they made the *hiṅkāra* sound. //4//
"Om! We eat; Om! We drink. Om! He is a god (deva) because of his shining (dyotana). Varuṇa because of his enveloping (varṣaṇa) the world.
Prajāpati because of his protecting (pālana) of creatures."
Savitṛ is called Āditya because he is the impeller (prasavitṛ) of all.
By these synonyms, [the meaning is]: "May that Āditya, being such as this, bring food to us here; may he bring it.
Having done so, they spoke again: "O Lord of Food, you indeed..."

For he is the lord (pati) because he is the progenitor of all food; indeed, without his cooking, not even a minute particle of abundant food is produced for living beings. Therefore, he is the Lord of Food (annapati).
"O Lord of Food, bring food to us here; bring it!
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
Thus ends the twelfth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
This world, indeed, is the syllable *hāu*.
The syllable *hā* is the wind;
the syllable *atha* is the moon;
the syllable *iha* is the self.
Fire is the syllable ī. 1.13.1.

Since the meditation on the object of devotion is connected with the constituent parts of the Sāman, other meditations concerning the *stobha* syllables belonging to other parts of the Sāman are taught next in a collective manner, because they are no different in being connected to the constituent parts of the Sāman: "This world indeed is the *hā-ukāra* *stobha*, well-known in the *Rathantara* Sāman, according to the text: ‘This [earth] is indeed the *Rathantara*’."
On account of this commonality of connection, one should meditate thus: "This *hāukāra* stobha is the world. For *hā* is Vāyu;
[moreover,] the *hāikāra* is well known in the *Vāmadevya* Sāman.

Furthermore, because the connection between wind and water is the source (*yoni*) of the *vāmadeva* sāman, on account of this similarity, one should meditate upon the syllable *dhāi* with the vision of wind.
The syllable *atha* is the moon;
one should meditate upon the syllable *atha* with the vision of the moon.
For this world is established in food; the moon is the self of food,
because of the commonality of the letter *tha* and the vowel *ā*.
The syllable *iha* is the self (*ātman*). For the self is designated as "here" (*iha*), and thus the exclamation *iha* is the self.
Because of that commonality:
*agni* is the syllable *ī*; and all Sāmans dedicated to Agni have *ī* as their *nidhana*. Therefore, it is because of that commonality. //1//
The syllable *ū* is Āditya;
the syllable *e* is Nihava.
The All-gods are the syllable *auhoyi*; Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*;
breath is the *svara*.
Food is the Yajus;
speech is the Virāj.
The Sun is the syllable *ū*. Because the Sun is high and above, they sing of him as *ū*; and this musical interjection (*stobha*) is the syllable *ū*.
Since the *Sāman* has the Sun as its deity, the interjection *ū* [in that chant] is the Sun; thus, the Sun is the syllable *ū*.

*Nihava* means a call; the *stobha* is the syllable *ehi*, because they call out "Come! (*ehi*), and there is a similarity between them. The *viśve devāḥ* (All-Gods) are the syllable *auhoyikaḥ*, because this is seen in the *sāman* dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
Prajāpati is the *hiṅkāra*,
because the *hiṅkāra* is unmanifest due to its lack of explicit definition;
breath is the *svara*.
"Svara" is a stobha;
it is so called because of the commonality of being the cause of sound for the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Yā yā" is a stobha; it is food (anna).
Because it moves by means of food, on account of that commonality, "vāk" (speech) refers to the *stobha*, or else to the deity Virāj as food; for the *stobha* is seen in the *vairāja* sāman. //2//
The thirteenth is the undefined stobha, the moving *huṃ*-sound.

"Unspecified" (*anirukta*) means that because of its unmanifest nature, it cannot be specified as "this" or "that"; therefore, it is a "wandering" (*sañcara*), meaning its form is subject to conceptualization.

To the question "What is this?", he says: "The thirteenth is the *stobha*, the syllable *huṃ*. For this is indeed unmanifest; thus, the intention is that it should be meditated upon precisely as something whose specific character is unspecified. //3//
Speech yields for him its milk, which is the milk of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food.
He who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the Sāmans, he truly knows the secret doctrine.
"Speech yields for him its milk," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

The sense is that for one who knows this Upaniṣad—the vision concerning the Sāmans, specifically regarding the *stobha*-syllables which are parts of the Sāmans, possessing the characteristics as previously described—this aforementioned fruit belongs.
The double repetition is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
Or rather, it is for the purpose of completing the specific meditations concerning the various parts of the Sāman. //4//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the first chapter in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the second chapter. Om.
The meditation on the Sāman as a whole is indeed good. For what is good, they call "Sāman."
"What is not good, that is our sam. (ChU 2.1.1)
By the passage beginning with "Om, this syllable," meditation (upāsana) concerning the constituent parts of the Sāman was taught as having manifold fruits;
immediately thereafter, meditation concerning the *stobha* syllables was described.

In every respect, that [meditation] was connected only to a single part of the Sāman. Now, the Scripture begins by saying, "I shall describe meditations concerning the entire Sāman," referring to meditations whose object is the whole of the Sāman.
For it is logical that after the meditation on a single part, the meditation concerning the possessor of those parts is taught;
this means [the meditation] on the whole, characterized by all its parts, consisting of five or seven divisions.
The word "khalu" (indeed) serves as an embellishment for the sentence.

The meditation on the *sāman* as "the good" (*sādhu*) is intended to enjoin the perception of the whole *sāman* as being good; it does not aim at censuring the meditations previously mentioned. The word "good" (*sādhu*) signifies that which is beautiful or auspicious.
How is this understood? He says: indeed, that which is well-known in the world as "good"—meaning beautiful and blameless—is what the experts call *sāman*.
That which is improper and contrary is what we do not accept. //1//
Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with the *sāman*"; by this they mean: "He has approached him with what is good."
"He has come to him without the Sāman," they say of that.
In that very context, for the purpose of distinguishing between the right and the wrong, they also say: "He approached this king and the neighboring vassal with a *sāman*.
Who is he, from whom there is the apprehension of falling into wrongdoing?
Such is the intended meaning of the word "he" (*sa*).
People in the world, not seeing any improper act such as binding and so forth, say in that case, "He approached him with what is good," meaning he approached him with a noble intention.

But where the opposite occurs and they see an improper act such as binding and so forth, they then say, "He approached him with what is not good," meaning he approached him with what is improper. //2//
Furthermore, they also say:
"Sāman, indeed! when something is good; they mean "Good, indeed! by that.
"Alas, it has not been so for us"—when something is bad, they say, "Alas, it has not been so for us. Thus they speak. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.1.3)

Then they also say: "Alas! Our Sāman has become self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*) to us. They say this out of compassion. What they mean by this is: when something good occurs, they say, "Ah, how good! and when the opposite occurs, they say, "Alas! Our Sāman [has failed]!"
When something is not good, they say, "Alas, it is not good! Therefore, it is established that the words *sāman* and *sādhu* have the same meaning. //3//
He who, knowing this thus, venerates the Sāman as "the good"— verily, it is close at hand that good dharmas should come to him and incline toward him.

Therefore, whoever worships the Sāman as "the good" (sādhu)—that is, as possessing the quality of goodness—knowing the entire Sāman to possess that quality of goodness, for him this is the fruit: "abhyāśo ha," meaning quickly indeed. The word "yat" is used here as an adverbial modifier. It means that the "good" (sādhavaḥ), that is, auspicious qualities not contrary to Śruti and Smṛti, shall come toward this worshiper (ā ca gaccheyuḥ) and they shall approach him (āgaccheyuḥ). Moreover, it does not merely mean they shall come; they shall also "bow down toward him" (upa ca nameyuḥ), which means they shall present themselves to him as objects of enjoyment. //4//
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman with respect to the worlds.
The earth is the *hiṅkāra*;
fire is the *prastāva*;
the intermediate space is the *udgītha*.
The Āditya is the Pratihāra;
the sky is the Nidhana—
thus with respect to those things that are above.
But what are those Sāmans, distinguished by the vision of the virtuous (*sādhudṛṣṭi*), which are to be meditated upon as a whole?
These are stated as "the fivefold in the worlds" and so forth.
Now, is it not a contradiction that they are to be meditated upon with the vision of the worlds and also with the vision of the virtuous? No.
Because the object denoted by the word *sādhu*—which is the cause in effects such as the world—is pervasive, just as clay is in its modifications such as jars;
and because the object expressed by the word *sādhu*, whether it be *dharma* or *brahman*, is in every way pervasive within effects such as the world;
therefore, just as in whatever case the perception of a jar or the like is necessarily accompanied by the perception of clay or the like.
Likewise, the view of the world and so forth follows precisely from the view of the Sublime One (*sādhudṛṣṭi*),
because the world and so forth are effects of the Dharma and other such factors.
Even though the status of being a cause is indistinguishable between Brahman and the Dharma, [the distinction remains].

Nevertheless, it is logical that *dharma* alone is what is denoted by the word "good" (*sādhu*), because the word "good" is applied to *dharma* in the passage: "One who performs good deeds becomes good. [Objection: Since the cause is inherent in effects such as the worlds and so forth, that perception [of the cause in the effect] is already established by implication; thus, one need not say, "He should meditate on the *sāman* as 'good'. [Reply: No, because that perception is to be understood through scripture.
For in all cases, only those dharmas established by the scriptures are to be meditated upon, and not even existing things that are non-scriptural.

One should meditate on the *sāman*—which is fivefold, consisting of five types through the division of fivefold devotion—as being entirely auspicious within the worlds, such as the earth and so forth.
How so?
The earth is the *hiṅkāra*.
Regarding the phrase "in the worlds," that which is the seventh [note] is treated as the first.
Now, regarding the unenclosed [spaces]:
the sky is the *hiṅkāra*,
and the sun is the *prastāva*.
The intermediate space is the Udgītha;
fire is the Pratihāra;
the earth is the Nidhana.
Now, when the worlds are turned away and face downwards, the fivefold meditation on the Sāman is taught.

Since the worlds are characterized by coming and going, the meditation on the Sāman is prescribed specifically with that view in mind; therefore, it is performed regarding the worlds as they turn back.
The sky is the *hiṅkāra* because of its primacy;
the sun is the *prastāva*,
for when the sun has risen, the activities of living beings are set in motion (*prastūyante*).
The intermediate space is the *udgītha*, as before;
fire is the *pratihāra*,
because fire is brought forth (*pratiharaṇa*) by living beings.
The earth is the *nidhana*;
for those who have come from there, it is the *nidhana* here. //2//
The worlds, both ascending and descending, become available to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.2.3)

The fruit of the meditation is as follows: "The worlds—those above and those below, characterized by coming and going—become available; that is to say, they become capable and established as objects of enjoyment for him. This construction applies everywhere: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as the entire 'Good' (Sādhu) in the worlds," whether in the fivefold or the sevenfold [meditation]. //3//
Thus ends the second section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain.
The east wind is the *hiṅkāra*;
the cloud arises, that is the *prastāva*;
it rains, that is the *udgītha*.
When it lightens and thunders, that is the Pratihāra.
ChUpBh_2,3.1: One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain.
Because rain is the cause of the stability of the world, it follows immediately [after the meditation on wind].
The preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*.
For rain begins with the east wind and ends with its cessation; just as a *sāman* chant begins with the *hiṅkāra* and ends with the *nidhana*,
therefore the east wind is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because of its priority: "The cloud is born; that is the Prastāva.
For it is well known that when clouds arise in the rainy season, there is a "prelude" (prastāva) to the rain.
It rains—that is the *udgītha*, because of its excellence. It flashes and thunders—that is the *pratihāra*, because it is drawn back (*pratihṛta*). //1//
He takes it up; that is the finale. He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain, indeed causes rain.
He takes up that as the *nidhana*, because of the commonality of completion. He reveals the fruit of this meditation: "Verily, he obtains his desire."
Likewise, he causes it to rain even when there is no rain;
"he who [does this]" and so forth is as explained previously. //2//
Thus ends the third section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters.
When the cloud gathers, that is the *hiṅkāra*;
when it rains, that is the *prastāva*;
those [rivers] which flow eastward, that is the *udgītha*.
Those that flow westward are the Pratihāra;
the ocean is the Nidhana.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters. Since all waters are preceded by rain, the sequence begins with that.
When the cloud gathers—that is, when it becomes condensed through mutual union—it is said that the cloud "gathers" (*saṃplavate*). That cloud is the beginning of the waters; it is the *hiṅkāra*.
That which rains is the *prastāva*,
for the waters have begun (*prastuta*) to pervade everywhere.
Those waters that flow eastward are the *udgītha*, because of their excellence.
Those [waters] which flow westward are the Pratihāra, due to the commonality of the word "prati" (back/against).
The ocean is the Nidhana,
because the waters have that as their final resting place.
He does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters.
If he does not desire it, he does not pass into water; rather, the fruit is that he becomes possessed of water. //2//
Thus ends the fourth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman with reference to the seasons.
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*,
summer is the *prastāva*,
and the rainy season is the *udgītha*.
Autumn is the Pratihāra;
winter is the Nidhana.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. Its immediate succession [to the meditation on the year] follows because the establishment of the seasons has the aforementioned water as its cause. Spring is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because it comes first:
summer is the *prastāva*,
for the gathering of barley and other grains is indeed commenced for the sake of the rainy season.
The rainy season is the *udgītha* because of its preeminence;
the autumn is the *pratihāra*,
because it brings back those who are ill and the dead.
Winter is the end;
because of the lack of wind, it is the end of living beings. //1//
The seasons become favorable for him, and he becomes possessed of the seasons, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. (ChUp 2.5.2)
The seasons indeed become available as objects of enjoyment for this meditator, in accordance with his specific ritual arrangements;
the meaning is that he becomes endowed with the measures of the seasons and with seasonal enjoyments. //2//
Thus ends the fifth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals.
The goats are the *hiṅkāra*;
the sheep are the *prastāva*;
the cows are the *udgītha*.
The horse is the Pratihāra;
the man is the Nidhana.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals.
Since the season of well-behaved animals is the time favorable for cattle, there is an immediate sequence [of meditation].
The she-goat is the *hiṅkāra*.
Either because of its preeminence or its primacy, according to the Vedic revelation: "The goat is the first of animals.
Thus, the sheep (*avayaḥ*) is the *prastāva*.
Because of the observation of their association, as in "the cows are the *udgītha*"; because of preeminence, as in "the Brahmins are the *udgītha*."
The horses are the *pratihāra*,
because they carry men;
the man is the *nidhana*.
Because animals have man as their refuge. //1//
Cattle indeed come to him, and he becomes rich in cattle, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in cattle.
The fruit [of this] is that cattle come to him; he becomes possessed of cattle.
The meaning is that he is endowed with the fruits of cattle, such as the enjoyment [of their products] and the renunciation [of them]. //2//
Thus ends the sixth section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman, which is progressively higher, in the vital breaths (prāṇas).
The vital breath is the *hiṅkāra*;
speech is the *prastāva*;
the eye is the *udgītha*.
The ear is the Pratihāra;
the mind is the Nidhana.
These indeed are progressively more excellent.

ChUpBh_2,7.1: One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman as the vital breaths (prāṇas). The meaning is that one should meditate on the Sāman—characterized by the quality of being progressively more excellent—as distinguished by the vision of the vital breaths.
The vital breath, namely the sense of smell, is the *hiṅkāra*.
Because it is the first among those that become increasingly superior,
speech is the *prastāva*;
for by means of speech everything is introduced (*prastūyate*).
Speech is superior to the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
for speech can express even that which has not been reached,
whereas the vital breath is the perceiver only of a fragrance that has already been reached.
The eye is the *udgītha*.
Since the eye reveals a wider range of objects than speech, it is superior to speech; therefore, it is the *udgītha* because of its excellence.
The ear is the Pratihāra,
because it is drawn toward [objects];
and the mind is more extensive than the ear.

Because they pervade all the objects of the senses, even an object beyond the senses is indeed within the range of the mind. For the reasons stated above, these [elements], beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa), are progressively more excellent. //1//

"Superior and more excellent indeed becomes his lot, and he wins superior and more excellent worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as 'superior and more excellent' in the vital breaths.
Thus far with respect to the fivefold [Sāman]. (ChU 2.7.2)

"One who meditates upon the Sāman as distinguished by this view—that it is 'higher than the high' (parovarīya)—his life becomes higher than the high. This has already been explained. The statement "thus has the meditation on the fivefold Sāman been described" is intended to focus the mind on the subject about to be described regarding the sevenfold Sāman;
for one who is independent regarding the fivefold [Sāman], [the transition to the sevenfold is appropriate].
He intends to apply his intellect to what is about to be explained. //2//
Thus ends the seventh section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now follows [the meditation] on the sevenfold [Sāman].
One should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech.
Whatever there is of speech as "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*;
whatever there is as "pra," that is the *prastāva*.
That which goes is the beginning. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.8.1)
Now, immediately following this, the meditation upon the sevenfold Sāman in its entirety is commenced.
The locative case in "vāci" (in speech) is as before;
the meaning is that one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as characterized by the vision of Speech.

Whatever specific sound of speech there is, namely "hum," that is the *hiṅkāra*, because of the commonality of the letter *ha*. That form of sound which is "pra" is the *prastāva*, because of the commonality of the prefix *pra*. That which is "ā" is the *ādi*.
Because of the similarity of their forms;
"the first" refers to the syllable *oṃ*, because it is the beginning of all [mantras]. //1//
That which is "ut" is the *udgītha*;
that which is "prati" is the *pratihāra*.
That which it approaches is the *upadrava*; that which it leads to is the *nidhana*. ChUp 2.8.2.
That which is "ut" is the *udgītha*, because the *udgītha* begins with "ut. That which is "pra" is the *pratihāra*.
Because of their commonality:
that which it approaches is "distress" (*upadrava*), because distress consists of affliction;
that which it leads to is the "finale" (*nidhana*).
Because of the commonality of being soundless. //2//
Speech yields for him its milk, which is the milk of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food.
He who, knowing it thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech.
"He milks for him," etc.; the meaning has already been explained. //3//
Thus ends the eighth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
indeed, one should meditate upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman.
It is *sāman* because it is equal toward all;
it is *sāman* because it is equal toward everyone, thinking "toward me," "toward me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.9.1)
In the first chapter, the meditation on the fivefold *sāman* was taught by viewing the sun upon each individual part of the *sāman*.
Now, however, one should meditate upon the sevenfold *sāman* by superimposing that very sun upon the *sāman* as a whole, divided according to its parts.
But how, then, does the sun possess the nature of the *sāman*?
It is said:
just as there is a reason for the Sun being the *udgītha*, there is a reason for its being the *sāman*.

What is that? Because it is always equal (*sama*) due to the absence of increase or decrease, for that reason it is the *sāman*; it produces an identical cognition [in people], such that "the Sun is mine, the Sun is mine."
Therefore, it is equal to all; thus, *sāman* means "equality" (*samatva*).

Since the status of being preceded by *hiṅkāra* and so forth is understood from the very mention of the commonality of the *udgītha* section, as well as the commonalities stated regarding the worlds and so on, no further reason for its being preceded by *hiṅkāra* has been stated.
However, since the reason for the Sun's being a *sāman* was not previously stated, and that would not be easily understood, "equality" (*samatva*) has been mentioned. //1//
One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it. That which is before sunrise is its *hiṅkāra* (the introductory chant).
Therefore, cattle are dependent upon this;
hence they utter the sound *hiṅ*. For they are sharers in the *hiṅ* of this Sāman.
One should know that all these beings about to be mentioned are dependent upon—that is, follow after—that sun as its means of subsistence.
How so? That form of the sun which exists before its rising is the *hiṅkāra* chant-portion; in this regard, there is this correspondence:
the cattle, such as cows and the like, are dependent upon—that is, follow after—the *hiṅkāra* portion of this Sāman of the sun, meaning they subsist upon that form of its chant-portion.

Since this is so, therefore those animals utter the sound "hiṅ" before sunrise; for they are partakers of the *hiṅkāra* of this Sāman called Āditya, and because it is their nature to partake in its divisions, they behave in this manner. //2//
Now, that which is at the first rising [of the sun] is the Prastāva;
of that, human beings are dependent.
Therefore, those who desire to introduce [the subject] and those who desire praise are indeed entitled to participate in this Sāman.
Now, that form of the sun which first rises is the *prastāva* of this Sāman called Āditya; of it, human beings are dependent, as before.
Therefore, they desire praise (*prastuti*), because they partake in the *prastāva* of this Sāman. //3//
Now,
that which is at the time of the gathering of cattle is its *Ādi* (Beginning);
to it the birds are attached.
Therefore, having taken hold of those [worlds] which are without support in the intermediate space, they fly about;
for these are the portions of the beginning of this Sāman.

Now, as for that which is at the time of *saṅgava*—the time when there is a coming together (*saṅgama*) of the rays of the cows, or the time when the cows come together with their calves—that form belonging to Savitṛ at that time is the first specific division, the syllable *Oṃ*. To it, birds (*vayāṃsi*) are closely attached.
Because of this, those birds, having no support (*anārambaṇāni*)—that is, being without a hold—in the intermediate space, take hold of themselves alone as their very support.
Having grasped them, they fall away; therefore, because of the similarity of their forms, these [notes] indeed partake in the first division of this *sāman*. //4//
Now,
that which is exactly at midday is the *udgītha*;
the gods are dependent upon that part of it.
Therefore, among the offspring of Prajāpati, they are the best,
for they are the sharers in the Udgītha of this Sāman.
Now, that which is precisely at midday— meaning the straight midday— is the *udgītha* division; the gods are dependent upon that part of it, because of the excellence of its radiance at that time.
Therefore, they are the best and most distinguished;
for among those belonging to Prajāpati—the offspring of Prajāpati—they are the sharers in this Sāman, the Udgītha. //5//
Now, that which is after midday and before afternoon is the *pratihāra*;
to it are attached his embryos.
Therefore, they are turned back and do not descend,
for they are entitled to the *pratihāra* of this Sāman.
Now, that form of the sun which is after midday and before afternoon is its *pratihāra* (response). To it the embryos are attached.
Therefore, being held up by the *pratihāra* portion of the sun, they do not fall down; that is to say, they do not drop below even though that [opening] exists.
For the embryos partake of this *pratihāra* of the Sāman. //6//
Now, that which follows the afternoon and precedes sunset is the *upadrava*;
the forest animals are dependent upon that part of it.
Therefore, seeing a man, they run away, thinking he is a thicket or a pit;
for they are subject to the calamities of this Sāman.
Now, that which is after midday and before sunset is the *upadrava* [section] of this Sāman; it belongs to the wild animals of the forest.

Therefore, when they see a man, being afraid, they run toward—approach—the thicket, the forest, or the pit, thinking it is free from danger. Because they run away (*upadravanti*) upon seeing him, they are indeed the possessors of the *upadrava* of this Sāman.
Now, that which occurs at the first setting of the sun is the *nidhana*;
the ancestors are dependent upon it.
Therefore, they lay them down.
For these are the sharers of the finale of this Sāman.
Thus indeed one worships yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman.

Now, when the sun has first set and is about to go to invisibility, that is the *nidhana*; his ancestors are connected to that. Therefore, they lay them down—that is, they deposit them upon *darbha* grass in the form of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—or they place the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for their sake.
For the ancestors partake of the *nidhana* (concluding syllable) because of their connection with the *nidhana* of this Sāman.

Thus, the remainder of the sentence is that for one who meditates upon that sevenfold Sun as divided into seven parts according to its constituent members, the fruit is the attainment of that [Sun]. //8//
Thus ends the ninth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
indeed, one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman, which is commensurate with the Self and transcends death.
"Hiṅkāra" has three syllables;
"Prastāva" has three syllables; that is equal. ChUp 2.10.1.
The sun is death, because it causes the destruction of the world by means of time consisting of day and night and so forth.
For the purpose of transcending that [death], this meditation on the Sāman is taught— now, indeed,
immediately following the meditation on the Sāman concerning the sun as death.
"Measured by oneself" means measured by equality with one's own limbs or measured by equality with the Supreme Self (Paramātman). It is "beyond death" because it is the cause for conquering death.

Just as in the first chapter the syllables of the name of the *udgītha* division were stated to be objects of meditation as "ud-gī-tha," so here the syllables of the names of the sevenfold divisions of the Sāman are collected and, by being made equal in groups of three, are conceptually established as having the nature of a Sāman and are stated to be objects of meditation.

By means of meditating upon that, having reached death through the commonality of the number of syllables belonging to the imperishable (akṣara) which is within the sphere of death, one fashions a transition by means of the syllable exceeding that, for the very purpose of transcending that death of the Sun.

One should meditate on the sevenfold Sāman as "beyond death" (atimṛtyu), because it has transcended death by the number of its extra syllables; thus it is the "deathless" (amṛtyu) Sāman. Its first division (bhakti) consists of three syllables: *biṃ* and *kāra*—these are the three syllables. The measure of the division called *prastāva* is also exactly three syllables; it is equal to the former. //1//
"Ādi" consists of two syllables;
"pratihāra" consists of four syllables.
Then, here is one; that is equal. 2.10.2.
"Ādi" consists of two syllables; the syllable *oṃ* is called "Ādi" because it completes the number for the sevenfold *sāman*.
"Pratihāra" consists of four syllables.
Then, having subtracted one syllable from here, it is added to the two initial syllables;
by that means, it becomes exactly equal. //2//
"Udgītha" consists of three syllables; "upadrava" consists of four syllables. They become equal by means of three [syllables] each;
one syllable remains over, making three syllables.
That is equal. ChU 2.10.3.
"Udgītha" has three syllables; "upadrava" has four syllables. By means of the three [syllables] in each, they become equal, yet one syllable remains over—it is left over.

Since this results in inequality, he says [the following] in order to bring about the equality of the *sāman*: "That [remaining syllable], although being one, is a syllable"—thus it becomes three syllables.
Therefore, it is equal. //3//
"nidhana" consists of three syllables;
thus, it is indeed equal.
Now, these indeed are twenty-two syllables.
"Nibhanam" consists of three syllables; thus it becomes equal.

Having thus established the quality of being a *sāman* through the equality of these three syllables, the syllables are counted exactly as they occur: "These syllables of the names of the seven sections (*bhaktis*) are indeed twenty-two. (ChUpBh 2.10.4)
He attains the twenty-onefold Āditya;
for that Āditya up there is indeed twenty-onefold from here.
With the twenty-second [day], one conquers that which is beyond the sun;
that is the vault of heaven (nāka);
that is free from sorrow.
In that regard, by means of the number twenty-one syllables, one reaches the sun, which is death;
for from this world, that sun is the twenty-first in number, according to the Vedic revelation:

"Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. By means of the remaining twenty-second syllable, one conquers—that is, one attains—that which is beyond the sun, which is death. This is the meaning.
And what is that which is beyond the sun? It is *nāka*. *Ka* means happiness; its negation is *aka*, meaning that which is not happiness. Thus, *nāka* means that which is indeed happiness.
And it is *viśoka*; "free from sorrow" means devoid of mental suffering, since sorrow belongs to the domain of death.
"He obtains that," thus [it is said]. //5//

He attains here the victory of the sun; indeed, his victory surpasses the victory of the sun— he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman as commensurate with the self and transcending death— yes, he meditates upon the Sāman.

He states the summarized meaning of what has already been said: "By the number twenty-one, one attains victory over the sun; for one who knows thus, there is a victory beyond the sphere of death resulting from the victory over the sun"—the meaning is that it is by the number of twenty-two syllables.
"Whoever [knows] this thus" refers to the meaning already explained starting with the word "dvāniṣṭikī."
"This is its fruit as previously described"—this repetition is for the purpose of concluding the sevenfold classification. //6//
Thus ends the tenth section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. The mind is the *hiṅkāra*.
Speech is the Prastāva;
the eye is the Udgītha;
the ear is the Pratihāra.
The vital breath is the Nidhana.
This Gāyatra is woven upon the vital breaths.
In the preceding section, meditation on the fivefold and sevenfold *sāman* was taught without mentioning its specific names.

Now, however, other meditations on the *sāman* that yield specific fruits are described, preceded by the mention of their names, such as the *gāyatra*, etc., in the same order as they are employed in ritual practice.
The mind (*manas*) is the *hiṅkāra*, because the mind is the first among all the activities of the sense organs.
Immediately following that, speech is the Prastāva because it is the introduction; the eye is the Udgītha because of its preeminence;
the ear is the Pratihāra because it is drawn back [to the self];
and the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Nidhana, because at the time of sleep, those aforementioned [organs] find their dissolution (nidhana) in the vital breath.
This Gāyatra Sāman is woven upon the vital breaths (prāṇas), because the Gāyatrī has been praised as being identical with the vital breaths. //1//
He who thus knows this Gāyatra as woven upon the vital breaths becomes possessed of vital breath.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
He should be great in fame;
he should be high-minded.
That is his vow.
He who thus knows this Gāyatra as woven upon the vital breaths becomes possessed of vital breaths; that is to say, he becomes one whose organs are unimpaired. He reaches a full span of life.
According to the Vedic revelation that "a hundred years is the full lifespan of a man," he lives long and radiantly;
he becomes great through progeny and so forth, and great through fame.
This is the vow for the worshiper of the Gāyatrī: that he should be high-minded, meaning his mind should not be mean-spirited. //2//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He rubs [the fire-drills]; that is the *hiṅkāra*.
When smoke arises, that is the Prastāva;
when it blazes, that is the Udgītha;
when it becomes embers, that is the Pratihāra.
It becomes tranquil—that is its finale; it becomes completely stilled—that is its finale.
This is the Rathantara [Sāman] woven into Agni.
He rubs [the fire-drills]; that is the *hiṅkāra*, because it comes first.

From the fire, smoke is produced; that is the *prastāva*, because it follows immediately after. It blazes; that is the *udgītha*, because of its connection with the oblation, for blazing is preeminent.
They become embers; it is a *pratihāra* because the embers have been brought forth (*pratihṛta*).
It is "subsidence" (*upaśama*) because the fire still has a remainder;

it is "complete subsidence" (*saṃśama*) because it is the total cessation [of the fire]. Because of the commonality of completion, this *rathantara* is the "finale" (*nidhana*), and it is woven into the fire.
For it is said that fire is produced by friction. //1//
He who thus knows this Rathantara as woven into the fire becomes endowed with spiritual luster.
He becomes an eater of food;
he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long.
He becomes great in offspring and cattle,
and great in fame.
He should not sip water toward the fire, nor should he spit toward it.
That is the vow. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.12.2)
"Sa yaḥ" and so forth is as before. "Brahmavarcasī" refers to the splendor (*tejas*) caused by one's conduct and Vedic study;
"tejas," however, is merely the state of radiance.
One who eats food becomes possessed of a bright digestive fire.
One should not sip water facing toward the fire, nor should one eat anything, nor spit, nor discharge phlegm; this is his vow. 2.
Thus, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the twelfth section of the second chapter.
He invites [others] to eat; that is the *hiṅkāra*.
That which makes itself known is the *prastāva*;
that which lies with a woman is the *udgītha*;
that which lies back toward a woman is the *pratihāra*.
Time passes—that is death;
it goes to the further shore—that is death. This Vāmadevya [Sāman] is interwoven with the couple.
He addresses her—that is, he makes a secret signal—and because this occurs first, it is the *hiṅkāra*.
He makes himself known—that is, he pleases her—and that is the *prastāva*.
Lying together—that is, going to the same bed—is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence.
The facing toward the bed with the woman is *pratihāra*;
when one reaches the end—that is, the completion—of sexual union, that is *nidhana*. This *Vāmadevya* is woven into the couple, due to the connection between the couple of wind and water. //1//
He who thus knows this Vāmadevya hymn as woven into the couple becomes a couple himself.
From pair after pair he is born;
he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long.
He becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
He should not exclude anyone.
That is the vow. ChUp 2.13.2.
"Sa yaḥ... and so forth is as before.
"He becomes paired" means he becomes free from separation.
"From pair after pair he procreates" expresses the fact that his seed is unfailing.

One should not reject any woman whatsoever who has come to one’s own bed and seeks union, because this is prescribed as an ancillary to the meditation on the Vāmadevya Sāman; since the understanding of dharma arises from the authority of such scriptural statements, there is no contradiction between this and the prohibitive scriptures. //2//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The rising [sun] is the *hiṅkāra*.
The rising sun is the Prastāva; midday is the Udgītha;
the afternoon is the Pratihāra.
That which sets is the Nidhana;
this Bṛhat is woven upon the sun.
The rising sun is the *hiṅkāra*, because it is the first appearance; the risen sun is the *prastāva*, because it is the cause for the commencement of ritual actions;
the midday sun is the *udgītha*, because of its preeminence.
The afternoon is the *pratihāra*, because cattle and other animals are driven back toward their homes;
that which sets is the *nidhana*, because living beings are placed within their dwellings at night. This *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is woven into the sun, for the *Bṛhat* has the sun as its deity. //1//
He who thus knows this Bṛhat as woven upon the sun becomes radiant and an eater of food.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
One should not revile one who shines with great fame; that is the vow. ChUp 2.14.2.
"He who... and so forth is as before.
"One should not revile the one who is heating [the sun]; that is his vow. //2//
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The clouds gather together; that is the *hiṅkāra*.
The cloud forming is the *prastāva*;
its raining is the *udgītha*;
its lightning and thundering are the *pratihāra*.
He takes up that as the finale (nidhana).
This Vairūpa [sāman] is woven into Parjanya.
"Clouds" (abhrāṇi) are so called because they bear water; "megha" is so called because it sprinkles water.
The rest has already been explained.
This Sāman named Vairūpa is woven into Parjanya;
for Parjanya possesses a manifold form (vairūpya) through clouds and other such phenomena, owing to his lack of a single, uniform form. //1//
He who thus knows this Vairūpa [Sāman] as woven upon Parjanya secures both deformed and well-formed cattle.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
One should not revile a person who rains;
that is his vow. ChUp 2.15.2.
He acquires and obtains animals that are both deformed and well-formed, such as goats, sheep, and so forth; this is the meaning.
He should not revile one who is raining—this is his vow. //2//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Spring is the *hiṅkāra*.
Summer is the Prastāva;
the rainy season is the Udgītha;
autumn is the Pratihāra.
Winter is the Nidhana;
this Vairāja [Sāman] is thus woven into the seasons.
The spring is the *hiṃkāra* because of its priority;
the summer is the *prastāva*, and so forth, as explained previously.
He who thus knows this Vairāja [Sāman] as woven into the seasons shines forth with offspring.
Through cattle and through spiritual luster,
he reaches a full span of life; he lives long.
He becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame. He should not revile the seasons.
That is the vow. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.16.2)

He who knows this Vairāja [sāman] as woven upon the seasons shines like the seasons; just as the seasons shine with their seasonal attributes, so does the knower shine with offspring and other blessings—this has been stated elsewhere.
One should not revile the seasons; that is his vow. //2//
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. The earth is the *hiṅkāra*.
The intermediate space is the Prastāva; the sky is the Udgītha;
the quarters are the Pratihāra.
The ocean is their resting place.
These Śakvarī verses are woven into the worlds.
"The earth is the *hiṅkāra*" and so forth, as before.
"The *śakvarīs*" always takes the plural number, just like the *revatīs*.
They are woven into the worlds. //1//
He who thus knows these Śakvarī verses as interwoven in the worlds becomes a possessor of worlds and reaches a full span of life.
He lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle;
great in fame.
One should not revile the worlds; that is his vow. ChUp 2.17.2.
"He becomes possessed of a world; he is joined with the fruit of the world"—this is the meaning.
"One should not revile the worlds"—that is his vow. //2//
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The she-goat is indeed the *hiṅkāra*.
Sheep are the Prastāva; cows are the Udgītha;
horses are the Pratihāra.
The Puruṣa is the Nidhana. These Revatī verses are interwoven with cattle. // ChUp 2.18.1 //
"Goat is the *hiṅkāra*," and so forth, as before.
[The syllables] are woven into the animals. //1//
He who thus knows these *revatī* verses as interwoven with cattle becomes possessed of cattle.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
He should be great in fame;
he should not revile cattle. That is his vow.
One should not revile animals; that is his vow.
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The hair of the body is the *hiṅkāra*.
The skin is the Prastāva;
the flesh is the Udgītha;
the bone is the Pratihāra.
The marrow is the finale;
this Yajñāyajñīya chant is woven into the limbs.
The hair is the *hiṅkāra* because it is the first among the limbs of the body; the skin is the *prastāva* because of its immediate succession;
the flesh is the *udgītha* because of its excellence.
The bone is the *pratihāra* because it is held together;
the marrow is the *nidhana* because it is at the end. This Sāman named *yajñāyajñīya* is thus woven into the limbs of the body. //1//
He who thus knows this Yajñāyajñīya as woven upon the limbs becomes possessed of limbs.
He does not perish in his limbs;
he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long.
He becomes great in offspring and cattle;
he becomes great in fame.
For one year he should not eat marrow.
That is the vow:
"One should not eat marrow," so it is said.

"He becomes whole" means he becomes possessed of all his limbs. "He does not become crippled in any limb"—that is to say, he does not become deformed or crooked like a lame man or a man with a withered arm.
For one year—that is, for the duration of a full year—he shall not eat or consume marrow.
The plural number is used for the purpose of indicating fish in general. His vow is that he should never eat marrow, or rather, that he should never eat it at all. //2//
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Fire is the *hiṅkāra*.
The wind is the Prastāva;
the sun is the Udgītha;
the stars are the Pratihāra.
The moon is the Nidhana;
this is the Rājana chant woven among the deities.
Agni is the *hiṅkāra* because he occupies the first position;
Vāyu is the *prastāva* because of the commonality of being next in order;
Āditya is the *udgītha* because of his preeminence.
The constellations are the *pratihāra* because they are drawn forth;
the moon is the *nidhana* because it is the conclusion for those who perform ritual actions.
This is the *rājana* chant woven into the deities, because of the radiant splendor of the deities. //1//
He who thus knows this king woven into the deities attains the same world,
the same creation, and union with these very deities.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
he becomes great in offspring and cattle.
He is great in fame. He should not revile Brahmins;
that is his vow. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.20.2)

The fruit for the knower is this: co-residence (*salokatā*)—that is, residence in the same world—with these very deities, Agni and the others; equality of power (*sārṣṭitā*), which is equality of prosperity (*samānarddhitva*); and union (*sāyujya*), which is the state of being a single body and its inhabitant (*ekadehadehitva*).

Here, the word "or" (*vā*) is to be understood as elided, as in "or co-residence," and so forth, because a specific result is logically established through a specific mode of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
He goes; he attains [the goal]. And because a cumulative collection [of results] is not logically possible, the vow is: "One should not revile Brahmins."
“Indeed, these Brahmins are the gods manifest before our eyes”—according to this Vedic scripture, reviling a Brahmin is tantamount to reviling a deity. //2//
Thus ends the twentieth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The triple knowledge (the three Vedas) is indeed the *hiṅkāra*.
These three worlds are the Prastāva;
fire, wind, and the sun are the Udgītha;
the stars, birds, and rays of light are the Pratihāra.
The serpents, the Gandharvas, and the ancestors—this is their finale;
this Sāman is woven into everything.
The triple science (trayī vidyā) is the *hiṅkāra*.
The immediate sequence of the triple science after the Sāman beginning with Agni is due to the scriptural statement that the triple science has Agni and the others as its effects.
It is the *hiṅkāra* because it is the first of all things to be performed.
These three worlds are the *prastāva* because they are the immediate effects [of that].
The status of fire and the others as the *udgītha* is due to their preeminence;
