the status of the stars and the others as the *pratihāra* is due to their being held back (*pratihatatvāt*).

Because of the commonality of the sound *dhakāra* in words such as "serpent" (*sarpa*), this *Sāman* possesses the quality of being the end (*nidhana*). Since there is no distinction in name, the word *Sāman* refers to the entire collection of *Sāmans*.
Indeed, the constituent parts of the *Sāman*, beginning with the *hiṅkāra*, are to be meditated upon through the vision of the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) and so forth.
Even regarding the previous meditations on the *Sāman*, whatever *Sāman* was woven into each respective object, that *Sāman* was to be meditated upon through the vision of that very object.
Because the ritual wife (karmāṅganā) is to be consecrated by a specific gaze, just like the clarified butter (ājya). //1//
He who thus knows this Sāman as woven upon everything becomes everything indeed.
The fruit for one who knows the equality of all objects is that "he becomes everything" and "he becomes the lord of all"; this is the meaning.
For if he possessed the state of being everything in its primary sense, it would be impossible for him to receive offerings from those situated in the various directions. //2//
Concerning this, there is this verse:
"Those which are fivefold, three by three."
There is nothing else greater or higher than them.
Regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra:

"There is no other entity whatsoever that is greater than or more supreme than those fivefold triads—the three [Vedas] and so forth—which have been declared in five ways through the divisions of *hiṅkāra* and the rest. There exists no other distinct reality superior to or beyond those groups of five.
The meaning is that it does not exist;
for within that very [reality], everything is included. //3//
He who knows that knows all;
all the quarters bring tribute to him.
"One should worship it with the thought, 'I am all.
That is the vow; that is the vow."
He who knows this *sāman* as having the aforementioned nature of being the self of all—that is, he knows everything;
the meaning is that he becomes omniscient.
All the quarters—that is, those situated in all directions—bring tribute, meaning they offer enjoyment, to such a knower.
"One should meditate upon this Sāman as 'I am all; I am everything. This indeed is its vow.
The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the meditation on the Sāman. //4//
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"I choose the resounding Sāman, which is beneficial for cattle"— this is the *udgītha* of Agni.
That which is undefined belongs to Prajāpati;
that which is defined belongs to Soma;
that which is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu.
The voice of Indra is smooth and powerful;
that of Bṛhaspati is like the cry of a curlew;
that of Varuṇa is a deep, resonant sound.
One should serve all of them,
but one must avoid the one belonging to Varuṇa.
In connection with the meditation on the Sāman, the excellence of the specific singing and other qualities of the Udgātṛ priest are taught.

Because of its connection with a specific result, "vinardi" refers to a distinguished sound—a particular tone resembling the bellowing of a bull (*ṛṣabha*); the completion of the sentence is that such is the "vinardi" song. And that [song] belonging to the Sāman is beneficial for cattle (*paśavya*) and, having Agni as its deity, pertains to the *udgītha*, which is the act of chanting.
Thinking, "Therefore, I choose and pray for one who is distinguished in this way," a certain sacrificer or Udgātṛ considers [this].
It is *anirukta*—meaning unspecified as "such-and-such"—and thus undifferentiated; it belongs to Prajāpati, having Prajāpati as its deity, for that specific chant is not specified.
Because of Prajāpati’s being *anirukta* (unexpressed), it is *nirukta* (clearly expressed) for Soma.
The meaning is that the *udgītha* has Soma as its deity;
singing that is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu, having Vāyu as its deity;
and singing that which is smooth yet forceful, endowed with excessive effort, belongs to Indra, having Indra as its deity.

The *krauñca* chant, which resembles the cry of the *krauñca* bird, belongs to Bṛhaspati; it is the *bārhaspatya*. The *apadhvānta*, which resembles the sound of cracked bell-metal, is this song of Varuṇa.
One may practice or employ all of these, but one should avoid the *vāruṇa* alone. //1//
"May I sing forth immortality for the gods," thus he should sing;
"food for the ancestors, hope for men, grass and water for animals, the heavenly world for the sacrificer, and food for myself"— meditating on these in his mind, let him chant with vigilance.
"May I sing for the gods the attainment of immortality;
may I sing for the ancestors the *svadhā* offering; may I sing for men hope—'hope' meaning prayer, that which is prayed for;

may I sing for animals grass and water; may I sing for the sacrificer the heavenly world; and may I sing for myself, the singer, food"—thinking and meditating thus in his mind, he should chant the praise without negligence regarding the vowels, sibilants, consonants, and so forth.
All the vowels are the self of Indra;
all the sibilants are the self of Prajāpati.
All touches have death as their essence.
If someone should attack him while he is among the vowels, he should say to him:
"I have sought refuge in Indra; he will answer you. ChUp 2.22.3.

All vowels, beginning with *a*, are the selves of Indra—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose function is strength—and they occupy the position of the limbs of his body. All sibilants (*ūṣman*), beginning with *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*, are the selves of Prajāpati Virāj, or of Kaśyapa.
All consonants (*sparśa*), beginning with *ka*, are the selves of Death. If anyone should reproach this Udgātṛ priest who knows thus regarding the vowels...
Having been reproached thus, "The accent was wrongly applied by you," he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Indra, the vital breath, the Lord;
while I am applying the accents, that very Indra, who is to speak to you, will speak to you—he, the God himself, will give the answer. //3//
Now, if they should reproach him for the *ūṣman* sounds, he should say to them:
"I have fled for refuge to Prajāpati; he will look after you."
Now, if someone should challenge him regarding objects of touch, he should say to him: "I have sought refuge in Death; he will burn you. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.22.4)
Now, if they should likewise reproach him regarding the hot things, he should say to him: "I have fled for refuge to Prajāpati; he will look upon you and crush you to pieces.
And if they should reproach him regarding the tactile objects, he should say to him: "I have fled for refuge to Death; he will burn you up and reduce you to ashes. //4//
All vowels should be pronounced with resonance and strength, [thinking]: "I am bestowing strength upon Indra.
All sibilants should be pronounced unswallowed, unexpelled, and open, [thinking]: "I am surrendering my self to Prajāpati."
"One should say that all contacts have been avoided even in the slightest degree, thinking, 'I am avoiding death itself.'"
Since the vowels (svara), beginning with *s*, are the self of Indra and the others, therefore all vowels should be pronounced resonant and strong, thinking:
"Thus may I bestow strength upon Indra; thus may I impart strength.

Likewise, all sibilants (*ūṣman*) should be unswallowed—meaning not drawn inward—and unrejected—not thrown outward—but expanded, endowed with the effort of expansion, thinking: "I surrender my self to Prajāpati; I offer it to him."
All contacts should be described as slight, gradual, unapplied, and uncast down, as one who avoids himself from death slowly, like a child, thinking, "I shall avoid myself from death. //5//
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. There are three branches of dharma.
Sacrifice, study, and giving constitute the first [āśrama];
austerity alone is the second;
and the third is the student who dwells in the teacher’s household, exhausting himself completely while living in the teacher’s household.
All these become possessors of the worlds of merit;
but he who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality.
The section beginning with "The three branches of duty" (ChU 2.23.1) is commenced for the purpose of prescribing the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the syllable *Oṃ*.
One should not think that the fruit is obtained solely from meditating on the *Oṃ* as a constituent part of the *Sāman*, characterized by the *udgītha* and so forth.
What then? That fruit—immortality—which cannot be attained even through all the meditations on the *Sāman* or through ritual actions, is obtained from the meditation on the *Oṃ* alone.
Its mention in the context of the *Sāman* is for the purpose of praising it.
"Dharma-skandhas" means threefold divisions of Dharma; that is to say, classifications of Dharma.
To the question "What are they?", he says: sacrifice (*yajña*), such as the *agnihotra* and so forth.
Study consists of the repeated practice of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures according to the prescribed rules;
giving consists of the distribution of wealth to those who beg outside the sacrificial altar according to one's ability.
This is the first pillar of Dharma.

Because [the term] is associated with the householder, it is indicated by the householder who performs those [rites]; "the first" means "the one," and it does not mean "the beginning" because of the mention of "the second" and "the third.

"The second is austerity alone"—austerity refers to *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth; one who possesses that is an ascetic (*tāpasa*) or a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), but not one who is "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*), for the latter is established merely in the duties of his stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*).
This is because immortality is heard [to be attained] only by one who is established in Brahman.
The second aggregate of Dharma:
one whose nature is to dwell in the family of the preceptor as a celibate student is called a "dweller in the family of the preceptor" (*ācāryakulavāsī*).
The third aggregate of Dharma is one who, for the rest of his life, exhausts himself through observances in the family of the preceptor, wearing away the body.
From the qualification "absolutely" (*atyantam*) and so forth, it is understood that [the subject] is a *naiṣṭhika* (one who remains lifelong).

For one who is a *upakurvāṇa* (a student who returns after study), since the purpose of his Vedic study is to grasp the texts, the attainment of the world of merit does not result from his studentship alone.
All three of these types of *āśramins*, however, attain the world of merit through their respective duties as previously described.
Those for whom the world is merit are these "merit-world" (puṇyaloka) hermits.

But the remaining one, who has not been mentioned, is the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) established in Brahman—meaning he is perfectly situated in Brahman; he attains immortality, which is distinct from the merit-world and consists of the state of non-death that is absolute, not relative like the immortality of the gods and others, because immortality is distinguished here as being separate from the merit-world.
And if immortality were merely a preeminent state among the worlds attained through merit, then it would not have been taught as distinct from "the world of merit.
From this distinct designation, it is understood that immortality is absolute.

Furthermore, the presentation here of the fruits of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) is for the purpose of praising the practice of the syllable Om (praṇava), and not for the purpose of enjoining those fruits as ends in themselves.
For the sentence would have to be split [if it were taken as] praising the service of the *praṇava*, [and simultaneously] enjoining the fruits of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).
Therefore, by restating the fruits of the stages of life as established in the Smṛti, the text praises the service of the *praṇava* by declaring immortality to be its fruit.
It is just as when the service of Pūrṇavarman results in the mere wearing of a garment by his devotees, whereas the service of Rājavarman results in a fruit equal to sovereignty over a kingdom.
And the *praṇava* is that Truth, because it is the symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Brahman;

for the *Kāṭhaka* recites: "For this very syllable is Brahman, for this very syllable is the Supreme. Thus, it is logical that immortality results from its service, since there is no distinction among the four [classes] regarding their eligibility.
Furthermore, because there is no prohibition against being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃstha),
and because the capacity for being established in Brahman is possible even when one's own duties are interrupted;
nor is the term "brahmasaṃstha" conventionally restricted to the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) in the same way that words such as *yava* or *varāha* are restricted to specific meanings.
Because [the term] functions by taking its basis from being established in Brahman;
for conventional words do not depend upon a causal basis,
and the establishment of all things in Brahman is logically consistent.

Wherever a ground exists for being established in Brahman, it is not proper to restrict the word "established in Brahman"— which denotes anyone possessing such a ground— to the wandering mendicant alone, since there is no reason for such a limitation. Furthermore, immortality is not attained through the mere duties of the wandering mendicant stage of life.
Because it would follow that knowledge is purposeless.
If it is argued that only knowledge conjoined with the dharma of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is the means for attaining immortality, we say no;
for there is no distinction in its being a duty belonging to a particular stage of life (āśrama-dharma).
Furthermore, the principle that "dharma distinguished by knowledge is the means to immortality" applies equally to the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*).
Nor is there any scriptural statement to the effect that liberation belongs only to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) who is established in Brahman, and not to others.

Moreover, it is the established conclusion of all the Upanishads that liberation results from knowledge. Therefore, whoever among those who perform the duties prescribed for their own stage of life is established in Brahman, he alone attains immortality.
Injunctions regarding action, such as "Do this" and "Do not do that," have been set forth;
however, that [moral] cause is not created by the scripture,
because it is observed among all living beings.

The cognition produced by the scriptures— such as "Being alone, one, without a second," "All this is indeed the Self," and "All this is indeed Brahman"— which consists of knowledge, does not arise without first subverting the innate cognition of the distinction between action, agent, and fruit, which is the cause for injunctions regarding ritual acts;
for there is a contradiction between the cognitions of difference and non-difference.

For indeed, the cognition of the oneness of the moon and so forth does not arise upon the removal of the cataract without first subverting the cognition of the plurality of moons and so forth produced by the cataract;
this is because there is a contradiction between the cognitions of knowledge and ignorance.
This being the case, that cognition of plurality upon which the injunctions for ritual action depend is subverted for one [who has attained knowledge].

"That which is Being is one alone, without a second; that is the Truth, while the diversity of modifications is untruth"—by means of this cognition of unity produced by the authority of such scriptural statements, he desists from all ritual actions because the causes [for action] have ceased.
And he who has desisted from action is called "one who is firmly established in Brahman."
And that [one] must be a wandering mendicant alone, because no other state is possible.
For another person, in whom the cognition of difference has not ceased, perceives, hears, thinks, and cognizes one thing while thinking, "Having done this, I shall obtain that.
While acting in this manner, he does not possess the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*).

Because modifications are merely verbal designations and are based on the false notion of reality, when the cognition of difference is sublated as being unreal, the cognition of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge— such as "this must be done by this person" or "by me"— is no longer tenable. To the discerning person, it is like the perception of surface or impurity in the sky.

If one does not desist from actions even when the cognition of difference has been sublated, then— as before— the sentence that enjoins the cognition of unity would be rendered invalid. However, just as the validity of prohibitive sentences such as those forbidding the eating of forbidden food is established, so too is the validity of the sentence concerning unity appropriate,
because all the Upaniṣads have that [unity] as their ultimate purport.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) being invalid, we say no; for their validity is established with respect to those persons whose cognition of difference has not been sublated, just as dream-cognitions are valid prior to awakening. If it is argued that because the non-discriminating lack such realization, the validity of the ritual injunctions would be destroyed, we say no.
Because we observe that the injunctions for optional rites (*kāmyavidhi*) are not abolished.

For it is not the case that because those who know that "being driven by desire" (*kāmātmatā*) is not praiseworthy cease to perform optional rites, the injunctions for optional rites are thereby abolished; rather, they are indeed performed by those who possess desire. Similarly, although rites are not performed by those established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*), the knowers of Brahman, the injunctions for them are not abolished, as they are indeed performed by those who do not know Brahman.

If it is argued that, just as for wandering mendicants, householders and others—even though they have developed the realization of oneness—do not cease from performing rituals such as the *agnihotra*, we say no;
for when considering the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), human activity cannot serve as a precedent.

Indeed, one does not observe anyone performing a prohibited act such as sorcery (*abhicāra*) simply because it has been forbidden; nor would a discerning person, even if devoid of hatred toward an enemy, engage in such sorcery.

Furthermore, once the cognition of difference—which is the cause for engaging in the performance of ritual actions—is sublated, there remains no motivating cause for acts such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice;

just as hunger and so forth are the motivators for a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) to go about begging, one might argue that here too, the fear of sin (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance serves as the motivator. This is not so.
Because the subject under discussion is one who possesses the notion of difference.
We have stated that he who possesses the notion of difference—that is, whose cognition of difference has not been sublated by knowledge—is the one qualified for ritual action.

For there is sin in the non-performance of duty for one who is so qualified, but not for one whose qualification has ceased, just as there is no fault for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) in failing to perform the specific duties of a householder.
If it is argued that, in that case, everyone residing in their own stage of life (*āśrama*) would be a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) once the cognition of oneness has arisen, we say no;
because the cognition of the distinction between "self" and "owner" has not ceased,
and because the other stages of life exist for the sake of ritual action (*karman*).
For it is heard in scripture: "Then one should perform action.
Therefore, due to the absence of the relationship between property and owner, only the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is a wandering ascetic (*parivrāj*), not the householder and others.

If it is argued that for a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the practice of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is untenable because the cognition of difference caused by ritual injunctions has been sublated by the cognition of oneness produced by the rule of [the realization of] oneness; we say no.

For [restraints and observances] are established as being possible prior to the cognition of oneness, such as when one is afflicted by hunger and so forth, since they serve the purpose of cessation [from worldly activity].
Furthermore, there is no possibility of engaging in what is prohibited.
Because the notion of oneness has already been refuted prior to this;
for one who has fallen into a well or upon a thorn at night does not fall into that very same place when the sun has risen.
Therefore, it is established that only the mendicant whose karma has ceased is "established in Brahman."
Furthermore, as for what was said— that for all those devoid of knowledge there is the world of merit—
this is true.
And as for what was said— that by the word "asceticism" (tapaḥ) the wandering mendicant (parivrāj) is also included— [that too is true].
This is incorrect.
Why?
Because the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) is possible only for a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).
For we have already stated that he alone is what remains;

moreover, for one who possesses the knowledge of oneness, there is a cessation of austerity, just as there is with the Agnihotra and other rites. Indeed, the duty to perform austerity would belong only to one who possesses the notion of duality.

By this, the argument that the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) is impossible during a lapse in ritual action, as well as the lack of prohibition [against it], has been answered.
Likewise, the objection that knowledge would be useless—on the grounds that only one who possesses knowledge and has ceased from action is a wandering mendicant (parivrāj)—has been answered.

Furthermore, the claim that the term *brahmasaṃstha* is not conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a wandering mendicant, in the same way that words such as *yava* or *varāha* are not, has been refuted.
Because the state of being "established in Brahman" (brahmasaṃsthatā) is possible only for that [person] and not for anyone else.
As for what was further stated— that words established by conventional usage do not require a [specific] etymological cause—
that is not so.

Because we observe words such as *gṛhastha* (householder), *takṣan* (carpenter), and *parivrājaka* (wandering mendicant), these words are seen to be conventional (*rūḍha*) with respect to specific stages of life (*āśrama*)— namely, the householder and the wandering mendicant— and with respect to a person of a particular caste, namely the carpenter, even though they take as their basis the respective causes of residing in a house, wandering, and carpentry. They do not apply to every instance wherever those causes may be present.
Because [the term] is not commonly established [in that sense elsewhere],

so too here the word *brahmasaṃstha* must refer to the one who has retired from all ritual actions and their means— the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) known as the Paramahaṃsa who stands beyond the [lower] stages of life (*atyāśramin*).
This is because the fruit of immortality is heard [to be attained] through this primary [meaning].
Therefore, this alone is the renunciation (pārivrājya) declared in the Veda:
not the possession of the sacrificial thread, the triple staff, the water-pot, and so forth.
For the Śruti says, "Shaven-headed, without possessions, unattached," and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad states, "The supreme purifier beyond the senses," and so on.
And from such Smṛti passages as, "Free from praise, free from salutation," and "Therefore, the ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual action," and "Therefore,
the knower of dharma is without marks, possessing unmanifested marks," and so forth.
As for the renunciation of action accepted by the Sāṃkhyas,
that is false because they accept the reality of the cognition of distinctions between action, agent, and fruit;
and as for the non-agency accepted by the Buddhists due to their acceptance of emptiness (śūnyatā).
That too is incorrect,
because the one who accepts that [non-doership] must necessarily accept the existence of a being; furthermore, the acceptance of non-doership by the ignorant out of laziness is also invalid.
Because the notion of agency is not removed by any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

it is established that only for one who possesses the cognition of oneness produced by the Vedānta *pramāṇa* does there exist the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatva*) characterized by renunciation (*pārivrājya*), which consists in the cessation of ritual action.
By this, it follows as a matter of course that when a householder possesses the realization of oneness, renunciation is necessarily attained.

"Surely the wandering mendicant would incur the fault of extinguishing the sacred fire, according to the Vedic scripture: 'He who lets the fire go out is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods. No;
for it has been extinguished by the Veda itself, since that fire is truly extinguished when the vision of oneness arises."
Because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The nature of fire has departed from fire," therefore the householder who goes forth as a wandering mendicant does not incur any fault. //1//
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds.
From them, thus brooded upon, the threefold knowledge issued forth.
He brooded over it;
from it, thus brooded upon, these syllables flowed forth: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*.

In order to define that state wherein one attains immortality, he says: Prajāpati—whether Virāj or Kaśyapa—directed his attention toward the worlds; "he heated them" means he performed meditation (*dhyāna*), that is, austerity (*tapas*).
From those worlds thus heated, the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), which is their essence, flowed forth; this means it appeared within the mind of Prajāpati.
He brooded over her, as before.
From her, thus brooded upon, these syllables issued forth: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*—the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛtis*). //2//
He brooded over them;
from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable Om issued forth.
Just as all leaves are pierced by a pin, so is all speech pierced by the syllable *oṃ*.
The syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this; the syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this.
He brooded over those syllables; from them, thus brooded upon, the syllable *oṃ* flowed forth—that is Brahman.

He asks what it is like: "Just as all leaves—meaning all the various parts of leaves—are pierced, perforated, and pervaded by a stalk or a leaf-stem (*parṇanāla*), so too is the entire collection of words and speech pierced by the syllable *oṃ*, which is Brahman and serves as the symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self."
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The syllable 'A' is indeed all speech.
Furthermore, since even the modification of the Supreme Self is merely a name, it follows that "all this is indeed the syllable Oṃ.
The repetition at the end is for the sake of emphasis.
The purpose of explaining the accomplishment of the worlds and so forth is for the sake of praising the syllable Oṃ. //3//
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the second chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The exponents of Brahman say:
That which belongs to the Vasus is the morning libation; that which belongs to the Rudras is the midday libation;
and that which belongs to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas is the third libation.

In connection with the meditation on the Sāman, having set aside the syllable *oṃ*—which, being subordinate to ritual action, was previously subject to withdrawal—and having magnified it as a symbol of the Supreme Self and a cause of immortality, [the author], desiring to teach the Sāman, the oblation, the mantra, and the rising, which are constituent parts of the very sacrifice under discussion, says: "The exponents of Brahman say: 'That which is the morning libation belongs to the Vasus.'"
And by them—those who are the lords of the libations (savaneśāna)—this world was brought under control at the morning libation (prātaḥsavana);
likewise, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) was brought under control by the Rudras, the lords of the midday libation (mādhyandinasavana);
and the third world was brought under control by the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas, the lords of the third libation (tṛtīyasavana).
Thus, no other world remains for the sacrificer. //1//
"Then where is the world of the sacrificer? "If one does not know that, how could he perform it?"
Then the wise man should perform [the rite]. ChUp 2.24.2.
Therefore, where then is the world for the sacrificer for whose sake he sacrifices?
The intention is that there is no world for him at all, because of the Vedic scripture: "He who sacrifices sacrifices indeed for the sake of a world."

And in the absence of the worlds, that sacrificer who would not know—that is, would not understand—the means of acquiring those worlds, characterized by the Sāman, the oblation, and the rising of the mantra, being ignorant, how could he perform the sacrifice? In no way whatsoever is his status as an agent possible; this is the meaning. Since the intent is to praise the knowledge of the Sāman and so forth, the agency of one who is ignorant—meaning one who knows only the ritual action—is not being denied.
For this sentence is divided into two parts: for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Sāman and so forth, and for the purpose of prohibiting its performance by one who is ignorant.
Regarding the first part, we have already stated the reason in the *Oṣastya-kāṇḍa* that ritual action exists even for the ignorant;
however, one who knows the means consisting of the Sāman and so forth, which is about to be described, should perform it. //2//
Before the commencement of the Prātaranuvāka, sitting behind the Gārhapatya fire facing north, he sings the Sāman addressed to the Vasus.

"What is that which is to be known? he asks; [the text] says: Before—previously—at the commencement of the *prātaranuvāka* recitation, sitting behind the *gārhapatya* fire facing north, he sings the *sāman* sacred to the Vasus (*vāsava*). //3//
"Open the door to the world! Let us see you, O Lord of Radiance! *lo* 3 *kadvāram apāvā* 3 *rṇū* 33 / *paśyema tvā vayaṃ rā* 33333 *hu* 3 *m ā* 33 *jyā* 3 *yo* 3 *ā* 32111. (ChUp 2.24.4)
"O Agni, open the door to this world of earth for its attainment; through that door may we behold you, O King. //4//
Then he offers an oblation:
"Homage to Agni, who dwells on the earth, who dwells in the world!"
"Find a world for me, who am sacrificing!
This indeed is the world of the sacrificer;
I am she. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.5)

Then, immediately after that, he offers with this mantra: "Homage to Agni! We bow down before you, O dweller on earth—that is, the one who resides upon the earth; O dweller of the world—that is, the one who resides in the world of the earth.
Find—obtain—a world for me, the sacrificer.
This indeed is my world as a sacrificer; to it I shall go. (5)
At this point, the sacrificer says, "Svāhā! Beyond the span of life!
and having said, "Remove the crossbar," he stands up.
To him, the Vasus present the morning libation.

"In this world, I, the sacrificer, having passed beyond my lifespan—that is, having died—[I say] *svāhā* and offers [the oblation]. Having uttered the mantra, 'Cast away, remove the crossbar—the bolt of the door to the worlds'—he rises. Thus, by means of these [mantras], he [offers] to the Vasus."
The world connected with the morning pressing would have been ransomed; therefore, they bestow the morning pressing upon the sacrificer. //6//
Before the commencement of the midday libation, sitting behind the Āgnīdhrīya fire-altar and facing north, he sings the Sāman dedicated to Rudra.
"Open the door of the worlds! Open it! Open it!
May we behold you, O Vira! Huṃ! Ā! Jyā! Yo! Ā! (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.8)
Likewise, having sat down behind the Āgnīdhrīya fire, facing north, the sacrificer sings the Raudra Sāman, which has Rudra as its deity, for the sake of attaining sovereignty. (7–8)
Then he offers:
"Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, who dwells in the world!"
"Find a world for me, who am sacrificing!
This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; in this I abide. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.24.9)
There, the sacrificer says, "Hail! Beyond the span of life!
and having said, "Remove the crossbar," he stands up.
To him, the Rudras hand over the midday libation.
"Abiding in the intermediate space," and so forth, is the same as before. //9//
Before the commencement of the third pressing, sitting behind the Āhavanīya fire facing north, he sings the Sāman addressed to Āditya and that addressed to the Viśvedevas. (ChUp 2.24.11)
"Open the door of the world! Open it!
So that we may see you, O Self-radiant One! Hūm! Ā! Jyā! Yo! Ā!"—thus [he worships] the Sun. (ChU 2.24.12)
Now follows the Vaiśvadeva: "May we behold you with the Sāman—huṃ ā 33333 jyā 3 yo 3 ā 32111. (ChU 2.24.13)

Likewise, sitting facing north before the Āhavanīya fire, he sings the Sāman dedicated to Āditya, the Sāman dedicated to Āditya, and the Vaiśvadeva Sāman in succession for the sake of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*).
Then he offers the oblation.
Homage to the Ādityas and to all the gods who dwell in heaven and dwell in the worlds!
Find a world for me, the sacrificer!
"This indeed is the world of the sacrificer;
here am I, the sacrificer, beyond the span of life—svāhā! Having said, 'Strike away the crossbar,' he rises. (ChU 2.24.15)
"From those dwelling in heaven," and so forth—the rest is the same.
The only difference is the addition of the words "may he find" and "free from evil.
However, this [formula] pertains to the sacrificer.
Because of the indicative mark [found] in such passages as "I am here, O sacrificer. (14–15)
Therefore, both the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas bestow upon him the third libation. Verily,
he knows the measure of the sacrifice who knows this— who knows this.
This sacrificer, indeed, who knows thus—that is, who knows the measure and the true nature of the sacrifice as described, such as the Sāman and so forth—knows it as stated.
The repetition, "He who knows thus, he who knows thus," is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. 16.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa. Om.
Now begins the third chapter.
This sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods. Of it,
the sky itself is the cross-beam.
The intermediate space is the cake;
the rays are the sons.
The connection for the beginning of this chapter, starting with "That sun indeed," is as follows:

At the end of the immediately preceding chapter, it was stated that "one should know the measure of the sacrifice. Furthermore, specific chants (*sāman*), oblations (*homa*), mantras, and ritual standings (*utthāna*) pertaining to the sacrifice were taught as constituent parts of the sacrifice for the attainment of distinguished results.
And Savitṛ, who is the manifestation of the fulfillment of all sacrifices, shines with great splendor.
This very [sun], which is the fruit of the karma of all living beings, is directly perceived and subsisted upon by everyone.

Therefore, immediately after the description of sacrifice, the Śruti begins with the words, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," in order to enjoin the meditation on the Sun— the subject matter that constitutes the result of sacrifice— which yields the most excellent fruit among all human goals.
Because he gladdens the gods like honey, this Āditya is "honey" (*madhu*).
He will later explain that Āditya is the cause of joy for Vasu and the other classes of gods because he is the embodiment of the fruit of all sacrifices.
To the question, "In what way is he honey? he says: Of that honey, heaven itself is the horizontal beam (*tiraścīnavaṃśa*), just as there is a horizontal beam in the honey of bees.

For the sky appears as if turned sideways, and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) hangs down like a honeycomb attached to the beam of the sky; thus, due to this similarity with a honeycomb, and because it is the support of the honey of Savitṛ, the intermediate space is called a "honeycomb.

The rays are the light-beams, and the waters situated within those rays are the terrestrial waters drawn forth by Savitṛ, for it is known from scripture: "These indeed are the waters of Svarāj, which are the rays."

Because they are situated within the rays that have entered the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), they appear like bees placed inside honeycombs; thus they are called "sons" (*putra*) because they are like sons—just as the offspring of bees are found within the cells of a honeycomb. Of that [sun], those rays which extend toward the east are its eastern honey-cells.
The *ṛc*s are indeed the honey-makers;
the *Ṛgveda* is the flower;
they are the immortal waters.
Now, these indeed are those very verses.

Of that honey which has the Sun as its substratum, those rays which extend eastward—that is, toward the eastern direction—are his "eastern honey-ducts" (*madhunāḍyaḥ*), so called because they extend forward like the channels of honey;
the meaning is that they are apertures serving as receptacles for honey.

In this context, the *Ṛg* verses themselves are the "honey-makers," for they produce the honey—the red-colored essence resting in the Sun—just as bees, having taken up essences, produce honey. Thus, they are like honey-makers or bees.
The Ṛgveda alone is like the flower of that [tree].

Since the collection of Ṛks and Brāhmaṇas is designated as the "Ṛgveda," and because it consists of mere sound, it is impossible for the flow of nectar in the form of objects of enjoyment to issue from it; therefore, by the word "Ṛgveda" here, the ritual action prescribed in the Ṛgveda is intended.
For from that [action], the flow of nectar consisting of the fruit of the ritual becomes possible.
Just as honey is produced by bees from flowers, so too is honey produced by means of the *Ṛg* verses, taking the water from the ritual action prescribed in the *Ṛgveda*.

He asks: what are those waters? They are the waters employed in the ritual in the form of Soma, clarified butter, and milk; when cast into the fire, they become "immortal" (*amṛta*) waters—so called because they serve the purpose of immortality and because they possess extreme flavor—as a result of that cooking.
Taking up those essences, these very *Ṛg* verses are like bees that extract the juice from flowers; such are the *Ṛg* verses. (2)
They brooded over this Rigveda.
From it, thus brooded upon, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
These *ṛks*—employed in ritual action—“heated,” as it were, this *Ṛgveda*, that is, the action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda* which stands in the place of a flower.

For it is logical that action being performed with *ṛk*-mantras that have attained the status of constituent parts such as the *śastra* hymns should release the juice that produces honey, just as flowers do when they are sucked by bees.
This is what the text expresses: “of that *Ṛgveda* having been heated.”
What is this essence that is said to have issued forth from the heating of the *Ṛk*-bees?

It is fame, which is renown; splendor, which is the radiance residing in the body; the senses, which is the non-deficiency of the faculties endowed with capability; vigor, meaning capacity or strength;

and food, which is both "food" (*anna*) and "that which is to be eaten" (*ādya*), by the consumption of which the sustenance of the gods occurs day after day. This essence was produced from ritual action characterized by sacrifice and the like. //3//
It flowed away;
it took refuge around the sun.
Now, this which is the red form of the sun is indeed that very [Brahman].
That [water], beginning with fame and ending with edible food, flowed forth—that is, it issued out specifically;
and having gone, it took refuge on all sides, that is, on the eastern part, of the sun.

For people perform rituals for the sake of attaining results characterized by fame and so forth, thinking, "We shall enjoy the honey called the fruit of karma accumulated in yonder sun," just as one performs the cultivation of a field.
This is demonstrated before the eyes of the cultivators for the sake of inspiring faith; that is indeed this very thing:
the red form which is seen of the rising sun. //4//
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those which are its southern rays are its southern honey-cells.
The Yajus formulas themselves are the honey-makers;
the Yajurveda itself is the flower;
those are the immortal waters.

"Then, as for those rays of his which are to the south," and so forth, is the same [as before]. The *yajus* formulas themselves are the honey-makers; they are employed in the rituals prescribed by the *Yajurveda*, just like the honey-makers in the previous case.
The ritual action prescribed by the Yajurveda occupies the position of the flower and is thus called the "flower.
These very waters, beginning with Soma, are the nectar. //1//
These very sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) heated this Yajurveda.
From it, thus heated, there arose as its essence (rasa) glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
That flowed out;
it took refuge around the sun.
That indeed is this white form of the sun.
"These very *yajus* verses brooded over this *Yajurveda*"—all [this] is the same as before.
This is that honey which is seen as the white form of the sun. (2–3)
Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those rays of his which extend westward are its western honey-cells.
The Sāman chants are indeed the honey-makers;
the Sāmaveda is the flower; they are the immortal waters. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.3.1)
These very Sāmans heated this Sāmaveda.
From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence (rasa) fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
That flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That, indeed, is this black form of the sun.
Now, "those rays of his which face west," and so forth, is the same [as before].
Likewise, there is the honey of the Sāmans.
This is the black form of the sun. (ChUpBh 3.3.1–3)
Thus ends the third section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those rays of his which point northward are its northern honey-cells.
The Atharva-Angirasas are indeed the honey-makers;
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the flower;
those are the immortal waters.
These very Atharvaṅgirases brooded over this Itihāsa-Purāṇa;
from it, thus brooded upon, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food.
That flowed out;
it took refuge around the sun.
That, indeed, is this very form of the sun which is intensely black.
Now, "And those rays of his which point upward," and so forth, is the same [as before].
The *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the mantras seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras; employed in ritual action, they are the honey-makers (*madhukṛtaḥ*). Itihāsa and Purāṇa are the flower.
The application of these two—the *Itihāsa* and the *Purāṇa*—as constituent parts of the ritual during the *pāriplava* nights of the Aśvamedha sacrifice is established.
This "honey" is the supreme black form of the Sun; that is to say, it is exceedingly black. //1-3//
Thus ends the fourth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those rays of his that go upward are indeed its upward honey-cells.
The secret instructions are indeed the honey-makers;
Brahman is the flower;
they are the immortal waters.
These secret instructions, indeed, brooded over this Brahman.
From it, thus brooded upon, glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food—its essence—were born.
That flowed forth;
it took refuge around the sun.
That indeed is this which appears as if quivering in the middle of the sun.

3. Now, "those rays of his which go upward," and so forth, is as explained previously. The secret, hidden, and esoteric instructions (*adeśāḥ*)—namely, the ritual procedures concerning the "door of the world" and other such matters, as well as the meditations (*upāsanāni*) pertaining to the constituent parts of ritual action—are the honey-makers. Brahman alone, because of its connection with the word [in this context], is the flower called Prāṇa. The rest is the same [as before].
This honey-like [light] within the sun appears as if it were agitated, as if it were moving, to one whose vision is concentrated. //1-3//
These, indeed, are the essence of essences;
for the Vedas are essences.
These are their essences;
indeed, these are the nectars of the nectars,
for the Vedas are nectar.
These are their nectars. (ChU 3.5.4)
These aforementioned specific forms, such as the red and so forth, are the "essences of essences.

Of which essences? He says: because the Vedas are the "essences" (*rasa*) since they are the distillate of the world, these specific forms—red and so forth—are the essences even of those [Vedas] that have entered into the state of ritual action; the meaning is that they are the ultimate core.
Likewise, the Vedas are indeed immortal among immortals because they are eternal; therefore, these forms of his, such as the red and others, are immortal.
The statement "the essence of essences," and so forth, is a praise of the action (karma), meaning that for one who performs this, the fruit consists of such distinguished immortals. //4//
Thus ends the fifth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
that which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon it with Agni as their mouth.
The gods indeed neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.1)
Regarding the phrase "of form":
no, because fame and so forth are apprehended by the ear and other senses;
fame is that which is grasped by the ear.
The form of light is that which is perceived by the eye.
The sense-faculty (*indriya*) is the capacity of the instrument, inferred from the effect of grasping its respective object.
Vigor (*vīrya*) is strength, the enthusiasm residing in the body, and the state of being endowed with vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Food is that which is consumed daily and serves to maintain the body; for every such essence is of this nature.
"Seeing whom all the gods are satisfied"—the meaning of "seeing and being satisfied" is that they experience it through their own senses and thereby attain satisfaction.
Being dependent upon the sun, they are free from the defects of the body and the senses, such as foul odors and the like. //1//
They enter into this very form; from this form they emerge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.2)
"Do they live upon immortality without making any effort? "No.
"How then?
"Having perceived this very form and realizing, 'Now is not our time for enjoyment,' they enter into it [the state of absorption] and remain indifferent."
When indeed the occasion for the enjoyment of that nectar arrives, then they rise up from this nectar—for the sake of enjoying the nectar; that is the meaning.
They rise up from this form, meaning they become full of enthusiasm.
For it is never seen in the world that those who lack enthusiasm, who do not exert themselves, and who are lazy, attain enjoyments. //2//
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Agni as his mouth. He enters into this very form.
It arises from this form. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.3)

Whoever knows this exactly as it has been described— that the bees are the Ṛg-veda hymns, the honey is the essence protected by them, the flowers are the rituals prescribed in the Ṛg-veda, that [essence] rests upon the sun, its red color, its location within the vessels of the rays extending toward the eastern direction,

its being enjoyed by the Vasus, and how the knower of this, having attained oneness with the Vasus, lives upon the food offered by Agni and finds satisfaction through mere sight at the time of his own enjoyment— [attains these things].
He too knows the rising at the departure of that time and the reclining; he experiences everything just like Vasu. //3//
As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so long does he attain the lordship and sovereignty of the Vasus.

It is now stated for how long that wise one lives upon that immortality: as long as the sun rises in the east, in the eastern direction, and sets in the west, in the western direction—for that long is the period of enjoyment for the Vasus; for that same length of time he becomes the sovereign ruler over the Vasus, meaning he attains self-rule (*svārājya*) and moves everywhere.
He does not remain like one situated in the lunar orb—a mere performer of ritual action, dependent on others, and serving as food for the gods;
rather, he attains sovereignty and the state of being his own master. //4//
Thus ends the sixth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for the second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it with Indra as their mouth.
The gods indeed neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.7.1)
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.7.2)
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Rudras, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Indra as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.
Now, as for that second immortality, the Rudras subsist upon it; the rest is the same [as previously stated]. 1–2–3.

As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long it rises in the south and sets in the north; for so long he attains the sovereignty and self-rule of the Rudras. As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that time—that is, for a double duration—it rises in the south and sets in the north; such is the period of enjoyment for the Rudras.
Thus ends the seventh section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which is the third nectar, the Ādityas subsist upon it with Varuṇa as their mouth.
The gods indeed neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.8.1)
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.8.2)
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Ādityas, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Varuṇa as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he rises up again.

"As long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice as long will it rise in the west and set in the east; for that long he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas. Thus ends the eighth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for that fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it with Soma as their mouth.
Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Maruts themselves, becomes satisfied by beholding this very nectar with Soma as his mouth.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.

"As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long it shall rise in the north and set in the south; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts. Thus ends the ninth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for that fifth nectar, the Sādhyas subsist upon it with Brahmā as their mouth.
Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink;
they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar.
They enter into this very form;
from this form they emerge.
He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Sādhyas, becomes satisfied by seeing this very nectar through the mouth of Brahman alone.
He enters into this very form;
from this form he emerges.

"As long as the sun rises in the north and sets in the south, twice as long it shall rise above and set below; for so long shall he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Sādhyas"—thus [it is said] in the tenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Likewise, it shall rise in the west, in the north, and above, and set in the opposite directions.
The view that the duration of time increases twofold for each successive direction from the east is not found in the Purāṇas.
For the authors of the Purāṇas have stated that the time of sunrise and sunset is equal for the Sun in the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma in the four directions,
because its circumambulation of Meru on the summit of Mānasottara is uniform.
Regarding this, the solution has been stated by the Teachers:
the evacuation of the cities, such as Amarāvatī and the others, occurs at intervals that double successively;

and what is called the "rising" of the sun is simply its coming within the range of vision for the living beings dwelling there, while its "setting" is the passing out of that range—it is not that rising and setting exist in an ultimate sense.

Furthermore, when there are no living beings dwelling there, even though [the sun] moves along that very same path toward them, it neither rises nor sets, because there is neither the occurrence of its coming within the range of vision nor the cessation thereof.

Likewise, the city of Saṃyamanī remains for twice as long as Amarāvatī; therefore, with respect to the living beings dwelling there, it is said—relative to our own perception—that it rises as if from the south and sets in the north.
The same application [of the rule] applies to the northern cities as well;
for all of them, Mount Meru lies to the north.
When the sun reaches its meridian in Amarāvatī, it is seen rising in Saṃyamanī; when it reaches its meridian there, it is seen rising in Vāruṇī.
Likewise, in the north,
because the clockwise circumambulation is identical,
for the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta— whose solar rays are blocked on all sides by the mountain ramparts— the sun appears to rise directly overhead and set directly below.

From the entry of the light of the sun through the opening at the summit of the mountain, it is inferred that the immortals—who subsist on the nectar of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas—possess double the potency of each successive level, as evidenced by the doubling of the duration of their enjoyment.
The rising, setting, and so forth of the gods, beginning with Rudra, are the same for the wise man. (1.4)
Thus ends the eighth, ninth, and tenth sections of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, having risen from there upwards, he neither rises nor sets; he remains alone in the center.
Regarding this, there is this verse: ChUp 3.11.1.
Having thus performed the favor toward living beings through their rising and setting— which is the cause for their enjoyment of the fruits of their own karma—

and having withdrawn those multitudes of living beings into himself upon the exhaustion of the enjoyment of those karmic fruits, he then, immediately after that time of favoring living beings, rises up within himself; and having risen, because of the absence of those living beings for whom he rises, he remains established in his own self.
"He neither rises nor sets; he is alone, without a second, partless, and remains established in his own self in the midst [of all].

There, a certain wise man—who shares the same conduct as Vasu and the others, who partakes in the enjoyment of the immortals such as Rohita, and who, having approached the Sun as his own self according to the aforementioned sequence, remained concentrated—having seen this mantra, arose and spoke it to another who questioned him."

"Since you have come from the world of Brahmā, does the sun there also, revolving through day and night, exhaust the lifespan of living beings just as it does here for us? Being thus questioned, he replied.
Regarding that which was asked and that which was stated there, this verse occurs; "This was spoken by the Yogi"—this is the statement of the Śruti.
"Verily, there it never sets,
nor does it ever rise."
"O gods, by that truth, may I not be separated from the Brahman. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.2)
"Indeed, that which you ask about does not exist there—in that world of Brahman from which I have come.
For the sun never sets nor ever rises there; at no time, in any place whatsoever, has the sun gone to its setting or risen from anywhere.
When told that the world of Brahman is devoid of rising and setting, he accepted this as if it were true.

"O gods, you are witnesses; hear the truthful word as spoken by me. By that, may I not be at variance with Brahman—that is, with the one whose nature is Brahman—nor may I be opposed to Him; the meaning is: may there be no failure for me to attain Brahman. //2//
Verily, for him the sun neither rises nor sets;
for him it is always day.
He who knows this secret doctrine of Brahman (brahmopaniṣad) in this manner.

The Śruti says that what he has spoken is true: "Verily, for this knower of Brahman as described, neither does the sun rise, nor does it set, nor does it go down; rather, for this knower of Brahman, it is always day, as it were, because of his being self-luminous—provided he knows this secret Upaniṣad of Brahman as it has been described."

Thus, by means of the underlying principle (*tantra*), one understands the triad beginning with the bamboo staff (*vaṃśa*) as well as its connection to the nectar (*amṛta*), and whatever else we have stated;
the meaning is that "one who knows thus" becomes the eternal, unborn Brahman, which cannot be delimited by the times of rising and setting. //3//
Brahmā told this to Prajāpati;
Prajāpati told it to Manu.
Manu [taught it] to his offspring.
And this very Brahman, a father spoke to his eldest son, Uddālaka Āruṇi.

Now, this very knowledge of the honey (madhu-jñāna), Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha told to Virāj Prajāpati; he [Virāj] told it to Manu; and Manu proclaimed it to the subjects beginning with Ikṣvāku. Thus [the text] praises the knowledge as having come down through a distinguished succession starting from Brahmā.
Moreover, this very knowledge of the honey, [which was taught] by a father to Uddālaka Āruṇi—
this indeed a father should declare as the Brahman to his eldest son, or to a worthy disciple.
This very thing which has been described should indeed be taught by one to another—namely, to an eldest son who is worthy of all affection, or to a beloved disciple who is a fit student. //5//

He should not tell it to anyone else at all—even if someone were to give him this earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, he would say: "This is indeed less than that. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.6)
One should not proclaim this to anyone else; only two "sacrificial seats" (tīrtha) are permitted among the many seats—such as that of the teacher and others—that one might encounter.

Why, then, is there this restriction of the seats? It is for the sake of the redemption of the knowledge: by giving wealth to the teacher in its full perfection along with enjoyments and clothing, that [wealth] is not its redemption, because even compared to that gift, this very gift of the Madhu-vidyā is superior.
The meaning is that it yields even more abundant fruit. The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of showing emphasis. //6//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The Gāyatrī indeed is all this that exists, whatever there is here.
Speech, indeed, is the Gāyatrī.
Speech, indeed, sings and protects this entire world that has come to be.

Since this knowledge of Brahman yields such extraordinary fruits, it must be explained by another method as well; therefore, the passage beginning with "The Gāyatrī indeed" is commenced. It is taught by way of the Gāyatrī because Brahman—which is devoid of all specific attributes and is to be understood through the negations "not this, not this"—is difficult to comprehend.
Although there are many meters (*chandas*), the Gāyatrī alone is selected as the gateway to the knowledge of Brahman because of its preeminence.

Due to its fetching of the Soma, its filling out the syllables of the other meters, and its pervading all the libations (*savana*) in the sacrifice, the Gāyatrī holds primacy. Furthermore, because the Brāhmaṇa has the Gāyatrī as his essence, he does not find anything more venerable than the Gāyatrī—just as one would not abandon a mother for anyone more venerable—even though Brahman is said to be the highest. Thus it is said: "Even Brahman [is not more venerable]."
Because extreme reverence for her is well known,
Brahman is spoken of by means of the Gāyatrī alone.
In the phrase "Gāyatrī indeed," the word "vai" (indeed) serves the purpose of emphasis.
All this that has come into being, whatever is stationary or moving, all that is indeed the Gāyatrī.

It might be argued that it is impossible for that which is merely a metrical measure (chandomātrā) to be all beings; therefore, [the text] declares Speech to be the cause of the Gāyatrī, saying, "This is a cow," "This is a horse," and so forth; and it protects and guards [beings] by saying, "Do not fear from this," "What fear has arisen for you? and so on.
One who is being turned back from fear on all sides shall be protected by speech.
For that which has become speech both sings and protects; thus it is Gāyatrī itself that both sings and protects, because it is non-different from speech.
It is called Gāyatrī because of singing (gāna) and because of protecting (trāṇa). //1//
That which is indeed that Gāyatrī is this very earth;
for upon this earth all this being is established.
One does not go beyond this very [truth]. ChUp 3.12.2.
That Gāyatrī which is characterized in this way and consists of the forms of all beings is indeed this very earth.
But how is it that this earth is Gāyatrī?
It is said [that she is called "Earth"] because of her connection with all beings.
How is there a connection with all beings?
Because on this earth everything—both the stationary and the moving—is established; it does not exceed nor does it go beyond this very earth. This is the meaning.

Just as the earth is connected to the elements through its singing and protecting, so too the earth is connected to the elements because it is the foundation of the elements; therefore, the Gāyatrī is the earth. //2//
That which is indeed this earth is truly this body of the person here;
for upon this [body] these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are established.
They do not go beyond this very [truth]. ChUp 3.12.3.

That which is indeed this earth is this very Gāyatrī; what is that? It is this body within this person—this aggregate of cause and effect—which exists while living, because the body is composed of earth.
How is it that the body has the nature of the Gāyatrī?
It is said: For in this [body], these vital breaths (prāṇas), which are denoted by the word "beings" (bhūta), are established.
Therefore, because it is the support for the vital breaths denoted by the word "beings," like the earth, the body is the Gāyatrī.
This is precisely because the vital breaths do not exceed this body. //3//
That which is the body in the person is indeed this very thing, namely the heart within this person;
for upon this, these vital breaths are established.
They do not go beyond this very thing. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.4)
Or rather, that which is the body in the person—that indeed is the Gāyatrī.
That which is this heart, called the lotus, within the middle of this person, is the Gāyatrī.
How so? He says: for in this [heart] these vital breaths (prāṇas) are established; therefore, like the body, the heart is the Gāyatrī.
And the vital breaths do not exceed this very [number]:
"The vital breath is indeed the father;
the vital breath is the mother."
Thus, according to the Vedic scripture, "not harming any living beings," the term *bhūta* refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). //4//

This is that Gāyatrī, which has four feet and is sixfold. This very thing is declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: tāvān asya mahimā tato jyāyāṃś ca pūruṣaḥ | pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripād asyāmṛtaṃ divi || Such is his greatness; yet the Puruṣa is even greater than that. All beings constitute one foot of him; his three-footed immortal self is in heaven. tripād ūrdhva ud ait puruṣaḥ pādo 'syehābhavat punaḥ | tato viṣvaṅ vy akrāmat sāśanānaśane abhi || With three quarters the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter of him remained here again. From there he strode out in all directions, pervading both the eating and the non-eating worlds. tasmād virāḍ ajāyata virājo adhi pūruṣaḥ | sa jāto atyaricyata paścād bhūmim atho puraḥ || From him Virāj was born; from Virāj the Puruṣa was born. Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before. yad puruṣeṇa haviṣā devā yajñam atanvata | vasanto 'syāsīd ājyaṃ grīṣma idhmaḥ śarad dhaviḥ || When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation, spring was its clarified butter, summer its fuel, and autumn its offering. taṃ yajñaṃ barhiṣi praukṣan puruṣaṃ jātam agrataḥ | tena devā ayajanta sādhyā ṛṣayaś ca ye || They sprinkled that Puruṣa, born in the beginning, upon the sacrificial grass. With him the gods sacrificed, as did the Sādhyas and the Ṛṣis. tasmād yajñāt sarvahutaḥ sambhṛtaṃ pṛṣadājyam | paśūṃs tāṃś cakre vāyavyān āraṇyān grāmyāś ca ye || From that sacrifice, in which everything was offered, the speckled butter was collected. He made those animals—those belonging to Vāyu, those of the forest, and those of the village. tasmād yajñāt sarvahuta ṛcaḥ sāmāni jajñire | chandāṃsi jajñire tasmād yajus tasmād ajāyata || From that sacrifice, in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born. The meters were born from it, and from it the Yajus-formulas were produced. tasmād aśvā ajāyanta ye ke cobhayādataḥ | gāvo ha jajñire tasmāt tasmāj jātā ajāvayaḥ || From it horses were born, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth. Cows were born from it, and from it goats and sheep were produced. yat puruṣaṃ vy adadhuḥ kati dhā vy akalpayan | mukhaṃ kim asya kau bāhū kā ūrū pādā ucyete || When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms? What were his thighs and feet called? brāhmaṇo 'sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ | ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata || The Brāhmaṇa became his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms. That which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born. candramā manaso jātaś cakṣoḥ sūryo ajāyata | śrotrād vāyuś ca prāṇaś ca mukhād agnir ajāyata || The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born. From his ear came wind and breath; from his mouth fire was born. nābhyā āsīd antarikṣaṃ śīrṣṇo dyauḥ sam avartata | padbhyāṃ bhūmir diśaḥ śrotrāt tathā lokām akalpayan || From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved. From his feet the earth, and from his ear the quarters; thus they fashioned the worlds. saptāsyāsan paridhayas triḥ sapta samidhaḥ kṛtāḥ | devā yad yajñaṃ tanvānā abadhnan puruṣaṃ paśum || Seven were his enclosing sticks; thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared, when the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound the Puruṣa as the victim. yajñena yajñam ayajanta devās tāni dharmāṇi prathamāny āsan | te ha nākaṃ mahimānaḥ sacanta yatra pūrve sādhyāḥ santi devāḥ || With the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the Sacrifice; these were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the height of heaven where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.

This very Gāyatrī, being of the nature of *chandas*, consists of four feet and six syllables per foot; yet, being sixfold—consisting of speech, the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, and the vital breath—it becomes sixfold.
Although speech and the vital breath were mentioned for other purposes, they are nonetheless modes of the Gāyatrī;
otherwise, it would be impossible to complete the number six.

Therefore, regarding this matter, this Brahman called Gāyatrī—which follows the Gāyatrī and has been explained by way of the Gāyatrī—is also proclaimed and revealed by a Ṛk verse, that is, by a mantra. //5//
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than that. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6)
Such is the greatness—the extent of the manifestation of power—of this entire Brahman known as Gāyatrī;

that is, the extent of the four-footed and sixfold modification of Brahman which was explained as "the foot is Gāyatrī. Therefore, greater than that—which is characterized by modification and consists merely of a verbal handle—is the Puruṣa, who is the supreme reality, non-modified, and all-pervading, because he fills [all things] within the city (puri) of the body.
And from the context of "resting":
"of this" [Brahman], "one quarter" (pāda) consists of all beings—fire, water, food, and so forth, including everything stationary and moving.
It has three quarters; thus, it is "three-quartered" (tripāt).
The meaning is that the immortal three-quarters called the Puruṣa is established in the "heaven"—that is, in its own self which is luminous—of the entire Gāyatrī-self. //6//
"That which is indeed called Brahman is this very space that is outside the person. That which is the space outside the person— " *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.12.7.
That which was indeed described as the three-quarter immortal Brahman by way of the Gāyatrī—this, verily, is that;
it is this very thing, namely, that well-known elemental space which is outside the person. That which was called the space outside the person is indeed this. //7//
This indeed is that which is this space within the person;
for that which is this space within the person is indeed that [space].
This indeed is that which is this space within the person in the body; for that which is the space within the person is [the same as] that [space]. //8//
This indeed is that which is this space within the heart;
it is full and unchanging.
He who knows this obtains full and unswerving prosperity.
"This indeed is that which is the space within the heart, inside the lotus of the heart.
How can there be a threefold division of the one existing space?
It is said: in the space that is the waking state, the object of the external senses, an abundance of suffering is observed."
Then, within the body—which serves as the locus for dreaming—there arises a much milder suffering for one who sees dreams.
However, when [the self] is situated in the space within the heart, it desires no object whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever.
Therefore, space, which consists in the cessation of all suffering, is the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Therefore, it is logical that even a single [element] is explained as having a threefold division.
Starting from the external person and proceeding inward until the contraction of space within the heart is for the purpose of praising the locus for the concentration of the mind.
Just as it is said: “Of all the three worlds, Kurukṣetra is distinguished.”
"Half of it is Kurukṣetra and half is Pṛthūdaka"—just so.
This very Brahman, known as the space within the heart, should be understood as full and all-pervading, not limited merely to the heart.

Although the mind is concentrated upon the space within the heart, it is "non-active" (apravarti)—meaning its nature is such that it does not proceed from anywhere nor toward anything—and it possesses the quality of imperishability.
Just as other beings are limited and subject to destruction, the space within the heart (*hārda nabhas*) is not so;

one attains full, non-transmigrating, and imperishable glory, power, and the fruit of the qualities—he who knows, that is, understands, Brahman as described here as possessing the qualities of fullness and non-transmigration, attains its very state even while living in this world—this is the meaning. //9//
Thus ends the twelfth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
indeed, there are five divine apertures of this very heart.
That which is its eastern opening is the out-breath;
that is the eye;
that is the sun.
One should meditate upon this as "splendor" and "food-eating.
He who knows this becomes splendid and an eater of food. (ChU 3.13.1)
With the words "Of that, indeed," etc., the text begins for the purpose of prescribing the qualities of the door-keepers and others as ancillaries to the meditation on Brahman known as Gāyatrī.
Just as in the world, door-keepers who have been brought under control through service to a king become the means for attaining the king, so it is here as well.
"Of that" (tasya) refers to the previously mentioned heart.

Immediately following this, there are five divine apertures (*devasuṣayaḥ*)—that is, five openings serving as gateways for attaining the heavenly world—which are guarded by the gods, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the sun; therefore they are called "divine apertures. Of this heart, which is the abode of the heavenly world, that eastern aperture—the opening or door facing east—is the *prāṇa*; [the person] exists therein by means of it.
That specific vital air (*vāyu-viśeṣa*) which moves through the gateway [of the mouth and nose] is called *prāṇa* because it breathes forward (*prāṅ aniti*).

The eye is connected with that very [vital air] and is non-different from it; likewise, that [eye] is the sun (*āditya*), according to the Vedic revelation: "The external *prāṇa* is indeed the sun. Thus, by way of being the support for the form of the eye, it resides in the heart.
For it is said in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "On what is that sun supported? On the eye," and so forth.
For the deity of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*) alone, together with the eye and the sun along with their respective substrates, is intended;
and it will be stated: "By saying 'Svāhā to Prāṇa,' one satisfies all this as an oblation.
Thus, that which is called *prāṇa* is Brahman, because it acts as the gatekeeper of the heavenly world.

One who desires to attain the heavenly world should meditate upon this splendor as the Sun in the form of the eye, and because the Sun is the source of food, one should meditate on that splendor as food. By these two qualities, he becomes possessed of splendor and an eater of food, free from disease; for him who knows thus, this is the fruit of those qualities.
The gatekeeper, when brought under control through worship, becomes the cause for attaining the heavenly world; this is the primary fruit. //1//
Now, that which is his southern cavity is the *vyāna* breath;
that is the sense of hearing.
That is the moon.
One should meditate upon it as "Prosperity" and "Fame.
He who knows this becomes prosperous and famous. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.2)

Now, that which is its southern aperture, the specific wind situated therein, performing vigorous action by either separating or joining the prāṇa and apāna, is the vyāna; and the sense organ of hearing is likewise connected to it, as is that moon, according to the Vedic scripture:
"The quarters and the moon were created by the ear."

Together with their substrates, as before, this is *śrī* (prosperity) and *vibhūti* (power). Because they are the causes of knowledge through the ear and the moon, they possess the quality of *śrī*. Furthermore, for one who possesses knowledge, fame (*yaśas*)—that is, renown—arises; thus, because they are the cause of fame, they possess the quality of *yaśas*. One should meditate upon them by means of these two qualities, and so forth, as previously explained. //2//
Now, that which is its western cavity is the apāna;
that is speech.
That is Agni.
One should meditate upon this as spiritual luster and food. He who knows this becomes possessed of spiritual luster and becomes an eater of food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.3)

Now, that which is his western cavity facing backward, the specific vital air located there, is called *apāna* because it moves downward, carrying away urine, feces, and so forth; it is likewise speech.
Because of its connection with that [speech], the fire is also like that; this is *brahmavarcasa*, the splendor resulting from the performance of duties and the study of the Vedas.
Because it is connected with fire, the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) has its function fulfilled;
because it is the cause for the consumption of food, the *apāna* (downward breath) possesses the quality of being "eatable" (*annādya*).
The rest is the same. //3//
Now,
that which is its northern cavity is the Samāna;
that is the mind.
That is Parjanya.
One should meditate upon this as both fame and splendor.
He who knows this becomes famous and splendid.
Now, that which is its northern cavity—the opening situated in the north—is the specific vital air called *samāna*, because it carries what is eaten and drunk evenly (*samaṃ nayati*).

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) connected to that is the mind (*manas*); that is the deity Parjanya, whose nature is rain, and the waters have Parjanya as their cause, according to the Vedic scripture: "By the mind were created the waters and Varuṇa."
This is also fame (*kīrti*);
because mental cognition is the cause of fame,
and fame is the state of being well-known by others regarding oneself.
Fame (*yaśas*) is renown, which is cognizable by one's own sense organs.
Prosperity (*vyuṣṭi*) is radiance, the loveliness residing in the body. Furthermore, it is called "fame" (*kīrti*) because it arises from renown (*kīrti*).
The rest is the same. //4//
Now, that which is its upper cavity is the *udāna*;
it is Vāyu.
That is space.
One should meditate upon it as "vital power" (ojas) and "majesty" (mahaḥ).
He who knows this becomes possessed of vital power and majesty. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.5)

Now, that which is its upper opening is the *udāna* [breath]; it moves upward starting from the feet for the purpose of ascending and performing actions of excellence, hence it is called *udāna*. It is the wind (*vāyu*), and its support is space (*ākāśa*). Because these two—wind and space—are the cause of vigor (*ojas*), they are "vigor" (*ojas*);
and because of their greatness, they are "the Great One" (*mahaḥ*).
The rest is the same. //5//

These, indeed, are the five gatekeepers of the heavenly world, the attendants of Brahman. He who knows these five attendants of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world, in his family a hero is born.
He who knows these five persons of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world attains the heavenly world.

These aforementioned five, connected to the five apertures, are the five persons of the Brahman within the heart, like royal officers stationed at the gates; they are the gatekeepers of the heavenly world within the heart.
