For by these—the eye, ear, speech, mind, and breath—when they are directed outward, the doors to the attainment of the Brahman within the heart are obstructed.
For this is directly perceived: because the senses have not been conquered and the mind has grown attached to false external objects, it does not abide in the Brahman within the heart.
Therefore, what was said is true: these five persons of Brahman are the gatekeepers of heaven.
Consequently, he who knows and thus meditates upon these gatekeepers of the heavenly world as characterized by the aforementioned qualities, through that meditation—

He brings them under his control through worship, just as one might subdue the gatekeepers at a king’s palace; having brought them under his control, he proceeds unimpeded to the heavenly world, just as one approaches a king who is the Brahman within the heart.
Furthermore, in the family of this knower, a heroic son is born, due to his service to heroic persons.
Through the removal of that [impurity], it serves as the cause for engaging in the meditation on Brahman;
and since that leads, through a traditional succession, to the attainment of the heavenly world, the attainment of the heavenly world alone is the single fruit. //6//

Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme— this indeed is that light which is within this person here.

His vision is this: that wherein one perceives warmth through touch within this body. His hearing is this: that when one covers his ears, he hears as it were a roar, as it were a tumult, as of a blazing fire.
One should venerate this as both seen and heard.
He who knows this becomes pleasing to the sight and renowned; he who knows this becomes pleasing to the sight and renowned. ChUp 3.13.7.
Now, when that wise man attains the heavenly world through the service of heroic persons,

that which was stated in the verse, “Three quarters of him are the immortal in heaven,” must be brought within the range of the senses of sight and hearing by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), just as fire and other things are inferred by means of smoke and other marks.
For in this way, there would be a firm conviction regarding the matter as it has been stated, namely, "this is exactly so," and a certainty through [the realization of] non-difference.
Therefore, he says: "That which is beyond (paraḥ) this heaven (amuṣmāt divaḥ)," where the masculine gender has been changed [to neuter].
The light shines.
Because it is self-luminous and eternally radiant, it is said to "shine" as if it were shining,
since a radiance characterized by combustion— such as that of fire and the like— is impossible [in its case].
The explanation of the phrase "on all sides behind" (*viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*) is "behind everything" (*sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu*);
the meaning is "above *saṃsāra*.
For indeed, *saṃsāra* itself is everything.
Because it is non-transmigratory, unitary, and undifferentiated;

and in order to eliminate the suspicion that this might be a *tatpuruṣa* compound (meaning "among the unsurpassed"), he says "in the highest worlds," referring to Satyaloka and so forth. It is called "in the highest worlds" because the Supreme Lord, who resides within the effects such as Hiraṇyagarbha, is in close proximity there.
Or rather, this very thing is that which is the light within this person; it is perceived through the internal organ by means of the signs of heat and sound, which are grasped by the ear.
As for that which is grasped by the skin in the form of touch, that too is [perceived] by the eye alone, because the skin provides a firm basis for cognition.
And because color and touch are invariably concomitant, how is it that this mark of light comes within the range of the sense of touch? To this he says:
"When," that is, at which time.
The word "this" (*etad*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
In this body, by touching—that is, by means of contact—one perceives warmth, which is the state of hot touch coexisting with form.

For that warmth is the infallible mark (*liṅga*) of the light of the conscious Self (*caitanyātmajyotis*) which has entered the body for the purpose of differentiating name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*).
For heat does not deviate from a living self; indeed, it is known that "one who is warm shall live, one who is cold shall die.
Furthermore, at the time of death, [the text] states, "the fire [goes] into the highest deity," because it is accepted that [the self] becomes non-distinct from the Supreme.
Therefore, heat is an uncommon mark [of the self], just as smoke is of fire.
Therefore, this vision of that supreme [Self] is as if a direct perception; the meaning is that it is the means for perceiving it.
Likewise, this hearing of that light is also said to be the means for hearing it.

When—*yatra* meaning when—the person desires to hear (*śuśrūṣati*), that is, wishes to listen to the indicative mark of the light, then he covers his ears; *etat* (this) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
"Having grasped and covered"—the meaning is having enveloped [the ears] with the fingers—one hears a "ninada," like the roar of a chariot;

one hears a sound like the bellowing of a bull, and just as one hears the sound of a fire burning outside, so too one hears a sound within the body. Since this light has the characteristics of being both seen and heard, one should meditate upon it as "seen and heard."
Likewise, from meditating upon it, one becomes *cakṣuṣya* (pleasing to the sight) and *darśanīya* (beautiful to behold), as well as *śruta* (learned) and *viśruta* (famous).
The fruit that results from meditating on its quality of touch (*sparśa*) is realized in the form of being *cakṣuṣya*;
this is because color (*rūpa*) and touch (*sparśa*) always coexist.
And because being beautiful to behold is desirable,
in this way the fruit of knowledge would be logically established, but not through the possession of qualities such as softness to the touch.
He who knows these two aforementioned qualities in this manner [attains that fruit].
But the attainment of the heavenly world is said to be the unseen fruit;
the repetition [of the word] is for the sake of emphasis. //7//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"Indeed, all this is Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That (taj-jalān). One should meditate upon it with a tranquil mind."
Now, indeed, a person consists of resolve; as is his resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here.
Therefore, let him form a resolve.

ChUpBh_3,14.1: Furthermore, desiring to enjoin the meditation upon that very same three-quarter immortal Brahman—which possesses infinite qualities, infinite powers, and is to be meditated upon in its many diverse forms—as possessing specific qualities and powers, [the author] says: "All this, indeed...
The particle *khalu* is used for the purpose of poetic ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*).

This world, which is modified by name and form and is the object of perception and other means of knowledge, has Brahman as its cause; it is called *brahma* because it is the most fully grown (*vṛddhatama*).
To the question, "How is everything Brahman?", he says: *tajjalān*.
Everything has arisen from that Brahman through the sequence of fire, water, and food;
therefore, it is *tajja* (born from That).
Likewise, by that very same process of birth, through the reverse order, it dissolves into that very Brahman and merges with it as its own self; thus it is "tal-laya" (dissolution into That).
Likewise, during that very period of maintenance, it breathes and moves;
thus, through its identity with Brahman, it remains undifferentiated across the three periods of time, because it is not perceived apart from That.
Therefore, this very world is that [Brahman]; and how it is that this [world] is indeed that one, non-dual reality, we shall explain in detail in the sixth chapter. And because all this is Brahman,

Therefore, being peaceful—free from defects such as passion and hatred—and self-controlled, one should meditate upon all that is Brahman through the qualities about to be described. How should one meditate? One should perform *kratu*; *kratu* is resolve, determination, or an unwavering conviction that "it is exactly thus and not otherwise. One should perform that *kratu*, which is connected with the word "meditate" (*upāsīta*) mentioned earlier.

Furthermore, what purpose is to be served by the *kr̥t-karaṇa* (the instrument for performing the sacrifice), or how is the sacrifice to be performed? And how is it that the *kr̥t-karaṇa* is the means for accomplishing the intended goal? It is for the sake of explaining this matter that the passage beginning with "atha" (now) is provided.
Here, the word "atha khalu" (now indeed) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Because the person— the living self— is composed of resolve, consists primarily of resolve,

and is of the nature of determination; therefore, according to his resolve, according to what kind of resolve he has, according to his determination and what sort of conviction he holds while living here in this world, even so does he become after departing from and dying after this body.
The meaning is that it becomes characterized by a fruit corresponding to the ritual act (*kratu*).
For this is indeed seen from scripture:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when he leaves the body at the end," and so forth.
Since this systematic arrangement is thus seen in the scriptures, one who knows this should perform the sacrifice exactly as we shall describe it.
Because a result corresponding to the sacrifice is established through the authority of the scriptures, that sacrifice must be performed. //1//

Consisting of mind, having vital breath for its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, possessing all works, all desires, all odors, and all tastes; he has pervaded all this, yet is speechless and indifferent.
How so?

"Consisting of mind" means having mind as its primary constituent. That by which one thinks is the mind; it becomes engaged with objects through its own function, and [the self] consists of that mind.
Thus, it appears as if engaged in activity and yet, for the most part, appears as if withdrawn from it.
For this very reason, it has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its body; "prāṇa" here refers to the subtle body (*liṅgātman*), which is a fusion of the two powers of cognition and action.
As the Śruti declares: "That which is indeed *prāṇa* is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that which is wisdom is *prāṇa*."

He whose body is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is "one whose body is the vital breath" (*prāṇaśarīra*). This is also supported by another scriptural passage: "Consisting of mind, he is the leader of the body consisting of the vital breath. He is "whose form is light" (*bhārūpa*).
He whose form is light—that is, whose nature is characterized by consciousness—is "consisting of light" (bhārūpa).
He is "one whose volitions are true" (satyasaṅkalpa):
he whose volitions (saṅkalpas) are true, that is, non-false, is this one whose volitions are true.
The meaning is that the volition of the Lord is not of uncertain fruit, as is the case with those in saṃsāra.
Because it is obstructed by "untruth"—that is, by the cause of false results—the volition has false results.
As he will say: "For they are obstructed by untruth."
"Ākāśātmā":
he whose self (ātman), that is, whose essential nature (svarūpa), is like space (ākāśa), is Ākāśātmā.
Pervasiveness, subtlety, and the absence of form and so forth are the reasons for the Lord's similarity to space.
"Performing all actions":
since the entire universe (*viśva*) is created by that Lord, the whole world is his action; thus he is "the performer of all actions.
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "For he is the creator of all."

"Having all desires" (*sarvakāma*): he is one for whom all desires are free from fault; thus, he is "having all desires. This is according to the Smṛti: "I am desire among beings that is not contrary to Dharma."

Surely, because of the statement "I am Kāma," a *bahuvrīhi* compound is intended here; thus, the meaning of the Smṛti should be stated as "I am Kāma. [Likewise,] "possessing all fragrances" (*sarvagandha*):
he for whom all fragrances are sources of pleasure is this one who possesses all fragrances.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): "Fragrance on earth is meritorious.
Likewise, tastes are also to be understood in the same way, since it is heard in scripture that the perception of unmeritorious fragrance and taste is caused by a connection with evil:
"Therefore, by means of that [nose], one smells both the pleasant-smelling and the foul-smelling."
For it is stated in the Śruti: "He is indeed pierced by evil in these [bodies].
Moreover, there can be no association with evil for the Lord, because defects such as ignorance (avidyā) are impossible in His case.

This entire world is *abhyāttaḥ*, meaning pervaded; the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the active sense of the root *at*, which means "to pervade. Likewise, it is called *vāk* because one speaks by means of it; or rather, *vāk* is simply speech itself.
The word *vāk* is derived from the root *vac* with the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "an instrument of speech.
One who possesses that is *vākī*; one who does not possess it is *na-vākī*.
Furthermore, the negation of speech here is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Since the Lord possesses the hearing of smells, tastes, and so forth, the sense organs such as the nose would necessarily be obtained for the purpose of perceiving odors and the like;
therefore, they are negated by the negation of speech.
This is based on the wording of the mantra: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears. Etc.
Disrespect is a lack of reverence.
For reverence would indeed exist for one who has not attained what is to be attained and whose desires are unfulfilled;
but for the Lord, who has fulfilled all desires and is eternally satisfied, there is no reverence whatsoever. //2//
"This is my Self within the heart, smaller than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet.
This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds."

This Self of mine, endowed with the qualities described above, exists within my heart—that is, inside the lotus of the heart. It is subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, and so forth; this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating its extreme minuteness.

Having mentioned that it is subtler than *śyāmāka* grain or *śyāmāka* rice—thereby suggesting a limited dimension—one might suspect it possesses the dimension of an atom; therefore, to preclude that, he begins with: "This Self of mine within the heart is greater than the earth," and so on.
And by showing its greatness relative to a greater magnitude, he demonstrates its infinite magnitude. //3//
He contains all works, possesses all desires, has all fragrances, has all tastes; he pervades this entire world, is beyond speech, and is free from concern.
This is my Self within the heart.
"This is Brahman;
having departed from here, I shall attain this"—he who has such a conviction certainly has no doubt.
Thus said Śāṇḍilya, yes, Śāṇḍilya. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4)

By the passage beginning with "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and ending with "greater than these worlds," it might be argued that the Lord, characterized by the aforementioned qualities, is the object of meditation, but not as one qualified by those qualities; for just as when it is said, "Bring the king's man" or "Bring the one possessing brindled cows," one does not exert oneself to bring the qualifying attribute as well, so it would be here too. To preclude this, the text repeats the description with "all works" (*sarvakarma*) and so forth.
Therefore, the Lord alone, characterized by qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), is to be meditated upon.

For this very reason, unlike in the sixth and seventh chapters where [the teacher] consecrates [the disciple] to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) with such [identifications] as "That thou art" or "All this is indeed the Self," he does not do so here. This is evident from the indicative mark: "This is my Self; this is Brahman; from this world, I shall attain Him. Thus, it is not the inner individual self (*pratyagātman*) that is denoted by the word "Self" here.
Because the genitive case in "mameti" (of me) conveys the sense of a relationship, and because in "etam abhisambhavitāsmi" (I shall attain him) there is a designation of both object and agent;
[one might object]: "But does not the phrase 'atha sampatsye' (then I shall become united) in the sixth chapter show that the union with Being is separated by another time?
No, for that passage has the purpose of explaining the persistence of the remainder of the impressions of the commenced [life], and it does not have the meaning of being separated by another time.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting the meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Even though the word *ātman* has the sense of the inner self (*pratyak*), and although it is stated in the context of "All this, indeed, is Brahman" that "This is my Self within the heart; this is Brahman," nevertheless, without entirely abandoning even a slight sense of internal concealment, [the text speaks of] this Self from here...
It was said: "Having departed from this body, I shall attain [that state].

For one who knows thus, there is the thought, "I shall become the Self according to the form of my resolve (*kratu*). Indeed, it would be so; truly, it would be thus: "I shall be so after departing," or "I shall not be so. And there is no doubt regarding this matter, namely, the connection between the resolve and its fruit.
"The wise man attains lordship in that very manner"—this is what the sage named Śāṇḍilya, it is said, declared.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. //4//
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. The treasure-chest has the intermediate space for its interior and the earth for its base; it never decays.
For its corners are the directions, and the sky is its upper opening;
this is that treasure-chest, the container of wealth, in which this entire universe is supported.
It has been stated that "a hero is born in his family.
However, the mere birth of a hero is not sufficient for the protection of the father;
for another Vedic text declares: "Therefore, they say a son who has been properly instructed is what wins the world."

Therefore, for the purpose of explaining how that long life might be possible, the commencement of the description of the *kośa* (sheath) is made. It was not mentioned immediately after [the previous topic] due to the preoccupation with the more venerable forms of consciousness; it is now commenced right here: "He whose belly is the intermediate space"—that is, he whose internal cavity is the atmosphere; this is the *kośa*. It is called a *kośa* because of its similarity to a sheath in many respects.
And it has the earth as its base (*bhūmibudhna*)—meaning that whose root (*budhna*) or foundation is the earth. It does not decay nor perish, because it consists of the three worlds.
For he (the Self) abides for the duration of a thousand yugas;

all the directions are its sides and corners. The sky is the upper opening of this casket, situated above. This aforementioned casket is "the repository of wealth" (vasudhāna), because in it is deposited (dhīyate) the "wealth" (vasu)—namely, the fruits of the actions of living beings. Thus, it is called vasudhāna.

Within which [Brahman] this entire universe—the fruits of the actions of all living beings along with their means—is contained; that is to say, it is supported, dependent, and situated therein, as perceived by direct perception and other means of valid cognition. //1//
Of that [sacrificial ladle], the eastern direction is named Juhū;
the southern direction is named Sahamānā.
The western quarter is named Rājñī; the northern quarter is named Subhūtā;
their calf is Vāyu.
He who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters does not weep for the loss of a son. I, knowing this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters,
shall not weep for the loss of a son.

Of this [body], the eastern direction is its eastern part, named *juhū*; it is called *juhū* because ritualists, facing east, offer oblations (*juhvati*) in that direction. The southern direction is named *sahamānā*; it is called *sahamānā* because living beings in the city of Yama endure (*sahante*) the fruits of their evil deeds in that direction.
Likewise, the western direction is named *rājñī*; it is *rājñī* because it is presided over by King Varuṇa, or because of the connection with the glow of twilight.
The northern direction is called *Subhūtā* because it is presided over by prosperous lords such as Īśvara, Kubera, and others; thus it is named Subhūtā.
The wind belonging to those directions is the calf, because the wind is born from the directions, as seen in such expressions as "the east wind" (*purovāta*).

Whoever, desiring long life for his son, knows Vāyu—possessing the qualities described above—as the calf of the quarters and as immortality, he does not weep the "son's weeping," that is, he does not weep on account of his son; the meaning is that his son does not die.

Since this knowledge concerning the treasure-chest and the calf of the quarters is thus distinguished, therefore I, desiring life for my son, know and understand this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters in this manner.
Therefore, do not weep the "son's cry"; do not weep on account of the death of a son.
The meaning is: let there be no such thing as the "son's cry" for me. //2//
I enter the uninjured treasure-chest with this, with this, with this; I enter the vital breath with this, with this, with this.
I take refuge in Bhūḥ by means of this, this, and this; I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ by means of this, this, and this;
I take refuge in Svaḥ by means of this, this, and this.
"I take refuge in the unharmed, indestructible treasure-chest as described; I have taken refuge for the sake of my son's life.
He pronounces his son's name three times: "by this one, by that one, by that one.
Likewise, "I take refuge in Prāṇa: by this one, by that one, by that one."

"I take refuge in *bhūḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such; I take refuge in *svaḥ* with such-and-such, such-and-such, and such-and-such"—in every instance, he utters "I take refuge" three times, repeating it again and again. (3)
As for what I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa":
Prāṇa indeed is all this being that exists here, whatever there may be.
You have indeed attained that very thing.
As for what I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," that was introduced for the sake of explanation:
Prāṇa indeed is all this being, which is this world. As he will say later: "Or as the spokes are fixed in the hub."
Therefore, by that very surrender of my life-breath, I attained—that is, I became one who has sought refuge in—all of that reality. //4//
3.15.5 Now, when I said, "I take refuge in bhūḥ," I thereby said, "I take refuge in the earth, I take refuge in the intermediate space, I take refuge in the sky. //5//
Likewise, when I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant that I take refuge in the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ. //5//
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," that was indeed saying: "I take refuge in Agni, I take refuge in Vāyu, I take refuge in Āditya. (ChUp 3.15.6)
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I meant that I take refuge in Agni and the other deities.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in the light," I meant this: "I take refuge in the Ṛgveda, I take refuge in the Yajurveda, I take refuge in the Sāmaveda. Thus did I speak.
Now, as for what I said, "I enter into the light" (*svaḥ prapadye*), I meant that I enter into the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas.

Thereafter, one should mutter the mantras; having meditated correctly upon the previously mentioned undecaying chest together with its calves in the form of the quarters, the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. //7//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Man, indeed, is the sacrifice.
Those twenty-four years of his constitute the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*).
The *gāyatrī* meter consists of twenty-four syllables;
the morning libation belongs to the *gāyatrī*.
The Vasus are dependent upon him;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the Vasus,
for they cause all this to dwell.

The meditation on the life-span of the son and the recitation [of the mantra] have been explained. Now, in order to secure a long life for oneself, the text prescribes this meditation and recitation, stating: "For only by living does one become united with the fruits such as sons and so forth, and not otherwise. Therefore, one should accomplish the self as a sacrifice. "Puruṣaḥ puruṣaḥ" refers to the person characterized by life—the aggregate of causes and effects (the body and organs) as it is commonly known.
The word *eva* (or *vāva*) has the sense of restriction;
the meaning is that the person alone is the sacrifice.
For in this way, he accomplishes the nature of the sacrifice through commonalities.
How so?
Those twenty-four years of that person’s lifespan constitute the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) of the sacrifice.

By what commonality? He says: the *gāyatrī* metre consists of twenty-four syllables; the morning extraction (*prātaḥsavana*) of the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*) indeed possesses the *gāyatrī* metre.
Therefore, a person endowed with a twenty-four-year lifespan is identical to the morning extraction. Consequently, by virtue of this similarity to the ritual sacrifice, it is called a "sacrifice."

Similarly, for the two subsequent periods of life as well, the fulfillment of the two *savanas* (pressings) should be stated by virtue of the commonality in the number of syllables of the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters.

Furthermore, of this *puruṣayajña* (human sacrifice), the *prātaḥsavana* (morning pressing) has the Vasus as its presiding deities (*anvāyatta*), meaning they follow it as its masters by virtue of being the deities of the *savana*, just as in the case of the ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*).

Since it might be thought that in the "sacrifice of the person" (puruṣayajña), as in the "sacrifice of ritual injunction" (vidhiyajña), the Vasus—the gods beginning with Agni—are also included, he therefore specifies: "The Vasus are indeed the vital breaths," namely speech and the others, as well as the winds.
For it is because these [breaths] cause this entire collection of living beings, beginning with man, to dwell;
for when the vital breaths dwell in the body, all this dwells therein, and not otherwise.
Thus, because of their dwelling and their latent impressions, they are called the Vasus. //1//
If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him,
he should say: "O Prāṇas, O Vasus, extend this morning libation of mine to the midday libation, so that I, the sacrifice, may not be lost in the midst of the Prāṇas and the Vasus."
Having risen from there, he indeed becomes free from disease.

If, when this age has been completed by the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) of the sacrifice, some cause for fear of death such as disease or the like should afflict him and produce suffering, then that person who has accomplished the sacrifice, regarding himself as the sacrifice, should speak— that is, he should mutter— this mantra: "O Prāṇas, O Vasus, this morning libation of mine..."
"Let my sacrifice proceed; extend it through the midday pressing"—the meaning is: "make it continuous, unified, and joined with the midday pressing and with life.
"May I, the sacrifice, not be lost among you—the Prāṇas and the Vasus who are masters of the morning pressing"—the meaning is: "may I not perish, may I not be cut off."
The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the mantra.
By means of that recitation and meditation, he rises up—that is, emerges—from that affliction;
having emerged and being liberated, he indeed becomes free from disease and free from affliction. //2//
Now, those forty-four years constitute the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*);
the *triṣṭubh* meter consists of forty-four syllables.
The midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh;
the Rudras are connected with it.
The Rudras are indeed the vital breaths.
For these indeed cause all this to weep.
Now, the passage beginning with "the forty-four years" is the same as before.

They are called *rudra*s because they weep (*rudanti*) and cause others to weep; for they are cruel, since they cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to perish in the middle age, and thus they are *rudra*s. //3//

If, at this stage of life, something should afflict him, he should say: "O Prāṇas, O Rudras, extend for me this midday pressing and the third pressing, so that the sacrifice may not be lost in the midst of you, the Prāṇas and Rudras."
Having risen from there, he indeed becomes free from disease.
Now, those forty-eight years constitute the third pressing;
the Jagatī meter consists of forty-eight syllables,
and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī.
The Ādityas are dependent upon him;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the Ādityas,
for they take up all this.
If, at this age, anything should afflict him, he should say:
"O Prāṇas, O Ādityas, extend this third pressing of mine along with my life; may I not be deprived of the sacrifice in the midst of the Prāṇas and the Ādityas.
He rises from that very affliction and indeed becomes free from disease.

Likewise, the Ādityas are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). For they take up this collection of sound and other objects; therefore they are called Ādityas. "The third pressing is life"—the meaning is that [the sacrificers] should complete and sustain the sacrifice for one hundred and sixteen years. The rest is the same. (ChU Bh 3.16.4–6)
Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya used to say:
"Why do you afflict me with this, I who shall not depart because of it?"
He lived for one hundred and sixteen years;
he who knows this lives for one hundred and sixteen years.

Showing that knowledge, when certain, leads to its fruit, [the text] cites this illustration: "The seer of the sacrifice (yajñadarśana), namely the one named Mahidāsa, the son of Itarā (Aitareya), said:
'Why, O fever (roga), do you afflict me? Since I, who am the sacrifice, shall not perish—that is, I shall not die—on account of this affliction caused by you, your labor is therefore in vain.'"
This is the meaning.
The phrase "he spoke thus" is to be connected with what precedes.
Having reached such a certainty, he lived for one hundred and sixteen years.
Anyone else who has such a conviction also lives for one hundred and sixteen years; that is to say, he who knows and understands the accomplishment of the sacrifice as it has been described. //7//
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When he feels hunger, when he feels thirst, and when he does not find pleasure— these are his initiatory rites (dīkṣā).

The general reference to sacrifice beginning with "when he desires to eat" and so forth is connected with the preceding [section] concerning the person (*puruṣa*). "When he desires to eat" means he wishes to eat; likewise, "he thirsts" means he wishes to drink.

When he does not find delight because of the non-attainment of desired objects and the like, and when he experiences such suffering, those are his initiations (dīkṣās), due to the commonality of suffering with that of the ritual sacrifice (vidhi-yajña). //1//
Then, what he eats, what he drinks, and what he enjoys— that he performs with the Upasads.
Now, when he eats, drinks, and experiences pleasure through union with desired objects and the like, he attains similarity to the *upasad* rites.

For the *upasad* rites possess a happiness characterized by the vow of subsisting on milk; furthermore, because the days of eating little are near, there is a sense of relief (*praśvāsa*). Thus, there is a commonality between eating and the other acts and the *upasad* rites. //2//
Now,
when he laughs, when he eats, and when he engages in sexual intercourse, he goes by means of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns.
Now, when one laughs, eats, chews, or engages in sexual intercourse, he attains equality with those very acts through the commonality of possessing sound. //3//
Now, as for austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness— these are its sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
Now, as for austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness—these are its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), because they share the common quality of promoting the growth of dharma. //4//
Therefore they say,
"He will procreate" or "He has procreated"; this is merely his being born again.
Death itself is the final purificatory bath.

And because the sacrifice is a person, therefore when his mother gives birth to him, others say of his mother, "She will press [the Soma]"; and when she has given birth, they say, "Pūrṇikā has pressed it. Just as in the case of a ritual sacrifice, one says, "Devadatta will press the Soma," or "Yajñadatta has pressed the Soma."
Therefore, either because of the commonality of the word, the person is the sacrifice;

for that which is called the "person-sacrifice" has the commonality of being produced again, as indicated by the verbal connection "he will beget" (*soṣyati*) and "he begot" (*asoṣṭa*), just like a ritual sacrifice (*vidhiyajña*).
Furthermore, death itself is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of this person-sacrifice, due to the commonality of being its conclusion. //5//
Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught this to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, said:
"He indeed became free from thirst."

At the time of his end, he should perform these three [rites], reciting: "Thou art the imperishable; thou art the unswerving; thou art sharpened by life. Regarding this, there are these two verses: akṣitam asy acyutam asi prāṇasaṃśitam asi | prāṇasyedaṃ vaśe sarvaṃ tvayi sarvam idaṃ jagat || mā chitthā mā vyathiṣṭhāḥ śāntā viśvābhiṣṭhā āpaḥ | drupadaṃ manasā dhyāyan mūrdhānaṃ paryāvartaye || Thou art the imperishable; thou art the unswerving; thou art sharpened by life. All this is under the control of life; all this world is in thee. Do not be cut off; do not tremble; the waters are peaceful, supporting all. Meditating on the pillar with the mind, I turn back my head.

Now, this very vision of the sacrifice was told by one named Ghora, by lineage Āṅgirasa, to his disciple Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī; having said, "This triad," and so forth—as related in the distant [preceding] passage—he, even after hearing this vision, remained as thirsty for other forms of knowledge as before.

Thus, by showing that this particular knowledge caused the cessation of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī's thirst for other sciences, the text praises this knowledge of the Person as Sacrifice (puruṣayajñavidyā).

Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught this knowledge to Kṛṣṇa, said: "What did he say? To that he replies: One who knows the sacrifice as described above, at the time of departure—that is, at the moment of death—should resort to these three mantras; the meaning is that he should recite them. What is that? "Thou art the imperishable" (*akṣitam*), meaning undecaying or uninjured; this is one Yajus-mantra. By its power, he speaks of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) residing in the sun, having unified it [with the Self]. Likewise, he says of that very same [Self]: "Thou art the unfallen" (*acyutam*), meaning not fallen from its own nature; this is the second Yajus-mantra.

"Prāṇasaṃśitam" means that which is sharpened by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and "saṃśitam" means properly refined and subtle; "tat tvam asi" is the third Yajus formula. In this regard, there are two verses (*ṛc*) intended for the praise of knowledge, not for the purpose of recitation (*japa*), because that would contradict the prescription to "attain the triad."
For in that case, there would be a number of five. //6//
From the beginning, from the ancient seed;
we have risen up out of the darkness.
"Beholding the light above, beholding the sun above, we have gone to the god among the gods, Sūrya, the highest light—the highest light. Thus [he said]. ChUp 3.17.7.
In the word *āditya*, the letter *t* is an unnecessary suffix (*anubandha*) of the vowel *ā*, as is the particle *iti*.
"Of the ancient" means of that which is long-standing or primordial.
They behold the light—the illumination—of the cause, the seed-like world designated as *Sat*.

The word "ā" (on) has its grammatical suffix elided and is connected with the verb "paśyanti" (they see). What light do they see? It is that light of Brahman which pervades everything, like the day recurring day after day.

The meaning is that those who know Brahman, whose eyes have turned away [from sense objects] and whose inner organs (antaḥkaraṇa) have been purified by the means of practice such as celibacy (brahmacarya), perceive the Light on all sides.
The expression "paraḥ param" involves a change of gender (liṅgavyatyaya), because the Light is the supreme goal.
That which is kindled and shines in the sky—that which possesses radiance—abiding within that Brahman;
by which light Savitṛ is ignited and burns, the moon shines, lightning flashes, and the hosts of planets and stars gleam.
Furthermore, another seer of mantras, beholding the aforementioned light, has said:
"Up from darkness"—that is, beyond that which is characterized by ignorance;
or rather, "up from darkness," meaning we have risen up while beholding that supreme light situated in the sun which removes darkness.
That light is *svaḥ*—our own, abiding within our hearts.
And that is the one light abiding in the sun.
Having seen it—which is higher, more excellent, or more elevated in comparison to another light—they say, "We have risen up. To whom have we risen? He says: [to the world of heaven].

We have gone forth toward the shining god among all the gods, the Sun, so called because he impels the juices, the rays, the vital breaths, and the world; we have reached that light, the highest of all lights—the meaning is: "O, we have attained it!
This is that light which has been praised by the two Ṛg-verses and illuminated by the triad of Yajus-formulas.
The repetition twice is for the purpose of completing the ritual arrangement of the sacrifice. //7//
Thus, in the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the seventeenth section:
"One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman."
Thus with respect to the self;
now with respect to the divine:
space is Brahman.
Thus both have been taught: that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the divine.

The Lord has been described as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and as the "ether-self" (*ākāśātman*), being a single part of the qualities of Brahman. Now follows the beginning with the words "Mind is Brahman," etc., for the purpose of enjoining the meditation upon the mind and the ether as the complete Brahman. That by which one thinks is the mind; it is the internal organ. One should meditate upon that as the supreme Brahman. This vision concerning the self is the "internal" (*adhyātma*) perspective.
Now, we shall speak concerning the divine—that which pertains to the deities.
One should meditate upon space as Brahman.
Thus, both this internal [subject] and the divine [subject] are taught and instructed as objects for the vision of Brahman.
Because of the subtlety of both space and the mind, and because Brahman is perceivable by the mind, the mind is suitable for the contemplation of Brahman;
and space is also suitable because of its all-pervasiveness, subtlety, and freedom from limiting adjuncts. //1//
This very Brahman has four quarters:
speech is one quarter, breath is one quarter, the eye is one quarter, and the ear is one quarter.
Thus with respect to the self;
now with respect to the deities:
Fire is one quarter, Wind is one quarter, the Sun is one quarter, and the Quarters are one quarter.
Thus both have been taught: that which pertains to the self (adhyātma) and that which pertains to the divine (adhidaivata).
This very Brahman called "mind" (manas) has four quarters—that is, it has four parts.
How does the mind-Brahman have four quarters? He says: speech, breath, sight, and hearing—these are the quarters with respect to the internal self (adhyātma).
Now, with respect to the deities, these are fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters—these belong to the ether that is Brahman.
Thus, Brahman is declared to have four quarters in both respects: namely, with respect to the self and with respect to the deities. //2//
Speech indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman;
it shines and glows with fire as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge.
In this context, speech alone is the fourth foot of the mind as Brahman, with respect to the other three feet.
For by means of speech, as if by a foot, one stands firm toward the objects to be expressed, such as cows and so forth;
therefore, speech is like a foot of the mind.
Likewise, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a foot, as is the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*);
by means of that, one moves toward the object of odor.
Similarly, the eye is a foot and the ear is a foot; thus, with respect to the internal, the Brahman that is the mind possesses the nature of having four feet.
Now, with respect to the divine (adhidaivata), fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters are perceived as being attached to the ether—which is Brahman—like the feet of a cow.
Therefore, fire and the others are called the "feet" of that ether.
Thus, both with respect to the self (adhyātma) and with respect to the divine, it is established as four-footed.
In that context, speech alone is the fourth quarter of the mind-Brahman.
It shines, blazes, and glows with Agni as its presiding deity (adhidaivata) and light; it also produces heat and warmth.

Alternatively, the meaning is that speech, kindled by the consumption of oily substances, ghee, and other things related to fire, shines and glows—that is, it becomes capable of the exertion required for speaking.
And the fruit of the knower shines and blazes with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge—he who knows it thus as it has been described. //3//
Prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with Vāyu as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge.
The eye indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with the sun as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
The ear indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows with the quarters as its light.
He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge—yea, he who knows this, knows this.
6. Likewise, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is the fourth foot of Brahman.
It shines and glows for the sake of perceiving odors by means of the wind;
likewise, the eye [shines] by means of the sun for the perception of forms, and the ear by means of the quarters for the perception of sounds.
The fruit of knowledge is equal everywhere; the attainment of Brahman is the unseen fruit for one who knows thus.
The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the exposition. //4-6//
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the third chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"The sun is Brahman"— this is the instruction.
Its further explanation:
In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent;
that became existent.
That came into being;
it developed into an egg;
it lay for the duration of a year.
It burst open;
those two eggshell halves became silver and gold.

Since the sun has been declared a foot of Brahman, this section is commenced for the purpose of viewing that [sun] as the entire Brahman: "The sun is Brahman"—this is the *ādeśa*, the instruction; its detailed explanation (*upavyākhyāna*) is now being made for the sake of praise.
This entire world, prior to its origin—that is, in its previous state—was non-existent (*asat*), meaning unmanifested name and form, but it was not non-being (*asat*) in the absolute sense.
"How could one bring forth the existent from the non-existent?"—because this prohibits the theory that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production].
Now, one might argue that because the text here prescribes "from the non-existent alone," there would be an option;
but no, for an option is impossible regarding a real entity, just as it is not possible in the case of actions.
How then is it that this is "only non-existent" (asat)?
Have we not already said that because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) have not yet been manifested, it is "as if non-existent," hence "non-existent"?
Is it not the case that the word "eva" (only/just) has the sense of restriction?
This is true;

however, it does not determine the non-existence of sentient beings. What then? It determines the non-existence of name-and-form as they have been manifested; for the use of the word "existent" (sat) is observed in reference to the domain of manifested name-and-form.
And that manifestation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) for the world depends mostly upon the sun; for in its absence, this world would be blind darkness and nothing at all would be discerned.

Therefore, just as in a statement intended for praise, one might say, "Even though this royal lineage exists, it does not truly exist unless King Pūrṇavarman, who is endowed with every virtue, is present," so it is here.
Nor is it intended here to establish either the existence or non-existence of the world, for the passage is devoted to the instruction that "the sun is Brahman";
thus, at the conclusion, it will summarize with the words, "One should meditate on the sun as Brahman.

That which was "Being" (sat) prior to creation—that which is denoted by the word "Non-being" (asat)—was motionless and inert, like non-being, yet facing toward its effects, with activity having just slightly arisen.
Then that [Being], having gained momentum, became differentiated by a very slight manifestation of name and form, like a seed that has begun to sprout.
From that, as it gradually became more substantial, an egg (*aṇḍa*) emerged and formed from those waters.
The elongated form "āṇḍam" is a Vedic usage.
Then that Egg remained as a single, undifferentiated entity for the measure and duration of a year, which is the well-known unit of time.
Thereafter, from that period measured by a year, it burst open like the egg of a bird;
and of that split Egg, the two shells became silver and gold. 1.
In that regard, what was silver is this earth;
what was gold is the sky.
That which was your placenta are the mountains; that which was your amnion is the mist together with the clouds.
The veins are the rivers;
the water contained within them is the ocean.

Of those two shell-halves, that which was the silver shell became this earth—meaning the lower shell of the cosmic egg as indicated by the earth. That which was the golden shell became the sky—meaning the upper shell of the cosmic egg as indicated by the celestial realm.
That which was the *jarāyu*, the membrane enveloping the embryo, at the time when the gross egg split into two parts, became the mountains.
The subtle membrane that envelops the embryo, together with the fatty tissues, became the mist, the fog, and the hoarfrost; this is the meaning.
Those vessels and channels that exist in the body of the born embryo became the rivers. The water contained in its bladder became the ocean. //2//
Now, that which was born is yonder sun.
As he was being born, shouts and cries of joy arose after him, as did all beings and all desires.
Therefore, for its arising and for its manifestation, shouts and cries of joy arise, as do all beings and all objects of desire.

Now, that which was born in the form of an embryo within that egg was this very Āditya. As that Āditya was being born, shouts—sounds, cries, and loud, far-reaching roars—arose, just as they do here at the birth of the first son of a Lord; and all beings, both stationary and moving, and all those [beings']...
Desires (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are desired; they are objects such as women, clothing, food, and so forth.

Since the arising of the desires of living beings is caused by the birth of the Sun, therefore even today, with respect to that Sun, "returning" (*pratyāyanam*) means either its rising or its setting, or alternatively, its repeated coming back again and again.
"Corresponding to that" means having made that the cause.
All beings, all desires, sounds, and cries arise in response;
for this is well known at the rising and other phases of the sun. //3//
He who, knowing it thus, venerates this Āditya as Brahman—
surely auspicious sounds will quickly come to him and overwhelm him, they will truly overwhelm him.
The meaning is that whoever, knowing this [Āditya] as possessing the aforementioned greatness, meditates upon Āditya as Brahman, attains its very nature.

Furthermore, there is a visible result: "quickly" (abhyāśaḥ) is an adverbial phrase meaning "swiftly," referring to what happens to the knower of this. "The virtuous" (sādhavaḥ) refers to those who are excellent; "sounds" (ghoṣāḥ) refers to auspicious sounds.

The correctness (*sādhutva*) of the sounds (*ghoṣa*) and so forth consists in the absence of any connection with evil during their enjoyment. "They may go forth, they may come back, they may repeat themselves, and they may repeat themselves again"—the meaning is that it is not merely a matter of the sounds coming and going, but that they should bring comfort and produce pleasure.
The double repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter and for the sake of showing respect. //4//
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a liberal donor, and one who prepared many dishes.
He had dwellings built on every side, thinking, "People shall eat my food from all directions."
The superimposition of the view of the quarters of Brahman upon Vāyu and Prāṇa has been described previously.
Now, the subsequent section is commenced so that these two may be meditated upon as Brahman directly.
The narrative is for the sake of easy comprehension.

And for the purpose of demonstrating the procedure for the giving and receiving of knowledge, as well as the fact that faith, the giving of food, lack of arrogance, and so forth, are the means for attaining knowledge, this is shown by means of a narrative.
Jānaśruti is the descendant of Janaśruta.
The particle *ha* signifies traditional report (*aitihya*).

The grandson of that son was Pautrāyaṇa; he was indeed a "śraddhādeya," meaning one for whom gifts are to be given with faith (*śraddhā*)—that is, things to be given to Brahmins and others preceded by faith. He was a "bahudāyī," meaning one whose habit is to give abundantly. He was a "bahupākya," meaning one in whose house much was to be cooked day after day.
The meaning is that for those seeking food, much food was cooked in his house.
Endowed with such qualities, this Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa lived at a certain distinguished place and time.
He, indeed, had dwellings—meaning those places where people come and stay—constructed throughout all directions, in villages and cities; that is to say, he caused them to be built.
"In every way, those dwelling in those dwellings shall eat—that is, they shall consume—my food"; such was his intention. //1//
Then, indeed, at night some swans flew by. Thereupon,
one swan addressed another swan in this manner:
"Ho there, Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa! A light as vast as the sky is spread out for Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa; do not touch it, lest it consume you!
While the king was thus situated on the roof of his palace during that time of religious observance, some swans descended at night.
Being either sages or deities who had been gratified by the king's merit of giving food, they assumed the form of swans and descended within the range of the king's vision.
At that time, as those swans were flying, one falling behind addressed the swan flying in front, calling out "Ho! Ho! and "O!
O!", addressing him with the words "Bhallākṣa! Bhallākṣa! to show his regard, just as one might say, "Look! Look at this wonder!
He spoke thus, using the term "Bhallākṣa" to indicate the other's dull sight.

Alternatively, because he possessed the conceit of having correctly perceived Brahman, he was repeatedly censured by him; being thus afflicted, he indicates that [affliction] out of indignation by saying, "O Bhallākṣa! [The meaning is:

the radiant light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is equal to—that is, the same as—the heavenly world (dyuloka), produced by the power born from his giving of food and other such acts, spread out and pervading it, touching the heavenly world;
or rather, his light is equal to the day (divā).
"Do not touch it"—the meaning is that you should not form an attachment to it, nor establish a connection with that light.
"By touching it, let that light not burn you"—the meaning is that it should not consume you; the change in verbal person (from *pradhākṣīt* to *pradhākṣīḥ*) is used for the sake of meter. //2//
The other replied to him: "Who indeed is this person you call Raikva with the cart, as if he were such? And how, pray, is Raikva with the cart? ChU 4.1.3.
To him who had spoken thus, the other—the one walking in front—replied: "O Āre! This king is base and wretched;

why do you revile him, who is actually such a person, and endowed with what greatness? Why do you address him with such words of high esteem, as if he were Raikva Sayugvā—that is, Raikva who is accompanied by a *yugvan*, a vehicle for traveling?"
He said this to him: "It is improper and unsuitable for you to speak of him in such a way, as if he were Raikva"—this is the intention.
The other replied, "Who indeed is this Sayugvā Raikva of whom you speak? To him who had spoken thus, Bhallākṣa said, "Listen to how that Raikva is. //3//
"Just as all the lower throws of dice go to one who has won with the *kṛta* throw, even so everything that people do in a good way goes to him who knows what he [the Self] knows.
'He who knows that which he knows—this has been told by me. (ChUp 4.1.4)

Just as in the world, when the *kṛta*— the well-known four-pointed die used in gambling— is victorious in a game for those engaged in it, then for that victorious one, the others— the three, two, and one-pointed dice known by the names *tretā*, *dvāpara*, and *kali*— converge, meet, and become subsumed within it.
The meaning is that because the values of three, two, and one are present within the "made die" (kṛtāya), they are included within it.
Just as in this illustration, so too does everything—represented by the dice such as the tretā and others—converge and become included within this Raikva, who stands in the place of the kṛtāya.
What is that? Whatever good and beautiful collection of dharma all creatures in the world perform, all of that is included within the dharma of Raikva.
And the meaning is that within its fruit, the fruit of all living beings' dharmas is included.
Likewise, there is another who knows what he ought to know; what is it that he knows? That which Raikva knows.

The phrase "he attains that" carries over [from the previous verse]: whoever else knows that which is to be known—that entire collection of qualities belonging to all living beings as well as their fruit—he likewise attains it, just like Raikva.
The intention is this: when one who is thus constituted—a man of knowledge—is addressed by me with these words, he alone becomes the equivalent of the stake won by Raikva. //4//
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard this. As he was rising, he said to his charioteer, "My good man, have you spoken of Sayugvān Raikva as if he were a mere firebrand?"
"But how is Raikva with the cart? he asked.

Just as when one has won a prize in a game of dice, all the lower stakes are gathered together, even so everything that people do which is good converges upon him who knows what he knows—that is what I have told you. 4.1.6.

Now, while staying upon the roof of his palace, King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa heard this very speech of the swans, which was in the form of a censure of himself and in the form of praise for another wise man such as Raikva. And remembering that speech of the swans, he spent the remainder of the night by repeating it over and over again.
Then, being awakened by the bards with words of praise while still rising from his bed and even as he was abandoning sleep, the king said to the steward (kṣattṛ):
"O dear one, did you speak of me to that Sayugvā Raikva?
The intention is: 'He alone is worthy of praise, not I.'"
Alternatively, [the king may have thought: "I wish to see that Raikva Sayugvā; having gone there, I shall speak to him.
In this case, the word *eva* (indeed) must be explained as either serving the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or being redundant.
Then the attendant, desiring to bring Raikva and knowing the king's intention, replied: "How indeed is that Raikva Sayugvā?"
When the king had spoken thus, wishing to know that sign in order to bring him [Raikva], he asked, "Who indeed is this Sayugvā Raikva?
And he (Bhallākṣa) spoke only the words of Bhallākṣa.
The steward, having searched for him, returned saying, "I did not find him.
He said to him, "O friend, where one searches for a Brahmin, there one should seek him."
Remembering that, the steward went to the city or the village, searched for Raikva, and returned, saying, "I did not find him; I did not know him.
He said to the steward: "O, go to where one searches for and tracks down a Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman—in a secluded place such as a forest, on a riverbank, or in a solitary spot—go there to Raikva."
The meaning is: "perform a search. //7//
He sat down near a man who was scratching an itch beneath a cart.
He addressed him, saying, "Are you, venerable sir, Raikva with the cart?"
"I am indeed the spokes," he replied. Then the steward returned, saying, "I have found him. ChU 4.1.8.
Having been told this, the charioteer searched for him and, seeing in a secluded place beneath a cart— that is, a wagon—
a man scratching and rubbing his scabs and itch, he thought, "This must surely be Raikva with the cart," and approached him, sitting down near him with humility.
And he addressed that Raikva, saying:
"O Venerable One, you are indeed Raikva with the cart.
Thus questioned, he replied with disregard, "I am indeed Ara, Ara," thereby acknowledging [the name] without respect.
Having recognized him, he returned, thinking, "I have known what was not known"; the meaning is that he came back. //8//
Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, approached him.
He spoke to him.
Then, perceiving the sage’s intention toward the householder’s life and his desire for wealth,
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa took six hundred cows, a gold necklace for the neck, and a chariot yoked with two mules;
having taken that wealth, he approached Raikva.
And having gone to him, he addressed him, saying: //1//
"O Raikva, here are six hundred cows, this gold necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules;
teach me, O venerable sir, that deity whom you worship."
"O Raikva, these six hundred cows have been brought by me for you; here is this gold necklace, and here is this chariot drawn by mules. Accept this wealth, O Blessed One, and instruct me.
The meaning is: instruct me by teaching me that deity which you worship. //2//

But the other replied to him: "O Śūdra, let it be yours alone, along with the gold necklace and the mule-chariot. Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a mule-chariot, and his daughter, went back to him.
To the king who had spoken thus, the other, Raikva, replied: "Ah.
This particle *aha* is used elsewhere in the sense of restraint or prohibition, but here it is meaningless, since the word *eva* is employed separately.

"Having taken it away, having joined it with the necklace—this cart, having taken it away along with the cows, let it remain yours alone; let it not be mine, for I have no need for this which is insufficient for my purpose"—this is the intended meaning, O Śūdra.

But surely he was a king because of his connection to the *kṣattṛ* (steward), as it was previously stated that "he spoke to the *kṣattṛ*. Furthermore, since one approaches a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of acquiring knowledge and since a Śūdra lacks the qualification [for such study], how can Raikva speak this inappropriate thing, "O Śūdra"?

Regarding this, the teachers say: upon hearing the words of the swan, grief entered him; because of that grief, having heard of Raikva’s greatness, he ran toward him. Thus the seer, demonstrating his own indirect knowledge [of the man's identity], addressed him as "Śūdra.
Or else, he approached him for the sake of acquiring knowledge with wealth alone, like a Śūdra, and not with service.
"But he was not a Śūdra by birth. Others, however, say that he called him a "Śūdra" out of anger because only a small amount of wealth had been brought;
for it is a sign that the taking of wealth occurs when there is much to be brought.

Having understood that thought of Uddālaka Āruṇi, Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa once again took an additional thousand cows, his own daughter who was dear to the ṛṣi, and set out toward him. He approached him and spoke to him.
"Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this gold necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell; O venerable sir, instruct me further."
Lifting her face toward him, he said, "You have brought these [gifts]; you would have made me speak with this mouth of a Śūdra!
These are the Raikvaparṇas by name among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he dwelt for him. To him, he then spoke.

"Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this daughter of mine brought for you as a wife, and this village in which you dwell—this has all been prepared by me for your sake. Taking all this, please instruct me, O Venerable One. When he had spoken thus, [Raikva said: "The mouth—that is, the entrance—of that very daughter of the king who was brought for him as a wife..."
"Regarding the gift of knowledge, one who receives it at a sacred place (*tīrtha*)—meaning one who knows [the proper way]—is as follows:
a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), a giver of wealth, one who is intelligent, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), and one who is dear;
or else, through knowledge itself, knowledge declares these six to be my sacred places."
Thus the statement of Vidyā is understood.
Knowing this and supporting it, he spoke— that is,
he said— "O Sir, that you brought these cows and whatever other wealth there was, that is well," is the completion of the sentence.

"Śūdra"—this is merely an imitation of what was said before, and not due to any other cause as in the previous case. "By this very mouth," meaning by the channel for receiving knowledge, "you will cause me to speak"—that is, you are making me speak. These are those very villages known as Raikvaparṇa, famous in the Mahāvṛṣa regions, in which villages Raikva had resided; the king gave those villages to that Raikva.
To that king who had given him wealth, it is said, Raikva indeed imparted the knowledge.
Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Air, indeed, is the absorber.
When fire goes out, it enters into the wind;
when the sun sets, it enters into the wind;
when the moon sets, it enters into the wind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1)

"Vāyu indeed is the absorber. The word "indeed" (vāva) is for the purpose of emphasis, meaning that it is specifically Vāyu. It is called the "absorber" (saṃvarga) because of its absorbing, gathering, or swallowing [of other elements].
It is the absorber because it brings the deities to be mentioned hereafter—such as Fire and the others—into its own nature.
The quality called "the absorber" (saṃvarga) is to be meditated upon as being like the wind,
based on the examples found from the section beginning with "Kṛta" and ending with "Anta.
He explains how the wind possesses the nature of an absorber:

When, at whatever time, fire goes out—that is, reaches extinction and becomes still—then that fire enters into air alone; it attains the very nature of air. Likewise, when the sun sets, it enters into air alone;
when the moon sets, it enters into air alone.
But how can the sun and the moon, while remaining in their own essential forms, enter into the wind?
This is not a fault, because at the time of setting, their non-perception is caused by the wind.
For the sun is led to its setting by the wind, since motion is the effect of the wind;
or else, at the time of dissolution (pralaya), when the forms of the sun and moon perish, their essence as light would merge back into the wind alone. //1//
When the waters dry up, they merge into the wind alone;
for the wind indeed gathers them all together.
Thus with reference to the deities. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.2)
Likewise, when the waters dry up—that is, reach a state of desiccation—they merge into the air alone.
For it is because the air withdraws these very elements, beginning with fire, which possess great power;
therefore, the meaning is that the air, characterized by the quality of being the "absorber" (*saṃvarga*), is to be meditated upon.
Thus has been described the vision of the Saṃvarga (the absorber) with respect to the deities among the divine powers. //2//
Now,
with reference to the self:
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the absorber.
When he sleeps, speech indeed merges into the vital breath,
sight merges into the vital breath, and hearing merges into the vital breath.
"The vital breath is the mind;
for the vital breath indeed gathers all these together. (ChU 4.3.3)
Now, immediately following this, the vision of the absorber (*saṃvarga*) within the self is stated with reference to the internal realm.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), indeed, is the primary absorber.

When that person sleeps—at which time—the speech merges into the vital breath, just as fire merges into the wind; the eye merges into the vital breath, the ear into the vital breath, and the mind into the vital breath. For it is because the vital breath absorbs all these, beginning with speech, that it is called the absorber.
Thus [ends the third section]. //3//
These two, indeed, are the two absorbers:
Vāyu among the gods, and Prāṇa among the vital breaths.

These two, indeed, are the two absorbers (*saṃvarga*). Vāyu alone is the absorber among the deities, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the absorber among the vital functions, beginning with speech. //4//
Then, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served food, a religious student begged from them;
but they did not give to him.
Now, this narrative is commenced for the purpose of praising these two. The word *ha* indicates tradition (*aitihya*).
Śaunaka is the descendant of Śunaka; Kāpeya belongs to the lineage of Kapi; and Abhipratārin by name is the descendant of Kakṣasena.
While the son of Kakṣasena was seated for a meal and being served by the cooks, a religious student (*brahmacārī*) who was a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) begged of him.
Perceiving that the student was proud of his knowledge of Brahman, and desiring to test him, the two did not give him alms, thinking, "What will he say? //5//
He said:
"The one God has swallowed the four great ones; who is he, the guardian of the world?"
O Kāpeya, mortals do not perceive him, O Abhipratārin, though he dwells in many ways; for they think, "This food has not been given to him to whom it belongs. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.6)
He, the religious student, said: "The four of the Great Self"—this is the accusative plural.
"The one god" refers to Vāyu; "the breath" refers to Agni and the others, as well as speech and the rest.
Who is that Prajāpati who swallowed them, who has consumed them?

"Who is it that swallows?"—thus some ask. "The world" (*bhuvana*) means that in which beings (*bhūtāni*) exist; it refers to the entire world, beginning with the earth. Its "guardian" (*gopā*) means its protector, its preserver, its keeper.

O Kāpeya, mortals—those subject to death or lacking discrimination—do not perceive, do not know, that Prajāpati. O Abhipratārin, he dwells in many ways through the modes of the internal self (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaivata*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*).
"For to whomsoever this food is brought day after day for eating and prepared—that Prajāpati—this food has not been given to him."
Then Śaunaka Kāpeya, reflecting upon this, returned [to his position]:
"The Self of the gods, the progenitor of creatures, with golden tusks, the devourer, the wise one."

"O Somya, you truly shine like one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you?"
"Others say it is from human beings," he replied;
"but may the Blessed One himself tell it to me, according to my desire."
"O dear one, you truly shine like one who knows Brahman.
One who knows Brahman has serene senses, a smiling face, and is free from anxiety, having accomplished his purpose;
therefore, the teacher says, 'You shine like one who knows Brahman.'"
Reflecting on this with the thought, "Who indeed [taught you]?", he asked, "Who instructed you?
And he replied, "Satyakāma [instructed me], and others besides humans;
the deities have instructed me."

The intention is: "What other human being would dare to instruct me, a disciple of the Blessed One? Therefore, he made this declaration: "Others than humans [are my teachers]. The Blessed One alone may speak to me according to my desire; what is the use of what others say? I do not take that into account—this is his intention. //2//
"I have indeed heard from those like your venerable self that knowledge, when learned from a teacher, reaches its most perfect state. Therefore,
he said this very thing to him."
"In this, indeed, nothing whatsoever is lost—nothing whatsoever is lost. (ChU 4.9.3)
Furthermore, it has been heard by me from sages equal to the Blessed One that in this matter knowledge indeed exists;

for it is said that "knowledge, once understood from a teacher alone, attains its most excellent state"—that is, it reaches the highest degree of perfection. Therefore, the Blessed One himself should speak. Thus addressed, the teacher spoke to him that very same knowledge which had been declared by the deities.

In this regard, not even a single part, not even a mere portion of the knowledge of the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakalavidyā*), has been omitted—that is, nothing has been left out. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the instruction. //3//
Thus ends the ninth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a student of sacred knowledge with Satyakāma Jābāla.
He attended upon his sacrificial fires for twelve years;
while he allowed other pupils to return home, he did not allow him to do so.
"Furthermore, I shall explain the knowledge of Brahman in another manner," [the teacher] begins, setting forth both the path for those who know that and the knowledge of the fires.

The narrative is as before, intended to demonstrate that faith and austerity are the means to the knowledge of Brahman: "Upakośala by name, the son of Kamala (Kāmalāyana), [studied] with Satyakāma Jābāla"—here, *ha* has the sense of traditional report (*aitihya*).
He attended upon the fires of that teacher for twelve years; he performed the service of the fires.

That teacher, having caused the other religious students to master their private recitation, would have them perform the ceremonial bath (*samāvartana*), but he alone did not cause Upakosala to perform it.
His wife said to him: "The student has performed his penance; he served the fires well.
Let not the fires speak out against you."
"Tell us," they said.
But he, without having told him, went away on a journey.
The teacher’s wife said to him: "He was a disciplined student who attended to the sacred fires properly; he has served them well.
And the venerable one does not dismiss from studentship one who is devoted to the fires.
Therefore, knowing that he does not dismiss you because of your devotion to us, may the fires not speak ill of you, may they not bring reproach upon you."
"Therefore, tell him the knowledge desired by Upakosala. Although he was thus addressed by his wife, he did not speak at all; without saying anything, he simply went away on a journey.
He, however, resolved not to eat because of illness.
His teacher’s wife said to him, "O student, eat!"
"Why indeed do you not eat?
He replied, "There are many desires in this person, each with its own course;
I am filled with diseases."
"I will not eat," he said. ChU 4.10.3.

That Upakośala, afflicted by mental illness and suffering, resolved—that is, fixed his mind upon—undertaking a fast (*anaśanam*). While he was staying silently in the fire-sanctuary, the teacher’s wife said to him: "O student (*brahmacārin*), eat; why indeed, for what reason, do you not eat?
He replied: "In this person, who has not accomplished his purpose and is merely ordinary, there are many various desires regarding what ought to be done."
"Various perils" (*nānātyaya*) refers to those diseases and anxieties regarding what ought to be done; the meaning is that they are mental sufferings caused by the attainment of such duties.
I am filled with these.
Therefore, I shall not eat. //3//
Then the fires said to one another:
"The student has performed his penance; he has served us well."
"Come, let us explain this to him," they said, and they spoke to him:
"Brahman is Prāṇa; Brahman is Ka; Brahman is Kha."
When the religious student had spoken and become silent, the three fires—having been won over by his service and filled with compassion—consulted together and said:
"Come now, let us all instruct this religious student, who is devoted to us, distressed, ascetic, and full of faith; let us proclaim to him the knowledge of Brahman.
Having thus deliberated, they said to him: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman. 4.
He said:
"I know that breath is Brahman."
"I do not understand what *kaṃ* is and what *khaṃ* is.
They said,
"That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *khaṃ*."
"That which is space (kha) is indeed that which is bliss (kam). They told him this: both the vital breath (prāṇa) and the ether (ākāśa).

The religious student said: "I understand what you have said—that *prāṇa* is Brahman—because its meaning is well-established. Since life exists when it is present and ceases when it departs, and since that term is conventionally used in the world for a specific kind of air (*vāyu*), its status as Brahman is logical.
Therefore, because its meaning is well-established, I understand that *prāṇa* is Brahman."
"But as for *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*, I do not understand them. Now, since the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* are indeed well-known terms whose referents are pleasure (*sukha*) and space (*ākāśa*),
why is there ignorance on the part of the religious student?

He thinks: "Surely, how can that which is denoted by the word *ka*—pleasure—which perishes in a moment, and that which is denoted by the word *kha*—space—which is insentient, possess the nature of Brahman?
And how could your statement not be invalid?
Therefore, he says, "I do not understand."

When the religious student had spoken thus, those fires said to him: "That which we called 'ka' is indeed 'kha,' that is, space. Thus, being qualified by 'kha,' 'ka' would be distinguished from the pleasure born of the contact between the sense organs and their objects, just as a blue lotus, when qualified [by its color], is distinguished from red and other colors."

Know that what we have called "kha" (the void) is indeed "ka" (bliss). Thus, when the void is qualified by bliss, it is distinguished from the material, insentient void, just as a blue lotus is distinguished [from other lotuses].
This bliss resides in the space [of the heart], not the other, worldly kind.
The meaning is that space (*ākāśa*) is the locus of happiness, and not the other [element], which is composed of material elements (*bhautika*).
Now, if space is intended to be qualified by happiness, let there be only one of the two as the qualifier— either "that which is *kaṃ* is indeed *kha*" (where the latter is the surplus),
or "that which is *kha* is indeed *kaṃ*" (where the former is the surplus).
[Objection: But have we not already stated that the exclusion of both bliss (*sukha*) and space (*ākāśa*) from worldly bliss and space is intended?
If it is argued that when space is qualified by bliss, the exclusion of both [worldly bliss and space] follows as a matter of course, [the reply is: True, this is so;
however, it is specifically space as qualified by bliss that is enjoined as the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), and not the bliss which is merely a qualifying attribute of space.
The state of being an object of meditation would be established;
for the employment of a qualifier functions solely as a restrictor of the qualificand.
Therefore, bliss (*sukha*) is also qualified by "one's own" (*sva*) for the purpose of making it an object of meditation.
And from what is this determined?
That the word *kaṃ* is connected with the word *brahman*, such that "the bliss (*kaṃ*) is Brahman.
For if the fires had intended to teach that the ether (*kha*) qualified by the attribute of bliss is the object of meditation, they would have first said, "The bliss-ether (*kaṃ khaṃ*) is Brahman."
But they did not speak in this manner;
rather, they said, "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman.

Therefore, for the purpose of removing the confusion of the religious students, it is indeed appropriate to indicate the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the words *ka* and *kha*, beginning with the passage, "That which is Ka, etc."
The Śruti declares this very statement spoken by the fires for our understanding: "And [He gave] breath to that religious student (brahmacārin).
His space is that space.
The meaning is that the space within the heart is the space related to breath as its locus.

Because of the description of possessing the quality of bliss, both that ether—which is characterized by the quality of bliss—and the vital breath (prāṇa) residing therein, which is Brahman solely through its contact with Brahman, are both collectively designated as "Brahman" by the fires. Thus, having combined both the vital breath and the ether, they spoke of them as being Brahman.
Thus ends the tenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "The earth, fire, food, and the sun."
"That person who is seen in the sun, I am he; I am indeed he. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.11.1)
