The fires, having come together, spoke the Brahman to the religious student;
immediately thereafter, they began to teach their respective branches of knowledge individually.
Among them, first the Gārhapatya fire instructed this religious student.
"Earth, fire, food, and the sun—these are my four bodies.

Among them, that person who is seen in the sun is I; he is the Gārhapatya fire. And that which is the Gārhapatya fire is indeed I, the person in the sun. This statement, "I am that very one," is made by way of reversal.
The relationship between the earth and food, characterized by their being objects of consumption, does not exist between the Gārhapatya fire and the sun.
Since the attributes of being the eater, the cooker, and the illuminator are indistinguishable, there is absolute identity between these two;
however, the earth and food are related to them only as objects of consumption. //1//
He who, knowing it thus, worships this [Self] destroys his evil deeds.
He becomes a possessor of the world;
he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long.
His lower people do not perish;
we enjoy him both in this world and in the next, who, knowing it thus, meditates upon him. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.11.2)

Whoever thus meditates upon the Gārhapatya fire— as described above— divided fourfold as food and the eater of food, he destroys and annihilates evil deeds, that is, sinful action. He becomes a possessor of worlds, endowed with a world like our own, namely the world of Agni, just as we are here in this world.
He attains and reaches a full lifespan of a hundred years; he lives long and brilliantly, not remaining unrenowned—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, his "inferior men"—meaning those born in his lineage—do not perish;
that is, there is no interruption of his lineage. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, what do we enjoy and protect while living in this world and in the next world?
The meaning is that for one who, knowing this as it has been described, meditates upon Him, this is the fruit. //2//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire instructed him: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon."
"That person who is seen in the moon, I am he; I am indeed he. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.12.1)
He who, knowing it thus, venerates it, destroys evil-doing and becomes a possessor of the world.
He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long;
his descendants do not perish.
We enjoy that [fruit] both in this world and in the next,
who, knowing it thus, meditates upon it.

Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire, the southern fire, instructed him: "Water, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—these are my four bodies. Having divided myself fourfold, I abide as the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
Therein, that person who is seen in the moon—that am I; he indeed am I," as before.

The identity of the Anvāhāryapacana fire and the moon is established through their connection with food and their commonality as luminous bodies (jyotiṣṭva), as well as their connection with the southern direction.
The waters and the stars are connected as food, just as previously described.
Because the moon is well known to be the object of enjoyment for the stars;
and because it produces food, the Dakṣiṇāgni is "food," while the Gārhapatya is like the earth. The rest is the same. //1-2//
Thus ends the twelfth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him further: "Breath, space, heaven, and lightning."
"That person who is seen in the lightning—that am I; that very one am I. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.13.1)
He who, knowing it thus, worships it,
destroys his evil deeds and becomes a possessor of the world.
He attains a full lifespan; he lives radiantly;
his descendants do not perish.
We enjoy that [person] both in this world and in the next,
who, knowing it thus, venerates him.
Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, and lightning—these are my four bodies as well.
That person who is seen in the lightning, that am I," and so forth, as before, on account of their commonality.
However, because heaven and space are the substrata, they are related to lightning and the Āhavanīya fire solely by way of being objects of enjoyment.
The rest is the same. //1-2//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the fourth chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
They said:
"Upakosala, my dear, this is our knowledge of the Vedas and the knowledge of the Self;
but your teacher will tell you the way.
Then his teacher returned.
The teacher addressed him, saying, "Upakosala! three times.

Having come together again, they said, "O dear one, this is your knowledge from us—the knowledge of fire (agni-vidyā), meaning the previously mentioned knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā) and [the teachings] 'Breath is Brahman,' 'Bliss is Brahman,' and 'Space is Brahman.
But the Teacher will tell you the way for the attainment of the fruit of that knowledge. Having said this, the fires ceased speaking.
In time, his teacher arrived;
and the teacher addressed that disciple, saying, "Upakosala!"
"Yes, Venerable Sir," he replied.
"My dear, your face shines like that of one who knows Brahman."
"Who, indeed, has instructed you? "Who, sir, would instruct me? he thus conceals himself as it were. "Surely these [fires] are such, and yet otherwise," he thus reflects upon the fires.
"What, my dear, did they indeed say to you? [he asked].
"Indeed," he replied, "they have told you, my dear, about the worlds.
But I shall tell you that [which you seek]: just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this."
"Let the Blessed One tell it to me.
He said to him: "ChU 4.14.3"
"Venerable sir," he replied.

"My dear boy, your face shines serene like that of one who knows Brahman. Who, indeed, has instructed you? Being thus addressed, he replied: "Who, indeed, would instruct me? Who could provide such instruction, O venerable sir, while you were away? Here, he seems to deny it; the phrase "he denies as it were" connects with the word "seems" (iva) which is placed further back. He does not deny it entirely, nor does he state exactly what was said by the fires.
The intention is that he said this.

How so? [He thought: "These fires, having been served by me, must surely have spoken, since upon seeing you they appear as if trembling, whereas previously they were otherwise. Thus, pointing toward the fires with a questioning tone (*kāku*), he addressed them, asking: "What, my dear, did the fires indeed say to you? Being thus questioned, he replied, "They said this"—that is, he acknowledged only a mere hint (*pratīka-mātra*), something small, and did not state everything exactly as it had been spoken by the fires.
For the Teacher said: "O Somya, those [predecessors] of yours have indeed spoken of the worlds—earth and so forth—but not of Brahman in its entirety.
However, I shall tell you that Brahman which you desire to hear;
listen to the greatness of the knowledge of that Brahman as it is being spoken by me, just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf."
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so also, as I shall explain, evil action does not cling to one who knows Brahman; it does not adhere to him.
When he had spoken thus, the teacher said, "Let Upakosala tell me [more], venerable sir. To him the teacher spoke. //2-3//
"This person who is seen in the eye— that is the Self," he said. Thus ends the fourteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the two rims.

This person who is seen in the eye by those whose vision has turned inward, who are endowed with the means such as celibacy and the like, and who are peaceful and discerning—the seer of sight, according to another scriptural text: "The eye of the eye," and so forth.

Now, it may be argued that what was said by the Fires is false, because they stated, "But the Teacher shall tell you the path," implying he would speak only of the path; furthermore, there was a lack of understanding on the part of the Fires regarding the future matter.
This is not a fault.

Because it is stated that this very blissful space is seen in the eye, and because of the reference to the seer with the words, "This is the Self of living beings," he spoke thus; that which we have declared to be the reality of the Self is this very thing.

It is immortal, having the nature of being deathless and indestructible, and is therefore fearless—for fear arises only for one who has the apprehension of destruction—and since that absence exists, it is fearless. For this very reason, it is Brahman, the vast and infinite.

Furthermore, what is the greatness of this Brahman, the Person in the eye? It is this: even if one pours dust or water into that place, the eye, it goes only to the eyelashes or the eyelids; it does not adhere to the eye, just as water does not adhere to a lotus leaf.
This is the greatness of the location itself; what then need be said of the stainlessness of the Person in the eye who occupies that location? Such is the intended meaning. //1//
They call him "the one in whom all blessings converge" (saṃyadvāma), for indeed, all blessings converge upon him.
All blessings come together unto him who knows this.
They call this aforementioned Person "Saṃyadvāma.
Why?
Because all desirable things (*vāmāni*)—that is, things worthy of being sought after and beautiful things—converge upon and gather toward him; therefore, he is Saṃyadvāma.
In the same way, all blessings come together for one who knows this thus. //2//
He indeed is the leader of all that is desirable, for he leads all desirable things.
He who knows this leads all things that are desirable.

He is indeed the "Bringer of All Desirable Things" (vāmanī), for he leads, brings, and carries all desirable things—the fruits of meritorious deeds—to living beings according to their merit; and for the knower, he carries as his own attribute the fruit: he who knows this leads all desirable things [to himself]. //3//
He,
indeed, is the one who leads by light;
for he shines in all worlds.
He who knows thus shines in all the worlds.
This very one is indeed the "Light-bearer" (bhāmanī), for he shines—that is, he blazes—throughout all the worlds in the forms of the sun, the moon, fire, and so forth.
According to the Vedic scripture, "By his light all this is illumined," he leads (nayati) to the lights (bhāmāni); thus he is the Light-bearer.
He who knows this likewise shines in all the worlds. //4//
Now,
whether they perform the funeral rites for him here or not, they pass into the flame;
from the flame, into the day.
From the day [he goes] to the waxing fortnight;
from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward;
from the months to the year.
From the year [he goes] to the sun;
from the sun to the moon; from the moon to lightning.
Then a non-human person leads them to Brahman.
This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman.
Those who proceed by this path do not return to this human whirlpool; they do not return.
Now, the destination of the knower of Brahman as previously described is being stated:

whether or not the officiating priests perform the funeral rites (*śavyam*) for one who knows thus when he has died, in every case, such a knower is not obstructed by those unperformed funeral rites and attains the world of Brahman.
Nor does he gain any superior world by performing the funeral rites for the dead, because of another Vedic text stating: "He increases neither by action nor does he become less.
By showing disregard for the funeral rites, the text praises knowledge; it does not mean that one who knows this should not perform the funeral rites at all.
For it is inferred elsewhere that when the funeral rites (*śavakarma*) are not performed, there is some obstruction to the commencement of the fruit of an action;

therefore, here [the text] shows that for one who possesses knowledge, the commencement of the fruit occurs without obstruction, regardless of whether the funeral rites are performed or not at the time of the commencement of the fruit of knowledge.

This applies to those who meditate upon the blissful space within the eye, which has such qualities as being the "converging of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*), "leading downward" (*vāmanī*), and "leading upward" (*bhāmanī*), as well as the knowledge of the fires together with the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

And let there be another karma for them or let there not be; in any case, they "attain the light"—the meaning is that they attain and reach the deity presiding over the light. From the light, [they go] to the deity presiding over the day; from the day, to the deity presiding over the waxing fortnight (the white fortnight); from the waxing fortnight, to those six months during which the sun moves northward.
The sun goes toward those months, which are the deities of the northern course; from those months, to the year, the deity of the year;

from that year, to Āditya; from Āditya, to the moon; from the moon, to lightning. There, a certain person—some individual who has come from the world of Brahman, one who is not human (amānava), meaning he does not belong to the human creation—approaches those who reside there.

Brahman leads them to the world of truth (satyaloka), because of the designations of "the goer," "the goal to be reached," and "the leader"; for these [designations] would be untenable if there were attainment of Brahman as pure being (sanmātra), since in that case it would be more logical to say, "Being Brahman itself, he merges into Brahman."
He will explain the realization of pure Being (sanmātra) through the elimination of all distinctions;
for a path that has not been perceived does not stand ready for one to travel upon, according to another Vedic scripture: "If it is not known, it does not benefit him."

This is the path of the gods (*devapatha*); it is called the path of the gods because it is characterized by the gods, such as those beginning with *arciḥ*, who are appointed as its conductors. It is also called the path of Brahman (*brahmapatha*) because it is characterized by Brahman, which is the goal to be reached.
Those proceeding along this path—those going toward Brahman—do not return to this human whirlpool (*āvarta*), which pertains to Manu and is characterized by the creation of Manu.

They do not turn back; they do not turn back—this repetition is for the purpose of showing the completion of the fruitful knowledge. Those who have mounted the wheel of the continuous cycle of birth and death turn again and again like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*); thus, they do not attain that [state]. They do not turn back, they do not turn back. //5//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. This, indeed,
is the sacrifice which purifies here.
For as he moves, he purifies all this; since he purifies all this as he moves,
therefore he alone is the sacrifice.
His mind and his speech are the two paths.

In this section on the secret doctrine (rahasya-prakaraṇa), because of the context and the commonality of being "forest-treatises" (āraṇyaka), it is necessary to prescribe the *vyāhṛtis* as expiatory rites when a flaw occurs during a sacrifice; furthermore, silence (*mauna*) must be observed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), namely the Brahman.
For this reason, the following is commenced: "Verily, this wind that blows is indeed this sacrifice."
The particles *ha* and *vā* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) that indicate a well-known fact;
for it is well known in the Vedas (*śruti*) that sacrifice is established in air:
"Svāhā! Bestow [this] upon the wind."
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "This indeed is the sacrifice that purifies here," and so forth;
for it is wind alone that, by virtue of its nature as motion, is the substratum of action, and because of the Vedic revelation: "Wind alone is the initiator of the sacrifice; wind is its foundation."
Indeed, this very one, moving and going, purifies, cleanses, and purges this entire world;
for there is no purification for that which does not move.
Indeed, the removal of defects is seen in one who moves, not in one who is stationary.
And because this [sacrifice] purifies all this [universe], therefore it is indeed the sacrifice, since it purifies.
Of this very distinguished sacrifice, speech is occupied with the utterance of mantras,
and the mind is occupied with the knowledge of things as they truly are.
These two, speech and mind, are the two paths (vartanī), the two ways by which the sacrifice being performed proceeds; they are the two paths.
For another Vedic text states: "The sacrifice is the successive progression of speech and thought, which possesses the movement of the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna).
Therefore, since the sacrifice proceeds by means of speech and mind, speech and mind are called the two paths of the sacrifice. //1//
Of these two, the Brahman priest prepares one with his mind,
while the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare the other with their speech.
Whenever the Brahman priest interrupts [the recitation] while the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) has been commenced but before the concluding verse (paridhānīyā), [he incurs a fault].
He prepares only one of the two tracks;
the other falls away. Just as a cart traveling on one foot or moving with only one wheel comes to ruin, so too does his sacrifice come to ruin.
When the sacrifice is damaged, the sacrificer suffers accordingly;
having performed that sacrifice, he becomes worse off.
Of those two paths, one who possesses discriminative knowledge effects the purification of one path by means of the mind;
and the three officiating priests— the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ— purify the other path, characterized by speech, by means of speech alone, with the Brahman priest acting as the officiant.
In this case, speech and mind are the two paths to be purified in the sacrifice. Now,

at that time when the *prātaranuvāka* recitation has been commenced and begun, if the Brahman priest should speak— that is, abandon his silence— before the final concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) of the *śastra*, then [the sacrifice goes] to one of the two paths alone.
He prepares the path of speech by means of the sacred word (*brahman*); meanwhile, the path of the mind, being unprepared, falls away, perishes, and becomes riven.
That sacrifice, being unable to proceed by either one of them—the path of speech—comes to ruin.
He asks: "In what way? [and answers: "Just as..."

Just as a one-legged man, walking along a path, comes to grief, or as a chariot, moving while turning on only one wheel, comes to grief, even so does the sacrifice of this sacrificer come to grief— that is, it perishes— when performed by a wicked Brahmin.
As the sacrifice comes to grief, the sacrificer comes to grief.
For the sacrificer has the sacrifice as his life-breath;
therefore, when the sacrifice is injured, his injury is incurred.
Having performed such a sacrifice, he becomes more wretched—that is, more sinful. //2-3//
Now, when the morning litany has been commenced, if the Brahman priest does not speak out before the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), they prepare both tracks;
neither one is neglected. (ChU 4.16.4)

Just as a chariot moving on two wheels remains steady when traveling on both feet, even so his sacrifice remains steady; as the sacrifice remains steady, the sacrificer follows it in remaining steady. Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

Now, furthermore, where the learned Brahman priest, having taken up silence, remains without releasing his speech until the final concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) is recited— just so do all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) maintain both paths; neither one of them is neglected.
To the question "In what way?", he says:
the two examples are the reverse of those previously mentioned.
Thus, the sacrifice of this sacrificer, proceeding by its own two paths, becomes firmly established; the meaning is that it proceeds without perishing, by means of its own self.

As the sacrifice becomes firmly established, the sacrificer follows after it and becomes firmly established. That sacrificer, having performed the sacrifice thus endowed with the knowledge of *mauna* and Brahman, becomes superior; that is to say, he becomes the most excellent.
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds.
From them, as they were being brooded upon, he drew forth their essences:
Agni from the earth.
Vāyu from the intermediate space;
Āditya from the sky.

In this context, silence is prescribed for the Brahman priest; therefore, when that [silence] falters during his duty as Brahman or during other duties such as those of the Hotṛ priests, the offering of the *vyāhṛtis* serves as the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). To that end, he says that the *vyāhṛtis* must be enjoined: Prajāpati performed austerity characterized by meditation directed toward the worlds, with the desire to extract their essence.
As those worlds were being heated, he drew forth—that is, extracted and took—their essences in the form of refined substance.
Which ones?
The essence of fire from the earth.
Vāyu from the intermediate space;
Āditya from heaven. //1//
He brooded over these three deities;
from them, as they were being brooded upon, he drew out their essences.
The Ṛg-verses come from Agni;
the Yajus-formulas from Vāyu; and the Sāmans from Āditya.
Furthermore, in this very same manner, he brooded upon these three deities beginning with Fire;
from that as well, he extracted the essence, the sap, which is the triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā). //2//
He brooded over this threefold knowledge. From it,
as it was being brooded upon, he drew out its essences.
"Bhūḥ" from the Ṛg-verses;
"Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajus-formulas;
"Svaḥ" from the Sāman-chants.
If, therefore, it should be damaged on account of the Ṛgveda, one should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "Bhūḥ Svāhā!
By means of the essence of the Ṛcs, by the power of the Ṛcs, he thereby heals what was injured in the Ṛcs of the sacrifice.
He again brooded over this triple knowledge. From it, as it was being brooded upon, he drew forth its essence: the vyāhṛti "bhūḥ" from the Ṛg-verses, and the vyāhṛti "bhuvaḥ" from the Yajus-formulas.
The *svāhā* is the *vyāhṛti* for the Sāmans;
from these [three] alone come the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and the *rasas* of the great *vyāhṛtis*.

Therefore, if in that sacrifice anything should be impaired (*riṣyet*) on account of a *ṛc*—that is, due to a connection with a *ṛc* or because of a *ṛc*—the sacrifice would incur injury (*kṣatam*); in such a case, one should offer an oblation into the Gārhapatya fire with the words "Bhūḥ svāhā."
That is the expiation in that case.
How so? "Of the *ṛcs* alone" is an adverbial phrase;

by means of the essence (*rasa*) of the *ṛcs*, by means of the vigor (*vīrya*) and vitality (*ojas*) of the *ṛcs*, he joins together—that is, he repairs—the damage, the breakage, or the wound that has arisen in the sacrifice associated with the *ṛcs*. //3-4//
Now, if it should be damaged in respect of the Yajus, one should offer an oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the words, "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! By means of the essence of the Yajus,
by the power of the Yajus, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured in the Yajus.
Now, if it should be damaged in respect to the Sāman, one should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Svaḥ! Svāhā!
By means of the very essence of the Sāmans, by the vigor of the Sāmans, he thus mends the damage in the sacrifice caused by the Sāmans.
Now, if it should be damaged on account of the Yajus—that is, due to a cause related to the Yajus—one should offer an oblation into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with the words, "Bhuvaḥ svāhā.
Likewise, if there is damage on account of the Sāman, one should offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Svaḥ svāhā.
In this way, as before, one restores the sacrifice.
But if there is a flaw caused by a Brahmin, one should offer oblations in the three fires with the three *vyāhṛtis*;
for that flaw belongs to the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*).

“For by what [does one attain] the status of a Brahman? By this very triple knowledge,” according to the Śruti; or else, another principle must be sought for the cause of the status of a Brahman when there is a flaw. //5-6//
Just as one might join gold with salt, silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and leather with wood; so it is. (ChU 4.17.7–8)
Thus, by means of the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this threefold knowledge, he heals whatever is injured in the sacrifice.
Indeed, that sacrifice is made medicinal where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus.
It is just as one might join gold with salt,
or [join] iron with alkali such as borax and the like; for that makes it soft.
One might join silver with gold, though it is difficult to join;
likewise, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, wood with leather, and leather with a leather fastening.

In this same way, by the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this Ātreyī knowledge—by its vigor known as essence (rasa) and its vital energy—one joins together whatever is torn in the sacrifice.
This sacrifice is indeed like one prepared by a physician;
it becomes like a man afflicted by disease who is treated by a well-trained physician.
What is that [sacrifice]?
The meaning is: in whatever sacrifice there is such a Brahman priest—one who knows the expiatory rites involving the oblations of the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis*—that is the [true] sacrifice. //7–8//
This sacrifice indeed flows toward the north where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus. Concerning such a knowing Brahman priest, there is this traditional verse:
Whithersoever it turns, thither it goes.
Furthermore, this sacrifice indeed has its slope toward the north, its depression toward the north, and its elevation toward the south;
the meaning is that it is the cause for attaining the northern path.
Wherever there is such a Brahman priest, regarding such a knowing Brahman priest as the officiant, there is this following verse, which is intended as a praise of the Brahman.

From whichever part of the sacrificial area the ritual of the officiating priests turns back and becomes defective, the Brahman priest, by means of expiation, repairs that very defect of the sacrifice and proceeds, meaning he protects it.
Indeed, the Brahman priest alone is a Mānava; just as a charioteer protects the Kurus, so too does one who knows this protect the sacrifice and the sacrificer.

He protects all the officiating priests; therefore, one should appoint only such a person as this knower as the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know this, not one who does not know this. //10//
The human being;
indeed, the Brahman alone as the officiating priest protects the Kurus with his horses.
For one who knows thus, the Brahman protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests.
Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as this to be the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know this, not one who does not know this.

The Brahman priest is called *mānava* because he practices silence (*mauna*), or because he possesses knowledge through reflection (*manana*). Therefore, like a mare protects horses that have mounted for battle, the Brahman who knows this indeed protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by removing the defects committed by them.

Since the Brahman is thus distinguished as one who possesses such knowledge, one should therefore appoint only such a person—who knows the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis* and so forth—as the Brahman; never one who does not possess such knowledge.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. //10//
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the fourth chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the preceptor of the wandering mendicants and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
"Whoever knows the eldest and the best truly becomes the eldest and the best. Verily, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the eldest and the best. (ChU 5.1.1)
The northern path has been described for the knower of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahmavidyā*).

Now, in this fifth chapter, having referred back to that same path for the householder who knows the five fires, for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), and for the faithful practitioners of other forms of knowledge, another path connected with the southern direction is described for those who perform mere ritual works— a path characterized by smoke and so forth, consisting of return.

And now, beginning with the statement that the third course of transmigration is even more difficult than the previous ones and must be described for the sake of generating dispassion, it is commenced.
Furthermore, in the preceding text, the term "prāṇa" has been used many times, as in "Prāṇa is superior to speech and the other organs" and "Prāṇa indeed is the absorber.
How is it that he is superior among speech and the others, given that there is no difference in their being agents that act in combination?

And how is he to be meditated upon? Because of his preeminence and other qualities, this [section] is commenced immediately hereafter with the intent to teach those attributes: "Whoever knows the eldest and the best"—by age indeed he is the eldest, for he is the eldest among speech and the other organs;
for while the person is still in the womb, the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) first attains its own nature before that of speech and the others, by which the embryo [survives].

Since the eyes and other sense organs are produced first through the formation of their respective locations and constituent parts, the function of speech and the others is acquired only afterwards; thus, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the eldest in terms of age.
Its preeminence, however, will be demonstrated by means of the illustration beginning with "the well-bred horse" and so forth.
Therefore, in this aggregate of causes and effects, the vital breath (prāṇa) alone is both the eldest and the best. //1//
START ChUp 5,1.2:
He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) indeed becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech, verily, is the most excellent. CHUp 5,1.2.
He who knows the most excellent, the best at clothing, the best at covering, or the wealthiest—verily, he himself becomes the most excellent among his own kinsmen.
But who, then, is the most excellent? He says: Speech indeed is the most excellent; for eloquent men live surpassing others and become the wealthiest; therefore, speech is the most excellent. //2//
He who knows the foundation truly becomes established both in this world and in that world.
The eye, indeed, is the foundation.
He who knows the foundation indeed becomes firmly established both in this world and in that higher world.
What, then, is the foundation? He says: "The eye, verily, is the foundation.
For by means of the eye, one who sees remains firm on even ground and on difficult terrain; therefore, the eye is the foundation. //3//
He who knows attainment— for him indeed desires, both divine and human, attain. The ear, verily, is attainment.

"Whoever knows prosperity—for him indeed both divine and human desires become fulfilled. What, then, is prosperity? He says: the ear, verily, is prosperity. Because by means of the ear the Vedas are received, and from them comes the knowledge of their meaning; from that, rituals are performed; and from those, the fulfillment of desires arises. Thus, because it is the cause of the fulfillment of desires, the ear, verily, is prosperity. (ChUpBh_5.1.4)
"Whoever knows the abode (āyatana) becomes the abode of his own people. Mind, indeed, is the abode. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.5)
"Whoever knows the abode (āyatana) indeed becomes an abode for his own people; that is to say, he becomes their support."—What is that abode? He says: "Mind (manas), verily, is the abode.
Mind is the abode, the support, for those objects presented by the senses which have become perceptions for the sake of the enjoyer.
Therefore, it has been said that the mind, indeed, is the abode. //5//
Then, indeed, the vital breaths (prāṇas) disputed among themselves regarding who was superior,
saying, "I am superior! I am superior!"

Then, indeed, the vital breaths (prāṇas), possessing the aforementioned qualities, disputed— meaning they spoke variously and contradictorily— for the purpose of [determining] "I am the better, I am the better, I am the better."
Then those vital breaths (prāṇas) went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best?
He said to them:
"Whichever one of you, upon departing, makes this body appear most wretched, that one among you shall be the best. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.7)

They— indeed, while disputing in this manner, having approached their father Prajāpati, the progenitor, for the sake of knowing which among themselves was the most excellent, said: "O Venerable One, who among us is the most excellent, superior in qualities?"— thus they questioned him.

Their father said to them: "Among you, he by whose departure this body appears most wretched—even more so than when one is still alive—and after the vital breaths have departed, it is seen as even more wretched than before, like a corpse, untouchable and impure; he is the best of you. He spoke thus with an interrogative intonation, desiring to avoid causing them distress.
Then Speech departed.
Having been away for a year, it returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as the limbs live without speaking, breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—so it was.
Then Speech entered [the body]. ChUp 5.1.8.
The eye departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as the blind, though not seeing, breathe with the breath, speak with speech, hear with the ear, and think with the mind—so it is.
Then the eye entered [the body]. (ChU 5.1.9)
The ear departed.
Having been away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me? They replied:
"Just as the deaf live—without hearing, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and thinking with the mind—in that same way."
It entered the ear. ChU 5.1.10.
The mind departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said:
"How were you able to live without me?"
"Just as fools breathe with the breath, speak with speech, see with the eye, and hear with the ear," so [thinking], the mind entered. (ChU 5.1.11)
When the vital breaths had been thus addressed by the father, speech indeed departed;
having departed and stayed away for a full year, having ceased from its own function, it returned and said to the other vital breaths:
"In what way, by what means, were you able—without me—to live and maintain yourselves?"
They said, "As those without parts," and so forth. "Without parts" means mute; just as in the world people live by speech even while not speaking.
How? By breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and reflecting with the mind—meaning they perform all the activities of the sense organs in this manner.
The meaning is: "In this way we lived.
Having realized its own inferiority compared to the vital breaths (prāṇas), speech indeed entered back in; that is to say, it became engaged once more in its own function.
The rest is the same: "The eye indeed departed, the ear indeed departed, the mind indeed departed," and so forth.
Just as children are "unmindful," meaning their minds have not yet fully developed. // 8-11 //

Then, as the vital breath (prāṇa) was about to depart, just as a fine horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers, even so did it tear up the other vital breaths. They gathered around it and said: START ChUp 5,1.12: Now, as the vital breath was about to depart, just as a fine horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers, even so did it tear up the other vital breaths.
They gathered around it and said:
"O Blessed One, be! You are the best among us; do not depart," [he said]. ChU 5.1.12.

When speech and the other organs had thus been examined, immediately thereafter it is told what that principal breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) did when it desired to depart— that is, when it wished to go out. Just as in the world a fine horse— a noble steed— when struck by a whip by its rider for the sake of testing, might tear up, uproot, and pull out the tethering pegs— the spikes used for binding its feet— so did it tear up and extract the other vital breaths, such as speech and the rest.

Those vital breaths, being thus agitated and unable to remain in their own places, gathered together and said to that principal breath: "O Venerable One, come! Be our lord, for you are the best among us; do not depart from this body."
Then Speech said to him:
"Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent."
Then the eye said to him:
"Insofar as I am the foundation, you are that foundation."
Then the ear said to him:
"As I am the attainment, so are you that attainment.
Then the mind said to him:
"That which is my abode, that is your abode. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.14)
Then, indeed, speech and the other organs, establishing the pre-eminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) through their own functions, spoke to him—just as subjects bring tribute to a king.
How so? First, speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (vasiṣṭha).
The word "yat" is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is: "insofar as I possess the quality of being the most excellent."
"You are that Vasiṣṭha"—by this, the quality of being Vasiṣṭha was mistakenly conceived by me as "mine"; this is what is meant.
The same should be applied to the subsequent cases regarding the eye, the ear, and the mind. (13–14)
Indeed, they do not call them "voices," nor "eyes," nor "ears," nor "minds";
they call them simply "breaths" (prāṇas).
For it is breath alone that becomes all these things.
This statement of the Śruti is appropriate; for it was said by speech and the other organs with reference to the principal vital breath (prāṇa),
because neither worldly people nor those learned in the scriptures refer to speech and the other instruments as "speeches," "eyes," "ears," or "minds."

What then? They call them, they say, "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*), because the vital breath indeed becomes all these collections of instruments, such as speech and the rest; therefore, he wishes to conclude the meaning of this section by showing that what was said by speech and the others was entirely appropriate for the principal vital breath.
Now, one might ask: how is this logical—that these [organs], like sentient persons, should dispute with one another and vie for preeminence?

For it is not possible for the eye and the other organs to speak individually without setting aside speech; likewise, their departure from the body, re-entry, going to Brahman, or the praise of the vital breaths would not be tenable. In this regard, the fact that speech and the other organs possess consciousness is established by scripture, since they are presided over by conscious deities such as Agni and the rest. If it is argued that this contradicts the systems of the logicians regarding the presence of multiple consciousnesses in a single body—[we reply: [this is not so].
No;
for we accept that Īśvara is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Those logicians who do accept Īśvara maintain that the internal effects and instruments, such as the mind, and external things, such as the earth and so forth, proceed only by necessity when presided over by Īśvara.
It is like a chariot and so forth.
Furthermore, we do not admit that deities such as Agni, even though they are conscious, are the enjoyers within the self;
rather, what then?

For it is accepted that the Lord is the supervisor merely by his presence over those [energies] which possess instruments and effects, which consist of various distinctions of the individual self, the elements, and the divine, and which involve millions of conceptual variations;
he is indeed devoid of instruments.
And the followers of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad recite: "He brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning," and so forth.

We shall explain that the enjoyer, who is connected with the fruits of action, is the individual soul (*jīva*) which is distinct from the body. Furthermore, this dialogue among speech and the other organs is imagined here for the sake of determining the superiority of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

It is just as in the world when men, disputing among themselves for the sake of establishing their own superiority, ask someone who is an expert in specific qualities: "Who among us is the best by virtue of our qualities?"

He said to them, "Strive each one of you individually to accomplish this task; he by whom this task is accomplished shall be the best among you. Thus addressed, they strove accordingly, yet they could not determine whether the excellence belonged to themselves or to another. Therefore, the Śruti has attributed this worldly transaction to speech and the other senses.

How indeed could a wise person fail to realize the preeminence of the vital breath (prāṇa), seeing that life is observed to persist even in the absence of each of the others—speech and so forth—but not in the absence of the vital breath?

Thus says the Śruti of the Kauṣītakins: "One lives deprived of speech, for we see the mute; one lives deprived of sight, for we see the blind; one lives deprived of hearing, for we see the deaf; one lives deprived of mind, for we see infants."
"One whose arms are severed lives; one whose thighs are severed lives," and so forth. //15//
Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He said: "What shall be my food?"
"Whatever there is here, down to the dogs and down to the birds," they said;
that indeed is the food of the cart.
"Cart" (ana) is indeed its manifest name.
"Indeed, for one who knows this, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1)
He (the principal vital breath) said: "What shall be my food?

The Śruti, having imagined the principal vital breath as the questioner and speech and the others as the respondents, says: "Whatever kind of food exists in this world, well-known down to dogs and up to birds—that is the food of all living beings."

"Whatever food there is, that is your food," so said Speech and the others. Having turned away from the form of the invented narrative intended for the realization that "the Prāṇa is the food of all, and the Prāṇa is the eater of all food," the Śruti speaks in its own direct form: "Now, whatever food is eaten here in the world by living beings, that is food for this Prāṇa."
The meaning is that this food is eaten by means of the *prāṇa* alone. The word "ana" is the direct name of *prāṇa*, intended to demonstrate its quality of pervading all types of activity;
for if it were preceded by an upasarga such as *pra*, there would only be a specific, limited movement.

And thus, the mention of the names of all eaters of food is a direct designation of the eater of all foods in the words, "He is the Nameless. Indeed, for one who knows thus— for one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) as described, thinking, "I am the vital breath, abiding in all beings, the eater of all foods"—
there is indeed nothing whatsoever among the things to be eaten by living beings that is not food for him.
The meaning is that everything becomes such knowledge;
for the knower has become the vital breath (prāṇa).

This is known from another scriptural passage which, beginning with, "Verily, he rises from the vital breath and sets in the vital breath," concludes: "For him who knows thus, the sun indeed rises; for him who knows thus, the sun indeed sets. //1//
He said, "What shall be my garment?
They replied, "Water."
Therefore, indeed, those who are about to eat surround it with water both before and after;
he becomes a receiver of clothing and he remains unclothed [in the sense of being well-provided]. 5.2.2.
He, Prāṇa, spoke again;
the conceptualization is just as before.
"What shall be my clothing? they—the Speech and the others—said, "Water."
Since water is the dwelling place of the vital breath (prāṇa), therefore learned Brāhmaṇas, both before eating and after having eaten, perform this rite.
What is it?

With water, which serves as the place of clothing, they clothe themselves—that is, they perform the act of dressing—both before the meal and after the meal, being intent on obtaining and sustaining the principal vital breath.
"He becomes possessed of clothing";
the meaning is that he truly obtains clothing.
"He becomes unclothed" [is said] in contrast.
Since nakedness is already precluded by the fact that one has obtained a garment, the statement "he becomes non-naked" means that he possesses an upper garment (*uttarīya*).

Regarding the sipping of water (*ācamana*) for the sake of purification which is known to be performed by one who is about to eat or who has finished eating, what is prescribed here is merely the contemplation that "this is the garment of the vital breath" (*prāṇa*).
The phrase "they clothe him with waters" does not refer to another act of sipping water.

Just as the view that food being eaten by worldly living beings belongs to the *prāṇa* is a mere illustration, so too are the questions and answers—"What is my food? and "What is my clothing?"—equal in nature.
If the sipping of water (*ācamana*) were performed as something new for its own sake, then even the food of worms and such would have to be prescribed as fit to be eaten by the *prāṇa*.

Since both the question and the answer are equal in their purpose of providing knowledge, and since the context is intended for the sake of knowledge, it is not proper to assume the "half-old-woman" logic (where one part of a statement is taken literally while another is taken figuratively).

As for the objection that the well-known act of sipping water (ācamana) does not serve both the purpose of purification (prāyatya) and the purpose of providing clothing for the breath (prāṇa), we do not say that the sipping of water serves both purposes. Rather, we say that what is enjoined is the contemplation that the water used as a means for the purificatory sipping constitutes the clothing of the breath. In that case, the charge of the fault of implying that the sipping of water must serve both purposes is untenable.
If it is argued that the mention of clothing in the context of sipping water (ācamana) is intended for the purpose of obtaining clothing, we say no.

In the sentence whose purpose is the knowledge of clothing, there would be a split of the sentence (vākya-bheda) if one were to enjoin a previously unknown sipping for the sake of clothing, and simultaneously enjoin the visualization of non-nakedness therein; this is because there is no evidence for the sipping to serve both those purposes and another purpose at once. //2//
Having taught this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, Satyakāma Jābāla said:
"Even if one were to say this to a withered stump, branches would surely grow on it and leaves would sprout."
This very vision of the vital breath (prāṇa) is now being praised.
How so?
Satyakāma Jābāla, having explained this very vision of the prāṇa to Gośruti by name—the son of Vyāghrapada, a descendant of Vyāghrapada—said to him, "There is something else as well."

The speech that is about to be spoken—what was it that he said? He says: "Even if one were to say this teaching to a withered stump, living beings would arise from it, branches would sprout upon this stump, and leaves would grow;
how much more so if one were to speak it to a living person? (3)

Now, if one should desire to go to greatness: having been initiated on the new moon day, on the night of the full moon, having stirred a mash of all herbs with curds and honey, and having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "Svāhā to the eldest, to the best," [he should pour it] into the mash.
One should pour it down as a continuous stream.
Now, immediately after this, if he should desire to go to greatness— that is, if he should wish to attain greatness—
the following rite is prescribed for him;
for when greatness exists, prosperity approaches.

For one who possesses prosperity, wealth is naturally acquired; from that comes the performance of ritual action, and from that, one will attain either the path of the gods (devayāna) or the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa).
Having accepted this as the purpose, this ritual action is intended for one who seeks greatness, not for one who desires the enjoyment of sense-objects.

The rule regarding the time and other details for this [rite] is stated as follows: having been initiated on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), meaning that one has become possessed of the dharmas such as lying on the ground and so forth—characterized by austerity—and truthfulness of speech, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and the like; it does not mean, however, that one undertakes the entire collection of ritual acts belonging to initiation (*daikṣa*), because the rite called "the mash" (*mantha*) is not a modification (*vikāra*) of those [initiatory rites].
From another Vedic text, "one who observes the *upasat* vow," it follows that he undertakes an austerity consisting of consuming only milk, which serves as a means of purification.

On the night of the full moon, he begins the ritual; having taken as much as he is able of all herbs—both cultivated and wild—he husks them and grinds the flour while still raw, placing it in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood, shaped either like a *kaṃsa* or a *camasa*, along with curds and honey.

Having poured it in from another Vedic text and stirred it, he should place it before him; then, having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the *āvasathya* fire at the place for pouring offerings with the formula, "To the eldest, to the best, svāhā!", he should pour the residue clinging to the *sruva* ladle into the churned mixture, letting the remainder fall down. //4//
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To Vasiṣṭha, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To the Foundation, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To prosperity, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To the abode, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.5)

The rest is the same. Having offered each oblation with the words, "To Vasiṣṭha, for support; to Saṃpat, for the abode, svāhā," he should likewise pour out the remainder of the mixture after each offering. //5//
Then, having stepped back and placed the mash in his joined palms, he mutters:
"Amo by name you are."
For this entire world is yours;
he is indeed the eldest, the most excellent, the king, and the sovereign. May he lead me to preeminence, excellence, kingship, and sovereignty.
"May I indeed be all this," [he thought]. ChUp 5.2.6.
Then, having crept back and moved slightly away from the fire, he places the stirred mixture in his joined palms and mutters this mantra:
"Ama by name art thou, for Ama is indeed thine. "Ama" is a name for the vital breath (prāṇa).

For by means of food the vital breath (prāṇa) breathes within the body; therefore, because the substance of the churned offering (mantha) is the food of the vital breath, it is praised as being the vital breath itself with the words, "Thou art Amas. Why? Because "amas" means together (saha); for since this entire world is together with thee, who art the vital breath, it belongs to thee.
For this *mantha* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the eldest and the best;
for this very reason, it is the king, the radiant one, the sovereign who, presiding over all, is the protector.
May the *mantha*, as my own vital breath, cause me to attain the multitude of qualities such as seniority and so forth, so that I myself may become this entire world, like the vital breath itself.
The word "iti" serves the purpose of indicating the completion of the mantra. //6//
Then, indeed, with this verse he sips water foot by foot:
"That of Savitṛ we choose," with these words he sips.

"We are the food of the god," with these words he sips; "the best, the most all-pervading," with these words he sips; "we meditate upon the swift power of Bhaga," with these words he drinks the whole.

Having washed the bronze vessel or the wooden cup, he lies down behind the fire on a skin or on the bare ground, restraining his speech and remaining unyielding. If he should see a woman, he should know that the rite has been successful.
Immediately thereafter, he indeed sips—that is, consumes—the food with this verse that is about to be recited, taking it foot by foot;
he consumes each morsel with one foot of the mantra.
That meal belongs to Savitṛ, the progenitor of all.
Having unified the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun (*āditya*), it is said:
"We choose, that is, we pray for, the form of the sun as the *mantha*.
The intention is: "By means of this food belonging to Savitṛ, by consuming which as our nourishment, may we become possessed of the very nature of Savitṛ."
The phrase "of the god Savitṛ" is connected with what precedes.

"Most excellent" means most praiseworthy among all foods; "most sustaining" means the best supporter of the entire world, or that which provides sustenance in the highest degree. In every respect, it is an adjective qualifying food.
*Turam*, *tvaram*, *tūrṇam*, and *śīghram* mean "quickly.
The remainder [of the phrase] is: "the essential nature of the blessed god Savitṛ.
The intention is: "being purified by excellent nourishment and being pure-souled, we shall meditate upon [him], that is, we shall contemplate [him]."

Alternatively, thinking, "We have performed this ritual action to attain greatness, which is the cause of fortune and glory; let us reflect upon that sacrifice," he drinks all the residue of the churning, having rinsed and washed the *kaṃsa*— the vessel shaped like a *kaṃsa*— or the *camasa*—
the vessel shaped like a *camasa*— which is made of *udumbara* wood.

Having drunk [the water] and sipped it (ācamya), he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east, either on a skin of a sacrificial horse (vājina), or on a bare patch of ground (sthaṇḍila), or simply on the earth.

"Restraining his speech" (vācaṃyama) means being one whose speech is controlled. "Unassailable" (aprasāhaḥ) means not being overcome or overpowered by undesirable dreams such as those involving women and the like; that is to say, he remains with his mind fully composed.
If he, being in such a state, should see a woman in his dreams, then he should know: "This rite of mine will be successful. //7//
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects..."
One should recognize prosperity in that vision of a dream—in that vision of a dream.
Regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra:
"When, in dreams—that is, in dream-vision or at the time of dreaming—one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desire, one should know that there is success therein;
the meaning is that one should know that the accomplishment of the fruits of those rites will come to pass."
The intention is that this occurs when there is the vision of such auspicious dreams as women and so forth.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the ritual action. //8//
Thus ends the second section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas.
Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him:
"Boy, did your father instruct you?
"He did indeed, sir," he replied.

The states of transmigratory existence, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, must be described for the sake of detachment in those seeking liberation; therefore, this narrative is commenced: "Śvetaketu, by name—*ha* is used here for the purpose of traditional report—Aruṇi (the son of Aruṇa), his descendant Āruṇeya, went to the assembly, that is, the court, of the Pañcālas."

When he had arrived, Pravāhaṇa Jaibali—the son of Jīvala—said to him: "O boy, has your father instructed you? The meaning is: "Has your father given you instruction? or "What have you been instructed by your father?"
Thus addressed, he said, "Yes, indeed, I have been instructed, O Blessed One," speaking thus to indicate his understanding. //1//
"Do you know where creatures go from here after departing?
"I do not, venerable sir."
"Do you know how they return again? "No, Venerable Sir. "Do you know the point where the two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors—diverge? "No, Venerable Sir."
"No, Blessed One," he replied. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.2)

He said to him: "If you have been instructed, do you know where, from this world, upwards, those who depart as creatures go—that is, do you know that place? He replied, "No, venerable sir. The other said: "I do not know that which you ask. Well then, do you know by what manner they return again?"
"No, Venerable Sir," he replied.
"Do you know the point of divergence—the place of mutual separation—of the two paths, the ways traveled together, namely the path of the gods and the path of the fathers?
"No, Venerable Sir," he replied. (2)
"Do you know why that world is not filled?
"No, venerable sir."
"Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?
"I do not indeed know that, venerable sir."
"Do you know how that world connected with the ancestors—which they reach and from which they return again—is not filled even by many who depart?
[Nārada] replied, 'I do not know it, O Venerable One.
[The Teacher said: 'Do you know how, by what sequence, when the fifth oblation—numbering five—is offered, [the result] is produced from the oblation...'"

The waters, which are the means for the oblations, become "human-voiced" (*puruṣavacas*); that is, when they are offered in succession as the sixth oblation, they possess the designation "human-voiced," meaning they receive the name "person" (*puruṣa*). This is the sense.
Being addressed thus, he said, "No, Blessed One.
The meaning is: "I do not know anything at all in this matter. //3//
Then [Uṣasta said]: "But what did you say when you were instructed? For how could one who does not know these things claim to have been instructed?"
Distressed, he went to his father's side.
The father said to him, "The venerable one indeed told me, 'I have not instructed you,' even though he said, 'I have instructed you.'"
Then, being thus ignorant, why did you say, "I have been instructed"?
For how could one who does not know these matters asked about by me say among the learned, "I have been instructed"?
Thus, having been pressed and exhausted by the king, Śvetaketu went to his father’s presence, that is, he arrived there. Him—

And he said to his father: "O Venerable One, at the time of my graduation, you indeed told me—without having given me instruction or providing the formal precept—that you had bestowed a blessing upon me; that is what you said."
"Five questions a kinsman of royalty asked me,
and I was not able to explain even one of them."
He said, "Since you spoke of them to me in such a way, it is clear that I do not know even one of them. Had I known these, why would I not have told you? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.5)
Gautama went to the king’s court; when he had arrived, the king offered him the honors due to him. In the morning, having partaken of the hospitality, he departed.
He said to him:
"O venerable Gautama, choose a boon from among human wealth.
He replied:
"O King, human wealth belongs to you alone;
tell me that very word which you spoke in the presence of the boy. He became distressed. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.6)

"Because a kinsman of a king—a *rājanyabandhu* (meaning one who is related to a king but is himself of ill-conduct)—asked me five questions, numbering five, and I was not able to explain even one of them; that is, I was not able to determine their meaning specifically. His father said: 'My child, know me to be just as you were when you first arrived and spoke these questions, saying, "I am not able to explain even one of them. "
The meaning is: "By the sign of your ignorance, you should know that I too possess ignorance regarding those matters.
How so? Just as I do not know—not even one—of these questions, so too, my dear friend, you do not know these questions; thus, I too do not know them.
Therefore, you should not harbor a mistaken notion regarding me.

"How is it so? Because I do not know whether I would have known these questions if I had known them; otherwise, why would I not have told them to you, my dear son, at the time of your return home? Having said this, he went to the presence of King Jaivali Gautama.
When Gautama had arrived, [the king] offered him the hospitality due to those worthy of such honor; he performed it for him.

And that Gautama, having been received as a guest and having stayed there, departed on the following day at the time of dawn. "Sabhāga" means one who possesses a share (*bhāga*), which is to say, one who receives honor, service, or worship; thus, being honored by others, Gautama himself went forth to see the king.
The king said to Gautama: "O venerable Gautama, choose as a boon whatever you desire of human wealth—such as villages and the like—which is to be sought after.
Gautama replied: "O King, let that human wealth remain with you alone.
Speak to me that very speech which you uttered in the presence of my son, my boy—that speech characterized by the five questions. Thus addressed by Gautama, [the king spoke].
The king indeed became distressed and sorrowful, wondering, "How can this be? //5-6//
He commanded him, "Dwell here for a long time.
He then said to him:
"Do not speak thus, Gautama!
So that this knowledge, which previously did not go to the Brāhmaṇas from anyone before you, [remains so];
therefore, indeed, in all the worlds, the governance has belonged to the Kṣatriya alone."
He said to him: "ChUp 5.3.7"

Being thus distressed, and considering that the Brāhmaṇa could not be refused and that knowledge must be imparted according to the proper rule, he commanded Gautama, saying, "Dwell [with me] for a long time. By this—namely, by what the King had previously refused to give as knowledge and what he subsequently commanded him to dwell for a long time—he sought to propitiate the Brāhmaṇa through an explanatory statement of the reason, saying to him: "O Brāhmaṇa, you are one who possesses all knowledge."
"O Gautama, whatever way you have spoken to me, please tell me that very speech characterized by knowledge; understand this from my ignorance.
In this regard, there is something to be said: how it is that this knowledge has not gone, nor has it ever gone, to the Brahmins before you."
And the Brāhmaṇas did not instruct [others] by means of this knowledge;

for it is well known in the world that, therefore, in ancient times, in all the worlds, the instruction—that is, the authority as a ruler—of the Kṣattra alone, of the Kṣattriya caste itself, by means of this knowledge, existed and prevailed.
Thus, through the lineage of the Kṣatriyas alone, this knowledge has come down until this present time.
"Nevertheless, I shall tell this to you; after its transmission to you, it will go to the Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, you should forgive what I have said. Having spoken thus, the king imparted the knowledge to him. //7//
Thus ends the third section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"Yonder world, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire."
Of that [fire], the sun is the fuel;
the rays are the smoke;
the day is the flame.
The moon is its coals;
the stars are its sparks. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1)
The question regarding "water in the fifth oblation" is answered first;
this is done so that its resolution may facilitate the resolution of the others.
That commencement of the effect of the two Agnihotra oblations has been described in the Vājasaneyaka.
Regarding that, there are questions: the departure, the movement of the two oblations, their establishment, their satisfaction, the return, and the rising toward the world.
The resolution of these has been stated in that very same place: "When those two oblations are offered, they depart; they enter the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
they make the intermediate space itself the *āhavanīya* fire; they make the wind the fuel and the rays the bright oblation; they [enter] the intermediate space..."
"Having satisfied him, they then ascend," and so forth; in this very same manner as before, having satisfied him, they then return from heaven.
Having entered this [earth] and satisfied [the beings], they enter the person. Then, having entered woman, one arises again toward the world. Thus it is said.
In that context, it was stated that the mere commencement of the effect of the two *agnihotra* oblations occurs in such a manner.

Here, however, desiring to prescribe the meditation upon that commencement of the effect—characterized by the transformation of the *agnihotra*’s *apūrva*—as the fivefold fires, which serves as the means for attaining the northern path (*uttaramārga*), he says:
"That world indeed, O Gautama, is the fire," and so forth.

In this world, when the two morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations have been offered—with milk and other materials as the means, preceded by faith (*śraddhā*), and having been transformed through the states of smoke, flame, embers, and sparks in the *āhavanīya* fire, and further transformed by the causal factors such as the agent—they ascend in the sequence of the intermediate space and enter the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). These two, being subtle elements, are designated by the term "water" (*ap*) because they are essentially composed of water, and they are also designated by the term "faith" (*śraddhā*) because faith is their cause. The fire that serves as their substratum, as well as other things, [also enter there].
The connection with that [fire] is expressed by the words "the fuel and so forth.
Furthermore, that meditation (*bhāvanā*) upon the two oblations as being fire and so forth is also indicated in the same manner:
"Verily, that world is the fire, O Gautama—just as the *āhavanīya* is here the locus for the *agnihotra*."
Of that fire called the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), the sun itself is the fuel, for by it being kindled, that world shines;
therefore, because of this kindling, the sun is the fuel-stick (samidh).
The rays are the smoke, because they rise from it.
For from the fuel, smoke arises;
the day is the flame due to the commonality of luminosity and because it is the effect of the sun; and the moon is the embers.
Because they become manifest upon the subsiding of the flame;
for when the flame subsides, the embers are manifested. The stars are like sparks of the moon, due to the commonality of being scattered [in various directions]. //1//
In this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation;
from that oblation, King Soma comes into being.

In this very fire as previously described, the gods—the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer appearing in the form of Agni and the other deities from the perspective of the higher divinity (*adhidaivata*)—offer faith (*śraddhā*). These waters, which are subtle and consist of the transformation of the *agnihotra* oblation, are called "faith" because they are permeated by faith;
for it is stated in the question regarding the oblations, "At the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called man," that the waters are the substance to be offered.
It is also known from scripture: "Faith is indeed water; having begun with faith and having led it forth, one proceeds.
One offers that faith, which has taken the form of water.
From that oblation, King Soma arises as the transformation of those waters denoted by the word "faith" when they have been offered into the fire of the heavenly world.

Just as it was stated that the essences of the flowers from the *Ṛgveda* and other Vedas, brought by the bees that are the *Ṛk* and so forth, initiate an effect in the sun characterized by forms such as redness and designated as "glory" (*yaśas*) and so on;

in the same way, these subtle waters denoted by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*), which are inherent in the *agnihotra* oblations, enter the heavenly world and initiate the lunar effect, which is the fruit of the two *agnihotra* oblations.

The sacrificers, who are the performers of that rite, consist of oblations; they are permeated by the contemplation of oblations and, drawn by the ritual action in the form of an oblation, enter the heavenly world (dyuloka) as a union with faith (*śraddhā*) and come into being there.
For it was for that purpose that the Agnihotra was offered by them.

However, in this context, it is primarily the transformation of the oblation itself—through the sequence of its connection with the five fires—that is intended to be explained for the sake of meditation, and not the destiny of the sacrificers.
He will later describe that [path] for the ignorant by way of the sequence beginning with smoke, and the higher path for the wise, which is produced by knowledge. //2//
Thus ends the fourth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed the fire.
For him, the wind is indeed the fuel;
the cloud is the smoke;
the lightning is the flame.
The thunderbolt is the embers;
the hailstones are the sparks.
Regarding the second stage of the oblation, he says: "Parjanya, indeed—Parjanya himself, O Gautama—is the fire. Parjanya is a specific deity presiding over the instruments of rain.
Of that [fire], wind alone is the fuel, for by the wind the fire of Parjanya is kindled.
Because rain is observed when the preceding winds and other factors are powerful;
the cloud is smoke, because it is the effect of smoke and because it is perceived in the same manner as smoke;
and lightning is flame.
Because they share the common quality of luminosity; or because lightning and embers share the quality of hardness, or due to their connection with lightning.
The *hrādunayaḥ* are sparks;
the *hrādunayaḥ* are the sounds of thundering, because of their commonality with the scattering of clouds. //1//
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as an oblation;
from that offering, rain comes into being.
In this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as a libation, just as before.
From that oblation, rain comes into being.
The waters called *śraddhā*, having been transformed into the form of Soma, reach the fire of Parjanya in the second stage and transform into rain.
Thus ends the fifth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
The earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire.
Of that [fire], the year is the fuel;
space is the smoke;
night is the flame.
The quarters are the embers;
the intermediate quarters are the sparks.
"Earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," and so forth, as before.
Of that fire called earth, the year alone is the fuel;
for it is by the time of the year that the earth is kindled for the production of rice and other crops.
Space is smoke;
space is seen as if rising from the earth,
just like smoke from fire.
Night is indeed the radiance of the earth, for night is appropriate to that which is non-luminous by nature; because it consists of darkness,
it is like the radiance appropriate to fire.
The quarters are the embers, due to the commonality of being extinguished;
likewise, the intermediate quarters are the sparks, due to the commonality of being minute. //1//
Into this very fire, the gods offer rain;
from that oblation, food comes into being.
"In that" and so forth is the same [as before].
From that oblation, food consisting of rice, barley, and so on, comes into being. //2//
Thus ends the sixth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire.
Of that [sacrifice], speech is indeed the fuel,
breath is the smoke,
and the tongue is the flame.
The eye is the embers;
the ear is the sparks. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.7.1)
"Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire.
His speech is the fuel, for by speech—by means of the mouth—is man kindled; he is not mute."
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the smoke, because it issues from the mouth like smoke;
the tongue is the flame, because of its redness;
and the eyes are the embers, because they are the locus of light.
The ear is the sparks, because of their similarity in being scattered. //1//
Into this very fire the gods offer food;
from that offering, semen comes into being.
The rest is the same.
They offer food prepared from rice and other grains.
From that oblation, semen comes into being. //2//
Thus ends the seventh section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire.
Her lap is indeed the fuel;
when she addresses [him], that is the smoke;
the womb is the flame.
What he does within are the embers;
his rejoicings are the sparks.
"A woman, O Gautama, is indeed the fire; her lap is the fuel,
for by means of it she is kindled for the production of sons and so forth."
That which he whispers is smoke,
because whispering arises from woman;
the womb is flame, because of its redness.
That which one performs within constitutes the embers due to their connection with fire;
the delights are fragments of pleasure, like sparks, because of their insignificance. //1//
Into this very fire, the gods offer semen; from that oblation,
the embryo comes into being.
In this very fire, the gods offer semen as an oblation;
from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
Thus, through the sequence of the offerings of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen, it is the waters themselves that become the embryo.

In that context, because water is the constituent element of the oblation, there is an intention to emphasize its predominance in the statement, "In the fifth oblation, waters come to be called 'man'.
However, it is not the case that waters alone initiate the effects such as Soma and the rest;
nor do the waters exist here as non-tripartite (*atrivṛtkṛta*).

Even though they have been made tripartite, the acquisition of specific designations is observed—such as "this is earth," "these are waters," or "this is fire"—based on the predominance of one or another element.

Therefore, it is the elements in their combined state alone that, due to the predominance of water and being associated with action, are called "waters" when they initiate effects such as Soma and so forth.
And the predominance of liquidity is indeed seen in Soma, rain, food, semen, and the body.
And although the body consists largely of fluid and is composed of earth, when the fifth oblation has been offered there, the waters take the form of semen and become the embryo. //2//
Thus ends the eighth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"But it is thus that at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'."
Wrapped in the fetal membrane, that embryo, having lain within for ten or nine months, or for however long it may be, is then born.
Thus, with the words "But thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (ChUpBh_5.9.1), one question has been explained.

As for what was stated in the Vājasaneyaka—that the two oblations, having returned from the heavenly world and so forth, enter the earth, then the man, and then the woman in succession, and thereby arise again toward the world—that is mentioned here as a supplementary point.
And here, in the first question, it was asked: "Do you know where creatures go from here? (ChUp 5.3.2).
And this is its commencement:
that embryo is the fifth specific transformation of the waters— those which are associated with the act of offering and designated by the word "faith"— which,

enveloped by the *ulba* (the inner membrane) and further covered and encased by the *jarāyu* (the outer membrane), having lain within the mother's womb for ten or nine months, or for as long as it may be.
It is born immediately thereafter, in a duration of time that may be shorter or longer;

this is stated for the purpose of inducing detachment, beginning with the words "covered by the womb" (ulbāvṛta), for it is indeed miserable to be in the mother's womb— filled with urine, feces, wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth— wherein the embryo is smeared by those and enveloped by the impure cloth of the womb.

It instills detachment by showing that one who has grown through the entry of the mother’s consumed food and drink—possessing impure seed and red blood—is born with obstructed power, strength, vigor, splendor, wisdom, and activity; and that birth is an even more painful emergence as one is squeezed through the gateway of the womb, having lain within for a very long time—nine or ten months—which is unbearable even for a single moment. //1//
Once born, he lives as long as his lifespan lasts.
When he has departed and reached his destiny, they carry him from here to the very fire from which he came and from which he was produced.

Having been thus born, he lives for as long as his lifespan lasts, performing actions for the sake of going and coming again and again like a water-wheel, or for the sake of revolving horizontally like a potter’s wheel, until the lifespan acquired through his karma is exhausted.

When his life is spent and he has departed— being dead, deceased, and directed by his destiny toward the next world— if he was qualified during his life for Vedic ritual or knowledge, they carry him from this village to the fire for the sake of the fire, that is, to the officiating priests.
The sons carry [the body] for the final rite.

To that very fire from whose presence they came—by way of the sequence of oblations beginning with faith—and from whom they were produced and born, namely from the five fires, they bring it; the meaning is that they cause it to reach its own source, the fire. //2//
Thus ends the ninth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
those who know this thus—
And those who, in the forest, venerate faith as austerity—
they pass into the light;
from the light, into the day.
From the day [he departs] to the waxing fortnight;
from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward. ChU 5.10.1.
From the months [he goes] to the year;
from the year to the sun;
from the sun to the moon.
From the moon, to lightning;
there a person who is not human leads them to Brahman.
"This is the path of the gods. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.2)
"Do you know where creatures go from here?"—this question has now presented itself and must be answered.
