In that regard, those householders who are authorized and have set out toward the world, and who know—that is, understand—in this very way the aforementioned vision of the five fires, [thinking], "We were born in succession from the fires beginning with the heavenly world; we are of the nature of fire, having the five fires as our self"—they [know].
How is it understood that those described as "knowing thus" (*itthaṃ-vid*) are spoken of as exclusively householders and not others?

For it will be stated that those householders who do not know thus, but are devoted solely to sacrifices (*iṣṭa*), public works (*pūrta*), and gifts (*datta*), go to the moon by way of smoke and so forth;
whereas those characterized as forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) who worship with faith and austerity are [included] among those who "know thus."

He will later describe their departure by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*); and because of the remaining possibility (*pāriśeṣya*) and the connection to the *agnihotra* oblation, only householders are understood by the phrase "those who know thus" (*itthaṃ viduḥ*).

But surely, since there are also celibate students (*brahmacārins*) not included [by the householder rule] due to the mention of the village and the mention of the forest, how can the establishment of the remaining possibility be achieved?
This is not a fault.

On account of the authority of the Purāṇas and the Smṛtis, for those of "upward-directed semen"—that is, lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*)—the northern path is intended; thus, they do not require a specific instruction [regarding the means of attainment]. Now, if it is accepted that the state of having upward-directed semen is the cause for embarking on the northern path based on the authority of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, then the knowledge of "being thus" (*itthaṃvit*) would become purposeless. No, for it is purposeful with respect to householders.

For those householders who do not know "thus" (the qualified Brahman), the southern path consisting of smoke and so forth is well known by their very nature. But as for those who know "thus"—that is, those who know the qualified Brahman or the other [unqualified] Brahman—they go by the northern path, according to the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him or not, [they go] to light alone. [Objection:

Is it not improper to claim that while the state of being an *āśrama* is common to both celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*) and householders, only the celibates travel by the northern path and not the householders? [Response: No, because of the abundance of Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra* [performed by householders].
And even if that were the case, there is no fault;
for they are indeed impure.
For them, passion and hatred arise from the causes of association with enemies and friends;
likewise, merit and demerit arise from the causes of harming and favoring others.
Furthermore, many causes of impurity, such as violence, falsehood, deceit, and unchastity, are unavoidable for them.
Therefore, they are impure;
because of their impurity, there is no going by the northern path.

On the other hand, others—whose selves are purified by the avoidance of violence, falsehood, deceit, unchastity, and so forth, and who are free from passion (*rajas*) due to the avoidance of enmity, attachment, hatred, and the like—for them, the northern path is appropriate.

And so the authors of the Purāṇas say: "Those who desired offspring, the undiscerning, have resorted to cremation grounds; those who did not desire offspring, the discerning, have indeed attained immortality.
Thus they speak.
Since those householders who possess such knowledge and forest-dwellers follow the same path and attain the same fruit of immortality, it would follow that knowledge is useless for forest-dwellers;
and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti:
"Neither do the sacrificial gifts reach there, nor the ignorant ascetics."
And [the statement] "if it is not known, it does not benefit him" is contradictory;
this is not so, because what is intended is immortality (*amṛtatva*) as a state lasting until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*).
Regarding that very point, it has been stated by the authors of the Purāṇas: "Indeed, the state until the dissolution of all beings is called immortality."

With reference to that absolute immortality, such scriptural passages as "No sacrificial gifts go there" and "He does not benefit him who knows [Brahman] without knowing this" are intended; therefore, there is no contradiction.
If it be argued that there is a contradiction with such scriptural texts as "They do not return again" and "They do not return to this human whirlpool," we say:
No, because of the qualification "this human [whirlpool]" and because of the statement that for them there is no return here.
For if they were not to return at all, the qualification "to this human state here" would be meaningless.
If it is argued that "this" and "here" refer merely to the general form (ākṛti), we say no;
since the meaning of eternal non-return is already understood from the word "non-return" itself, the postulation of a "form" is redundant.
Therefore, for the purpose of making the qualification "here" meaningful, it must be understood that there is no movement elsewhere.

Furthermore, for those who possess the realization that "Being is one alone, without a second," there is no departure through the artery at the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*) by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*), as it is said:
"Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman."
"Therefore, all that became it";
"His vital breaths do not depart;
they are merged right here"—from hundreds of such scriptural passages.

If it is argued that the meaning intended here is that when the living self (jīva) desires to depart from the body, the vital breaths (prāṇas) do not depart separately but go along with it—this is not so;

for in that case, the qualification "they are merged right here" would be redundant. Furthermore, since the departure together with the vital breaths is already established by the statement, "all the vital breaths follow after [the self] as it departs."
Therefore, the doubt regarding [the prāṇas] departing is entirely unfounded.

Even when it is stated that "they do not depart from there" because liberation is distinct from the course of transmigratory existence and one might suspect the prāṇas accompany the individual soul (jīva), even then the qualification "they are merged right here" would be purposeless.
Furthermore, for one who is deprived of the vital breaths (prāṇas), neither movement nor the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) is possible.

Since the Self is omnipresent and partless, the mere connection with the vital breaths—like sparks from a fire—is indeed the cause of the distinction known as the state of being a living soul. Therefore, in the absence of that [connection], it is impossible to conceive of either the state of being a living soul or movement, provided that the Śruti scriptures are the authority.
It cannot be imagined that a minute part called the *jīva*, being real, departs by splitting off from the [real] existent while making a hole in that which is of the nature of reality.

Therefore, it is understood that for one who meditates on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*), the passage through the artery along with the vital breaths as expressed in the text, "Going upwards by those two, he attains immortality" (*tadyordhvamāyannamṛtatvameti*), is dependent [on something else], and that this immortality is not liberation itself.
This is because, after stating, "That is the unconquered city; that is the lake Airammadīya," the text specifies, "This is the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) only for them."

Therefore, those householders who know the five fires, and those who dwell in the forest—namely the *vānaprasthas* and *parivrājakas*—together with the lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacāris*), worship [the path] by means of faith, austerity, and so forth; that is to say, they are full of faith and are ascetics.
The word "worship" (*upāsate*) signifies intentness (*tātparya*), as in the expression "they worship sacrifice, public works, and charity."

Furthermore, according to another scriptural passage, those who meditate upon Brahman as the True (Satya), known as Hiraṇyagarbha, all attain—that is, they reach—the Radiance, the deity presiding over the Radiance.
The rest is the same as explained in the commentary on the fourth path.
This path of the gods has been described as terminating at Satyaloka, not extending outside the cosmic egg.
This is because of the wording of the mantra: "That which is between the father and the mother. (1.2)
Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, "Sacrifices, works of public utility,
and gifts are [the path]," they pass into smoke.
From smoke [he goes] to the night;
from the night to the waning fortnight;
from the waning fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves southward.
These do not reach the year. ChU 5.10.3.

Now, the word "atha" (now) serves to introduce a different subject. "Those householders who are in the village"—the term "village" is a specific qualification of householders intended to distinguish them from those who dwell in the forest.
Just as "forest" is a qualification for forest-hermits and wandering mendicants intended to distinguish them from householders, so it is here.
They worship such things as *iṣṭāpūrta*: *iṣṭa* refers to Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra; *pūrta* refers to the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, gardens, and so forth;
and *datta* refers to the distribution of wealth to worthy recipients outside the sacrificial altar according to one's ability—these forms of service, protection, and the like, they revere.
Because the word "iti" has the sense of indicating a manner, they—being devoid of such vision—attain, that is, reach, smoke, which is the deity presiding over smoke.

Carried by her, they go from smoke to night, the deity of night; from the deity of night to the deity of the dark fortnight, who presides over the dark half of the month; and from the dark fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves southward, toward the southern solstice.

"Savitṛ": the meaning is that they reach those deities presiding over the six months of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). Since the deities of the six months move in groups, the plural "months" (*māsān*) is used; these performers of ritual action do not [reach] them.

The context concerns the year; for the southern and northern solstices are constituent parts of a single year. In that regard, it was stated that for those who have set out on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), there is the attainment of the whole—the year—from the months of the northern solstice. Therefore, here too, having heard of the attainment of the months of the southern solstice which are its constituent parts, [one understands] the attainment of the year as well, which is their whole.
As before, since "attainment" (prāpti) implies "reaching" (āpanna), the attainment of that [year] is prohibited by the statement, "these do not reach the year. //3//
From the months, [they go] to the world of the fathers;
from the world of the fathers, to space.
From space [he comes] to the moon;
this is King Soma,
the food of the gods.
The gods consume it.
From the months [they go] to the world of the fathers (pitṛloka); from the world of the fathers to space; from space to the moon.
Who is this moon that is reached by them? It is this very one seen in the atmosphere, King Soma, the food of the Brāhmaṇas;
that moon is the food of the gods, and the gods, Indra and the others, consume it.
Therefore, having traveled by means of smoke and so forth and become the moon, those performers of ritual acts are consumed by the gods.
[Objection: But surely the performance of sacrifices and other rites would lead to misfortune if they were to be consumed as food by the gods.
[Response: This is not a fault.
This is because by the word "food" (anna), only the means of subsistence is intended;
for they are not consumed by the gods by being taken up as mouthfuls.
Rather, they serve merely as resources for the gods, like women, cattle, servants, and so forth.
Furthermore, the word *anna* (food) is seen used for objects of enjoyment, as in: "Women are food, cattle are food; the subjects are the food of kings," and so forth.
And although these women and others are objects of enjoyment for men, their own experience of enjoyment is not absent.
Therefore, even while being objects of enjoyment for the gods, those who perform ritual actions remain happy and sport with the gods.
And for them, a body suitable for the enjoyment of happiness, composed of water, begins to form in the lunar orb.
This was stated previously: "The waters, signified by the word 'faith,' when offered into the fire of the heavenly world, become King Soma.

Those waters, conjoined with karma and accompanied by the other elements, having reached the heavenly world and attained the state of the moon, become the originators of the bodies of those who worship the sacrifices and other such rites.

And when the final oblation of the body has been offered into the fire and the body is being consumed by the flames, the waters arising from that [oblation] rise upward with the smoke; having enveloped the sacrificer and reached the lunar orb, they become the external constituent of the body, serving as the place for the *kuśa* grass and clay.
Then, abiding in the body thus commenced, they remain experiencing the fruits of sacrifices and other rites. //4//
Having dwelt there until the exhaustion of their merit, they then return again by this very same path to the ether.
From space, it goes to the air;
having become air, it becomes smoke;
having become smoke, it becomes mist. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5)

"Until the exhaustion of that karma which is the cause for its enjoyment"—the term *sampāta* means "that by which [they] fall together," namely the exhaustion of karma; thus, *yāvat-sampātam* means "until the exhaustion of karma.
Having dwelt in that lunar orb for that long, immediately thereafter they return again along this very path (*adhvan*) that is about to be described.
From the use of the expression "they return again," it is understood that they have previously gone to and returned from the lunar orb more than once.
Therefore, having accumulated karma such as sacrifices and other rites in this world, they go to the moon;
and upon the exhaustion of that [karma], they return.
It is not possible for them to remain there even for a single moment.
It is due to the exhaustion of the karma that serves as the cause for their continued existence,
just as a lamp goes out when its oil is exhausted.
In this regard, does one descend from that state upon the total exhaustion of all the karma by which one ascended to the lunar disk, or rather with some residue remaining?
What follows from that?
If there is the exhaustion of all karma, then liberation would occur for one who remains precisely on the lunar orb.
Let us set aside for a moment whether liberation would actually occur right there or not.
Consequently, for one who has arrived here [in the world of men], the experience of a body and so forth would not be possible;
furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such Smṛti texts as, "Then, by what remains...
Now, it may be argued that even apart from sacrifices, public works, and gifts, there exist many other karmas in the world of men that serve as causes for the experience of a body.
Furthermore, they do not experience enjoyment within the lunar disk;
therefore, those [limbs] remain undiminished.
There is no contradiction, for it is precisely those [limbs] by reason of which he ascended to the lunar disk that have become diminished.
Furthermore, the word "remainder" (śeṣa) is not contradictory because all [karmas] share the commonality of being objects of experience (*karman*).
For this very reason, there is no fault in the claim that liberation occurs precisely therein;
for it is possible for each individual sentient being to initiate [the fruition of] those various karmas whose results consist in the enjoyment of diverse and conflicting births.
Furthermore, the exhaustion of all karma in a single birth is not tenable;
for it is recorded in tradition that even a single act such as the killing of a Brahmin initiates multiple births,
and because those who have reached the state of stationary beings and are utterly deluded cannot possibly initiate the karma that serves as a cause for upward progression.
Furthermore, for those who have become embryos and are falling away [from conception], since action (karman) is impossible, transmigration would not occur.
Therefore, the experience of all actions does not take place within a single lifetime.
As for what some say—that at the time of death, through the destruction of the "glory" (śrī) of all actions, actions initiate a new birth—[that is incorrect].
In that regard, it is not tenable to say that some karmas remain merely uncommenced while others initiate a birth;
for death manifests all karmas, just as a lamp manifests its own range of objects.
That [objection] is incorrect.
Because it is accepted that everything has the nature of everything,

for if everything were of the nature of everything, then— given that things are restricted by place, time, and causal conditions— it would not be possible for anything anywhere to be suppressed in its entirety, nor could there be a manifestation in its entirety.
The same would apply to actions as well, provided they possess their respective substrata.

And just as the various contradictory latent impressions (*vāsanā*) formed by previous births as humans, peacocks, monkeys, and so forth, are not destroyed when a birth as a monkey begins through the karma that brings about that monkey-birth, so too it is logical that the karmas which are the causes for attaining other births are likewise not destroyed.

For if all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the experiences of previous births were to be obliterated, then when a monkey birth is commenced by karma having that monkey birth as its cause, a newborn monkey would not possess the skill of clinging to its mother’s belly while she moves from one branch to another;
this is because such a thing has not been practiced in this present life.

Nor can it be said that in his immediately preceding past birth he was actually a monkey, because of the scriptural text: "Knowledge, action, and the impressions of previous experience (pūrvaprajñā) all follow him.
Therefore, just as with latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no total destruction of all karma; thus, the possibility of residual karma remains.
Since this is so, there is no contradiction in the fact that transmigration occurs from the remainder of karma that has been experienced.
What is this path toward which they are said to return?
They return "by the same way," that is, as they came.

But surely, the sequence of going was stated as "from the months to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to space, and from space to the moon," whereas the return is not stated in that same way;
rather, it says "from space to air," and so forth.
How, then, can it be said to be "by the same path as they came"?
This is not a fault.

Since the attainment of space and the attainment of earth are equal, there is no restrictive rule here that they must proceed "exactly as they came. Rather, the rule is that they return even in a manner other than that; they return again and again.
Therefore, the phrase "as they came" is intended merely as an illustration.
Therefore, they first attain elemental space.
Those waters which had constituted their bodies while on the lunar orb dissolve there upon the exhaustion of those karmas that were the cause of their enjoyment,
just as the form of clarified butter dissolves through contact with fire.
Having dissolved, they become subtle, as if having become space while situated in the intermediate region; from that intermediate region they become air.
Established in air and having become air, being carried hither and thither, the one whose karma is exhausted becomes air along with them.
Having become air, together with them he becomes smoke.
Having become smoke, it becomes a cloud, whose nature consists merely of bearing water. //5//
Having become a cloud, he becomes rain;
having become rain, he falls as rain.
These are born here as rice and barley, herbs and trees, sesame and beans; indeed, it is very difficult to emerge from this state.
For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the semen, he becomes that very being again.
Having become mist, it then becomes a cloud capable of pouring rain; having become a cloud, it rains down upon elevated regions.
The meaning is that, with its residual karma remaining, it falls in the form of rain-showers.
These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, beans, and so forth.
The plural designation is used because those whose karma has been exhausted are many;
the singular designation is used for the preceding elements such as clouds because they possess a single uniform nature.
This is because there are thousands of locations—such as mountain slopes, fortresses, rivers, oceans, forests, and desert regions—into which [the waters] fall as showers of rain.
For this very reason, indeed, it is *durniṣprapataram*— difficult to emerge from, difficult to depart from, difficult to escape from.
For once they have been carried by the flow of water down from the mountain slopes and reach the rivers, and from there the ocean, they are devoured by creatures beginning with the letter *m* (fish,
etc.), and these in turn are devoured by others.

And right there in the ocean, they dissolve along with the crocodile; drawn up again by clouds from the waters of the sea, they fall through rain-showers onto an inaccessible rocky slope in the desert region, where they remain until perhaps they are swallowed or eaten by predatory beasts and the like, or consumed by others;
and those too by yet others—in this manner, they undergo such cycles of transformation.
Sometimes those born among immobile beings that are unfit for consumption may wither away right there.

Even among those born in immobile beings that are fit for consumption, the connection with the body of a seed-discharging being is indeed difficult to obtain because immobile beings are so numerous; therefore, it is difficult to escape from that state.
Alternatively, "durniṣprapataram" means more difficult to emerge from, or more difficult to exit, than this state of being rice, barley, and so forth.
Regarding the word *durniṣprapataram*, one *t* should be understood as having been elided.
The state of being rice, barley, and so forth is difficult to escape from; even more difficult to escape than that is the connection with the body of one who emits semen (*retaḥsig*).
This is because those who have eaten [the food] are destroyed in the interval—whether they be children whose semen has not yet risen, or men devoid of virility, or the elderly.

Because food-eaters are numerous, it may happen by some chance that they are eaten by semen-dischargers; when this occurs, the activity of the karma belonging to those who have attained the state of being semen-dischargers gains its functional manifestation.
How so?

For whosoever eats food that is conjoined with residual impressions (*anuśaya*) and pours semen into a woman during her fertile period, he becomes predominantly of that very nature and of that very form. This "predominance" refers to the abundance of the limbs and form [of the previous life]. The residual impression, having entered within the womb of the woman in the form of semen, comes to possess the form of the semen-seeder (the father), because the semen is permeated by the form of the semen-seeder.
For from another Vedic text we learn: "From all its limbs, heat was produced.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the intermediate being] takes on the very form of the one who emits the seed.
For it is so stated:
From a man a man is born, and from a cow only one having the form of a cow, not one of a different species; therefore, it is logical that "he becomes that very thing again.

However, for those others who, unlike those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*), do not ascend to the lunar orb but instead, due to their terrible evil deeds, attain the state of rice, barley, and so forth in this very world, and subsequently the state of humans and the like—for them, as for those possessing residual karma, the crossing back out is not difficult.
Why?

Because by means of their karma they have acquired bodies such as rice, barley, and so forth; thus, when the cause for that enjoyment is exhausted and the bodies of rice-stalks and the like perish, they—possessing consciousness (*savijñāna*)—migrate to ever-new other bodies according to what has been earned by their karma, just like a leech. "Possessing consciousness... [as in the original text].
For another scriptural passage states: "He enters [the womb] endowed with consciousness.

Even though they depart for another body with their organs withdrawn, they nevertheless go to that other body endowed with consciousness, by means of the knowledge of latent impressions (vāsanā) manifested through karma which is the cause for attaining another body—just as in a dream.
This is because of the authority of scripture (*śruti*).
Likewise, the journey by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and the path beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) occurs through an emergent consciousness, as if in a dream,
since the journey is caused by karma that has attained its functional manifestation.

In the case of those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) who have been born as rice and so forth, it is not possible for their semen to be endowed with consciousness upon its connection with the body of the woman who conceives;
for there is no persistence of consciousness during the stages of the rice being cut, threshed, and ground.
[Objection: But since the transition to another body is the same even for those descending from the lunar orb, it is logical that they possess consciousness, just like a leech.

If that were so, then for those who perform sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*), there would result a terrible experience in hell, beginning from the lunar orb and continuing until their birth as Brahmins and others; and if this were the case, the practice of sacrifices and works of public utility prescribed by scripture would lead only to misfortune.
Furthermore, the authority of the Veda would be undermined, because Vedic rituals would be followed by undesirable consequences.
No, for there is a distinction [between the two cases], like climbing a tree and falling from it.

It is appropriate that one who intends to transition from one body to another possesses consciousness (*savijñānatva*) through the cognition manifested by karma, since the karma has acquired its functional activity;
this is just as for one who wishes to grasp fruit while climbing toward the top of a tree.
Likewise, those traveling by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) possess consciousness, as do those ascending to the lunar orb by way of smoke (dhūma-ādi).
However, it is not so for those descending from the lunar orb; they lack consciousness, like those falling from the top of a tree.
And just as it is observed that those struck by a mallet or similar instrument— who, due to the sensation caused by that blow, have their faculties rendered unconscious and obstructed—
are devoid of consciousness while being carried from one place to another by their own bodies; likewise, for those descending from the lunar orb toward the bodies of humans and others,
whose watery bodies have been dissolved through the exhaustion of the karma that was the cause of their heavenly enjoyment, and whose faculties are thus obstructed.

Therefore, as if swooning due to the waters which have not yet abandoned their status as the seed of the body, they descend through this world in the sequence beginning with space; they become conjoined with the bodies of stationary beings according to the class determined by their karma, their cognitive faculties being obstructed so that their consciousness remains unmanifest.
Likewise, during the stages of cutting, threshing, grinding, processing, eating, the transformation into chyle and other fluids, and the emission of semen, they remain as if in a state of swoon.

Because the karma that initiates another body has not yet attained its fruition, the intermediate beings exist in all stages without abandoning their connection to the water that serves as the seed of the body; thus, their possession of consciousness is not contradicted, just as in the case of a leech. However, there is no fault in the fact that they lack distinct cognition during the interval, being like those in a state of swoon.
Nor can it be inferred that Vedic rituals possess a dual nature (as both causes of merit and demerit) simply because they involve violence;
for such violence is enjoined by the scriptures.

According to the Śruti, "One should not harm any living beings except at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*)," it is accepted that violence prescribed by the scriptures does not constitute a cause of unrighteousness (*adharma*).

Even if it were admitted that [Vedic rites] are causes of demerit, their removal by means of mantras—just as poison and the like are removed—is possible; thus, it is not logical for Vedic actions to initiate the effect of suffering, just as the consumption of poison [is neutralized] by a mantra. Therefore:
"Those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, most likely, enter a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya."
Now, those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is certain, enter a foul womb—either the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla.

In this context, among those who possess residual karma (*anuśayin*), those whose conduct (*caraṇa*)—meaning their character (*śīla*)—was pleasant and beautiful in this world are called "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*). By means of such pleasant conduct, they are characterized by a beautiful residual tendency (*anuśaya*), namely meritorious action (*puṇya-karma*);
these are what are termed "those of pleasant conduct."
For it is possible to perceive the existence of virtuous latent dispositions (*śubhānuśaya*) in those who are free from cruelty, falsehood, and deceit.
By means of that merit resulting from such latent dispositions, and by the remainder of the karma to be experienced in the lunar sphere, they indeed quickly approach [their next birth].

The word "that" (*yat*) is an adverbial modifier; thus, they would enter—that is, attain—a pleasant womb free from cruelty and the like, namely, a Brahmin womb, a Kṣatriya womb, or a Vaiśya womb, in accordance with their own past actions.

On the other hand, those who are the opposite of that— whose actions are characterized by foul conduct, who possess impure latent tendencies— it is highly probable that they will attain a foul womb according to their karma; indeed, being devoid of connection with dharma, they will attain a loathsome and foul womb,
such as the womb of a dog or the womb of a pig, precisely in accordance with their own past deeds.

But those twice-born ones who have performed pleasant conduct, if they remain steadfast in their own duties as performers of sacrifices and other rites, they go by the path of smoke and so forth, returning again and again like a water-wheel;
yet if they should attain knowledge, then they go by the path of light and so forth. //7//
Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning creatures, subject to the cycle: "Be born!
Die! This is the third station.
Therefore, that world is not filled up. One should therefore feel aversion toward it. On this point there is this verse: Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.8.

But when they neither practice knowledge nor perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*, then they go by neither of these two aforementioned paths characterized by light, smoke, and so forth; these become those small creatures, such as gadflies, mosquitoes, and insects, which return repeatedly.
Therefore, the meaning is that, having fallen away from both paths, they are indeed born and die again and again.
This is said to be a description of the succession of their births and deaths;
the activity caused by Īśvara is expressed as "be born and die.
In this way, time is spent solely through the characteristics of birth and death.
The meaning is that there is no time for ritual actions or enjoyments [in that state].
This third station, characterized by small creatures, belongs to those wandering in *saṃsāra* when compared to the two paths previously mentioned.
For this reason, even those who travel the southern path return again; indeed, for those not qualified for knowledge and action, the very act of going by the southern path is what defines them.
Therefore, that world is not filled.
As for the fifth question, it has been explained by means of the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).

The first [question] is resolved by means of the southern and northern paths; for although the casting of the dead into the fire is common to both the southern and northern paths, those who turn away from the two paths proceed by the way of light (*arcis*) and so forth, while others do not.
By means of smoke and so forth, they again reach the six months of the northern and southern solstices; having joined together, they turn back once more.
Others [attain] the year, and others the world of the ancestors after the months; thus it has been explained.
Furthermore, the return of those whose latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted is described as proceeding from the lunar sphere through space and so forth.
The non-filling of this world is stated by its own specific term: "Therefore, that world is not filled.
Since the course of saṃsāra is thus miserable, one should feel revulsion toward it.

And because small creatures, whose moments are consumed by the experience of sensations born of birth and death, are cast into a terrible, impassable darkness like a bottomless ocean without a boat, and are without hope of crossing over; therefore, one should feel disgust for such a course of saṃsāra, one should loathe it, one should be filled with revulsion, thinking: "May I never fall into such a terrible great ocean of saṃsāra."
Regarding this matter, there is this verse for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the five fires. //8//
A thief of gold, one who drinks liquor,
one who violates the teacher’s bed, and a slayer of a Brahmin— these are the four.
"These four fall, and the fifth falls by associating with them. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.9)
A thief of gold—that is, one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa;
a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor;
and one who dwells upon the bed of his guru—that is, the wife of his teacher.
The killer of a Brahmin, the slayer of a Brahmin—these four fall; and the fifth is he who associates with them. //9//

Now, he who knows these five fires in this way is not smeared by evil even while associating with those [evil people]. He becomes pure, cleansed, and possesses a world of merit—he who knows thus, he who knows thus. ChUp 5.10.10.
Now, furthermore, he who knows the five fires as they have been described—even if he associates with those who commit great sins—he is not tainted by evil; he remains pure.

Because he has been purified by that vision of the five fires, he becomes one for whom there is a "meritorious world"—that is, the world of Prajāpati and the like—and thus he becomes a possessor of a meritorious world, provided he knows this entire collection of matters as they were asked in the five questions.
The repetition is for the purpose of demonstrating the resolution of all the questions. //10//
Thus ends the tenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi— these were all great householders and great Vedic scholars.
Having come together, they deliberated:
"Who is our self? What is Brahman?"
It has been stated that for one who goes by the southern path, the state of being food is intended, such that "he is the food of the gods, and the gods consume him";
furthermore, the miserable course of transmigratory existence characterized by small creatures has been described.
Desiring to eliminate both these defects, the subsequent text is commenced for the purpose of attaining the state of being the eater through Vaiśvānara.
This is known from such indicative marks as, "You shall eat food; you shall see what is dear.

The narrative, however, is for the sake of easy understanding and for the purpose of demonstrating the proper method of transmitting knowledge. Prācīnaśāla is his name; he is an Aupamanyava, the descendant of Upamanyu.
Satyayajña is his name; he is a Pauluṣi, the descendant of Puluṣa.
Likewise, Indradyumna by name was the descendant of Bhallavi, thus a Bhāllavi; his descendant was Bhāllaveya.
Jana by name was the descendant of Śarkarākṣa, thus a Śārkarākṣya.
Buḍila by name was the descendant of Aśvatarāśva, thus an Āśvatarāśvi.
All five of these were great householders (*mahāśāla*), meaning they were endowed with extensive halls;
they were great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriya*), meaning they were perfected in learning, study, and conduct.
Being such as they were, having come together and assembled, they engaged in some philosophical inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) or deliberation.
How so?
[The question] "Who is our Self (ātman)? What is Brahman? establishes a relationship of mutual qualification between the words "Self" and "Brahman.

The term "Brahman" excludes the Self as limited to the internal body (adhyātma), while the term "Self" excludes the worshipability of a Brahman distinct from the Self, such as the Sun and other deities.

Through non-differentiation, it is established that the Self alone is Brahman and Brahman alone is the Self; thus, Vaiśvānara, who is the Self of all, is Brahman and He is the Self—this is proven by such indicative marks as, "Your head would have fallen off," and "You would have become blind. //1//
They made an agreement:
"Venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self."
"Come, let us go to him.
So they went to him.
Though they deliberated, they failed to reach a certain conclusion and so they made arrangements to find an instructor for themselves.
"Uddālaka Āruṇi"—well-known by name, venerable, and the son of Aruṇa—is currently studying this very Vaiśvānara Self that we have in mind.
"Come, let us go to him now. Having thus decided, they went to him; they approached that Āruṇi. 2.
He made a resolution:
"These great householders, these great Vedic scholars, will question me."
"I shall not accept everything from them; come now, I will instruct another. ChU 5.11.3.
Upon seeing them, he understood the purpose of their arrival and prepared himself accordingly.
How so?
"These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me regarding Vaiśvānara; I shall not be able to provide a complete answer to everything they ask. He did not venture to speak.
Therefore, thinking, "I shall now instruct another among them; I will speak as their teacher," [he departed]. //3//
He said to them:
"Venerable sirs, this Aśvapati Kaikeya is currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara."
"Come, let us go to him.
So they went to him.
Having thus prepared them, he said to them: "Venerable sirs, this man named Aśvapati, the son of Kekaya—a Kaikeya—is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self thoroughly," and so on, as before. 4.
When they had arrived, he had separate honors prepared for each of them.
Then, rising in the morning, he said:
"In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, and no drunkard;
there is none who has not established the sacred fires, nor any who is unlearned, nor any who acts wantonly—how then could there be a wanton woman?
Indeed, venerable sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice."
"As much wealth as I shall give to each individual officiating priest, so much shall I give to the venerable ones.
May the venerable ones dwell here. (ChU 5.11.5)
They said:
"Whatever purpose a person may pursue, that indeed one should declare.
You are currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara."
"Tell us that very thing," they said.
He said to them,
"I shall answer you in the morning.
With fuel in their hands, they returned in the forenoon.
Having initiated them without the usual formalities, he said this to them:
When they had arrived, the king had the priests and servants provide them individually with various honors and hospitable receptions.
On another day, as the king was rising in the morning, he approached them with humility and said, "Accept this wealth from me.
When he was refused by them, he thought, "They surely perceive some fault in me, since they do not accept wealth from me," and desiring to demonstrate his own virtuous conduct, he spoke as follows.
In my realm, there is no thief who steals the property of others;
no miser who fails to give despite possessing wealth; and no one who drinks liquor, especially among the best of the twice-born.
One who has not maintained the sacred fires shall not possess a hundred cattle;
nor shall one who is ignorant [of the law] [possess them] in accordance with his entitlement;
nor shall one who acts according to his own will go unto the wives of others.
For this very reason, the meaning is that how could a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) not be one of evil conduct?
When they replied, "We do not seek wealth," he said: "Thinking it to be small, these [women] do not accept the wealth;
indeed, O venerable ones, I am about to perform a sacrifice in a few days."
"For that purpose, I have set aside wealth such that I shall give to each venerable one as much wealth as is prescribed for each officiating priest (ṛtvij).
May the venerable ones stay and witness my sacrifice. Having been thus addressed, they said:
"Whatever purpose or need a man has for which he would approach someone, he should indeed state that very purpose."
"This alone is the purpose of our coming"—this is the principle of the virtuous.
We are seekers of the knowledge of Vaiśvānara;
you indeed now teach us this very Self as Vaiśvānara, that is, you know it correctly.
"Therefore, tell that very thing to us. Being thus addressed, he said to them:

"In the morning, I shall answer you; I shall give you a reply. Having been told this, they—knowing the king's intention and with fuel in their hands—that is, carrying loads of sacrificial wood—approached the king on the following day in the forenoon.

Since it was thus that these great *mahāśāla* Brāhmaṇas, who were great *śrotriya*s, having abandoned the pride of being *mahāśāla*s, approached with fuel-bundles in their hands and with humility the king—who was inferior by birth—in order to acquire knowledge; so too should others who desire to acquire knowledge act.
And he imparted knowledge to them even without having initiated them, that is, without performing the *upanayana* ceremony for them.
The meaning of the narrative is that, just as [Prajāpati] bestowed knowledge out of pride upon those who were worthy, so too should knowledge be given by another.
This connects with what is to be said next: "He spoke this very knowledge of Vaiśvānara. (5–7)
Thus ends the eleventh section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"Aupamanyava, upon which Self do you meditate?"
"O Venerable King," he said, "it is indeed heaven.
This is the self named Sutejas (the Brilliant), the Vaiśvānara self, which you venerate as the self.
Therefore, in your lineage, pressed soma, further-pressed soma, and continuously pressed soma are seen."
He states how he spoke: "O Aupamanyava, which Self as Vaiśvānara do you meditate upon?"—thus he questioned him.
Now, one might object: "Is this not improper, for a teacher questions his disciple?
This is no fault.
"Approach me with what you already know; thereafter I shall tell you what is beyond that," according to the principle seen [in this teaching].

Furthermore, in another instance, a question is observed to have been asked by Ajātaśatru for the purpose of generating insight in a disciple who lacked it: "Where was he then? Whence did he come? [The son replied:
"O Venerable King, I meditate upon heaven itself as Vaiśvānara. He said: "So be it."

This indeed is Vaiśvānara known as "Sutejas" (the One of Excellent Splendor), he whose splendor is beautiful; for he is a part of the Self, you meditate upon him as the Self or a portion of the Self. Therefore, from this meditation on Sutejas Vaiśvānara, your soma—which is pressed out (*suta*) in the ritual, poured forth (*prasuta*), and abundantly extracted (*āsuta*) in the multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*) and other rites—shall be excellent.
"In your family, those born of your lineage are seen to be exceedingly active in ritual works"—this is the meaning. //1//

"He eats food and sees what is dear; he eats food and sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family—he who thus worships this Vaiśvānara Self. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.12.2)
"But you are the head," he said. "Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me. (ChU 5.12.2)

"Being one whose digestive fire is kindled, you shall eat food and see what is dear and desired—sons, grandsons, and so forth. Others also eat food and see what is dear; he possesses the state of being a performer of rites such as the Suta, Prasuta, and Āsuta sacrifices, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family—he who, in whatever way described, meditates upon this Vaiśvānara."
This is indeed the head of Vaiśvānara as the Self, but it is not Vaiśvānara in his entirety.

Therefore, because you meditated upon Vaiśvānara with the notion that he was the whole, your head—your crown—would have fallen off, having been struck down by your erroneous grasp, had you not come to me. Had you not come, you would not have arrived.
The intended meaning is: "It is well that you have come to me. //2//
Thus ends the twelfth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi:
"Prācīnayogya, as what do you meditate upon the Self?
"The sun alone, O Venerable King," he replied.
"This indeed is the Self known as Vaiśvānara, the one of all forms, which you meditate upon as the Self."
Therefore, many forms of yours are seen in your lineage.
Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi: "O Prācīnayogya, upon what Self do you meditate? He replied, "Sir, O King, I meditate upon Āditya alone. [The teacher asked:

"Because of its white, blue, and other colors, Āditya is 'possessed of all forms' (*viśvarūpa*), or because it consists of all forms. For all forms indeed belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; therefore, Āditya is *viśvarūpa*. From meditating upon him, much wealth of manifold forms is seen as an instrument for your purposes here and in the hereafter within your family. //1//
A chariot drawn by mules, female slaves, and gold neck-ornaments shall attend you;
you shall eat food and behold what is dear.
"He who venerates this Vaiśvānara Self in this way sees food and becomes beloved; there is spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) in his family.
"But this," he said, "is only the eye of the Self. You would have become blind had you not come to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.13.2)
Moreover, following you shall be a chariot yoked with two mules—a mule-chariot—and a necklace of slave-girls—a necklace accompanied by slave-girls.
"You shall eat food," and so forth, is the same as before.
However, Savitṛ is the eye of Vaiśvānara.
"Because you did not come to me, you would have become blind, you would have been deprived of sight, due to your worshiping him with a collective intellect," as before. //2//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he spoke to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya:
"Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate?
"On Vāyu alone, O venerable King," he replied.
"This Vaiśvānara Self, whom you meditate upon as the Self, is indeed the 'Manifold-pathed' (pṛthagvartman) Self."
Therefore, offerings come to you from all sides, and rows of chariots follow you from every direction.
Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate? and so forth, as before.

The wind that moves along various paths—that is, whose paths are manifold due to its divisions such as the *āvaha*, *udvaha*, and others—is this "pṛthagvartman" (multi-pathed) wind. From meditating upon Vaiśvānara as that multi-pathed Self, various offerings—consisting of garments, food, and the like—come to you from various directions. These are the "balayaḥ" (offerings) that arrive.
Separate rows of chariots, even lines of chariots, follow after you. //1//
"He eats food and sees what is dear;
he eats food and sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), for one who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self."
"But this, indeed, is the breath of the self," he said.
"Your breath would have departed had you not come to me."
"You shall eat food," and so on, is the same as before.
He said, "This breath of yours has indeed perished; your vital breath would have departed—that is, it would have left you—if you had not come to me."
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya:
"Śārkarākṣya, as which Self do you worship?
"As space alone, O Venerable King," he replied.
"This Vaiśvānara Self that you worship is indeed the manifold (bahula) Self."
Therefore, you are abundant in offspring and in wealth.
Then he said, "Janam," and so forth; the rest is the same.
This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self, the manifold (*bahula*). Its manifoldness is due to the all-pervasiveness of space (*ākāśa*).

And because you have worshipped many virtues, you are "bahula," abundant, in terms of progeny—characterized by sons, grandsons, and so forth—and in terms of wealth, such as gold and other riches. //1//
"He eats food and sees what is dear;
he eats food and sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), for him who thus worships this Vaiśvānara Self."
"But this doubt regarding the self," he said,
"would have dissolved away from you had you not come to me."

"But this doubt—this 'sandeha'—is the middle body of Vaiśvānara. Since the root *dih* means 'to accumulate,' the body is abundant with flesh, blood, bones, and so forth; that is your 'sandeha. Your body would have perished—it would have been shattered—if you had not come to me. //2//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi:
"Vaiyāghrapadya, as what do you meditate upon the Self?
"As water alone, O Venerable King," he replied.
"This indeed is the Self Vaiśvānara, the Wealth, which you meditate upon as the Self."
Therefore, you are possessed of wealth and possessed of nourishment.
Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, and so forth, as before.
"This indeed is Rayi; the Vaiśvānara Self is of the nature of wealth.
From water comes food, and from that, wealth."
Therefore, you are possessed of wealth, possessed of riches, and possessed of nourishment in your body; for nourishment has food as its cause. //1//
"You shall eat food; you shall see what is dear.
He who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster.
"This bladder is your own," he said.
"Your bladder would have burst had you not come to me."

"But this bladder is the bladder of the Self, Vaiśvānara; the bladder is the place for collecting urine. Your bladder would have burst—that is, it would have been torn asunder—if you had not come to me. //2//
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Then he spoke to Uddālaka Āruṇi.
"Gautama, as what do you meditate upon as the Self?
"The earth alone, O Blessed One, O King," he replied.
"This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is the foundation, which you meditate upon as the Self."
Therefore, you are established with offspring and cattle.
"You eat food and you see what is dear;
he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).
But these, he said, are merely the feet of the Self."
"Your feet would have withered away had you not come to me. (ChU 5.17.2)
Then he said to Uddālaka, and so forth, as before.
"O venerable King," he replied, "the earth itself.
"This indeed is the foundation; it is the feet of Vaiśvānara."
"Your feet would have withered, they would have become faded and limp, had you not come to me. //1-2//
Thus spoke [the teacher] to them. *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, Fifth Chapter, Seventeenth Section.
Indeed, you all eat food while knowing this Vaiśvānara Self as if it were separate.
But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self as the measure of a span, as the all-pervading,
eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.

He said this to those who possessed the aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara: "You indeed,"—the words *vai* and *khalu* here are merely expletives—"you, though knowing this single Self, Vaiśvānara, as being non-different, eat food as if it were separate, because of your perception of a limited self; you are like those born blind [who do not see] an elephant."

But he who [meditates upon] this one [Self] as thus distinguished by the aforementioned members, beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet, is "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*); that is, it is measured (*mīyate*) or known through the internal [members] beginning with the sky as the head and ending with the earth as the feet, which are the "spans" (*prādeśa*).
Or, it is "measured by a span" because it is measured as the eater within the organs, such as the mouth.
Alternatively, "measuring a span" (prādeśamātra) refers to the extent of the space from the heavenly world down to the earth;
for the heavenly world and so forth are designated (adiśyante) as "spans" (prādeśāḥ) by means of the pre-eminent scripture (pra-śāsreṇa), and its measure is that much.
However, in another Vedic branch, they conceive it as measuring a span because it extends from the head down to the chin.
But here, that is not intended;

for [the text] concludes with "Of this very Self," and so forth. It is called *abhivimāna* because it is measured out as the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) and known as "I"; this very Self is Vaiśvānara.

He leads all men to a destination corresponding to their merit and demerit; this Lord Vaiśvānara is indeed the Self of all. Or, he is Vaiśvānara because he is the "all" (viśva) and the "man" (nara), since he is the Self of all.
Or, he is Vaiśvānara because he is led by all men as their innermost self (pratyagātman). One should meditate upon him in this manner.
He who knows Vaiśvānara as the eater of food—being the Self of all—eats food in all worlds, beginning with the heavenly world; in all beings, both moving and non-moving;
and in all selves, that is, in bodies, senses, minds, and intellects (for it is in these that the designation "self" is applied). He eats food while being the universal Self;
the meaning is not that he eats like an ignorant person who identifies only with the physical body. //1//
Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform),

the breath is *pṛthagvartmātmā* (the self of diverse paths), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), the feet are the earth itself, and the chest is the sacrificial altar, with the hairs being the sacrificial grass.
The sacrificial grass is the heart; the Gārhapatya fire is the mind; the Anvāhāryapacana fire is the mouth; and the Āhavanīya fire is the breath.
Why is it so?

Because of this: of that very same Self, Vaiśvānara, who has been under discussion, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly shining), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (of various paths), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), and the feet are indeed the earth.

Alternatively, this statement is for the purpose of an injunction, meaning "one should meditate thus. Now, desiring to identify the Agnihotra sacrifice with the eating of food by one who knows Vaiśvānara, he says: Of this eater, Vaiśvānara, the chest itself is the altar (*vedi*), because of the similarity in shape.
The hairs on the chest are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); they are seen spread out upon the chest just as sacrificial grass is spread upon an altar.
The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, for from the heart the mind is, as it were, led forth and remains immediately adjacent to it; therefore, the Anvāhāryapacana fire is the mind.
The mouth is the Āhavanīya fire, for food is offered into it, just as oblations are offered into the Āhavanīya. //2//
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
whatever food arrives first, that is to be offered as an oblation.
The first oblation he should offer, let him offer with the words, "Svāhā to Prāṇa!
Thereby Prāṇa is satisfied.
This being the case, whatever food may come at the time of eating for the purpose of a meal, that is to be offered as an oblation.
Since what is intended here is merely the completion of the *agnihotra* itself, the detailed procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of the *agnihotra* do not apply here.

Regarding how the eater should offer that first oblation which he might offer, the text says: "To Prāṇa, Svāhā!"—by this mantra; the meaning is that, because of the word "oblation" (*āhuti*), one should cast into the mouth a portion of food of the same measure as a sacrificial cutting (*avadāna*).
By that, the vital breath is satisfied. //1//
When the vital breath is satisfied, the eye is satisfied;
when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied.
When the Āditya is satisfied, the sky is satisfied.
When the sky is satisfied, whatever the sky and the Āditya preside over is satisfied.
Following that satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is satisfied, the eye, the sun, the sky, and so forth are satisfied; and whatever else the sky and the sun preside over as their domain, that too is satisfied.
Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied oneself while eating—this is directly perceived.
Furthermore, [one is satisfied] through offspring and the like.
*Tejas* is the radiance, brilliance, or confidence residing in the body;
*brahmavarcasa* is the splendor resulting from virtuous conduct and the study of the Vedas. //2//
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, when he should offer the second oblation, he should offer it with: "Svāhā to Vyāna!"
The vyāna breath is satisfied.
When the vyāna breath is satisfied, the ear is satisfied;
when the ear is satisfied, the moon is satisfied;
when the moon is satisfied, the quarters of space are satisfied.
When the quarters are satisfied, whatever the quarters and the moon preside over—that is satisfied.
Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Now, as for that which is the second, the fourth, and the fifth—this is the same [as before].
Thus ends the twentieth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which he should offer as the third oblation, he should offer with the words: "Svāhā to Apāna!"
The apāna breath is satisfied. // ChUp 5.21.1 //
When the apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied;
when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied;
when Agni is satisfied, the earth is satisfied.
When the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and fire preside over is satisfied.
Through their satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge. Thus it is said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.21.2)
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for the fourth [oblation] which one might offer, one should offer it with the formula: "Svāhā to Samāna!"
Being the same, he is satisfied.
When the breath is satisfied, the mind is satisfied;
when the mind is satisfied, Parjanya is satisfied;
when Parjanya is satisfied, lightning is satisfied.
When lightning is satisfied, whatever lightning and rain preside over is satisfied.
Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, as for the fifth oblation he should offer, he should offer it with the words: "Svāhā to Udāna!"
The *udāna* breath is satisfied. // ChUp 5.23.1 //
When the upward-moving vital breath (udāna) is satisfied, the skin is satisfied; when the skin is satisfied, the wind is satisfied;
when the wind is satisfied, space is satisfied;
when space is satisfied, whatever the wind and space preside over is satisfied.
Following his satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He who, not knowing this, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice—it would be as if, having removed the live coals, he were to offer the oblation into ashes. Such would that [sacrifice] be.

Whoever, being ignorant of this aforementioned vision of Vaiśvānara, performs the well-known Agnihotra sacrifice— that act of his offering in the Agnihotra would be equivalent to casting oblations into ashes instead of embers fit for an offering, in the place where no offering is made; this is said by way of censuring the ordinary Agnihotra in comparison with the Agnihotra of one who knows Vaiśvānara.
The Agnihotra sacrifice is praised for those who know Vaiśvānara. //1//
Now, when one who knows this thus offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, for him the offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.
And for this reason, this Agnihotra is distinguished.
How so?

"Now, he who, knowing it thus, performs the Agnihotra"—that is, one who possesses the aforementioned knowledge of Vaiśvānara—for him [the results accrue] "in all worlds," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
Because these two [expressions], "he eats the offered food" and "he eats the oblation," have the same meaning. //2//
Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all the evils of one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice consumed.

Furthermore, just as the tip of a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass, when cast or thrown into a fire, would be consumed and burnt away instantly, even so all the evils— known as merit and demerit— accumulated over many births, as well as those existing prior to the arising of knowledge and those coexisting with knowledge, are consumed without remainder for this wise man who has become the Self of all and is the eater of all food.

They would be burnt away, with the exception of the evil karma that initiated the present body; for that [karma] has already begun to bear fruit—like an arrow aimed at a target—and thus it is not burnt.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice or eats [his food], [is liberated]. //3//
Therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give even the remnants of his food to a Caṇḍāla,
it would be as if he had offered it into Vaiśvānara himself.
On this point, there is this verse: ChUp 5.24.4.

Even if he were to give leavings—that is, offer leavings—to a Caṇḍāla, one who is unworthy of receiving leavings, even if he were to perform that which is forbidden, namely the giving of leavings—nevertheless, that would be offered into the Vaiśvānara fire residing within his own self; it would not be a cause for demerit. Thus, [the text] praises knowledge itself. Regarding this matter of praise, there is also this verse, a mantra: //4//
Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother,
so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra.
Just as in this world hungry children, being famished, wait upon their mother, thinking, "When will our mother give us food?",
even so all beings who subsist on food wait upon the Agnihotra meal of one who knows this, thinking, "When indeed will he eat?"
The meaning is that the entire world becomes satisfied by the meal of the wise. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter. //5// //
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
START ChUp 6.1.1 Śvetaketu Āruṇeya was once a youth.
His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student."
"Indeed, my dear, one born of our family does not become like a mere Brahmin in name (brahmabandhu) without having studied the Vedas. (ChU 6.1.1)
The connection of this chapter begins with the words, "Now there was Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi.

It has been stated that "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it. How this world is born from it, dissolves back into it, and lives by it—that must now be explained.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that when one wise person eats, the entire world becomes satisfied; this is possible only if the Self, which dwells in all beings, is one, and not if there were a plurality of selves.
And as to how that oneness [is established], this sixth chapter is commenced for that purpose.
The narrative of the father and son is intended to demonstrate the supreme excellence of this knowledge.
Śvetaketu by name—*ha* is used in the sense of tradition—he was the grandson of Āruṇi (*Āruṇeya*). He existed [in the past].

Thinking that his son was a worthy vessel for knowledge and observing that the time for his initiation (upanayana) was passing by, the father, Āruṇi, said: "O Śvetaketu, go to a teacher suitable for our family and dwell there in the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). It is not fitting, O gentle one, that you, being born of our lineage, should become like a mere Brahmin in name (brahmabandhu)—one who merely designates Brāhmaṇas as his kinsmen without having studied
