Having lived away for twelve years, he returned at twenty-four years of age, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he came home. His father said to him: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2*
From this, it is inferred that the father was away on a journey, since,

though he himself was possessed of the necessary qualities, he did not initiate his son. That Śvetaketu, having been addressed by his father, approached a teacher when he was twelve years old and remained with him until he was twenty-four.

Having studied all four Vedas and understood their meaning, he was "high-minded"— one whose mind is great and profound, and who considers himself superior to others; being such a high-minded person, he was "conceited about his learning," one whose nature is to think of himself as learned, and thus, being "stiff" or unyielding in disposition, he returned home.
Seeing his son in such a state—possessing a character so unbecoming of himself, arrogant, and conceited—the father spoke out of a desire to lead him into the True Dharma:

"Śvetaketu, since you are so high-minded, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and yet so arrogant, what excellence have you obtained from your teacher? Or have you asked the teacher about that *ādeśa*? By *ādeśa* is meant that which is to be understood solely through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher; it is that by which the Supreme Brahman is pointed out—that *ādeśa* you have not asked of your teacher.
"Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so conceited, considering yourself well-versed in the Vedas, and so arrogant—
have you perhaps asked for that instruction by which what is unheard becomes heard, what is unthought becomes thought, and what is unknown becomes known?"
"How, O Blessed One, does that instruction come about? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3)

He specifies that instruction: by hearing which instruction, even what has not been heard becomes heard; what has not been thought becomes thought; what has not been reasoned out becomes reasoned out; what has not been understood becomes understood; and what was uncertain becomes certain. It is understood from the narrative that even after one has mastered all the Vedas and attained all other objects of knowledge, one remains truly unfulfilled as long as one does not know the reality of the Self.

Having heard this wonder, he said: "How indeed can this unknown become known through the knowledge of something else? Thinking thus, he asks: "In what way, O Venerable One, does that instruction come to be? //3//

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known— the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'— so it is. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4)
Listen, my dear, to how that instruction is given:
just as in the world, when one clod of clay—the cause—is known, all other things made of clay, the entire range of products of clay, become known.
How is it that by knowing the cause, the clod of clay, the effect, which is otherwise, becomes known?
This is not a fault,
because the effect is non-different from its cause.
As for what you think— that when one thing is known, another is not known— [that is not so].
This would indeed be so, if the effect were something other than the cause; however, the effect is not something other than the cause.
How then is it that in the world one says, "this is the cause" and "this is its transformation"?
Listen:
"a mere verbal handle" means a beginning in speech, or an object of speech;
what is this modification? It is a name—*nāmadheya* being simply *nāman*, with the suffix *-dheya* added in its own sense.

Name is merely an object of speech; it is only a designation and not a modification. In the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "modification" that exists as a reality. Rather, it is only the clay—clay alone—that is the real, existing entity. //4//

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold, everything made of gold might be known— the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.5)
Just as, my dear, by means of a single piece of gold—a lump of gold—all other products made from it, such as bracelets, crowns, and armlets, would be known;
the phrase "a mere modification of speech" and so forth is the same [as before]. //5//
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—
the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'iron' alone is the reality."
"In this way, my dear, that instruction is given," so it was said.
"Surely those venerable ones did not know this;
for if they had known it, why would they not have told me?
Let the venerable one himself tell it to me."
"So be it, Somya," he said.
"Just as, my dear, by means of one piece of black iron— meaning, by means of a nail-cutter characterized by it—
all black iron, that is, the entire range of objects made from black iron, would be known; the rest is the same."

The employment of numerous examples is for the purpose of following the various distinctions among the subjects of the illustrations and for the sake of firm conviction. When the father had said, "My dear, that instruction which I have spoken is thus," the other replied: "Surely those venerable, worshipful teachers of mine did not know, they did not understand, this very matter which you have spoken."
"For if they had known this matter, how would they not have told it to me—me, who am virtuous, devoted, and a follower? Therefore, I think they did not know it.
[The son spoke thus] even though he was stating an unmentionable humiliation of his teacher, out of fear of being sent back to the teacher's house.
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Tell me that very thing by knowing which I may attain omniscience; please explain it to me. Thus addressed, the father replied, "So be it, my dear. (6–7)
Thus, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the first section of the sixth chapter:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
Regarding this, some say: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-being (asat), one only, without a second;
from that non-being, being (sat) was born. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)

"Being indeed" (*sadeva*) means that which is mere existence (*astitāmātra*), a subtle, undifferentiated, all-pervading, one, stainless, partless consciousness, as is understood from all the Vedāntas.
The word "indeed" (*eva*) is for the purpose of restriction.
To the question, "What is being restricted? he says:
This world, which is perceived as modified by name, form, and action, was indeed that very Being (sat); thus it is connected with the word "was" (āsīt).
When it is asked, "When was this indeed Being? it is said: "In the beginning," that is, prior to the origin of the world.
Is it not the case that this [world] is now being qualified by the statement "that which was at the beginning"?
No; how then is there a qualification?
Even now this is indeed existent, but because it is characterized by name and form, it becomes the object of the word and the cognition "this," and thus it is called "this."
But prior to creation, this [world] was accessible only through the mere cognition of the word "Being" (sat); thus it is determined that "In the beginning, this was Being alone.
For prior to creation, it is not possible to apprehend this entity as being possessed of name and form, just as during the state of deep sleep.
The intention is that, just as one who has arisen from deep sleep perceives only existence, realizing that in deep sleep the reality was solely Being alone, so it was prior to creation.

Just as it is said in the world: when a potter, desiring to create a jar or the like in the forenoon, has observed a lump of clay spread out and has gone to another village, and having returned in the afternoon, observes there the very same effect divided into many varieties such as jars, bowls, and so forth, he says, "This jar, bowl, and so on, existed only as clay in the forenoon"; in the same way, it is said here also: "In the beginning, this was indeed Being alone."
"Only one" means that there is nothing else apart from what has fallen within its own causal sphere; thus it is said to be "only one.
"Without a second" means:

Just as, apart from clay, another instrumental cause such as a potter is observed who transforms the clay into the form of a jar and so forth, so too, in the case of Being (*sat*), a second distinct entity that would serve as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) apart from Being itself is logically required; however, this is negated by the term "without a second" (*advitīya*).
It is called "without a second" because no second distinct entity exists for it.

But surely, even in the Vaiśeṣika position, co-referentiality with "existent" (sat) is established for everything, because the word and cognition "existent" recur in the case of substances, qualities, and so forth; for we observe such expressions as "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action."

It may be true that this is so now; however, prior to its production, it is not accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas that this effect was indeed existent, because they accept the non-existence of the effect prior to its production.
Nor do they maintain that the Existent alone, without a second, existed prior to production.
Therefore, this "Existent" is said to be a cause other than the "Existent" imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, as evidenced by the analogies of clay and the like.

Regarding this very matter of determining the nature of reality prior to its origination, certain Nihilists (vaināśika), while attempting to determine the nature of reality, say: "Prior to its origination, this world was one alone, without a second, consisting merely of the non-existence of Being.
For the Buddhists postulate that the reality prior to origination is merely the absence of Being;
they do not, however, accept any other entity that stands as the opposite of Being.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that reality consists in that which is grasped as "existent" or "non-existent," being the opposite of what is perceived as it truly is.

But if the nihilists (Vaināśikas) intend for there to be a mere absence of existence prior to origination, how can they speak of a connection with time—saying "this was non-existent before origination"—as well as a connection with number, and their claim of "being without a second"? How can these things be predicated of them?
"Certainly, it is not tenable for those who accept the mere existence and non-existence [of things];
even the acceptance of mere non-existence is untenable, because an accepter cannot logically exist if there is no act of accepting.
If you argue that the accepter is accepted only now and did not exist prior to the production [of the object], we say: no."

Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-existence of that which exists prior to its production, the conceptualization that "prior to production it was simply non-existent" is untenable.

If it is objected: "But how can the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence—namely, 'In the beginning, this was non-existent, one only, without a second'—be established if the referent of a word is the form of a real entity (*vastvākṛti*)?
And if these are not established, would it not follow that this sentence lacks authority (*apramāṇa*)? [The response follows:]...
This is not a fault,
because the sentence is intended to exclude the apprehension of existence.
To begin with, this word "existent" (sat) denotes the universal form (ākṛti) of existence.
Furthermore, the two [phrases] "one only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*) are in grammatical apposition with the word *sat* (Being);
likewise is the phrase "this was" (*idamāsīt*).

In that context, the negative particle (*nañ*) employed in the sentence concerning Being (*sadvākya*) depends precisely upon that sentence concerning Being; it produces a cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence concerning Being, characterized as: "Being is one only, without a second, and this was."
Therefore, just as one mounted on a horse, while holding onto the horse, turns it away from objects facing it, so too [the teaching] turns one away from the meaning of the "existent" (sat).
It does not, however, assert the non-existence of the existent itself.
Consequently, this statement beginning with "this is indeed non-existent" (asadeva) is employed solely for the purpose of removing a person's erroneous apprehension.

For once a misconception has been shown, it is possible to turn one away from it; thus, because the statement "from non-being, etc. possesses purpose, its status as revealed scripture (*śrauta*) and its authority are established, and there is no fault.
Therefore, from "non-being," which consists of the total absence of everything, "being"—that which exists—was born, i.e., it arose.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is a Vedic usage. //1//
"But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? he said. "How could being be born from non-being?"
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
Having shown this contrary apprehension to be the position of the great nihilists (mahāvaināśika), [the text] refutes it:

"But from what source of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), my dear, could it be that 'being is born from non-being'?"—that is to say, how could this be possible? It means that it is not possible from any source of valid knowledge whatsoever.
As for the claim that a sprout is seen to arise from the very non-existence of the seed upon its destruction, that too contradicts their own tenets.
How so?

For those parts of the seed which are characterized by the specific configuration of the seed continue to persist even in the sprout; it is not through the destruction of those parts that the sprout is produced.

Furthermore, that which is the shape and configuration of the seed is not accepted by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) as being a real entity distinct from the parts of the seed, such that it would be destroyed upon the arising of the sprout.
If, on the other hand, it exists as a real entity distinct from its parts, then there is a contradiction with their own tenets.
If it is argued that it is the conventional form of the seed’s configuration that is destroyed, [then...]
What is this so-called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*): is it a non-entity (*abhāva*) or an entity (*bhāva*)?

If it is a non-entity, there is no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If, on the other hand, it is an entity, even then a sprout does not arise from a non-entity; for the sprout arises from the parts of the seed.
If it is argued that the parts are also destroyed, we say no;
for the same [reasoning] applies to their parts.

Just as for the Nihilists (vaināśika) there is no whole (*avayavin*) consisting of the form and configuration of a seed, so too its parts do not exist; thus, for them as well, destruction is untenable.

Since the parts of the seed have their own subtle parts, and those parts have yet other subtler parts, this regressus ad infinitum never ceases; thus, the destruction of everything is untenable. Furthermore, because the cognition of "existence" persists, existence itself does not cease. Therefore, for those who maintain that existence [is real], the arising of existence from existence alone will be established.
However, for those who maintain non-existence, there is no example for the arising of existence from non-existence.
The production of a jar from a lump of clay is observed by proponents of existence (*sadvādins*), because [the jar] exists when that [clay] exists and does not exist when it is absent.
If the jar were produced from non-existence alone, one seeking a jar would not take up a lump of clay;
furthermore, the persistence of the word and the cognition of "non-existence" would result even in the case of the jar and so forth.
But this is not the case; therefore, there is no arising of existence from non-existence.

As for what they say—that the cognition of clay is the cause of the cognition of a jar, and thus the cognition of clay is called the cause of the cognition of the jar, but that in ultimate reality neither the clay nor the jar exists—this too [is untenable], because the existing cognition of clay [arises] only from an existing [cognition].
If it is argued that "the cause of the cognition of a jar" does not imply the arising of the existent from the non-existent—

because there is merely a sequence between the cognition of the clay and the cognition of the jar by way of cause and effect, but no actual relationship of material cause and product— the answer is no;
for while a sequence of cognitions may be perceived, the nihilists (Vaināśikas) lack any external example [to support such a claim].
"Therefore, my dear, how indeed could it be so? he said. "In what manner, by what means, could being be born from non-being?

The intention is that there is no illustrative example whatsoever for the production of being from non-being. Having thus refuted the position of the proponent of non-being, he concludes with the establishment of his own view: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone."

But surely, for the proponent of existence (*sadvādin*) as well, there is no example whatsoever for the claim that "from the existent, the existent arises," because one does not observe the production of another jar from [the clay of] a jar.
True; it is indeed so that from an existent, another existent is not produced. Rather, the existent itself persists in a different configuration.
Just as a snake becomes coiled,
and just as clay exists through its various manifestations such as powder, a lump, a jar, or shards—
if this is so, since everything exists in every state, how can it be said that "this was non-existent prior to its production"?
It is said:

Have you not heard that the restrictive particle "eva" (indeed) applies to the effect denoted by the word "this"? In that case, it would follow that before its production, that which is denoted by the word "this" was simply non-existent, and now it has become "this. No.
This world exists precisely as the object of the word and cognition "Being" (sat), just as clay alone exists as the object of the words and cognitions "lump," "jar," and so forth.

Now, one might object: just as the substance clay exists, so too do the lump, the jar, and the like; therefore, because the cognition of the effect is an object distinct from the cognition of "Being," the entire collection of effects must be a different entity from "Being," just as a cow is a different entity from a horse.
[We reply: No, for although the lump, the jar, and so forth mutually exclude one another, they do not deviate from their nature as clay.
Although a jar deviates from a lump and a lump deviates from a jar, nevertheless, they do not deviate from the nature of clay; therefore, the lump and the jar are merely clay.
(A cow deviates from a horse, or a horse deviates from a cow.
Therefore, jars and the like are merely the particular configurations of clay and other materials.
Thus, it is logical that prior to its origination, all this is merely the configuration of the existent;
for it was "only the existent," since the mere configuration of the modification is a mere beginning in speech.

[Objection: But how can a modification or a structural form be possible for that which is partless, given such scriptural passages as, "It is without parts, without activity, tranquil, blameless, and stainless," and "For the divine Person is formless, existing both within and without, and unborn"?
[Reply: This is not a fault.

Just as the form of a snake and so forth arises from the constituent parts of a rope and so forth when conceptually constructed by the intellect, so too the state of modification arises from the constituents of Being (sat).
For the Śruti declares: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the clay alone is real. In this way, Being alone is real.
Thus, even at the time of the cognition of "this" (idam), it is in reality one without a second. //2//
It thought:
"May I be many; may I procreate."
It created fire. That fire thought: "May I become many; may I procreate."
He emitted the waters.
Therefore, whenever a person grieves or perspires, from that very heat the waters are produced.
"That [Being] thought" means it performed the act of seeing, that is, vision.
For this reason, the Pradhāna postulated by the Sāṃkhyas is not the cause of the world;
for the Pradhāna is admitted to be insentient.
But this [Brahman] possesses consciousness because it is a seer. To explain how it "saw," he says: "May I become many, may I be abundant, may I be born forth, may I be produced in abundance.
This is just as clay becomes a jar or similar forms, or as a rope appears in the form of a snake through the conceptual construction of the intellect.
[Objection: Then everything that is perceived is indeed non-existent, like a rope perceived in the form of a snake and so forth through mental construction. [Reply: No;
we say that because it is the existent itself that is perceived otherwise through the distinction of duality, nothing whatsoever is non-existent anywhere.

Just as logicians, having imagined another distinct entity apart from what exists, then declare that very thing to be non-existent prior to its arising and after its destruction, we do not at any time or in any place imagine any other designation, object of designation, or entity apart from what exists.
Indeed, everything that is designated and everything that is designated as something else is [actually] Being alone.

Thus, just as a rope is designated as a "snake" by one who perceives it through the cognition of a snake, or as in common worldly usage a lump of clay, a jar, and so forth, are designated by the words "lump," "jar," and so on through the cognition of things other than clay; and just as for those who perceive the distinction from the rope, the designation and cognition of a "snake" cease, and for those who perceive the distinction from clay, the words and cognitions of "jar" and so forth cease—in the same way, for those who perceive the distinction from Being, the words and cognitions of other modifications cease.
They turn back,
according to such scriptural passages as: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it," and "The undefined, the non-abiding," and so forth.

Having perceived thus, it emitted heat; having created heat. Now, an objection is raised: since another scriptural passage states, "From this very Self, space was produced," and from space, air, and from that, as the third, heat—how is it that here heat is created first from that very source, and space is said to arise from that same source? This appears contradictory.
This is not a fault;
for it is logical to conceive that after the creation of space and air, [the Self] created that being, fire.

Alternatively, the sequence of creation is not intended here; rather, what is intended is that all this is an effect pre-existent in its cause (satkārya), and therefore "Being alone was one without a second."
This is because of the examples of clay and so forth;
or rather, since the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is intended to be explained, [the text] describes the creation of fire, water, and food alone.
"Fire" is well-known in the world as that which burns, cooks, illumines, and is red.
That Being which had emitted that fire, having become established in the form of fire, reflected; the meaning is that the Being itself reflected, as before: "May I be many, may I procreate.
It emitted water.
Water is well known in the world as being liquid, cohesive, flowing, and white.

Since water is an effect produced from fire, therefore, wherever and at whatever time a person feels cold, suffers from heat, perspires, or breaks into a sweat, from that very fire water is then produced.

6.2.4 Those waters thought: "May we become many; may we procreate. They created food. Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant; from water alone, indeed, does this edible food arise.
is born. //4//
Those waters reflected, as before; the meaning is that *Sat*, abiding in the form of water, reflected.
"May we become many, may we become abundant, may we be procreated, may we come into being. They created food, characterized by the earth.
Since food is essentially earth, and food is produced from water, therefore in whatever region it rains, in that very place food becomes most abundant and plentiful.
Thus, that edible food is born from water alone.
Although the earth was previously said to have "created food," here, by the specific qualification "food and that which is edible," rice, barley, and so forth are meant as the illustration.
Food is heavy, stable, retentive, and black by form; this is well known.

But surely, the act of seeing is not perceived in fire and the other elements, since there is no prohibition against harming them and no observation of effects such as fear; how then can it be said that "that fire saw," and so forth?
This is not a fault.

Because fire and the other elements are transformations of the causal Seer, and because they produce their specific effects in a fixed sequence, the element is said to "behold," as if the Seer were beholding fire and the rest.
[Objection: But even for the Existent (Sat), the status of being a Seer is merely figurative. [Reply: No;
since the beholding of the Existent is cognizable solely through the word, it is not possible to assume that it is figurative.
However, in the case of fire and the other elements, since direct seeing is absent, it is logical to assume that "seeing" is used figuratively.
But could it not be inferred that even though [the Pradhāna] exists, it is insentient because it is a cause like clay?

Therefore, since the insentient Pradhāna exists for the sake of a sentient being and produces effects characterized by a fixed temporal sequence, one might infer that it "saw," as if it were seeing; thus, "seeing" is indeed merely figurative.

Furthermore, in the world, metaphorical treatment as if something were conscious is observed even for that which is unconscious, such as when one says "the bank wishes to fall. It might be the same in the case of the existent [Self]. No;
for it is taught that the Self is that very reality, stating "That is the Truth, That is the Self" (*tat satyam sa ātmā*).

If it is argued that the designation of a self (*ātman*) is also metaphorical—just as one says, "Bhadrasena is my self," applying the term "self" metaphorically to a non-self that performs all tasks for oneself—that is not so;
for there is the teaching of liberation for one who intends the Real and the True, thinking "I am Being," according to the statement: "For him, there is delay only so long [as he is not released].
If it is argued that this too is merely a metaphor, [we reply: no.
For one who intends [to attain] the Self consisting of Pradhāna, the proximity to liberation exists; thus, even the teaching of liberation is merely figurative.

It is just as in the world, when someone has set out to go to a village and might say, "I have reached the village," out of consideration for his haste. This is not so, because the text begins with: "By knowing which, that which was unknown becomes known."
When this [Brahman] is known, everything becomes known, because everything is non-different from it and because of the scriptural statement that it is "without a second.

There remains nothing else to be known—whether taught by the Śruti, or inferable through a logical mark (*liṅga*)—by which the instruction on liberation could be considered figurative. Furthermore, if one were to assume that the entire meaning of this chapter is figurative, the effort of the one who so assumes would be in vain; for the knowledge that accomplishes the human goal has already been attained through reasoning alone.
Therefore, because of the authority of the Veda, there is no abandonment of the meaning heard therein;
thus, it is established that the world has an intelligent cause. //4//
Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, for these beings, there are indeed only three origins: the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born.
Regarding these beings such as birds and so forth, which are entered by the individual soul (jīva), the word "these" (*eṣām*) refers to them because they are indicated through direct perception;

it does not refer to fire and the other elements, because their tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is yet to be described, and since tripartition has not yet occurred, a reference to them by direct perception would be untenable.
Furthermore, the term "deities" (*devatā*) is applied to fire and the others, as in the passage: "These are the three deities."
Therefore, for those beings—birds, animals, plants, and so forth—there are exactly three seeds as causes, and no more.
What are they? It is said:
"the egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) is that which is born from an egg; the egg-born is indeed the egg-born, such as birds and the like.
For it is observed that birds, snakes, and so forth are born from birds, snakes, and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is that a bird is the seed of birds, a snake is the seed of snakes, and likewise anything else born from an egg is the seed of those of its own kind.
Now, one might object: "That which is born from an egg is called *aṇḍaja* (egg-born); therefore, it is logical that the egg itself is the seed. How can it be said that the *aṇḍaja* is the seed?"

This would indeed be true if the Veda were dependent upon your will; however, the Veda is independent of you, since it states that "only those born from eggs and so forth are the seeds, not the eggs and so forth.

Furthermore, it is observed that in the absence of those born from eggs and so forth, there is an absence of their respective lineages, whereas this is not the case in the absence of the eggs and so forth.
Therefore, only those born from eggs and so forth are the seeds of those born from eggs and so forth.

Similarly, "born from a living being" (*jīvaja*) means that which is born from a living being, namely the *jarāyuja* (viviparous), such as humans, cattle, and so forth. "Born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*) refers to that which sprouts; *udbhit* is the stationary [being], and what is born from that is *udbhijja*. Alternatively, a sprout (*udbhit*) is a seed; what is born from that is *udbhijja*, meaning the seed of stationary beings—the sense being the seed of stationary things. The categories of "sweat-born" (*svedaja*) and "mold-born" (*saṃśokaja*) are included within "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) and "sprout-born" (*udbhijja*) respectively, according to their possibility.
In this way, the restriction that there are only three seeds is established. //1//
This deity reflected:
"Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form."
This very deity, under discussion, designated as "Being" (sat), which is the source of fire, water, and food, is said to have reflected—just as before—as "May I be many.
That very purpose of becoming many has not yet been accomplished; therefore, having once again undertaken that same purpose of becoming many, she reflected further.
How so?
Now, [the text says]: "Come, let me enter these three deities—fire and the others—as previously described, with this living self (jīva).
By saying "with this living self," she refers to her own self, which resides in her own intellect and is the sustainer of the vital breaths experienced during the previous creation.
By the statement "by the Self which sustains the vital breaths," it is shown that [the Self] is not distinct from one's own self, being characterized by the nature of consciousness.
Having entered [therein], she—
having acquired specific cognition through contact with the subtle elements consisting of fire, water, and earth— [proceeds].
"Name and form"— the meaning is that "I shall differentiate name and form," that is, "I shall make them distinct," "I shall define them such that 'this one has this name' and 'this one has this form.

But surely, it is not logical for the omniscient Deity, who is beyond the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), to have the intention, "Having entered a body that is the locus of hundreds of thousands of evils through conscious deliberation, I shall experience suffering," nor is entry itself logical, given her independence.
It is true that this would not be logical if she had intended, "I shall enter by my own unmodified form" and "I shall experience suffering," for it was not so.
How then?
Because of the statement: "having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman)."
The so-called *jīva* is merely a reflection of the Deity.

It is produced by the contact with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other subtle elements (*tanmātra*), like the reflection of a person entering a mirror, or like that of the sun and other luminaries in water and similar surfaces.

This appearance of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) resulting from the connection of the Deity—who possesses inconceivable and infinite power—with the intellect and the rest, arises from the failure to grasp the distinction between the true nature of the Deity and [the reflection]. It is the cause of various conceptual cognitions such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded."
Because it has entered [the body] merely as a reflection in the form of the individual soul (jīva), the deity is not connected by itself with the bodily experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Just as a person, the sun, and others, having entered into a mirror, water, and the like merely as reflections, are not affected by the defects of the mirror, the water, and so on—so too is the deity.
As the sun, though the eye of the entire world, is not tainted by external ocular defects.
Likewise, the one inner self of all beings, being external [to the world], is not tainted by the suffering of the world.
And in the Vājasaneyaka it is said: "It is all-pervading and eternal like space.
Now, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were merely a shadow, it would follow that it is entirely false, and consequently, its existence in the next world, this world, and so forth, would also be false.
This is not a valid objection.

Because it is accepted that [the cause] is real by virtue of its nature as Being (*sat*). And the entire collection of modifications, such as name and form (*nāmarūpa*), is real only through its nature as Being; in itself, however, it is indeed unreal, because it has been stated: "The modification is a mere handle of speech, a mere name."
The same applies to the individual soul (jīva) as well;
for it is a well-established principle that "the offering corresponds to the recipient.
Therefore, since all worldly transactions and all modifications are real in their nature as Being (sat), yet unreal insofar as they are other than Being, no fault can be raised here by the logicians.
Thus, it can be said that the various dualistic doctrines, which are mutually contradictory, are merely the conceptual constructions of one's own intellect and do not abide in reality. //2//
"Let me make each of these three deities threefold.
This very deity, having entered into these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), differentiated name and form.

Having thus entered those three deities, and having willed, "Let me manifest name and form, which exist in an unmanifested state as seeds established within my own self," [He thought], "And let me make each one of these three deities threefold. In making each one threefold, there is a predominance of one and a subordinate status for the other two; otherwise, there would be only a single threefold-making, like that of a rope, and not a distinct threefold-making for each of the three.
For in this way, fire, water, and food would each obtain their own distinct names and designations, such as "this is fire," "these are waters," and "this is food.
And when distinct names and designations are obtained, the purpose is the successful accomplishment of the proper practical dealings with these deities.
Having thus reflected, that very deity entered into these three deities by means of this very living self (jīva), like the reflection of the sun's orb within [water].

Having entered the Vairāja body first, and having subsequently entered the bodies of the gods and others, he manifested names and forms according to his own resolve, saying: "This one has such a name; this one has such a form. //3//
Of these, he made each one threefold, threefold.
"But as to how, my dear, each of these three deities becomes threefold, threefold, learn that from me."
And of those deities, she—the deity—made each one threefold by way of the relationship between the subordinate and the primary qualities.
Let it be for now that the aggregates of the deities and so forth, having been differentiated by name and form, consist of the three elements of fire, water, and food;
however, as to how indeed each of these many deities from the aggregates becomes threefold, each one by one, understand that from me as I speak it, and grasp it firmly through examples. 4.
Thus, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the third section.
That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat.
That which is white is of water;
that which is black is of food.
The "fire-ness" of fire has departed.
The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone are real.

Regarding that tripartition of the deities which has been mentioned, an illustration of it is now stated. An "illustration" (udāharaṇa) is so called because it is cited for the purpose of establishing [the principle] through a single instance. This is what he says: "That which belongs to fire, of the triply composed [elements]..."
Know that whatever is black is the very form of that fire, which belongs to food and to the earth when they have not yet been made tripartite.
This being so, that notion of "fire" which you held regarding this [earth] as distinct from the three forms—that fire-nature of the fire has now departed;
the meaning is that the cognition of fire and the word "fire" which existed previously, before the discernment of the three forms, have both now vanished.

Just as a crystal, when perceived in conjunction with a visible red substrate, becomes the cause for the word and the cognition "this is a ruby," yet those words and cognitions of a "ruby" cease once there is a discerning knowledge of the distinction between the substrate and the crystal for one who has realized that distinction— so it is in this case.

Now, what is achieved here by this conceptualization of intellect and word? It might be argued that it is proper to say, "Before the discernment of the three forms was made, there was only fire; the 'fire-ness' of that fire departed upon the discernment of its red and other forms," just as a cloth ceases to exist when the threads are pulled away.
But it is not so; for fire is merely intellect and word, since it says, "Fire is a modification, a mere handle, a mere name"—the meaning being that it is name-only.
Therefore, even the cognition of fire is merely false.
What, then, is true therein? It is precisely these three forms that are true; the meaning of the restriction is that there is not even an atom's worth of truth apart from these three forms. //1//
That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water.
That which is black is of the food.
The solar nature has departed from the sun.
This modification is a mere handle of speech, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of the moon is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The moonhood of the moon has departed.
A modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.
That which is the red form of lightning is the form of fire;
that which is white is the form of water;
that which is black is the form of food.
The lightning-nature of lightning has vanished;
it is a modification, a mere handle of speech, a mere name; "the three forms" alone is the truth.

4. Likewise, the passage beginning with "What of the sun, what of the moon, what of lightning" is the same [as before]. Now, having said, "My dear, understand from me how each of these three deities becomes threefold," the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) was shown through four examples—fire and so forth—pertaining only to *tejas* (heat/light), but no example was given for food (*anna*) and water (*ap*).

This has been shown in the section on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). This is not a fault; for the Śruti considers that even the examples concerning food, water, and fire are to be understood in exactly this same way.

The example of fire (*tejas*) is given for the sake of illustration; this is because it possesses color-form (*rūpavat*) and because its meaning is clearly established. Smell (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*) are not cited as examples because they cannot occur in all three [of the elements].
For smell and taste do not exist in fire.
Touch and sound are not cited as examples because they cannot be shown separately.

If the entire world has been made tripartite, then—just as in the case of fire and so forth—the three forms alone are real; thus, just as the "fire-ness" of fire has departed, the "world-ness" of the world has likewise departed.

Likewise, since food is a shoot of water, "water" alone is the truth, and food is a mere modification based on speech; similarly, since water is a shoot of fire, it is a mere modification based on speech, and "fire" alone is the truth; and since fire is a shoot of Being, it is a mere modification based on speech, and "Being" alone is the truth—this is the meaning intended to be expressed.
But surely, air and space remain unaccounted for, as they are not included among fire and the other elements;

likewise, smell, taste, sound, and touch remain unaccounted for. Thus, how could everything else become known by knowing the "Being" (sat), or else some other method must be stated for their knowledge?
This is not a fault.
Because everything is perceived within a substance possessing form:
first, since both sound and touch are apprehended in fire, which possesses form, the existence of wind and space—possessing the qualities of touch and sound respectively—is inferred therein.
Likewise, taste and smell are included within water and earth, which possess form.

By demonstrating the threefold transformation (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of the three material elements—fire, water, and earth—the Śruti considers everything that is included within them to be known, because it possesses the three forms, being a modification of those [elements].
For there is no apprehension of air or ether, nor of their qualities of smell or taste, apart from a material substance possessing form.
Alternatively, the Śruti considers the threefold transformation even of those things possessing form to be merely for the sake of illustration.

Just as it is true that when the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) has been performed, there are indeed three forms, so too the same principle applies to the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa). Therefore, since everything is a modification of Being (sat), by knowing Being, all this becomes known; thus it is established that Being alone is the one, non-dual reality.
Thus, it is well said: "When that one is known, all this becomes known. (2.4)
Knowing this, indeed, those former great householders and great Vedic scholars used to say:
"Nowadays, no one will be able to cite anything to us that has not been heard, not thought, or not understood."
For thus they understood from these [words].

Knowing this, the ancient great householders (*mahāśāla*) and great wealthy men (*mahāśrotriya*), having realized it, used to say: "Indeed, in our family, there shall be no one who will utter anything unheard, unthought, or unknown—meaning, because those born in our lineage possess true knowledge, everything is already known to them. They did not say this out of pride, but rather with the intention that, for those possessing the aforementioned realization, nothing remains unperceived.

Furthermore, as to how they came to know everything, he says: because they understood that from these three—the red and other forms—which had been made tripartite and were thus known, all else that remained was exactly like this, therefore they were indeed omniscient; the meaning is that they became so through that knowledge.
Or else, "they came to know from these"—that is, from the known examples such as fire and so forth—they came to know everything else. //5//
"As for that which appeared as if red, they understood: 'That is the form of fire.
As for that which appeared as if white, they understood: 'That is the form of water.'"
And when they said, "That which appeared as if black," they recognized that as the form of food.

Or, as for that which seemed as if unknown, they understood it to be the combination of these very deities. "Now, my dear, learn from me how each one of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7)
How so?

When that which was perceived as something else—such as the form of a dove or similar—appeared as if red, those ancient knowers of Brahman understood that to be the form of fire (*tejas*). Likewise, that which was perceived as if white, they understood to be the form of water (*āpas*).

They understood that whatever form was perceived as if black belonged to food; likewise, they understood that even that which was extremely difficult to discern, which was as if unknown and not specifically perceived, was simply a combination, a collection, of these same three deities.

Thus, first, the external object has been understood, like fire and the others. Now then, my dear, understand from me as I speak how these three aforementioned deities, having reached the person—the aggregate of cause and effect characterized by the head, hands, and so forth—and being utilized by the person, each become threefold; thus he spoke. 6–7.
Thus ends the fourth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts.
Of that [food], the coarsest constituent becomes feces; the middling becomes flesh; and the finest becomes the mind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1)
Food that is eaten and consumed is divided into three parts by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) as it is being cooked.

How so? Of that food which is thus divided into three, the coarsest part—the most substantial portion of the divided matter—becomes feces. That middle part of the food’s constituent elements, having been transformed through the sequence beginning with chyle (*rasa*), becomes flesh. That which is the subtlest... [text ends]

That subtlest element, having reached the heart and entered the subtle channels known as *hitā*, brings about the stability of the aggregate of the organs such as speech; transforming itself into the form of the mind (*manas*), it effects the accumulation of the mind.
Consequently, because the mind is accumulated from food, it is understood to be merely material (*bhautika*), and not eternal or partless as defined in the Vaiśeṣika system.

As for what will be stated—that the mind is its divine eye—that too is not with reference to eternity; rather, it is with reference to its pervading all objects of the senses, such as those that are subtle, concealed, or distant. Furthermore, we shall explain that even the eternity [of the mind] relative to the objects of the other senses is merely relative, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "Being, one, without a second. //1//
The water that is drunk becomes divided into three parts:
its coarsest constituent becomes urine.
That which is middling is blood;
that which is most subtle is the vital breath (prāṇa).

In the same way, the water that is drunk is divided into three parts: its coarsest constituent becomes urine; its middle constituent becomes blood; and its finest constituent becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
For it will be said: "The vital breath consists of water; it will not be cut off for one who drinks. //2//
The heat consumed is divided into three parts.
Of that, the coarsest constituent becomes bone.
That which is the middle is marrow;
that which is the subtlest is speech.
In the same way, the fire [element] in food—such as oil, ghee, and so forth—that has been eaten is divided into three parts: its coarsest constituent becomes bone;
its middling constituent becomes marrow, which is the oily substance within the bones; and its subtlest constituent becomes speech.
For it is well known in the world that by consuming oil, ghee, and other such substances, the speech becomes clear and one becomes capable of speaking. //3//
"For the mind, my dear, consists of food;
breath consists of water."
"Speech consists of light.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
Since it is thus that the mind, my dear, consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire—[one might object:

"But surely those who eat only food, such as mice and the like, possess speech and vital breath; likewise, those who consume only water, such as fish and crocodiles of the sea, possess mind and speech; and even those who drink only oil possess vital breath."
And if that [subtle body] were the object of inference, then how could it be stated that "the mind, my dear, consists of food" and so forth?
This is not a fault,
because everything has been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), and thus everything is possible everywhere.

For no one eats food that has not been made tripartite, nor are waters drunk that have not been made tripartite, nor does anyone eat fire that has not been made tripartite; thus, it is not contradictory that even food-eaters such as mice possess eloquence and the possession of breath, and so forth. Having been thus instructed, Śvetaketu said: "Venerable sir, please explain to me once more—that is, again—how the mind consists of food, my dear, and so on; let the venerable one cause me to understand this through an illustration, for I have not yet fully grasped this matter."

A correct certainty has arisen: since, within a single body which is indistinguishable in its composition of fire (*tejas*), water (*ap*), and food (*anna*), the various foods consumed—consisting of water and oil—are accumulated by the mind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and speech in the form of their subtlest constituents (*aṇiṣṭhadhātu*) without overstepping their own respective natures, this is difficult to discern; it is with this intention that he says, "Furthermore... and so forth.
To him who had spoken thus, the father said, "So be it; yes, Soma. Listen here to an illustration so that what you ask may be understood. //4//
Thus ends the fifth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"My dear, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence which rises upward emerges."
That becomes clarified butter (sarpis). ChUp 6.6.1.
"My dear, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence which rises upward, having gathered together, goes upward in the form of fresh butter; that becomes clarified butter.
"In exactly the same way, my dear, when food is being eaten, that subtle essence which rises upward—"
That becomes the mind. ChUp 6.6.2.

Just as in this illustration, my dear, so indeed it is with food—such as boiled rice and the like—when it is being eaten and consumed, and when it is churned by the digestive fire in the stomach together with the vital air (vāyu) as if by a churning-stick: that subtle essence (*aṇimā*) which rises upward becomes the mind (*manas*).
This means that, having combined with the constituents of the mind, it accumulates the mind. //2//
"My dear, when water is being drunk, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes breath."
"In the same way, my dear, of the water being drunk, that which is the subtlest part rises upwards; it becomes the vital breath."
"My dear, of fire being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward;
it becomes speech."
In the very same way, my dear, when fire is being consumed, that which is its subtlest essence rises upward; it becomes speech.
"For the mind, my dear, consists of food;
breath consists of water."
"Speech consists of light.
"Revered sir, please instruct me further.
"So be it, my dear," he said.
"The mind, my dear, consists of food; the vital breath consists of water; and speech consists of fire"—the intention [of the father] was that what I have said is indeed logical.
Therefore, let all this be so regarding water and fire.

However, as for the statement that "the mind consists of food," I have not attained absolute certainty; therefore, may the venerable sir please explain further to me, by means of an illustration, how the mind consists of food.
"So be it, my dear," the father said. //5//
Thus ends the sixth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"O gentle one, a person consists of sixteen parts."
"Do not eat for fifteen days; you may drink water as you wish.
Breath consists of water; it will not be cut off from one who drinks. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.7.1)

Of the food that has been eaten, that which is the subtlest constituent (dhātu) bestows power upon the mind; this power of the mind, accumulated by food, is intended to be designated as the "sixteenfold part" (kalā) of the person, having been divided sixteenfold.
Endowed with that power—accumulated by food and divided sixteenfold—which resides in the mind, the aggregate characterized by the body and the organs becomes possessed of it.

The body qualified by the living self (jīva) is called the "Person" (puruṣa) consisting of sixteen parts; for as long as that [food] exists, the person becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, a knower, an agent, and a cognizer, capable of all actions, whereas when it diminishes, there is a loss of capacity.
And he will say: "Now, one who does not eat food... and so forth.
The capacity of every instrument of action is produced by the mind alone;
for in the world, those endowed with mental strength are seen to be strong,
and some even subsist on meditation because food constitutes the very essence of everything.

Therefore, the mental vigor produced by food constitutes sixteen parts for this person; he is thus the "sixteen-part person. If you wish to perceive this directly, do not eat—that is, do not take food—for fifteen days.

However, drink water according to your desire, because if you do not drink water, your vital breath (*prāṇa*) will be severed—it will undergo interruption—since we have already stated that the vital breath consists of water and is a transformation of water.
For an effect is not able to remain without falling away without the support of its own cause. //1//
He did not eat for fifteen days.
Then he approached him and said, "Sir, what shall I say?"
"O gentle one, the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants.
He replied, "Indeed, they do not come to my mind, sir."
Having heard this, desiring to perceive for himself that the mind consists of food, he did not eat for fifteen days.
Then, on the sixteenth day, he approached his father; having approached him, he said, "Sir, what shall I recite?
The other replied, "O dear one, recite the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants."
Thus addressed by his father, he said: "No, indeed; it is not that deer and other animals do not appear to me in my mind; such is the meaning, O venerable sir. (2)
He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large kindled fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left,
it would not burn much more than that."
"In this way, my dear, of your sixteen parts, one part remains.
By that [part], you do not now perceive the Vedas. Eat."
"Then you will understand me," he said.
When he had spoken thus, the father said: "Hear the reason why those [Vedas], the Ṛgveda and the others, do not manifest themselves to you. (He said to him:

"Just as in the world, my dear, from a great, large-sized fire that has been kindled and built up with fuel, a single ember the size of a firefly might remain or be left over when it has been extinguished; from that ember, even slightly more than that size—"

"It would not burn much; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts nourished by food, only one part remains, a single fragment that has been left over. It would not burn much; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts nourished by food, only one part remains. With that—now, at this time, like a spark of fire the size of a firefly—you do not experience or comprehend the Vedas."
And having heard my words in their entirety, you shall understand; for now, eat, O Aśana. //3//
He laughed;
then he approached him.
Whatever he asked him about, he understood it all.
He ate exactly as he had been told, and immediately thereafter, desiring to serve his father, he approached him.

When the son had arrived, the father questioned him regarding whatever there was in the Rigveda and other branches—whether it were the textual form or the collection of meanings—and Śvetaketu understood all of that, both in terms of the meaning and the text of the Rigveda and so forth. 4.
He said to him:
"Just as, my dear, if from a large kindled fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left, and one were to fan it with grass and make it blaze up, it would burn much more than before."
The father said to him again: "Just as, my dear, from a large fire that has been kindled," and so on, the rest is the same.
Suppose a single ember, the size of a firefly, remains of a fire that has gone out; if one were to kindle it by adding grass and powder, one would make it blaze up and increase it.
By means of that blazing ember, one could burn much more than its previous size. //5//
"In this way, my dear, of your sixteen parts, one part remained.
That was nourished by food and it blazed up."
By means of that, you now experience the Vedas;
for, my dear, the mind consists of food,
and the vital breath consists of water.
"Speech consists of light. He understood this from him—yes, he understood it. ChU 6.7.6.

"Thus, my dear, of those sixteen parts of food which were of the nature of vital powers, one part remained; it was left over. For fifteen days you did not eat, and by each day one part was consumed, just as the moon wanes during the dark fortnight. That remaining part of yours, once replenished, increased, and grew through the food you ate, and it blazed up."
The lengthening [of the vowel] is Vedic; it means "blazed up" or "increased.
"She blazed up" (prājvālīt) means that the digit (kalā), being nourished by the food you have eaten, was increased, augmented, and thus blazed up.
The lengthening is Vedic; it means "blazed up" or "increased."
"Prājvālīt" is an alternative reading; in that case, the meaning is that [the fire], having been kindled by him, blazed up of its own accord.
By means of that [fire] being increased, you now—this very moment—experience and perceive the Vedas.

Thus, he concludes that the mind's consisting of food (*annamayatva*) is established through both its departure and its persistence, with the words: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food," and so forth.

The intention is that just as this quality of mind being composed of food (*annamaya*) is established for you, so too is it established that breath (*prāṇa*) is composed of water (*apomaya*) and speech (*vāk*) is composed of fire (*tejomayī*).
Śvetaketu understood—that is, he came to know—this which had been stated by his father regarding the composition of mind and the other faculties from food and the rest.
The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is intended to mark the end of the section concerning the triadic transformation (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). //6//
Thus ends the seventh section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep."
When a person here is said to "sleep," my dear, then he has become united with Being;
he has gone to his own self. Therefore, they say of him, "he sleeps" (svapiti).
For he has gone back into his own self.

In that mind, the supreme deity has entered by means of the living self (jīva), just as a person [is seen] in a mirror by means of a reflection, or as the sun and other luminaries [are seen] in water and the like by means of their reflections.
That mind consists of food (annamaya) and is joined with, and attained through, speech and breath, which consist of fire and water.

Of whatever nature and in whatever state the living self exists, it is capable of the worldly activities of thinking, seeing, hearing, and so forth; and upon the cessation of those [activities], it returns to its own true form as the deity.

This has been stated in another Vedic scripture: "As if meditating, as if moving, becoming a dream with the intellect, he transcends this world"; "That very Self is Brahman, consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind," and so forth;
"By means of dream, [he transcends] the bodily [self]," and so forth;
and "In breathing, one becomes what is called breath," and so forth.

Desiring to explain to his son that state of abiding in that supreme deity— who is manifested as one's own self— of this very person who resides in the mind, who has attained the designation "mind," and who has withdrawn from the objects of the senses by means of the pacification of the mind, Uddālaka Āruṇi, it is said, spoke to his son Śvetaketu.
"End of dream" (*svapnānta*) means the middle of the dream; it is called "dream" because of the occurrence of seeing, and its "end" (*anta*) is deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Alternatively, "end of dream" means the true nature (*satattva*) of the dream; even in that case, by implication, it is indeed deep sleep, according to the statement: "He has gone to his own self."

For the knowers of Brahman do not maintain that the merging of the individual soul (*jīva*) occurs anywhere other than in deep sleep. For just as when a mirror is removed, the reflection of a person existing within the mirror merges back into its own source, the person itself; so too, upon the cessation of the mind and other faculties, the individual soul—which is of the nature of a reflection of consciousness—merges into the Self that had entered the mind for the purpose of manifesting names and forms.
That supreme deity attains its own true self, having abandoned the state of being a living soul (jīva) known as the mind.
Therefore, it is understood that the state of deep sleep alone is what is denoted by the term "the end of dream" (svapnānta).
However, where one who is asleep sees dreams, that dream-vision is associated with pleasure and pain; for it is well known that merit and demerit are the originators of pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, it is only through the support of ignorance (*avidyā*) and desire (*kāma*) that merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*) can initiate their effects, namely pleasure and pain, and the perception thereof; it cannot be otherwise. Thus, while one is joined with ignorance, desire, and action—the causes of transmigratory existence—one is indeed in the state of dreaming, and therefore does not become "merged even in oneself. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "He is untouched by merit, untouched by evil; for at that time he has crossed beyond all the sorrows of the heart"; "This, verily, is his state free from desire"; and "This is the supreme bliss," and so forth.
He says, "I shall show you your own form as a deity, entirely free from the state of being a living soul (jīvatva)," while in deep sleep itself.
"O gentle one (somya), understand from me as I describe it," meaning grasp it clearly.
It is now stated when this end of the dream occurs.
At whatever time this name belongs to a person who is about to sleep—
it being well-known in the world that he "sleeps"—
he states that this name is figurative (*gauṇa*).

When it is said that "the person sleeps," at that time he becomes united with, that is, merged into, the Being—the deity denoted by the word "Being" which has been introduced as the subject. Having abandoned the form of the individual soul (jīva) produced by contact with the mind and other faculties that had entered the mind, he has gone back to, or entered into, his own true nature, which is the ultimate reality. Therefore, for this reason, worldly people say of him, "he sleeps."
For he has indeed gone back into his own self;
consequently, there occurs a cessation from their respective functions of the organs, which have become exhausted due to the fatigue caused by their manifold activities.
And this is confirmed by scripture: "Speech indeed becomes weary; the eye becomes weary," and so forth.

And thus, the organs such as speech, the ear, and the mind—as in the passage beginning "Speech is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, the mind is withdrawn"—are swallowed up by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
When the single, unwearied *prāṇa* awakens within the nest of the body, then the individual soul (*jīva*), in order to dispel its exhaustion, attains its own self in the form of its deity.
It is logical that there can be no removal of exhaustion except through abiding in one's own true nature; hence the well-known worldly expression: "He has gone to his own."
For it is observed in the world that those afflicted by diseases such as fever find rest when they are freed from them and established in their own self; the same would be logical here as well.
This is also supported by scriptural passages such as, "Just as a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary... and so forth. //1//
"Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at its very bond;
even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down at the vital breath (prāṇa) alone."
"For the mind, my dear, is bound by the vital breath. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2)

In this regard, there is this illustration for the meaning as stated: just as a bird, bound by a string held in the hand of a bird-catcher, having flown in every direction seeking release from its bond,
and failing to find or obtain any other abode or refuge for rest elsewhere than the bond itself, finally resorts to the bond alone.

In this very way, O Śaubhya, just as in this illustration, that mind—which is composed of sixteen parts, nourished by food, and determined to be the primary subject—is designated as "the mind" because the *jīva* has entered it, resides within it, and is characterized by it, just as one might refer to the occupants of a bed by the name of the bed itself (*mañcākrośana*).

That *jīva*, having the mind as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), falls and goes toward various directions—characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth—as taught by ignorance, desire, and karma; the meaning is that it experiences these during the states of waking and dreaming.

Except for her own Self, which is called "Being" (Sat), having found no abode— that is, no place of rest— she, the supreme deity called "Being," is designated as "Prāṇa," being characterized by Prāṇa, which is the support for the performance of all functions.
This is according to such scriptural passages as, "the breath of breath," and "having Prāṇa as her body, she whose form is light."
Therefore, one takes refuge in that deity, Prāṇa—indeed, the one called Prāṇa.
For, my dear, the mind has Prāṇa as its bond; that is, the mind has as its support the deity characterized by Prāṇa, and the individual soul (jīva) is characterized by that [mind]. //2//
"Learn from me, my dear, about hunger and thirst.
When a person is said to 'be hungry,' it is simply the waters that lead away what has been eaten."
"Just as one says 'cow-leader,' 'horse-leader,' or 'man-leader,' so they call this 'food-leader' (aśanāya).
In this regard, my dear, understand that this sprout has sprung up;
it cannot be without a root. (ChU 6.8.3)

Having thus shown the son the true nature of the living self (jīva)— which is the root of the world— by means of the well-known term "he sleeps" (svapiti), the Teacher now says this, desiring to show that the Existent (sat) is also the root of the world by way of the causal series beginning with food and so forth:
"Hunger and thirst"— hunger is the desire to eat, [the word *aśana* being formed] by the elision of the suffix *ya*.
The desire to drink is thirst; "hunger and thirst" refers to these two. Understand the true nature of hunger and thirst:
at what time does a person receive this name? What is it? It is when one desires to eat—that is, when one wishes to consume food.
He explains what the cause of that person’s name is at that time:

when the solid food eaten by the person is led away by the water he has drunk and, having been liquefied, is transformed into the state of essence (*rasa*) and so forth, then the consumed food is digested;
and yet, there arises for him the derivative name "he wishes to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*).
For every living being desires to eat when the food has been digested; thus, in this sense, it is well known as "aśanāyā" (hunger) because water leads that which has been eaten.
Just as a cowherd is called "gonāya" because he leads the cows, so too is it named.
Likewise, one who leads horses is called an *aśvanāya*, meaning a horse-herder;
one who leads men is an *puruṣanāya*, such as a king or a general.
In this way, worldly people refer to those waters as *aśanāya* (the "lead" or "guidance"), with the elision of the visarga.

In this regard, since it is so, know this: this body, produced by food that has been eaten and transformed into the state of the seven fluids and so forth, has arisen and emerged like a sprout from the seed-pod of a banyan tree; O Śvetaketu, understand this effect called the body to have arisen just like a sprout from a banyan or similar tree.

"What is to be understood in this regard? he asked. [The father replied: "Listen; since this thing called the body has a cause, like a sprout, it cannot be rootless—that is, devoid of a root. To this, Śvetaketu said: //3//
"Where could its root be, if not in food? In this very way, my dear, seek water as the root by means of food as the sprout."
"My dear, seek the root of fire by means of water as its sprout;
my dear, seek the root of being by means of fire as its sprout.
My dear, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support."
"If this body, like the sprout of a banyan tree or similar plants, is thus rooted, where might its root be?"—having been asked this, the father said:
"Where might its root be? Nowhere else than in food; food is its root"—this is the intended meaning. How so?
For food that has been eaten is liquefied by water and, being cooked by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), it is transformed into the state of nutrient-essence (*rasa*).
From the essence comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, bones; from bones, marrow; and from marrow, semen.
Likewise, the food eaten by a woman is transformed through this same sequence of essence and so forth, becoming menstrual blood (*lohita*).

The meaning is that this sprout of the body, rooted in food, has been fully developed— growing day by day like a wall built up with lumps of clay— as those two, semen and blood, which are products of food, were joined together and filled daily by the very food being consumed.
And as the sprout of the body is thus rooted in food, even so, my dear, seek out and understand water as the root of this sprout of food, which is its product.

Since water, too, possesses destruction and origination, it is indeed a sprout. O dear one, by means of water as a sprout—that is, the effect—seek its cause, fire, which is the root. Since fire, too, possesses destruction and origination, it is a sprout. By means of fire as a sprout, O dear one, seek that which has Being (*sat*) as its root—the one, non-dual, ultimate reality, in which all this world is superimposed through ignorance, being a mere verbal handle, a modification, a name, and an unreality, like the collection of mental constructs such as a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
Therefore, this is the root of this world; hence, O gentle one, all these creatures characterized as stationary and moving have "Being" as their root—that is, they have Being as their cause.
Not only are they rooted in Being, but even now, during the time of their existence, they have Being as their abode—that is, they have Being as their very support.
For indeed, there is no existence or stability for a jar or similar object without depending upon clay.
Therefore, because they have Being as their subtle root, those beings for whom there is always a foundation are "those whose foundation is Being" (sadāyatanāḥ prajāḥ).

And at the end, those for whom there is Being as their support—wherein "support" (pratiṣṭhā) means dissolution, completion, conclusion, and remainder—are "those whose support is Being" (satpratiṣṭhāḥ). //4//
Now, when a person is said to "thirst," it is the fire-element itself that leads away what has been drunk.
Just as one says "cow-leader," "horse-leader," or "man-leader," so does one call that fire-element "water-leader" (*udanyeti*).
"In this regard, my dear, understand that this very sprout has emerged;
it cannot be without a root. (ChU 6.8.5)
Now, he says that the tracing of the root of Being must be performed by means of the water-branch:

"When," at which time, "this name" occurs—namely, when a person "desires to drink" (pipāsati), meaning he wishes to drink. Like the expression "he desires to eat" (*aśiśiṣati*), this too is merely a figurative name.

The waters that carry the food which has been liquefied and eaten moisten the body—the "shoot" of food—and would cause it to become flaccid due to the excess of water, were they not dried up by heat (*tejas*). Furthermore, when they are thoroughly dried up by heat and transformed into the state of the body's own fluids, a desire to drink arises in the person; then the person is said to "thirst. This is what is meant:

at that time, the heat itself dries up the water and other substances thus drunk, and leads them—that is, transforms them—into the state of blood and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) residing within the body.
Just as [the word] "gonāya" and so forth are explained in the same way, so too the world designates that fire as "udanya," meaning "it leads water" (*udakaṃ nayati*), thus it is "udanya.
The form "udanyeti" is Vedic; there too, it is to be understood as before.
This very sprout called the body belongs to water as well, and nothing else; everything else is the same as previously stated. //5//
"Where could its root be, other than in water? My dear, seek the root of heat by means of water as its sprout."
"By means of the shoot of fire, my dear, seek the root that is Being.
All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support.
Now, my dear, how each of these three divinities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold—each one becoming threefold—has already been explained previously."
When this person departs, my dear, his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the highest deity.
By implication, this very thing called the body is also the sprout of fire;
therefore, by means of the body as the sprout of water, water is understood as the root,
and by means of water as the sprout, fire is understood as the root.

By means of the sprout that is fire (*tejas*), one reaches the root that is Being (*sat*), as before. Thus, having led his son to seek the root that is Being—the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) which is fearless, free from terror, and effortless—the father instructs him, saying: "This sprout of the body, composed of fire, water, and food, is a mere modification of speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*); it has its root in Being. [The father then says: "Seek the root that is Being," and he exhorts him: "One who seeks the root that is Being desires to eat and desires to drink."

By way of establishing the names, he refers back to what was previously stated: that which remains to be said here in this section—namely, how fire, water, and food, when consumed by the person, cause the growth of the body-sprout (the aggregate of causes and effects) without confusion of their respective natures—is already explained here and should be understood as such.
Thus, he points to what was mentioned before.

Indeed, as to the manner in which each of these three deities—known as fire, water, and food—becomes threefold upon reaching the person, that has already been stated previously: "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," and so forth.
In that very context, it was stated that those middle constituents (*dhātu*) of the food and other substances that have been consumed nourish the body consisting of seven constituents.

It is said: "There is flesh, there is blood, there is marrow, there is bone; and those most subtle elements which build up the mind, the vital breath, speech, and the aggregate of the internal organs of the body"—and it is further stated: "That becomes the mind, that becomes the vital breath, that becomes speech."
