Another body must be initiated in this [life];

and once knowledge has arisen, one necessarily performs actions—whether enjoined or prohibited—for as long as one lives; therefore, for the sake of experiencing their fruits, another body must inevitably be initiated, and from that [body] come further actions, and from those another body; thus, knowledge would be rendered purposeless.

Because actions possess fruits, if it were held that actions are destroyed for one who possesses knowledge, then liberation would occur at the very moment knowledge is attained; since knowledge is the cause of attaining Being (*sat*), the body would fall away immediately.

In that case, there would be an absence of a teacher, contradicting the scriptural statement, "A person who has a teacher knows [the truth]," and it would follow that liberation cannot result from knowledge due to the impossibility of possessing a teacher.
Nor can it be argued that knowledge has an uncertain result, like the knowledge of the means for reaching another country;
for there is a logical distinction between actions whose results have already begun to manifest and those whose results have not yet begun.

As for the claim that because actions whose results have not yet begun possess a certain fruit, another body must be commenced for the knower of Brahman after the fall of the current body in order to experience the fruits of those unmanifested actions—that is incorrect.
This is because of the authority of the Vedic scripture stating, "For the wise man, the delay is only so long. [Objection:
But surely the authority of other scriptures such as, "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action," and so forth, is also established. [Reply:
That is indeed so.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction between actions whose results have already begun to manifest (*pravṛttaphala*) and those whose results have not yet begun to manifest (*apravṛttaphala*).
How so?
Those actions whose results have already begun to manifest—by which the body of the wise person was initiated—are exhausted solely through their experience.

Just as an arrow or a missile released toward a target comes to rest only through the exhaustion of its momentum—and not because there is no purpose for it at the very moment it pierces the target—so it is here.

However, other actions whose fruits have not yet begun—whether performed before or after the arising of knowledge, whether committed in this life or in past lives—are burnt away by knowledge, just as they are by expiatory rites; as it is said in the *Atharvaṇa*: "And his actions are destroyed."

Therefore, even though for the knower of Brahman there is no purpose such as living on, the enjoyment of the fruits of those actions whose momentum has already been set in motion must necessarily take place; thus, the statement "for him [the delay] is only so long as he is not released from the body" is perfectly justified, and the objection regarding the aforementioned defect is untenable.

"My dear, when people sit around a man who is suffering from illness, they ask, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?'"
As long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, so long does he know.

"O dear one, when a man is afflicted—meaning, when he is suffering from fever or some other ailment—his kinsmen and relatives surround him and wait upon him, asking, 'Do you know me, your father? Your son? Your brother? As long as speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, [they remain there]—the meaning of this has already been explained. (ChUpBh_6,15.1)
Now, when his speech merges into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and his heat into the highest deity, then he no longer knows.

The very same process of death that belongs to the transmigrating soul is also the process by which the knower attains union with Being; this is what the text declares: "When he has attained union with the supreme deity, with light, then he no longer knows.
However, the ignorant person, having risen from Being, enters again into a state previously cultivated—such as that of a tiger, or the state of a god or a human.

The knower, however, having entered into Being-Brahman-Ātman, which is illuminated by the lamp of knowledge produced through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, does not return; such is the process of attaining union with Being.

Others, however, say that [the soul] departs through the artery at the crown of the head and goes to Being (sat) by way of the sun and other gates; but that is incorrect, because movement is observed to be preceded by a mental conception of place, time, means, and fruit.
For one who perceives the oneness of the Self with Being and whose resolve is fixed on Truth, a false conception regarding place, time, means, fruit, and so forth, is not possible.
Because of contradiction;
and since ignorance, desire, and karma—which are the causes for going—are consumed by the fire of true knowledge, going is simply impossible.
As stated in the Atharva Veda: "For one whose desires are fulfilled and who has realized the Self, all desires vanish right here. And so forth.
And because of the scriptural teaching of the analogy of the rivers and the ocean. //2//
That which is this subtle essence— this whole world has that as its self;
that is the Truth.
"That is the Self;
that art thou, Śvetaketu.
"Venerable sir, please instruct me further."
"So be it," he said, "Yes."
The passage beginning with "He who... is the same [as before].

Since the attainment of Being (*satsampatti*) is equal for one who is about to die and for one who desires liberation, [the question arises: what is the reason that the knower, having attained Being, does not return, whereas the ignorant one returns? "May the Blessed One explain this further by means of an illustration."
"So be it," he said, "yes. //3//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"O Somya, they bring a man, seized by the hand."
"He has stolen; he has committed theft; heat the axe for him!
If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false.
Being intent on falsehood, having concealed himself with falsehood, he takes up the heated axe.
He is burned;
then he is killed.

"Listen, my dear, to how it is: suppose the king's men bring a man suspected of the crime of theft for the purpose of arrest or examination, having seized him by the hand with his hands bound, and when asked, 'What has this man done? they reply, 'He has stolen this person's wealth.
They [the king's men] then say, 'Does he deserve imprisonment merely for the act of stealing?'"
Otherwise, even if the wealth were returned, there would be the risk of imprisonment; thus they spoke. They further said, "He committed theft; he took the wealth by means of music.
While they were speaking thus, the other denied it, saying, "I did not do that.
(They then said, "You have committed a doubtful theft regarding this wealth.")
And regarding that denial, they say, "Heat the axe for him," meaning, "Let him purify himself.

If he is the doer of that theft and yet denies it outwardly, being such as this, he then makes himself otherwise than he truly is—he makes a false representation of himself while being otherwise. Thus, with his mind fixed on falsehood, having concealed himself within by means of untruth, he remains hidden.
Having fashioned a heated axe, he accepts it out of delusion; he is then burned and punished by the king's men due to the fault of his own false promise. //1//
Then, if he becomes a non-doer of that [evil],
he thereby makes himself true.
He, being committed to truth, conceals himself with truth and takes up the heated axe;
he is not burned,
and thus he is released.
Now, if he is not the doer of that deed, then by that very truth he makes himself real.
Having concealed himself by means of that truth—the fact of his not having committed the theft—he takes hold of the heated axe.
Being one whose resolve is fixed on truth, he is not burned because of the intervention of truth; thus he is released from those who falsely accused him.

Even though the contact with the surface of the hand is equal in both cases, when the heated axe is applied, the thief who harbors a false intention is burned, but not the one who harbors a true intention. //2//
Just as there he would not be burned,
so this whole world has that as its self (ātman).
That is the Truth;
that is the Self;
"That thou art, Śvetaketu."
He understood it from him—yes, he understood it. ChU 6.16.3.

Just as one who has a true resolve (*satyābhisandha*) is not burned— because his palm is shielded by truth— when he grasps a heated axe, so too, for both the knower and the other who have a resolve on Being-Brahman (*sad-brahma-satyābhisandhin*), at the time of the body's fall when their attainment of Being (*satsampatti*) is equal,
the knower, having attained Being, does not return to assume the bodies of tigers, gods, or others.

But the ignorant person, identifying with the unreal modifications of nature, attains again the state of a tiger or the like, or the state of a deity or the like, according to his karma and according to his learning.

That which is the cause of liberation and bondage through identification with or non-identification with the Self; that which is the root of the world, the abode of all, the support of all creatures, and that of which everything consists—namely, that which is unborn, immortal, fearless, auspicious, and non-dual—that is the Truth.
"That is the Self; you are that, O Śvetaketu"—this statement, whose meaning has already been explained, is repeated more than once. But who is this Śvetaketu, the referent of the word "you"?

He is the one who knows himself as "I am Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka," having heard the instruction, reflected upon it, and realized it—thereby understanding what was previously unheard, unthought, and unknown.

Desiring to understand his father, he asked: "Venerable sir, how indeed does that instruction come about? This very person—the hearer, the thinker, and the knower—is the Supreme Deity itself which has entered into this aggregate of causes and effects composed of fire, water, and food, for the purpose of manifesting its own name and form, just as a man [is reflected] in a mirror, or as the sun [is reflected] in water and other media. Thus was he awakened by his father through analogies and reasons, with the words "That thou art."
"Indeed, he said: 'I am indeed Being'—thus he realized, he understood.
The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the chapter.
But what, then, is the fruit produced here in the sixth [chapter] by means of the authority of the statement?"

The fruit of that [knowledge] is the cessation of the cognition of being authorized for agency and enjoyership with respect to the Self, which we have described as the meaning denoted by the word "Thou," for the purpose of hearing and reflecting upon it, and for the sake of the fruit of knowing what was previously unknown. Prior to this knowledge, one thinks: "I shall perform these actions such as the Agnihotra; I am authorized here; and I shall enjoy the fruit of these actions both in this world and the next, or, once the actions are performed, I shall have fulfilled my duty. It is thus.

The cognition that arose within him— "I am the one authorized for agency and enjoyment"— is sublated for him once he has awakened through the sentence "That thou art," which reveals the single, non-dual root of this existent world;
this occurs because of their mutual contradiction.

For when this Self, which is one and without a second, is realized as "I am this," the cognition of duality—such as "this other thing is mine," "this must be done by me," or "having done this, I shall enjoy its fruit"—is no longer tenable.
Therefore, it is logical that upon the realization of the existent, true, non-dual Self, the cognition of the individual self (jīvātman), which is a modification and unreal, ceases.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the idea of Being (*sat*) is intended to be superimposed upon the referent of the word "thou" (*tvam*), just as the idea of Brahmā and others is superimposed upon the sun, the mind, and so forth.
And just as in the world one has the cognition of Viṣṇu and others in images and the like, so it is here; but it is not the case that Śvetaketu was already "Being" itself.

For if Śvetaketu were already Being itself, how could he not know himself, such that the instruction "That thou art" would have to be given to him? No, for this is distinct from the passages concerning the sun and other deities.
In passages such as "The sun is Brahman," the direct nature of Brahman is not understood because of the intervention of the word "iti.

Furthermore, because the sun and others possess form and other qualities, and because space and the mind [are mentioned] with the intervention of the word "iti," they are not Brahman. However, in this case, having shown the entry of Being (sat) itself here, the text teaches the unrestricted identity of the self with Being through the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi).
[Objection: But would it not be like saying "You are a lion" based on qualities such as prowess? [Reply: No.
Because of the teaching that "Being alone is real, one and without a second," like clay and so forth;
furthermore, the attainment of Being— expressed as "for him there is delay only so long"— would not be taught through a figurative cognition,
because a figurative cognition is false.
It is not a praise, because Śvetaketu is not an object of worship— just as in the statement, "You are Indra, you are Yama.
Nor would he be praised by being taught that he is truly Śvetaketu.

For a king would not be worthy of praise by being told "you are a slave," nor is it logical for the existent Self, which is the whole, to have its one part suppressed— just as it would be absurd to tell a provincial governor, "you are a village headman. Furthermore, no other possibility exists here that is distinct from the instruction regarding the Self's nature as Being.
If it is argued that here it is merely the cognition "I am Being" that is enjoined as something to be performed, and not that the unknown fact "I am Being" is being made known, [we reply]:
even on this view, such statements as "the unheard becomes heard" would be untenable.
No; for the injunction of the cognition "I am Being" is intended as a glorification (stuti).
No; for there is the instruction: "The man who has a teacher knows; for him, the delay is only so long [as he is not liberated].

For if it were merely the thought "I am Being" that was enjoined as something to be performed, and not the fact that the referent of the word "thou" is itself of the nature of Being, then the instruction regarding the means of knowledge—"the man who has a teacher knows"—would have to be stated [as a mere injunction], just as in cases such as "one should perform the Agnihotra," where having a teacher is already implied by the purpose [of the rite]. But this is not the case here.
Furthermore, the formulation of a time-limit in the words "for him, the delay is only so long" would be inappropriate;
for even if the reality of the Self were not known, liberation would follow from the mere production of a single cognition [of it].

Nor can it be said that when "That thou art" is uttered, the cognition produced by the authoritative statement—"I am not the [empirical] self"—can be prevented from arising or that it has not arisen at all.

Because all the statements of the Upaniṣads culminate solely in that [realization], just as it is impossible to say that the cognitions of the duty to perform the Agnihotra and other rites—produced by the injunctions for those rites—are either false or non-existent, so it is here.
As for what was said: "How could the Self, being existent, not know itself? [the answer follows].
This is not a fault.

Since living beings do not naturally perceive themselves as "I am the individual soul (jīva), the agent, and the enjoyer," distinct from the aggregate of the body and its organs, how could they possess knowledge of the True Self?
How indeed, while such a perception of distinction exists, can their perception of being an agent and so forth be possible—and yet it is observed?
Similarly, because one possesses the notion of a self with regard to the body and so forth, the knowledge of the true Self would not arise.

Therefore, it is established that this sentence, "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), serves solely to sublate the knowledge of the individual soul (jīvātman) which is subject to modification and unreality. //3//
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
thus ends the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
"Teach me, Venerable Sir!"—with these words Nārada approached Sanatkumāra.
He said to him: "Approach me with what you already know."
"Then I shall tell you what is beyond that," he said. He [the son] replied: "Tell me. ChU 7.1.1.

The sixth chapter, which is primarily devoted to the instruction on the reality of the ultimate truth, is employed solely for the purpose of determining the eternal unity of the Self. Since the principles characterized as modifications prior to Being have not yet been pointed out, [the author] intends to point them out in succession—beginning with Name and ending with Breath—and by means of them, to point out the unsurpassed reality called the "Full" (bhūman), just as one points out the moon by means of a branch. Thus it is said: "In this manner..."
He begins the seventh chapter.

For, even though the principles lower than Being (sat) have been mentioned and Pure Being itself has been pointed out, someone might still harbor the doubt that something else remains unknown; thus, he intends to point them out so that this doubt may not arise.

Alternatively, like ascending a staircase, having first made known the gross and then the subtle—the objects of the intellect—he intends to point out Name and the rest, thinking, "I shall consecrate [the seeker] in the sovereignty that transcends those."

Alternatively, since the principles (tattvas) beginning with Name and so forth are progressively more distinguished, and the principle called the Plenum (bhūman) is the most excellent among them, they are presented in sequence for the purpose of praising that [Plenum].
The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is for the purpose of praising the higher knowledge (paravidyā).
How so?

Even Nārada, the celestial sage, though he had accomplished all that was to be done and possessed all branches of knowledge, still grieved because of his lack of self-knowledge; what then need be said of any other being of little learning who has not performed superior meritorious deeds and has not achieved his purpose? Alternatively, this narrative of Sanatkumāra and Nārada is commenced to demonstrate that there is no means for attaining unsurpassed bliss other than the knowledge of the Self, by which even the celestial sage Nārada—though endowed with the power of all means of knowledge—did not attain the highest good, and by which [the goal is reached] through the excellence of noble lineage, learning, conduct, and the power of the means.

Having abandoned pride, he approached Sanatkumāra like an ordinary person for the sake of attaining the means to the highest good; thus, it is made known that the knowledge of the Self is the means for attaining the unsurpassed.
He indeed approached him, saying, "Teach me, O Blessed One, teach me! (adhihi-adhīṣva).
"Teach me, O Blessed One"—this is the mantra.
Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, the lord of yogis and most devoted to Brahman.
To him who had approached according to the proper rule, he said: "If you know anything regarding the Self, approach me by proclaiming that; this is what I [desire]."
When he had said, "I know; therefore, from your knowledge, I shall speak further to you," Nārada replied. //1//
"Venerable sir, I have studied the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth,

the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, phonology, the science of the gods, and the science of ritual."

"I know the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of beings, the knowledge of the ruling power, the knowledge of the stars, and the knowledge of the serpents and divine beings; this, O Venerable Sir, is what I have studied."
"Venerable sir, I study and remember the Ṛgveda"—since it is the knowledge [of these] that is being questioned by the words "whatever you know";

likewise, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth Veda (the word *veda* being the subject under discussion), and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth Veda among the Vedas of which the Mahābhārata is the fifth; for it is through grammar that the Ṛgveda and the others are understood according to the division of words and so forth.
The ancestral rites according to the *śrāddha-kalpa*,
the calculation of *kāśī*,
and the divine knowledge of portents.
*Nidhi* refers to the treatises on treasures such as those concerning Mahākāla;
*vākovākya* refers to the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*);
and *ekāyana* refers to the science of ethics (*nīti-śāstra*).
The science of the gods (devavidyā) is etymology (nirukta).

The science of Brahman—that is, the science of that which is called the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—is the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), consisting of phonetics (śikṣā), ritual codes (kalpa), and metrics (chandas).
The science of beings (bhūtavidyā) is the tantra of spirits.
The science of the Kṣatriyas is the Dhanurveda (the science of archery).
The science of the stars is Jyotiṣa (astronomy and astrology).

The science of the serpents and the divine beings consists of the science of serpents (Gāruḍa) and the science of divine beings, which includes knowledge of the preparation of perfumes, dancing, singing, instrumental music, the arts, and so forth.
"O Venerable One, I have studied all of this. //2//
"Venerable sir, I am indeed a knower of the mantras, but not a knower of the Self.
For I have heard from those like your reverence that one who knows the Self overcomes sorrow."
"Therefore, O Blessed One, I grieve;
may the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of this grief.
He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here, it is indeed only name."
"O Venerable One, although I know all this, I am merely a knower of the mantras (*mantravit*"; the meaning is that I possess only the knowledge of words and their referents.
For every word is merely a designation (*abhidhāna*), and every designation is included within the mantras.
"I am merely a knower of the mantras" means I am a knower of the mantras, which is to say, a knower of ritual actions (*karmavid*)."
For it will be stated later that "rites [are accomplished] by means of mantras. One who knows the mantras does not know the Self;
for surely, the Self is also revealed by the mantras—so how can one who knows the mantras not be a knower of the Self? No;
because the distinction between the designator and the designated is a product of transformation (vikāra).
Furthermore, modification is not accepted as being the Self.
But surely the Self is also denoted by the word "Self"? No, because [the scripture says]: "from which words turn back."
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Where one sees nothing else," and so forth.
[Objection: How then do words such as "The Self alone is below" and "That is the Self" convey the Self?
[Response: This is not a fault.

When a word is employed with reference to the inner self (pratyagātman) as embodied—which is the object of the notion of difference—and when the body and other such things are rejected as being the self, that which remains conveys the reality even though it is inexpressible.

Just as when an army is seen together with its king, although the king is not visible because he is concealed by umbrellas, banners, flags, and so forth, the linguistic usage "the king is seen here" occurs; and in that case, when one seeks to determine the specific identity of the king by asking "Who is this king?", [the answer is given].
Just as when another king who is not currently visible is excluded from view, the cognition of "king" still arises [regarding him], so it is here.

Therefore, [the ignorant person thinks]: "I am indeed a knower of mantras and a knower of rituals; I am one who knows all ritual action and its effects, which are modifications (vikāra). Thus, he is merely a knower of modifications, meaning he is not a knower of the Self, nor a knower of the true nature of the Self's primordial essence (prakṛti).
For this very reason it is said: "The person who has a teacher knows [the truth]."

And from such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back," it follows that there certainly exists the knowledge of the scriptures (*āgama-jñāna*). For since one who knows the Self transcends—overcomes—the sorrow, the mental anguish, and the sense of unfulfilled purpose, therefore, O Blessed One, because I do not know the Self, I grieve; I am constantly tormented by the conviction that my purpose has not been achieved. Therefore, [protect] me, who am thus.

"May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore, the end of this ocean of grief; may he bring my intellect to fulfillment through the boat of self-knowledge and lead me to fearlessness"—this is the meaning. To him who had spoken thus, [the teacher] said: "Whatever indeed you have studied here—by 'studying' (adhyayana), the knowledge of its meaning is indicated—you have known it; this is merely a name."
For the Śruti declares: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name. //3//

"Name," indeed, is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvana as the fourth, the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge, and the science of elemental beings.
"The science of the Kṣatriyas, the science of the stars, and the science of the serpents and divine beings—this is merely a name. Meditate upon the Name. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.4)
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and so forth—this is merely Name.
Worship Name as Brahman, that is, with the thought that it is Brahman; just as one worships an image with the thought that it is Viṣṇu, so it is here. //4//
He who meditates on "Name" as Brahman—
so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom, provided he meditates on "Name" as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than name?
"There is indeed something greater than name. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.1.5.

Now, hear what the fruit is for him who meditates upon Name as Brahman: as far as Name extends, as far as the range of Name, within that sphere of Name, he has freedom of movement according to his desire, just like a king within his own domain.

The concluding statement is: "He who meditates on Name as Brahman. The intention is: "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than Name—which is more significant—that is worthy of being viewed as Brahman?
Sanatkumāra said: "There is indeed something greater than Name. When this was said, [Nārada] replied: "If there is such a thing, may the Venerable One tell it to me. (5)
Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Speech, indeed, is greater than name.

Speech indeed makes known the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth among the Vedas, the ritual for the ancestors, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, dialogues, monistic doctrine, the science of the gods,
the science of sacred knowledge, the science of elemental beings, the science of weaponry, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings, and the heavens.

Earth and wind, space and water, and fire; gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and forest trees, and beasts of prey, down to worms, moths, and ants; dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, and that which is pleasing to the heart and that which is not.
If speech did not exist, neither dharma nor adharma would be made known; neither truth nor falsehood, neither the good nor the bad, neither that which is pleasing to the heart nor that which is not.
Speech alone makes all this known. Meditate upon speech. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1)
"Speech indeed.
Speech is the sense organ situated in the eight locations, such as the tongue and the roots of the teeth, which manifests phonemes;
and since phonemes constitute names, it is said that speech is greater than name.
In the world, it is observed that the cause is greater than the effect, just as a father is greater than his son;

in the same way, how is speech greater than name? He says: "Speech indeed makes the Ṛgveda known, [informing us] 'This is the Ṛgveda,'" and similarly for the Yajurveda and so forth—the rest is the same.
"Knowing the heart" means being dear to the heart;
the opposite of that is "not knowing the heart.

If speech did not exist, then dharma and so forth would not have been made known. In the absence of speech, there would be an absence of study; in the absence of study, there would be an absence of hearing its meaning; and in the absence of hearing it, dharma and so forth would not have been made known.
The meaning is that it would have been known.
Therefore, speech alone makes all this known through the utterance of sounds; thus, speech is greater than name. For this reason, meditate upon speech as Brahman. 1.
He who venerates speech as Brahman—
he has freedom of movement as far as speech extends, for him who venerates speech as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than speech?
"There is indeed something greater than speech. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.2)
The rest is the same. //2//
Thus ends the second section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Mind, indeed, is greater than speech.
Just as one's fist encompasses two *vāmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* fruits, or two *akṣa* fruits, even so the mind encompasses both speech and name.
When he intends with his mind, "I shall study the mantras," then he studies;
when he intends, "I shall perform rituals," then he performs them.
"One might desire sons and cattle," and so he desires them; "one might desire this world and the next," and so he desires them;
for the mind is indeed the self.
For the mind is the world;
for the mind is Brahman. Meditate upon the mind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.3.1)
The mind (*manas*), which is the internal organ characterized by the activity of thinking, is greater than speech.
For it is the mind, possessing the function of thinking, that impels speech toward what is to be spoken;
therefore, speech is included within the mind.
And whatever is included within something else is more extensive than that, because it pervades it.
Just as in the world, a fist encompasses two *āmalaka* fruits, or two *kola* (jujube) fruits, or two *akṣa* (bibhitaka) fruits; the fist pervades those fruits, for they are contained within the fist.
In this way, speech and name are experienced by the mind, just as in the case of the *āmalaka* fruit and so forth.
When, at whatever time, a person reflects with the mind—that is, the internal organ—the reflection being the desire to speak (*vivakṣā-buddhi*). How so?

Having formed the desire to speak, thinking, "I shall study and recite the mantras," he then studies them; likewise, having formed the desire to act (*cikīrṣā-buddhi*), thinking, "I shall perform ritual acts."
The meaning is: having first formed the desire, "I wish to obtain sons and cattle," one then desires them—that is, one obtains sons and so forth—by performing the means for their attainment.

Likewise, having formed the desire, "I wish to obtain this world and the next by means [of ritual action]," one then desires them—that is, one obtains them—by performing the means for their attainment.

For the mind is indeed the self; since agency and enjoyership belong to the self only when the mind exists and not otherwise, the mind is said to be the self. For the mind is indeed the world; for it is only when the mind exists that the world comes to be, as well as the practice of the means for attaining it. Since the mind is indeed the world, therefore the mind is indeed Brahman.
Because this is so, meditate upon the mind. //1//
He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—
so far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on the mind as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than the mind? "There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. (ChU 7.3.2)
"That which... and so forth is the same [as before]. //2//
Thus ends the third section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Volition, indeed, is greater than the mind.
When one indeed forms a mental resolve, then one intends; then one utters speech,
and that [speech] one projects into a name.
The mantras are one in Name;
the ritual acts are one in the mantras.
Volition (saṃkalpa) is indeed greater than the mind.

Volition is a function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that consists of mental deliberation; it is the determination [of what is] to be done and what is not to be done by means of discrimination.
For when an object has been determined through discrimination, the desire to act arises immediately after the stage of mental deliberation.

How so? When one indeed forms a volition (*saṃkalpayate*), differentiating objects such as what ought to be done— thinking, "It is proper to do this"— then one intends (*manasyati*) such things as, "I shall study the mantras," and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, one utters speech for the purpose of pronouncing mantras and the like. And one utters that speech by first forming the intention (*vivakṣā*) to utter a name; [this means] that within the name—that is, within the general category of names—the specific words that are mantras become one, or rather, are included within it.
For it is the particular that is included within the general.
Ritual actions are one with the mantras;
ritual actions are performed as revealed by the mantras, for there is no ritual action that exists without a mantra.
For it is that very action, which acquires its existence through the revelation of the mantra, that is prescribed as "this must be performed by the Brahmin for this specific result."
Even that appearance of the origin of rituals within the Brāhmaṇas is merely the clarification of those very rituals whose existence was already established in the Mantras;
for no ritual not revealed by the Mantras is seen to have originated in the Brāhmaṇas.
It is well known in the world that ritual action is prescribed by the Trayī (the three Vedas).
The word *trayī* (the triad) is a designation for the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas].
Furthermore, in the *Atharvaveda* it is said: "The sages beheld those rituals within the mantras.
Therefore, it is appropriate that rituals are contained within the mantras. //1//
These, indeed, have volition as their sole point of convergence, have volition as their essence, and are established in volition. Heaven and earth were willed into existence.
The wind and space were in harmony; the waters and fire were in harmony. Through their harmony, rain was brought into being.
Through the intention regarding rain, food is intended; through the intention regarding food, the vital breaths are intended;
through the intention regarding the vital breaths, the mantras are intended.
Through the volition of mantras, ritual actions are willed; through the volition of ritual actions, the world is willed;
through the volition of the world, everything is willed.
This is that very resolve.
Meditate upon resolve. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.4.2)
These, indeed, are the mind and the others, which have volition as their single goal; "single goal" means that volition is their one path—their course and their dissolution.

They consist of volition at the time of origination and are established in volition during their duration. For heaven and earth are observed to be as if they had formed a volition, remaining motionless.
Likewise, Vāyu and Ākāśa also "resolved," as it were; they too formed a resolution. Similarly, Āpas and Tejas "resolved" and are observed to be motionless in their own form.
Because of the resolution of those elements—Heaven, Earth, and the rest—they resolve upon rain, which is the cause of that resolution.
For the vital breaths (prāṇas) consist of food and are supported by food.

“For food is to be given,” so says the Śruti. The mantras become effective for the purpose of their intended application; for it is one possessed of vital breath who studies the mantras, not one who is weak.
For rites such as the Agnihotra are intended for the purpose of the manifestation of mantras; when performed as revealed by the mantras, they become capable of yielding their fruit.
Therefore, the world intends toward the fruit, meaning it becomes capable through its inherence in the agent of the action.
For the purpose of the world's intention, the entire universe intends, so that there may be no deficiency in its own nature.

For all this entire world, which culminates in results, has its root in volition (*saṃkalpa*). Therefore, this volition is preeminent. Having said, "Meditate upon volition," he states the result for one who meditates upon it. //2//
He who meditates upon volition as Brahman—being himself steadfast, he attains steadfast worlds;
being established, he attains established worlds; being unshakable, he attains unshakable worlds; and being well-ordered, he attains well-ordered worlds.
As far as the reach of resolve extends, so far one has freedom of movement therein who meditates upon resolve as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than resolve? "Indeed, there is something greater than resolve."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.4.3)

He who meditates upon volition as Brahman with the thought that it is Brahman—for him, these worlds are prepared by the Creator as his fruit; that wise man obtains them as they have been prepared, established, and intended. They are "firm" (dhruva) in the sense of being eternal relative to the extremely non-eternal, and he himself is firm. For if the inhabitant of the worlds were non-firm, the preparation of the worlds as firm would be purposeless; thus, being firm, he obtains them as "well-established," meaning endowed with all necessary means and resources.

Because it is seen that one becomes established through cattle, sons, and so forth, and because he himself is established—being endowed with his own means of subsistence and free from distress—he, being undistressed and devoid of fear of enemies and the like, attains and reaches [his goal]; this is the meaning.

"As far as the range of his resolve extends"—that is, within the sphere of his resolve; therein he has freedom of action according to his will. This refers to the resolve of the self (the liberated one), and not to the resolves of all people, for that would contradict the subsequent description of the fruit.
"He who meditates upon volition as Brahman," and so forth, as previously stated. //3//
Thus ends the fourth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Mind, indeed, is greater than volition.
When one indeed perceives, then one forms an intention;
then one reflects;
then one utters speech.
And they lead her up by means of the Name;
for the mantras become one in the Name,
and the ritual acts are contained within the mantras.
The mind, indeed, is greater than volition.

The mind is that which possesses the nature of a thinker—that is, the state of having an awareness appropriate to the time at hand—and the capacity to discern the purposes and objects of both the past and the future; it is greater even than volition.
How so?

When one indeed perceives, "It has been obtained," then one intends to give it away or to discard it; then one forms a resolution, then one reflects upon it, and so forth, as described previously. //1//
These, indeed, have thought as their single path, thought as their self, and are established in thought.
Therefore, even if one is a man of many kinds of knowledge, if he is without thought, people say of him: "This man does not exist."
Thinking, "Whatever this man knows, or whatever he knows as a learned man,
may he not be thus lacking in discernment," people indeed desire to listen to him if he possesses even a little discernment;
for discernment alone is their common goal.
"The mind is the self;
the mind is the foundation.
Meditate upon the mind. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.5.2)

Those [faculties], beginning with volition (saṃkalpa) and ending with action and its fruit, have the mind as their single path, the mind as their essence, arise from the mind, are established in the mind, and abide in the mind—this is also to be understood as before.
Furthermore, what is the greatness of the mind?
Since the mind is the root of volition and the rest, therefore, even one who possesses extensive knowledge of many sciences and so forth is [nothing] if he is without the [properly directed] mind.
He becomes devoid of the capacity for volition regarding what has been attained and so forth; the wise say of him, "Though this man exists, he is as good as non-existent.
And whatever of the scriptures and such he knows or has heard, they declare that even that is in vain for him.
Why?
The meaning is that they say: "If this person were truly wise, he would not have such a mind; therefore, even though he has heard [the teachings], it is as if he had not heard them at all.

Conversely, even if one knows little, if he possesses the right mental disposition, people will indeed desire to listen—that is, they wish to hear—in order for him to grasp the meaning of what has been said.
And therefore, the mind alone is the single point of convergence for these—volition and the rest—as described previously. //2//

He who meditates on Brahman as thought (citta) indeed attains, through thought, worlds that are firm, being himself firm; established, being himself established; and unshakable, being himself unshakable.
As far as the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement therein—he who meditates upon the mind as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than the mind?
"There is indeed something greater than the mind."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (ChU 7.5.3)
Those who have not accumulated [merit] through mental qualities, that worshiper of the mind, along with the words "the eternal" and so forth—this has already been explained in meaning. //3//
Thus ends the fifth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Meditation, indeed, is greater than thought.
The earth, as it were, meditates; the intermediate space, as it were, meditates; the sky, as it were, meditates.
The waters seem to meditate; the mountains seem to meditate;
gods and humans seem to meditate.
Therefore, those among humans here who attain greatness become, as it were, like participants in the attainment of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Now, those who are insignificant, quarrelsome, slanderous, and backbiters—they are [the opposite]. But those who are powerful become, as it were, like participants in the attainment of meditative absorption.
"Venerate meditation."—ChU 7.6.1.
He who meditates upon meditation as Brahman—
so far as meditation extends, there he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon meditation as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than meditation?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than meditation.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Meditation (dhyāna) is indeed greater than thought (citta).
Meditation is defined as a continuous stream of cognitions that is unshakable and uninterrupted by heterogeneous states when directed toward objects such as deities prescribed in the scriptures;
this is what they call one-pointedness (ekāgratā).
And the greatness of meditation is seen through its fruit.
How so?
Just as a yogi becomes motionless while meditating upon attaining the fruit of meditation.
Thus, the earth appears as if meditating, motionless;
"the atmosphere appears as if meditating," and so forth—the rest is the same.

"Gods and humans" (*devamanuṣyāḥ*) refers either to gods and humans, or specifically to humans who are like gods; the meaning is that these humans, perfected in qualities such as tranquility (*śama*), do not abandon their divine nature.

Since meditation (*dhyāna*) is thus distinguished, therefore those among men in this world who attain greatness—meaning they obtain the cause for greatness through wealth, knowledge, or virtues—are like those possessing a mere fraction of the attainment of meditation. "Attainment" (*āpāda*) refers to the acquisition of meditation, that is, the obtaining of its fruit; a "fraction" (*aṃśa*) is a part or portion. Thus, the meaning is that they are like those who possess only a small portion of the fruit of meditation.
They appear as if motionless and not at all mean-spirited.
On the other hand, those who are few, petty, and have not attained even a fraction of greatness in wealth and so forth, are the opposite of those previously described:
they are quarrelsome, having a disposition for strife, slanderous, exposing the faults of others, and censorious—bringing to light the faults of others as if they were right before one's eyes.
Those whose nature is to speak ill of women become slanderers.

Furthermore, those who have attained greatness through wealth and such means exercise power over others; thus, "the powerful" refers to learned teachers, kings, lords, and so forth, being like those who have attained the stages of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

This is the meaning already stated. Therefore, the greatness of meditation is seen in its fruit; since it is even greater than the mind itself, one should practice it—this is the meaning of what was said. //1-2//
Thus ends the sixth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Knowledge, indeed, is greater than meditation.

Or, by means of consciousness, one discerns the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth, the *Itihāsa-purāṇa* as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, dialogue, monistic doctrine, the science of the gods,
the science of sacred knowledge, the science of elemental beings, the science of weaponry, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings, and the heavens.
By means of discernment alone, one discerns the earth, wind, space, water, and fire; gods, humans, cattle, birds, grasses, forest trees, and beasts of prey, down to worms, moths, and ants;
righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant, food and flavor, and this world and the yonder world.
"Worship consciousness."—ChU 7.7.1.
Consciousness (vijñāna) is indeed greater than meditation (dhyāna).
Consciousness is knowledge regarding the subject matter of the scriptures; because it is the cause of meditation, it is greater than meditation.

And how is it greater? He says: "By means of consciousness one knows the Ṛgveda, [thinking] 'this is the Ṛgveda,'" for it is through its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the knowledge of its meaning serves as the cause of meditation.
Likewise, [the text mentions] the Yajurveda and so forth;
furthermore, animals and the like, as well as dharma and adharma, are established by the scriptures,
while the good and the bad are established by worldly consensus.
Or rather, the meaning is that through consciousness alone one discerns everything pertaining to the sphere of the Smṛti, as well as all objects both seen and unseen.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the knowledge of meditation and so forth is more abundant; hence, "meditate upon consciousness. //1//
He who venerates Brahman as consciousness (vijñāna) indeed attains worlds that are conscious and endowed with knowledge.
To whatever extent there is the range of consciousness, he has freedom of movement therein who venerates consciousness as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than consciousness?
"Indeed, there is something greater than consciousness."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.7.2)

Listen to the fruit of meditation for one who possesses discernment (*vijñāna*): he attains, that is, reaches, those worlds belonging to those who possess discernment as well as those who possess knowledge (*jñāna*). Discernment is knowledge concerning the subject matter of the scriptures; knowledge is proficiency regarding other subjects. The meaning is that he does not fail to reach the worlds inhabited by such persons. "As far as discernment extends," and so forth, is as explained previously. //2//
Thus ends the seventh section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Power, indeed, is greater than understanding.
Indeed, even a single powerful person can shake a hundred wise men;
when he becomes strong, he becomes one who rises up;
rising up, he becomes one who serves.
By serving, one becomes an attendant;
by attending, one becomes a seer, a hearer, a thinker, a knower, an agent, and a perceiver.

By strength indeed the earth stands firm; by strength the intermediate space, by strength the sky, by strength the mountains, by strength gods and humans, by strength domestic animals and birds, grasses, trees, and wild beasts.
"From worms, moths, and ants, the world stands by means of strength; meditate upon strength. (ChU 7.8.1)
He who worships strength—
so far as the reach of strength extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who worships strength as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than strength?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than strength.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Power, indeed, is greater than understanding.
"Power" refers to the capacity of the mind for intuitive insight regarding objects of knowledge, generated by the consumption of food.
This is based on the Vedic text: "From lack of food, the *ṛc* and other [Vedas] do not indeed manifest to me, O sir."

In the body as well, that same capacity for rising and so forth exists, because even a single strong living being can shake a hundred conscious men, just as a single rutting elephant can shake a hundred men gathered together. Since strength is thus caused by the consumption of food and other such things, when that person becomes strong—that is, possessed of strength—he then rises, being an agent of rising;
and while rising, he becomes an attendant of his elders and teacher, being an agent of attendance, which is to say, service.
The meaning is that by serving them, one who approaches them becomes their intimate associate.
And as he approaches—going into their presence—he becomes a beholder of the teacher or another instructor with one-pointed attention;
thereafter, he becomes a listener to what has been spoken by them.

Then, thinking "this is established by these [reasons] in this way," one becomes a thinker through logical justification; and being a thinker, one becomes a knower, realizing "this is exactly so. Having thus ascertained it, one becomes the doer and performer of the meaning of what was said, and the experiencer of the fruit of that performance—this is the sense.
Furthermore, the greatness of power is shown by such statements as "by power indeed the earth stands," and so forth. //1-2//
Thus ends the eighth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Food, indeed, is greater than strength.
Therefore, even if one were not to eat for ten nights—
if indeed one should live—
one becomes a non-seer, a non-hearer, a non-thinker, a non-understander, a non-doer, and a non-knower.
Then, for the sake of food, one becomes a seer, one becomes a hearer, one becomes a thinker, one becomes a knower, one becomes a doer, and one becomes a cognizer.
"Meditate upon food," [he said].
Food, indeed, is greater than strength, because it is the cause of strength. How is it that food is the cause of strength? This is explained as follows.

Since food is the cause of strength, therefore, even if someone were not to eat for ten nights, he would die due to the loss of the strength caused by the consumption of food; or, if he should live—though it is indeed observed that people live even without eating for a month—even while living, he becomes one who does not see, and likewise, he does not hear from his teacher and so forth; thus, everything becomes the opposite of what it was before.
Now, when, having not eaten for many days, he becomes incapable of activities such as seeing and the like, he is one who has *āya* of food;
*āya* means the coming (*āgamana*) of food, that is to say, its acquisition.
He in whom that exists is "one who has *āya* of food" (*annasyā’yī*).
The word *āya* is [derived] through a transposition of syllables;
furthermore, there is also a reading *annasyā'yāḥ*, which has the same meaning,
because of the hearing of effects such as "the seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth.
For it is observed that the capacity for seeing and other such functions exists when food is consumed, but not when it is not obtained; therefore, "partake of food. //1//
He who meditates on food as Brahman attains worlds that abound in food and drink.
As far as food extends, so far he has freedom of movement there who meditates upon food as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than food?
"There is indeed something greater than food."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (ChU 7.9.2)

And as a fruit for one who possesses food, he attains worlds that abound in food; and for one who possesses drink, worlds that abound in water—since food and drink are eternally connected—he attains these worlds.
The rest is the same. //2//
Thus ends the ninth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Water, indeed, is greater than food.
Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings become distressed, thinking, "Food will become scarce.

But when there is good rain, living beings become joyful, thinking, "Food will be abundant. These very waters have taken form as this earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the mountains, gods and humans, domestic animals and birds, grasses, trees, wild beasts, and even down to worms, moths, and ants.
"These very things are water in embodied form; meditate upon water. // ChUp 7.10.1 //
Water indeed is greater than food, because it is the cause of food.

Since this is so, when—at whatever time—there is no good rain, meaning a beneficial and auspicious rain for the crops, then living beings become afflicted and suffer. He asks: "For what reason? and says: "In this year, our food will become less, that is, more meager."

Furthermore, when there is good rain, living beings—possessing breath—become joyful, happy, and delighted, thinking, "There will be an end [to scarcity]; there will be much, there will be abundance. Since material food originates from water, these very waters have transformed into the forms of the differentiated categories of the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta). That which is this earth, that which is the intermediate space, and so forth—all these are the formed waters. Therefore, meditate upon the waters. //1//
He who venerates water as Brahman obtains all desires and becomes satisfied.
"As far as water extends, so far he has freedom of movement who venerates water as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than water? "There is indeed something greater than water."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.10.2)

The fruit [of this meditation]: he who meditates upon water as Brahman obtains all desires—that is to say, all desirable objects that possess form. Furthermore, because satisfaction arises from water, by meditating on water one becomes possessed of satisfaction. The rest is the same [as before]. //2//
Thus ends the tenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Fire, indeed, is greater than water.
Now, when that [heat] seizes the wind and heats the space, they say, "It is glowing; it is scorching; it will rain.
Having first displayed its brilliance, it then emits water.
Then these thunderclaps proceed with lightning flashes both upward and across; therefore they say, "It lightens; it thunders; it will rain."
Having first manifested heat itself, it then creates water;
"Meditate upon heat," he said.
Fire, indeed, is greater than water, because fire is the cause of water. To the question, "How is it the cause of water? he says:

Since fire has its source in the wind, therefore that very fire, having seized and held fast the wind—having made it motionless by means of its own self—heats the space, and while pervading the space, he heats it. When that happens, people in the world say: "It is glowing; it is burning;
it is heating the world in general and the bodies; therefore it will rain."

For it is well known in the world that one who has seen a cause being exerted possesses the cognition that "the effect will come to be. That fire first manifests itself, and immediately thereafter creates water; therefore, because it is the creator of water, fire is prior to water.
Furthermore, this very same fire becomes the cause of rain in the form of thunder.
How so?
Together with upward-moving lightning flashes and horizontal ones moving across, there arise sounds of thundering and rumbling.
Therefore, upon seeing that, people in the world say, "It is flashing," "it is thundering," or "it will rain," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
"Therefore, worship the fire as the light," [he said]. //1//
He who meditates on Brahman as splendor indeed becomes splendid; he attains splendid worlds that are luminous and free from darkness.
As far as the reach of fire extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon fire as Brahman.
"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than fire? "Indeed, there is something greater than fire."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. ChUp 7.11.2.

The fruit of the meditation on that *tejas* is this: he indeed becomes radiant. And he attains radiant worlds—luminous, full of light, and with darkness dispelled, meaning that the darkness of external and internal ignorance has been removed.
The rest is of straightforward meaning. //2//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Space, indeed, is greater than fire.
In space indeed are both the sun and the moon, lightning, the stars, and fire;
by means of space one calls out,
and by means of space one hears.
He glides through space;
he delights in space;
he does not delight in space.
"It is born from space;
it is born from space;
meditate upon space. // ChUp 7.12.1 //
Space, indeed, is greater than fire.

Because space is the cause of fire together with air, and since air was mentioned along with fire in the previous statement by including it in the phrase "having grasped air," it is not mentioned separately here as the cause of fire.
For in the world, a cause is observed to be greater than its effect.
Just as clay is greater than jars and other such objects, so too is space greater than fire accompanied by air; for it is its cause.
How so?
Indeed, both the sun and the moon, which are forms of light, as well as lightning, the stars, and fire—all these forms of light—are contained within space.
Furthermore, that which is contained within something else is small, while the other is the greater.
Moreover, one person calls out to another by means of space, and being called, the other hears by means of space; one hears the sound spoken by another and another responds;
they delight and play with one another in space, whereas no one delights in space when separated from a wife and so forth.
Space is not produced where it is already occupied by a material object;
likewise, sprouts and the like grow directed toward space, not in its opposite direction.
Therefore, take recourse in space. //1//
He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that are spacious,
luminous, unconfined, and wide-extending.
As far as the reach of space extends, so far he has freedom of movement who meditates upon space as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than space?
"Indeed, there is something greater than space."
"May the Blessed One explain that to me. ChU 7.12.2.
Listen to the fruit: that wise man attains worlds that possess space, which are expansive and luminous;

because light and space are eternally connected, he attains luminous worlds that are free from obstruction—obstruction being the state of being crowded, where there is mutual oppression—and thus he attains worlds that are unobstructed, possessing wide-reaching paths and vast scope for movement.
The phrase "as far as space" and so forth has its meaning already explained. //2//
Thus ends the twelfth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Memory, indeed, is greater than space.
Therefore, even if many were to sit together, if they were not mindful, they would not hear anything, nor would they reflect upon it, nor would they understand it.
But when they become mindful, then they hear, then they reflect, then they understand.
Indeed, by means of mindfulness one recognizes one's children; by means of mindfulness, one recognizes one's cattle.
"Meditate upon Smara."—ChU 7.13.1.
He who meditates on memory as Brahman—
so far as the reach of memory extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on memory as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than memory?"
"Indeed, there is something greater than memory.
May the Blessed One explain that to me."
Memory indeed is greater than space.
Memory is the act of remembering, which is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

It should be understood that it is greater than space, despite the change in grammatical gender [from neuter *ākāśam* to masculine *smaraḥ*]. For when there is memory on the part of the rememberer, everything beginning with space becomes purposeful, because it serves as an object of enjoyment for one who possesses memory.
But when there is no recollection, even that which exists is as if non-existent, because it lacks its functional effect upon sentient beings.
Furthermore, in the absence of recollection, it is impossible to perceive the existence of space and so forth; therefore, recollection is more vast than space.

For it is observed in the world that there is a great deficiency in memory; therefore, even if many people were to sit together in one place, if those sitting there do not remember what was said by one another, they would not hear any sound at all, nor would they reflect upon it—if they were to reflect, they would reflect only if they remembered; because of the absence of memory, they would not reflect, and likewise, they would not understand.
"When they indeed remember what is to be reflected upon, what is to be understood, and what is to be heard, then they hear; then they reflect; then they understand.
Thus, by means of memory, one recognizes, 'These are my sons,' and by means of memory, one recognizes one's cattle.
Because it is greater than these, meditate upon memory."
The rest has already been explained. //1-2//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Hope, indeed, is greater than memory.
"Desire indeed is memory; one who possesses desire studies the sacred hymns, performs ritual acts, desires sons and cattle, and desires both this world and the world beyond.
Meditate upon desire. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.14.1)
Hope, indeed, is greater than memory.
Hope is the longing for an object not yet attained; it is what they call by synonyms such as thirst and desire. And that is greater than memory.
How so?
For by means of the *āśaya* residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one remembers that which is to be remembered.
Remembering that which has the form of the object of desire (*āśā*), he becomes *smara*; therefore, being kindled by *āśā* and increased by *āśaya*, he becomes *smara*.
Remembering the *Ṛg* and other mantras, he studies them; having studied them, he hears their meaning and the injunctions from the Brāhmaṇas and performs rituals with the desire for their fruits.

He desires sons as the fruits of those rituals, and out of that very desire, he practices the means to achieve them. And desiring this world as well, he seeks it through the means for maintaining the world, all while remembering [the scriptures].

And having kindled this world with hope, one desires it through the performance of the means for its attainment; therefore, the entire universe—beginning with memory and space and extending to names—is bound by the tether of hope and revolves around every living being.
In this regard, since hope is even greater than memory, worship hope. 1.
He who meditates on hope as Brahman—
his every desire is fulfilled through hope.
His blessings become unfailing.
As far as his hope extends, there he has freedom of movement according to his desire—he who venerates hope as Brahman.
"Is there, O Venerable Sir, anything greater than hope? [he asked.]
"Is there anything greater than hope?
May the Blessed One tell me that. ChUp 7.14.2.
"But as for him who meditates upon hope as Brahman, hear the fruit thereof:
because he has constantly meditated upon hope, all desires of this meditator prosper—that is, they reach fulfillment.
Indeed, all his prayers and petitions become unfailing; the meaning is that whatever he has prayed for, all that necessarily comes to pass."
"Extending as far as the reach of hope," and so forth, as previously stated. //2//
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Breath, indeed, is greater than hope.
Just as spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The vital breath moves by means of the vital breath;
the vital breath gives the vital breath.
He gives it for the sake of the vital breath;
the vital breath is indeed the father,
the vital breath is the mother.
The vital breath is the brother;
the vital breath is the sister;
the vital breath is the teacher.
The Brahmin is the vital breath.
Beginning with Name and extending to Hope, all this exists as cause and effect, and as the signified and the signifier, established in a state of ever-increasing multiplicity;
it is bound on all sides by the snares of the rope of Hope, which serve as the basis for memory, and is dedicated to that Prāṇa like lotus fibers to their stalks.
Furthermore, by that [Prāṇa], which is all-pervasive and extends both within and without, everything is strung together and held fast, like a multitude of gems upon a thread.
This very vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed greater than hope.
To explain how it is greater, he provides an illustration to establish that greatness:
"Just as in the world the spokes of a chariot wheel are fixed, joined, and inserted into the hub of the chariot. This is what is meant.

Thus, in this primary vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of an aggregate of the bodily organs and whose nature is intelligence (*prajñātman*), the supreme deity is established by means of the individual self (*jīva-ātman*) for the purpose of manifesting names and forms—just as a reflection appears in a mirror—and who, like a great king, is the sovereign lord with authority over all. For the Śruti declares: "Thinking, 'Upon whose departure shall I depart, and upon whose remaining shall I remain? he created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). And it is this [breath] that follows the Lord like a shadow.

"Just as the rim is fixed on the spokes of a chariot wheel and the spokes are fixed on the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrā) are fixed on the elements of discernment (prajñāmātrā), and the elements of discernment are fixed on the vital breath (prāṇa).
This very vital breath is the self consisting of discernment"—so says the Kauṣītakins.
Therefore, everything as described is fixed upon this vital breath.

Therefore, this very vital breath (*prāṇa*) is independent; it moves by its own power alone through the vital breath. The meaning is that its capacity for actions such as going and so forth is not produced by anything else.
The purport of the entire section is that the entire collection of distinctions consisting of actions, instruments, and results is the vital breath alone; nothing exists outside of the vital breath.
When the vital breath gives the vital breath, that which it gives is indeed its own self.
That to which one gives [the gift] is also for the sake of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone;
therefore, even that which is designated as "father" and so forth is indeed the vital breath. //1//

"You are indeed a slayer of your father; you are indeed a slayer of your mother; you are indeed a slayer of your brother; you are indeed a slayer of your sister; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin. [Question:
How is it that the words "father" and so forth, by setting aside their well-known meanings, have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their referent?
[Answer: It is said: because the words "father" and so forth are applied to the father and others only when the vital breath is present, and because they are not applied when it has departed.
To explain how that is so, he says:

if anyone should reply to one of his parents or others with some speech that is excessively harsh, as if unbecoming, and filled with insults such as "thou," then those discerning people standing nearby say to him:
"Fie on you! Fie upon you! Thus it is.
"You are indeed a slayer of your father; you have killed your father," and so forth. //2//

Now, even if one were to burn these [bodies] while their vital breaths have departed, piling them up and burning them together with a spit, they would not say of him: "You are a slayer of your father," nor "a slayer of your mother," nor "a slayer of your brother," nor "a slayer of your sister," nor "a slayer of your teacher," nor "a slayer of a Brahmin. (ChUp 7.15.3)

Now, even if one were to take those very persons whose vital breaths have departed and who have abandoned their bodies, and were to burn them by cutting them up piece by piece and rearranging them, or by burning them after rearranging them— performing such an extremely cruel act characterized by burning upon that which is connected to the body through various methods such as cutting and rearranging— even so, people would not say of him, "He is a parricide," and so forth.
Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance, it is understood that even those called "father" and so forth are indeed the vital breath (prāṇa) itself. //3//
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed becomes all these things. He who sees thus, thinks thus, and understands thus, becomes one who speaks beyond [the ordinary].
If they should say to him, "Are you a master of speech?", he should say,
"I am a master of speech," and he should not deny it.
Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) indeed becomes all these things—the father and so forth—both moving and stationary.

He who knows the vital breath, seeing it in the manner described, experiencing its fruit, reflecting upon it with reasoned arguments, and understanding it by joining it with logical proofs, reaches the firm conviction that "it is exactly thus. This is the meaning.
For it is through both reflection (*manana*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) that the meaning of the teaching becomes ascertained and seen.

Therefore, seeing in this way, one becomes an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādī*); the meaning is that one possesses the habit of speaking by transcending the limit of names and so forth. If they should say to him: "If you are such an exceeding speaker who always functions by transcending the limit of names and so forth with all words..."

If they should say to Prāṇa— who speaks thus, who sees thus, who is habituated to superior speech, and who declares, "I am the Self of the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass"— "Are you one who speaks with superiority? he should say, "Yes, I am one who speaks with superiority," and he should not deny it.
For why would he deny it, since he has accepted as his very self that Prāṇa, the Lord of all, saying, "I am this"? //4//
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of the Truth."
"Therefore, O Blessed One, I speak by means of truth.
"But truth itself must be sought to be understood. "I wish to understand truth, O Blessed One. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16.1)
Having heard that this Prāṇa—his own self—is the Self of all and transcends everything else, Nārada desisted, thinking, "There is nothing beyond this.
He did not ask as before, "Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than Prāṇa?

For, seeing that he was satisfied with the knowledge of Brahman as a mere modification and an unreal thing, and considering him an unfit disciple who imagined himself to have attained the ultimate truth while actually being one who had not yet achieved his goal, the Teacher spoke in order to disabuse him of that particular false conviction.
The Blessed One Sanatkumāra said:
"But he indeed is a superior speaker (ativādin) whom I shall describe; one who knows the vital breath (prāṇa) is not a superior speaker in the ultimate sense.
His status as a superior speaker, however, is dependent upon [the knowledge of] names and so forth."

But he who knows the reality called the Plenum (bhūman), which transcends all and is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), is a "super-speaker" (ativādī); therefore, it is said: "But he indeed is a super-speaker who speaks by means of the Real. The intention is this: "I, being possessed of the knowledge of the ultimate truth, speak as a super-speaker; O Blessed One, I have taken refuge in you. May the Blessed One so instruct me that I may speak as a super-speaker by means of the Real. When it was thus stated, "If you desire to speak as a super-speaker by means of the Real, then the Real itself must first be sought to be known," Nārada replied:
"So be it, O Venerable One; I wish to know the truth, that is, I desire to understand it from you in detail. //1//
Thus ends the sixteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When, indeed, one discerns, then one speaks the truth.
One who does not know does not speak the truth;
only one who knows speaks the truth.
Therefore, knowledge itself is that which must be sought to be known.
“Venerable Sir, I desire to understand consciousness.”

When one truly understands reality in its ultimate sense—that "this is the ultimate reality, the Truth"—then, having abandoned the unreal collection of transformations which are merely "the starting point of speech," one speaks only that which is the Truth: namely, that Being alone, existing in all states of transformation, is the one Reality.
But is it not the case that even the transformation is indeed real?
"Name-and-form being real, by them this vital breath (prāṇa) is concealed";

"The vital breaths are indeed real, and of them, this [Self] is the reality"—from such another scriptural passage. It has been stated that the reality of the modification is mentioned in another scripture, but it is not stated with reference to the ultimate truth; rather, it is with reference to its being an object of the senses.

It has been stated that "the real" (*satya*) means "that which is so" (*tyat*); and by means of that, the apprehension of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is intended. It has also been stated: "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the real; of them, this [Self] is the real.
Here too, that very same point is intended.

In this context, however, the specific intended meaning is as follows: having raised Nārada up from his conceit regarding the knowledge of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) concerning the syllable *praṇava*, [the Teacher] intends to make known that which is truly existent (*sat*) and ultimately real—the "Plenum" (*bhūman*)—saying, "I shall make you understand that.

One who does not know the truth does not speak the truth; rather, he who speaks while not knowing it speaks while imagining fire and other things to be ultimately real by means of words such as "fire," yet those things have no ultimate reality apart from the three forms [of the *praṇava*].

Just as those [entities] do not exist from the perspective of reality, so too those forms do not exist at all from the perspective of reality; therefore, one who does not understand does not speak the truth,
whereas only one who understands speaks the truth.

Furthermore, that knowledge of truth (satya-vijñāna) is not known without being sought after or without inquiry; thus he says, "But knowledge itself is what must be sought after. [The disciple replies: "If that is so, O Venerable One, I wish to seek after knowledge. In this manner, the fact that each preceding element among the series beginning with truth and ending with action is the cause for each subsequent one should be explained. //1//
Thus ends the seventeenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When one indeed thinks, then one understands.
"One understands by means of thought;
one understands only by means of thought;
indeed, thought itself is what one must seek to understand."
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand intelligence. ChU 7.18.1.
"When one reflects" (yadā vai manute): reflection (*mati*) is the act of thinking (*manana*), reasoning (*tarka*), and the earnest application of the mind toward the object of thought. //1//
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the seventh chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When, indeed, one has faith, then one reflects.
One who lacks faith does not reflect;
only one who possesses faith reflects.
Indeed, faith itself is that which must be sought to be understood.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand faith. 7.19.1.
Faith (śraddhā) is the conviction that there is such a thing [as the afterlife]. //1//
Thus ends the nineteenth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When one has indeed completed [the work], then one has faith.
"One does not have faith without having reached a firm conclusion; one has faith only by having reached a firm conclusion.
Indeed, that firm conclusion itself is what one must seek to understand."
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand the ultimate goal."
Perfection consists in devotion to the service of the teacher and so forth, directed toward the knowledge of Brahman. //1//
Thus ends the twentieth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When one acts, then one accomplishes.
One does not reach completion without having acted;
one reaches completion only after having acted.
Indeed, action itself is what must be thoroughly investigated.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand action."
