When one indeed performs [the practice]—
where "performance" consists of the restraint of the senses and the concentration of the mind—
then, provided that this exists, the stages beginning with steadfastness (niṣṭhā) up to discernment (vijñāna), as previously described, come to be. //1//
Thus ends the twenty-first section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
When, indeed, one obtains happiness, then he acts.
One does not act having obtained what is not pleasant;
one acts only having obtained pleasure.
Indeed, pleasure alone is that which should be sought to be known.
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand happiness."
The meaning is that even that action occurs when one attains happiness—that is, when one thinks, "I must attain the unsurpassed happiness to be described.
Just as an action performed for the sake of visible results is undertaken only after obtaining happiness, so it is here as well; one does not act without having obtained happiness.
Even a future result is spoken of as "having been obtained."
Because activity toward that [Truth] is logically possible;

for now, since the subsequent stages such as "what is to be done" (*kṛtya*) and so forth exist, it might follow that Truth manifests of its own accord and thus no separate effort need be made to cognize it—therefore, this is said:
"But happiness alone is what one should desire to understand," and so on.
To her who had thus become intent, he said: "O Blessed One, you desire to understand happiness. (1)
Thus ends the twenty-second section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is bliss."
"In the finite there is no happiness; only in the infinite is there happiness. Therefore, the infinite alone is that which one must desire to understand."
"Venerable sir, I desire to understand plenitude."

That which is indeed the *bhūman*—synonymous with "great," "limitless," and "much"—is happiness. That which is less than that is small because it possesses a superior beyond it; therefore, there is no happiness in that which is small.
Because even a small amount [of wealth] is a cause for excessive craving,
and craving is the seed of suffering;
for in the world, the seed of suffering is never seen as happiness, such as in the case of fever and the like.

Therefore, it is logical that there is no happiness in the limited; hence, bliss belongs only to the Infinite (Bhūman), because in the Infinite the seeds of suffering such as craving cannot exist. //1//
Thus ends the twenty-third section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else— that is the Infinite (bhūman).
Now, where one sees something else, hears something else, or cognizes something else—that is the finite.
That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is indeed the immortal;
but that which is finite is mortal.
"Venerable sir, on what is he established?
"In his own greatness, or perhaps not even in greatness."

"What is the characteristic of that *bhūman*? he asks, and replies: "In which *bhūman*, in which reality (*tattva*), one does not see anything else as an object to be seen by means of another distinct instrument, nor does one hear anything else;

for since all distinctions of objects are included within name and form (*nāmarūpa*), only seeing and hearing—the perceivers of those objects—are mentioned here, while the other senses are intended as being implied."
And here, "thinking" (manana) should be understood as that which is spoken of, for there is nothing else that thinks;
this is because cognition (vijñāna) is generally preceded by thinking. Likewise, there is nothing else that cognizes.
That which has such characteristics is the Bhūman.

In this context, is it being said that the absence of the perception of anything else—which is well-known—constitutes the Bhūman by means of the phrase "he sees nothing else," and so forth; or rather, is it meant that he does not see anything else [but] sees the Self?

What follows from this? If it is said that [the state of] "Bhūman" is merely the absence of the perception of anything else, then it is stated that Bhūman is distinct from the conventional dealings of duality (*dvaita-saṃvyavahāra*).

On the other hand, if it is said that one perceives the Self by means of the negation of specific perceptions of other things, then a distinction between action, agent, and result would have to be admitted within that very same [Self].
If this were so, what fault would there be?
Is it not precisely this that is the fault: the non-cessation of saṃsāra?
For saṃsāra is indeed the differentiation of action, agent, and fruit.
If it is argued that even within the oneness of the Self, there exists a distinction of action, agent, and fruit which is distinct from the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), we say no.
For if one accepts the absolute, undifferentiated oneness of the Self, the acceptance of a distinction between actions such as seeing, their agents, and their fruits is merely verbal.

If it is further argued that even in the position where the absence of other perceptions and so forth is stated, the two qualifiers "wherein" (*yatra*) and "he sees nothing else" (*anyat na paśyati*) would be redundant; [we reply: they are not.

If it is argued that this is just as seen in the world, where when it is said of an empty house, "one sees nothing else," it is understood that one does not fail to see the pillars and so forth, nor oneself;
[we reply: no, because in this case, due to the instruction of identity in "That thou art," the distinction between the locus and the subject is untenable.
If it is argued that the qualification "wherein" (yatra) is rendered meaningless because it has already been determined in the sixth chapter that "Being alone is real,

one without a second," and because of such scriptural passages as "In the invisible, the bodiless," "His form does not stand within the range of vision," and "O, by what could one know the knower?"— which establish that seeing and other such activities are impossible with respect to the Self—
[we reply: No.
This is because it depends on distinctions created by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Just as, while the notion of unity and non-duality is already present, one says "Being is one only, without a second"— describing it as being beyond number and so forth—
so too, although the Infinite (*bhūman*) is one alone, the qualification "in which" is employed.

Furthermore, because in the state of ignorance there is a restatement of another's view, and because it is intended to characterize the abundance [of Brahman] as being devoid of that [duality], the qualification "he sees nothing else" is employed.
Therefore, the collective meaning is that the empirical transactions of saṃsāra do not exist in the Abundance (bhūman).
Now, where—in the sphere of ignorance—another sees another as something else, that is "the small" (alpa), meaning it exists only during the time of ignorance.

Just as an object seen in a dream exists only at that time prior to awakening, so too is that [world] mortal and perishable, exactly like a dream-object. That which is the opposite of this is the "Full" (bhūman), which is immortal;
the word "that" (tat) refers to immortality.
To Nārada, who had asked, "In that case, O Blessed One, in what is this *bhūman* of such characteristics established?", Sanatkumāra replied:

"In its own greatness (*sve mahimni*). This means the *bhūman* is established in its own greatness, its majesty, its manifestation. Whether you desire to know its support somewhere, or whether you are asking about the ultimate reality itself, we say that it is not even established in its own greatness.
The meaning is that he is non-abiding and non-dependent, not established anywhere at all. //1//
"Regarding this, they call cattle and horses 'greatness,' as do elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings.
I do not speak thus."
"I say so," he said,
"for one thing is established upon another."
If the Infinite (*bhūman*) is established in its own greatness, why then is it said to be "without support" (*apratiṣṭha*)?
Listen:
in this world, cows, horses, and so forth are called "greatness."
"Cows and horses" (*gavāśvam*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) treated as a singular.
Everywhere, the term "greatness" (*mahiman*) is well known to refer to such things as cows and horses; Caitra is dependent upon that and established therein.

Just as I am not thus dependent on some other greatness [like Caitra], I say that the Infinite (*bhūman*) is not like Caitra. Here, the connection with the remote phrase "for one thing is established in another" is made as the reason for this.
"But I speak thus," he said—"he alone," and so forth. //2//
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
He alone is below; He is above; He is behind; He is in front; He is to the south; He is to the north.
"He indeed is all this.
Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the "I":
"I am below, I am above, I am behind, I am in front, I am to the south, I am to the north—I indeed am all this."
Why, then, is it said that he is not established anywhere?
Because that very *bhūman* (the Infinite) exists below, and there is nothing else apart from it in which he could be established.
Likewise, "above" and so forth is the same.
If there were something else greater than the Infinite (bhūman), then the Infinite would indeed be established in that; but such a thing does not exist.
He alone is everything.
Therefore, for that reason, He is not established anywhere.

Lest someone should suspect that the "plenum" (bhūman) might be something other than the individual soul (jīva), the seer—based on the indication of a locus and its subject in the passage "where one sees nothing else," and based on the indirect reference in "that itself is below"—the teaching by means of the "I-maker" (ahaṅkārādeśa) follows immediately after this. It is called the "teaching by means of the I-maker" because it is taught through the "I-maker. For the purpose of showing the non-difference from the seer, the plenum itself is pointed out by means of the "I-maker" in such passages as "I myself am below," and so forth. //1//
Now, therefore, follows the instruction concerning the Self alone:
the Self is below, the Self is above, the Self is behind, the Self is in front, the Self is to the south, the Self is to the north— the Self indeed is all this.

Indeed, he who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who understands thus, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has union with the Self, and finds bliss in the Self; he becomes his own sovereign.
For him, there is freedom to move at will in all worlds.
But those who know otherwise than this have other rulers; their worlds are perishable.
For them, there is no freedom of movement in all the worlds.

Since even the aggregate of the body and so forth is designated by the term "I" through the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) by those lacking discrimination, the instruction regarding the Self (ātmādeśa) follows immediately thereafter to prevent such doubt; it is taught solely by means of the pure Self, whose nature is Being.

Seeing that the Self alone is everything everywhere—unitary, unborn, as all-pervasive as space, and devoid of anything else—that wise person, through both reflection and direct realization, finds delight in the Self alone; his delight, his pleasure, is in the Self.
He who possesses this is "one whose delight is in the Self" (ātmarati); likewise, he is "one whose play is in the Self" (ātmakrīḍa).
Delight has the body alone as its means, whereas play has external means.

The meaning is this: from the observation that in the world one plays with "glories" (śrī) and "companions" (sakhi), it is not so for the knower; rather, both of these exist solely on account of the realization of the Self.
Even that pleasure born of the couple—that is, the pleasure arising from duality—is independent of duality for that knower.

Likewise, while the bliss of the Self for the ignorant is a bliss caused by sound and other sense-objects, it is not so for this knower; rather, everything is at all times and in every way caused by the Self alone, being independent of external objects such as the body, life, and enjoyments.
This is the meaning.
A wise person characterized in this way, even while living, is consecrated in self-sovereignty (svārājya); even when the body has fallen away, he remains a self-ruler (svarāṭ).
Since he becomes such, for that very reason, he possesses freedom of movement at will in all worlds.

In the preceding stages, such as those beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it was stated that he possesses "unrestricted movement" (*kāmacāra*) limited only to those respective levels, and his status as a sovereign (*arājatva*) was implied by the fact that those states were still subject to gradation. Here, by restating the attainment of self-sovereignty (*svarājya*) and unrestricted movement as they were previously established, their cessation is described through the passage beginning with "He is a sovereign" (*sa svarāṭ*). Now, however, those who otherwise—that is, contrary to the aforementioned vision, or in the opposite manner, or even if they have heard it as stated, do not know it correctly—become "ruled by others" (*anyarājānaḥ*); that is, they have another, a superior, as their ruler and master.
They are the kings of others.
Furthermore, those for whom the world is subject to destruction are "those for whom the world is perishable" (*kṣayyaloka*).
We have already stated that because the vision of duality has a limited scope, that which is mortal is "limited."

Therefore, those who perceive duality possess worlds that are subject to decay, corresponding precisely to the nature of their own perception; for this very reason, they lack freedom of movement in all worlds. //2//

Thus, in the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the twenty-fifth section. Now, for one who sees thus, who reflects thus, and who understands thus, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arises from the Self (*ātman*), [and] from the Self...

From the Self comes hope; from the Self comes memory; from the Self comes space; from the Self comes fire; from the Self comes water; from the Self come appearance and disappearance; from the Self comes food; from the Self comes strength; from the Self comes perception; from the Self comes meditation;

from the Self comes thought; from the Self comes volition; from the Self comes the mind; from the Self comes speech; from the Self comes name; from the Self come mantras; from the Self come actions—from the Self alone indeed all this arises.
Thus [it is said]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1)
Regarding the passage beginning with "Of this very one" (ChUpBh_7,26.1), the meaning is: of that aforementioned knower who has attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).

Prior to the realization of the Self as Being (*sadātman*), there occurred the origination and dissolution of everything from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) down to names, which were perceived as other than one's own Self; however, once the realization of the Self as Being is present, all these things now resolve back into one's own Self, and likewise does every other worldly transaction.
For the wise person, [the fruit] arises from the self alone. //1//
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering."
"The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way.
Thus, he becomes onefold, he becomes threefold, he becomes fivefold.
It is recorded as sevenfold, ninefold, and again elevenfold;
it is one hundred and ten and one, and twenty thousand.
Through purity of food comes purity of being.
When the self (sattva) is purified, mindfulness becomes firm;
upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the complete liberation from all knots.
To him whose impurities have been rubbed away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra reveals the further shore of darkness.
They call him Skanda.
Furthermore, regarding this matter, there is also this verse, which is a mantra: "The seer does not see. The term "seer" (paśyaḥ) means the wise one who possesses the vision described above;
he does not see death—that is, dying—nor disease, such as fever, nor even suffering, that is, the state of misery.

"The seer sees everything indeed as everything; he sees the Self alone as everything. Thereupon, he attains everything in every way, in all its various forms. Furthermore, that wise one, prior to the differentiation of creation, exists as a single unity; yet at the time of creation, through the distinctions of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjoined) and other such modes, he becomes possessed of infinite varieties of difference. Then, at the time of reabsorption, he returns to his own fundamental, ultimate state of oneness, remaining entirely independent. Thus, the text praises knowledge by extolling it with its fruit, thereby inspiring a desire for it.

Now, the means for the purification of the aforementioned knowledge—which is the cause of its correct manifestation, just as the cause of the clarity of a mirror is the cause of its surface’s manifestation—is taught: "In the purity of food" (*āhāraśuddhau*).

That which is brought in (*āhriyate*) is "food" (*āhāra*); that is, the cognition of objects such as sound and so forth, which is brought in for the enjoyment of the enjoyer. [Thus] the means for its purification is taught. In the purity of food...

It is called *āhāra* because it is brought forth (*āhriyate*); that is, the cognition of objects such as sound and so forth, which is brought forth for the enjoyment of the enjoyer. The purity of that cognition, characterized by the perception of objects, is "purity of food" (*āhāra-śuddhi*), meaning a cognition of objects unadulterated by the defects of attachment, aversion, and delusion. When there is such purity of food, there arises the purity—that is, the stainlessness—of the *sattva*, the internal organ, which possesses that [cognition].

And when the purity of the inner being (*sattva*) has been attained, there arises a firm and uninterrupted mindfulness (*smṛti*), which is non-forgetfulness, regarding the Self as it has been understood.

And when that mindfulness has been acquired, upon the attainment of mindfulness, there occurs a complete liberation— a specific release or destruction— of all those knots of the heart, which are of the nature of nooses of misfortune created by ignorance, hardened by the impressions (*bhāvanā*) from experiences throughout many previous births, and situated within the heart.
Since this successive sequence has been stated as having its root in the purity of food (*āhāra-śuddhi*), the meaning is that it must be practiced.

Having explained the entire meaning of the scripture without exception, the Śruti concludes the narrative: "To him whose impurities have been rubbed away"—for impurity, like the resin of a tree, consists of defects such as passion and hatred because it has the nature of staining the mind; [it is removed] by the alkaline solution consisting of the practice of knowledge and dispassion.

To that worthy one, Nārada—who had been washed, rubbed, and destroyed of his impurities (kaṣāya)—the Blessed One showed, or rather has shown, the further shore, the supreme reality, beyond darkness characterized by ignorance. Who is he? The Blessed One: "The origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of beings..."
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance is to be called "Bhagavān."
“Such is the nature of Sanatkumāra.
Those who know him speak of that very god Sanatkumāra as Skanda. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of concluding the chapter. //2//
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section of the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad-Brahmaṇa.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Om.
Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space.
That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. (ChU 8.1.1)

Although it has been understood in the sixth and seventh chapters that Brahman is devoid of distinctions such as direction, space, and time, is Being alone, one, and without a second, and that "all this is indeed the Self," nevertheless, the intellect of those of dull understanding— which has been conditioned to perceive objects as possessing distinctions of direction, space, and so forth— cannot be suddenly directed toward the ultimate reality. Furthermore, since the human goal is not accomplished without the realization of Brahman, [this chapter is begun] for the sake of attaining that realization.
The region of the heart-lotus (hṛdayapuṇḍarīka) must be taught.

Although Brahman is the sole object of the right cognition of "Being" (sat), and since the human goal is not accomplished without realizing it, the region of the heart-lotus must be taught for the sake of that realization. Furthermore, although the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and is the sole object of the right cognition of "Being," nevertheless, because those of dull intellect desire it to possess qualities, its possession of qualities such as having true desires (satyakāma) and so forth must be stated.

Likewise, although for those who know Brahman there occurs a spontaneous cessation from objects such as women and the like, nevertheless, the thirst directed toward sense-objects—which has been produced by the practice of indulging in such objects over many lifetimes—cannot be turned back all at once; therefore, specific means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be prescribed.

Similarly, although for those who know the oneness of the Self there is an absence of a goer, a going, and a destination, because the cause for the persistence of the particular state of ignorance has perished, [the following applies].
Just as lightning vanishes into the sky, as wind subsides, or as fire ceases once its fuel is consumed, so too does [the soul] find rest within its own self; nevertheless,

for those whose intellects are conditioned by notions of a traveler and a journey, and who meditate upon Brahman as characterized by qualities located in the region of the heart, the departure via the artery at the crown of the head must be explained— thus the eighth chapter begins.
For the non-dual Brahman, which is real in the ultimate sense and devoid of distinctions such as direction, place, quality, state, or fruit, appears as if non-existent to those of dull intellect.
The Śruti thinks: "Let them first abide on the path of the existent (sanmārga); thereafter, I shall gradually cause them to grasp that which is real in the ultimate sense.

Immediately following this, there is that which is about to be described: the small (*dahara*), lotus-like (*puṇḍarīka*)—meaning resembling a lotus—dwelling (*veśma*), so called because it possesses gatekeepers and other such features.

In this city of Brahman—the city of the Supreme Brahman—just as a king’s city is provided with many constituent parts such as subjects, so too is this [city] endowed with the various sense organs, mind, and intellect, which act for the sake of their Master; thus it is called the "city of Brahman.
And just as there is a palace within a king's city, so too within that city of Brahman, the body, there is a small dwelling (dahara-veśma), meaning the locus for the perception of Brahman;
just as Śālagrāma is the locus for Viṣṇu.

For it has been stated that Brahman, which is designated as "Being" (Sat), entered this body— which is like its own transformed horn— in order to effect the differentiation of name and form by means of the individual soul (jīva).

Therefore, within this house of the heart-lotus, Brahman is perceived by those who have withdrawn their senses, who are dispassionate toward external objects, and who, through the specific disciplines of celibacy and truthfulness, meditate upon It as endowed with the qualities to be described hereafter.
Such is the meaning of the section.
"Dahara" means very small; because this dwelling (veśman) is small, that which exists within it is also very small.
The "interior space" (antarākāśa) is Brahman, known as Ākāśa.
For it will be said, "It is indeed named 'space' (ākāśa)";
because of its bodilessness, and due to the common characteristics of subtlety and omnipresence, it is like space.
That which is within—that is, in the middle of—that which is called space, is what must be sought.

The meaning is that this very thing must indeed be specifically desired to be known; having sought it out through means such as hearing from a guru and taking refuge in him, it must be directly realized. //1//

If they should say to him: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped abode; within it is a small space. What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand?"

He should say: "Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.2" (Note: This appears to be a citation marker rather than part of the original Sanskrit text provided). However, based on the standard phrasing of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad at that point, the response would be: "He should say: 'I am he. (sa brūyāt // "aham asmi" iti //)
If the disciples should challenge the teacher who has spoken thus, saying:
"How can it be that within this limited city of Brahman, inside the small lotus-palace, there is an ether even smaller than that?"
"What might there be in a house as large as a lotus?
What might there be in a space even smaller than that? they asked. "In this small space within, what exists? Nothing at all exists," such is the intended meaning.
"If there were indeed something [there] the size of a jujube fruit, what would be the use of searching for it or desiring to know it for the one who desires to know?
Therefore, there is no purpose in that which must be searched for or desired to be known"—this is the statement of the Śruti spoken by the teacher. 2.
As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
Both heaven and earth are contained within it.
"Both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars—whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is contained within him. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3)
Listen!
Regarding that which you say— that because the space within the lotus is small, that which resides therein must be even smaller—
that is incorrect.
For I did not say, "The small space within this [lotus]," thinking that the space had entered the lotus-heart and was smaller than the lotus-petal.

What then? The lotus is small; the internal organ (antahkarana) situated within it conforms to its shape and is delimited by the space of the lotus. When that [space] is purified, for yogis who have withdrawn their senses, it appears like a reflection in clear water or in a mirror.

And when [the mind] is pure, the light of consciousness, which is its own nature and appears as transparent, is perceived as being merely that much; thus we said, "In this small inner space," referring to the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
But in its own nature, this space within the heart—in which one must seek and desire to understand—is as large in extent as this well-known elemental space. This is what we have stated.
Nor is it said that [Brahman] is "so great" with the intention of implying that its magnitude is equal to that of space.
What then? It is because there is no other illustration corresponding to Brahman.
But how, then, is it understood that Brahman is not indeed equal to space?
"By which the sky, heaven, and earth are covered";

"From this very Self, indeed, space was produced"; and "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, is space," and so forth—from such scriptural passages [it is known]. Furthermore, both heaven and earth are contained within this space of Brahman (brahmākāśa), as qualified by the limiting adjunct of the intellect (buddhyupādhiviśiṣṭa); they are properly placed and situated therein, just as it has been said: "as the spokes are in the nave."
Likewise, both fire and wind, and so forth, are the same;
and whatever belongs to this embodied self by way of ownership exists here in this world,
as well as that which does not exist by way of ownership.
That which has perished and that which is yet to come are said to be "non-existent," but they are not absolutely non-existent;
for it would be impossible to concentrate the mind upon them in the space of the heart. //3//
If they should say to him: "If everything is contained within this city of Brahman—namely all beings and all desires—and yet it is overtaken by old age or perishes, what remains of it?

If the disciples should say again to him who has spoken thus: "In this [space]—meaning, in the internal space characterized by the city of Brahman—all this is contained, as well as all beings and all desires.
[Objection: How is it that the disciples speak of "all desires" when they were not mentioned by the teacher?
This is not a fault, for the Teacher has already stated what exists here and what does not exist;
moreover, all desires have indeed been mentioned by the word "all.

When—at whatever time—this body, called the city of Brahman, undergoes decay characterized by wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth, or when it is cut down by weapons and the like, it perishes, falls apart, and is destroyed.
What remains over from that?

The intention is as follows: just as milk, curd, oil, and so forth residing in a jar perish when the jar perishes, so too, upon the destruction of the body, that which resides in the body perishes successively because each preceding [substratum] has been destroyed.
When such destruction has thus occurred, what else remains over—that is, what persists—beyond what has been described? The intention is that nothing whatsoever persists. //4//
He should say:
"This does not decay with his decay; it is not slain by his being slain."
This is the true city of Brahman; within it all desires are contained.
This is the Self (ātman), free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true.
For just as subjects here follow according to their instructions, so do they enter [into that state].
Whatever end they desire, whatever country or whatever portion of land it may be, upon that very thing they subsist.
Thus urged by his pupils, that teacher should speak, removing their misconception.
How?

He should say: "By the decay of this body, this Brahman called the internal space—in which everything is contained—does not decay; the meaning is that, unlike the body, it does not undergo modification."

Nor is this [Brahman] destroyed by its slaughter—that is, by the blow of weapons and the like—just as space is not; how much less so Brahman, which is subtler than even that, soundless, and intangible?

It should have been stated at this point that Brahman is not touched by the defects of the body, senses, and so forth; however, it is not stated here so that there may be no interruption of the current subject at hand.
We shall explain this later, with logical reasoning, in the narrative of Indra and Virocana.

This is the truth, the non-false Brahmapura; "Brahmapura" means that Brahman itself is the city. However, the so-called body is called Brahmapura only because it serves as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for Brahman. In reality, however, it is indeed false.

According to the Vedic scripture, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," even though this sprout-like body is unreal as a modification, Brahman is perceived within it; thus it is called the "City of Brahman" (brahmapura) from a conventional standpoint.
But the truly real City of Brahman is this very Brahman itself.

Because it is the locus of all worldly transactions, therefore, within this city of Brahman characterized by the lotus, all desires—which are sought after by you externally—are contained right here within one's own self.
Thus, the intended meaning is: "Practice the very means for attaining that [Self] and abandon thirst for external objects."
This Self is your own true nature; hear its defining characteristic:
it is free from evil.
He whose evil—consisting of what is called dharma and adharma—has been struck away is "one whose evil has been struck away" (apahatapāpman).
Likewise, he is free from old age (vijara) and free from death (vimṛtyu).
This was already stated previously: "He is not slain by the slaying of this [body]."
Why, then, is it stated again?
Even if he is not bound by old age and death associated with the body, there might still be a connection with them in another way; therefore, this is said for the purpose of removing such a doubt.
"Free from sorrow" (*viśoka*) means one whose sorrow has departed.
Grief (*śoka*) is a mental torment caused by separation from what is desired and so forth.
Free from hunger (*vijighatsa*) means having no desire for food;
free from thirst (*apipāsa*) means having no desire for drink.
But surely, by the state of being "free from evil," old age and the rest ending with sorrow are already excluded,
because their cause has been negated;
for they are indeed the effects of merit and demerit.

Alternatively, by the negation of old age and so forth, if there were an absence of effects for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), then even though they exist, they would be equivalent to non-existence; thus, their separate negation would be purposeless. This is true; nevertheless, one might suspect that just as there is natural bliss distinct from the effect of merit—as in the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma*)—so too, there might be a nature consisting of the suffering of old age and so forth that is natural, even apart from the effects of demerit such as old age. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "By the negation of old age and so forth... and so on.
Therefore, it is logical that there is a separate negation of old age and so forth from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) for the sake of their cessation.
The mention of "old age and so forth" is intended as an illustration of all suffering.

Since the sufferings caused by evil are infinite and it would be impossible to negate each one individually, the statement "having evil removed" (*apahatapāpman*) is indeed appropriate for the purpose of negating all suffering.
He whose desires are true and not false is "Satyakāma" (one whose desires are true); for the desires of those in saṃsāra are indeed false,
whereas those of the Lord are the opposite.
Likewise, he whose volitions (saṃkalpa) regarding objects of desire are also true is "one of true volition" (satyasaṃkalpa).
For the Lord, both volitions and desires have as their cause the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of pure being (śuddhasattva), like a painter;
they do not exist in themselves, because it has been stated that He is "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Those who desire self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) must understand the Self exactly as it has been described—through the teachers, through the scriptures, and through its own direct realization.
If it is not understood, what fault would there be?
Listen to the fault in this matter by means of an illustration.
For just as in this world subjects enter into and follow [the will of] others,
according to their instruction— just as subjects here, considering another to be their master, enter into and follow the instructions of their own master in whatever manner—
what is it?
Whichever border region, frontier territory, district, or portion of land they desire, those seekers, in accordance with their own intellects, subsist upon that very border region and so forth;
this is the illustration regarding the fault of lack of independence in the enjoyment of the fruits of merit. //5//
Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes. Therefore,
those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires— for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds.
Now, those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

Now, there is another illustration regarding their destruction, beginning with the words "Just as here," and so forth. "There" (tat) means in this world; just as for those subjects who follow the commands of their master, the world won through service and the like is dependent on others for enjoyment and perishes—that is, it becomes finite—so now he concludes the application to the case at hand: "In exactly the same way, the world won by merit such as the Agnihotra and other rites is dependent on others for enjoyment and perishes indeed. Thus, the defect of these [works] has been stated; he now shows the scope [of that defect]: "Therefore, those..."

By these and other such statements, it is shown that those who, being qualified and entitled to knowledge and action in this world, do not follow the Self as described by its characteristics— that is, they do not realize it through their own direct experience according to the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher— but depart from this body and pass away; and those who [neglect] these aforementioned [means].

Without having realized the Truths and the desires situated within their own self— which are the effects of true resolve— they proceed [into the worlds], and for them there is a lack of freedom of movement and a lack of autonomy in all the worlds,
just as in the case of subjects who follow the commands of a king; this is the meaning.

Now, as for those others in this world who, having learned the Self according to the instruction of the scriptures and teachers, and having brought it to the state of being personally realized within themselves, proceed [to the worlds] and [attain] the true desires as previously described—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds, just as that of a sovereign emperor in this world. //6//
Thus ends the first section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, [he goes there].
By his mere volition, his ancestors arise;
endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified.
"How does one come to have freedom of movement in all worlds?

It is said in reply: he who has directly realized within his heart the Self characterized as previously described, being endowed with the means such as the celibacy to be mentioned hereafter, and having [realized] those true desires residing therein—he, upon leaving the body, if he desires the world of the fathers (pitṛloka)—the fathers being the progenitors—[attains it].

Thus, because they are objects of enjoyment by virtue of being causes of happiness, they are called "worlds. For one who has a desire for those worlds—that is, one who possesses a longing for a connection with those ancestors—the ancestors arise by his mere volition and attain a state of connection with him.

Because he is of pure essence (*viśuddhasattva*) and thus possesses true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), like the Lord (*īśvara*), he becomes endowed with that world of the ancestors as his object of enjoyment; being enriched by that attainment—attainment being the reaching of what is desired—he is magnified, honored, and prospers.
or experiences its greatness. //1//
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of mothers,
by his mere volition, mothers arise for him.
Endowed with that world of the mother, he is glorified.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers,
his brothers arise for him by mere resolve;
endowed with that world of brothers, he prospers.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters, by his mere volition sisters arise for him;
endowed with that world of sisters, he prospers.
Now, if he desires the world of friends,
his friends arise by his mere will; endowed with that world of friends, he is magnified.
Now, if he has a desire for the world of perfumes and garlands,
by his mere volition, perfumes and garlands arise for him;
endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands, he exults.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of food and drink, by his mere volition food and drink arise for him;
endowed with that world of food and drink, he is magnified.
Now, if he has a desire for the world of song and instrumental music, by his mere volition, song and instrumental music arise for him;
endowed with that world of song and instrumental music, he rejoices.
Now, if he becomes desirous of the world of women, women arise for him by his mere volition;
endowed with that world of women, he rejoices.
The rest is the same.
"Mothers" refers to those who have passed away and were causes of happiness due to their capacity;

for it is not fitting that a yogin of pure being should have a desire for, or a connection with, mothers who were causes of suffering and the instrumental conditions for births such as those of village pigs. (2-9)
Whatever end he desires,
whatever wish he longs for— whatever he desires.
By his mere volition, it arises for him;
endowed with that, he is magnified.

To whichever region he is desirous of going, and whatever desire he desires—even apart from what has been mentioned above—that desired object which he wishes to attain within himself arises for him through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Thus, being endowed with the absence of frustration in his desires and the attainment of his intended objects, he "thrives" (*mahīyate*); this has already been explained. //10//
Thus ends the second section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
These true desires have falsehood as their covering.
For these true beings, untruth is a covering.
Indeed, whoever departs from this world does not obtain them here for the purpose of seeing.
In order to generate enthusiasm among practitioners for the practice of the means of meditation on the Self as described, [the text], out of compassion, says: "Alas, this is indeed a hardship!
That these true desires, which reside within one's own Self and are capable of being attained, are yet covered by untruth.

Although they reside within the Self and have the Self as their very support, there exists "untruth"—namely, the thirst for external objects such as women, food, drink, clothing, and so forth, which is caused by that [desire].
Furthermore, because it functions according to one's own whims and is caused by false knowledge, it is called "unreal" (*anṛta*).
Since it is the cause for the non-attainment of true desires, it is like a covering; thus it is called a "covering" (*apidhāna*).
How is it that their non-attainment is caused by this unreal covering? [The answer follows:]...
It is said: Whosoever—whether a son, a brother, or a beloved one—departs from this world, goes forth, and dies;
that beloved son or brother, though existing within the space of one's own heart, one does not obtain again here, even while desiring to see him. 1.
Now, those of his which are living here, and those which are deceased, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain— all that he finds upon going there;
for here indeed are his true desires, covered by untruth.
Just as those who do not know the location might pass over a hidden treasure of gold again and again without finding it,
even so all these creatures, though they go there day after day, do not find this world of Brahman, for they are held back by untruth.

Now, furthermore, whatever living beings— such as sons, brothers, and so forth— who are alive here for this wise person, and those beloved relatives who have passed away and died, and whatever else he desires in this world, such as clothing, food, drink, or jewels, and does not obtain—
all that he finds and obtains here by going into this Brahman called the space within the heart, according to the method already described.
For here, in this space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*), these aforementioned true desires exist, uncovered by a lid.

How could that be improper? It is explained as follows: just as there might be a treasure of gold—a "treasure" (*nidhi*) being so called because it is deposited (*nidhīyate*) by depositors for the sake of future retrieval—that treasure of gold, once buried beneath the earth, remains unnoticed by those who do not know the site.

Just as those who do not know the science of treasures (*nidhi-śāstra*) would not find a treasure—even though it is capable of being found—even while walking directly over the location of that treasure;

even so, all these creatures, being possessed of ignorance, do not perceive that world of Brahman called the space within the heart—which is indeed Brahman itself—although they go there every day at the time of deep sleep. They do not perceive it.
"May they obtain [this]; today I have attained the state of the world of Brahman.
For they are indeed obstructed—meaning led away from their true nature and drawn outward by defects such as ignorance—by the aforementioned untruth.
Therefore, the intention is that this is a miserable condition for living beings: that although Brahman is within their own reach, it is not obtained. //2//
This very Self is in the heart. This is its etymological derivation: "He is here in the heart" (hṛdi ayam); therefore, he is called "Hṛdayam."
Day after day, indeed, one who knows this goes to the heavenly world.

The word "vai" (verily) serves to remind one of that Self which was introduced as "free from evil," etc. This very Self intended here is located in the heart—that is, within the lotus of the heart—and it is denoted by the term "ether.
This is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of this heart, and nothing else.

Since this Self resides in the heart (*hṛdi*), therefore it is called the "heart" (*hṛdaya*); the intention is that through the established etymology of the name "heart," one should understand that the Self is indeed in one's own heart.
Day after day, indeed, every single day, one who knows thus—"This Self is in the heart"—attains the heavenly world, that is, the Brahman within the heart.

Now, one might object: even one who does not know this attains the Brahman within the heart at the time of deep sleep, since it has been said, "At the time of deep sleep, my dear, he is then merged with Being.
Certainly, it is so; nevertheless, there is a distinction.

Just as every living being—whether knowing or not knowing—is indeed the Real Brahman, yet the wise person, having been awakened by the instruction "That thou art," knows "I am indeed the Real, I am nothing else," and thus becomes the Real;
even so, although both the wise and the ignorant attain union with the Real during deep sleep, it is said that "only the one who possesses such knowledge goes to the heavenly world.
This is the distinction, because the fruit of knowledge necessarily manifests even upon the fall of the body. //3//
"Now, that serene being who, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form—this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
The name of this very Brahman, indeed, is "Truth."

At the time of deep sleep, being united with his own self which is Being, he becomes perfectly serene; thus, he abandons the turbidity born from the contact between the senses and their objects during the waking and dreaming states. Although the term "perfect serenity" (*saṃprasāda*) is common to all living beings, nevertheless—because it is the subject under discussion that "one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world"—the phrase "this perfect serenity" refers specifically to him through a particular effort directed toward what is proximate. He [then], this body...
"Having departed from this body" means having abandoned the identification with the body as the self;
it is not appropriate here to understand "departed" in the sense of rising from a seat or similar,
because of the qualification "in its own form."
For one's own nature cannot be attained by arising from something else;
indeed, if it were to be attained, it would not truly be one's own nature.
Rather, this means that having reached the supreme light characterized as the Supreme Self, whose essence is consciousness (*vijñapti*), one attains well-being.

One is manifested in one's own form; prior to this attainment of one's true nature, however, through ignorance, one had identified the body alone as another form for oneself. It is with reference to that [prior state] that it is said, "in one's own form.

For bodilessness is the true nature of the Self—that which is its own supreme luminous essence. As it has been said: "This serene being (saṃprasāda) is the Self; having attained its own supreme luminous nature, it becomes manifest.
He should say this—meaning the teacher who is enjoined by the Śruti to instruct his disciples.
Moreover, this is the immortal and indestructible plenitude (*bhūman*); for it has been said, "That which is plenitude is indeed the immortal.
Precisely because of this, it is fearless, since there is no second to it; therefore, this is Brahman.
Now, the name of this very Brahman is its designation.
"What is that truth?
Truth is indeed the non-false Brahman;
for it has been said, "That truth is the Self."
Now, for what purpose is this name stated again? It is for the purpose of praising the method of its meditation. //4//
8.3.5 These, indeed, are those three syllables: *sat*, *ti*, and *yam*. That which is *sat* is immortal; that which is *ti* is mortal; and by *yam*, he holds both together.
Because he holds both together with this [syllable], therefore, one who knows thus goes to the heavenly world day after day. //5//

These, indeed, are the three syllables of the name of Brahman: *sat*, *ti*, and *yam*. In the word *satīya*, there is the letter *sa*, the letter *ta*, and the letter *ya*. The letter *t* in *tyam* is an auxiliary (*anubandha*) for the purpose of pronunciation.
This is because they are subsequently referred to by means of short syllables alone.

In this regard, that which is the syllable *sa* is the immortal; because it denotes the immortal Brahman, the syllable *sa* is indeed the immortal, though it is pointed out as ending in the letter *t*.

Now, that which is the syllable *ti* is mortal. Now, by means of that syllable *ya*, he restrains, controls, and governs—meaning he brings under his own power—both the preceding syllables called the immortal and the mortal.
Since one restrains both [the breaths] by means of this syllable *yam*, therefore it is called *yām*;
for by means of it, the two breaths (*yama*) appear as if restrained.

This greatness—the possession of attributes such as immortality—is stated even of the single syllable of the name; how much more so, then, of that which possesses the name? Thus it is praised for the purpose of being an object of meditation.
By the very etymological derivation of the name "Brahman," one who knows thus becomes a knower of that which possesses the name.
The statement, "Indeed, day by day, he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world," has already been explained. //5//
Thus ends the third section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
that which is the Self is the bridge and the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded.
Day and night do not cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds [cross it].
All evils turn back from here, for this world of Brahman is free from evil.

ChUpBh_8.4.1: Now, as for "that which is the Self"—the serene being (*saṃprasāda*) whose characteristics have been described is further praised by means of the qualities about to be stated and those already mentioned, for the purpose of connecting it with the means of *brahmacarya*.
This Self, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, is like a bridge; it is a bridge.
Vidhṛti means the sustainer.
For by him the entire world is sustained, ordaining through the regulations of distinctions such as caste (varṇa), stage of life (āśrama), actions, agents, and fruits, in accordance with the doer.
Indeed, if this universe were not sustained by the Lord, it would perish; therefore, he is the bridge (setu) and the sustainer (vidhṛti).

For what purpose is he a "bridge"? He says: for the sake of the non-confusion, the non-disruption, and the non-destruction of these [worlds] beginning with the earth, which are the substrates of agents and their actions.
And of what nature is this bridge? He says: day and night—though they are the delimiters of everything that has birth—do not cross over this bridge, which is the Self.
The intention is that, unlike other transmigrating beings who are delimited by time characterized as day and night, this one is not delimited by time.
Because of another Vedic text stating, "Since the year revolves by means of days," for this very reason, old age does not overcome—that is, does not reach—him;
likewise, neither death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [overcome him]; here, "good and evil deeds" refers to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
In this context, "attainment" (prāpti) is intended by the word "crossing over" (taraṇa), not "transcendence.
For the self is the cause;
indeed, it is impossible for an effect to transcend its cause.
And everything, such as day and night, is an effect of that which exists;
for the attainment or the transgression of one thing can be effected by another,
but not by that very same thing itself.
For a jar does not reach or transcend clay.

Although the negation of evil and so forth was already stated previously by the passage beginning with "the Self that is free from evil," nevertheless, here this distinction is made: by the words "he does not cross over," the state of being an object of attainment is negated.
In that previous instance, the mere absence of old age and so forth was stated without such distinction.

The sins already mentioned, such as those of day and night, and all others not mentioned, are said to be "evil" (pāpman). Therefore, they turn back from this Self, which is like a bridge, without even reaching it—this is the meaning.
For this is indeed the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), described as the world of Brahman because it is the very Brahman that is free from evil. //1//
Therefore, indeed, having crossed this bridge, one who was blind becomes non-blind;
one who was pierced becomes non-pierced.
Being afflicted, he becomes unafflicted;
therefore, having crossed this bridge, even night becomes day for him,
for this world of Brahman is indeed always luminous.

And because the effects of evil, such as blindness and so forth, belong to one who possesses a body and not to one who is bodiless, therefore— having crossed and reached this Self as a bridge— one becomes sighted,

even though previously one was blind while possessing a body; likewise, even though pierced while possessing a body, upon the separation from the body, having crossed and reached the bridge, one becomes sighted, even though previously one was blind while possessing a body.
Thus, one who was pierced while still possessing a body becomes unpierced upon reaching the bridge and attaining separation from the body.
Likewise, one who was afflicted—possessing the affliction of disease and so forth—becomes unafflicted.

Furthermore, because neither day nor night exist at the bridge, therefore, having crossed and reached this bridge, even the night—which is of the nature of darkness—and indeed all [time] results as nothing but day.
The meaning is that for the wise man, this light of the self, whose nature is consciousness, becomes like the day—always of one form.
Shining once, it shines forever; always of one form, this world of Brahman exists by its own nature. //2//
Therefore, those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy (brahmacarya)— for them alone is this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

This being so, those who—by means of *brahmacarya*, that is, by abandoning thirst for women, and by following the instructions of the scriptures and the teacher—attain this aforementioned world of Brahman, bringing it to the state of direct personal realization;

for them alone, who possess the means of *brahmacarya* and are knowers of Brahman, there is this world of Brahman, and not for others, even if they are knowers of Brahman, provided they still possess thirst born from contact with the objects of women; such is the meaning.
"For them, there is freedom of movement in all worlds"—the meaning of this has already been explained.
Therefore, the intention is that this practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the supreme means for those who know Brahman. //3//
Thus ends the fourth section of the eighth chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (yajña) is in fact celibacy (brahmacarya).
For indeed, by means of celibacy alone does one who knows find that [Self].
Now, what people call "sacrifice" (iṣṭa) is actually celibacy;
for by means of celibacy alone, having sacrificed, one finds the Self.

The commentary on ChUpBh 8.5.1 states that for the attainment of that Self which has been praised through attributes such as being a bridge, another means known as *brahmacarya* (celibacy/study), acting as a cooperative factor for knowledge, must be understood.

He praises it by means of sacrifice and other duties for the sake of its performance: "Now, that which they call 'sacrifice' (*yajña*) in the world—the means to the supreme human goal that the learned proclaim—that is indeed *brahmacarya*.
One who possesses *brahmacarya* obtains even the fruit of sacrifice; therefore, sacrifice itself should be understood as *brahmacarya*."

How is it that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is sacrifice (*yajña*)? He says: because by means of celibacy alone, he who knows finds—that is, attains—that world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), which is the ultimate fruit of sacrifice through a traditional succession; therefore, sacrifice is indeed celibacy.
Since the word "he who knows" (*yaḥ jñātā*) continues from the preceding [verse], sacrifice is indeed celibacy.
Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (iṣṭa) is actually celibacy (brahmacarya).
How so?
By means of celibacy alone as the instrument, having sacrificed to—that is, having worshipped—that Lord, or alternatively, having directed one's longing toward the Self, one finds that very Self.
Even that which is desired through seeking is indeed the holy life itself. //1//
Now, that which they call the *sattrāyaṇa* is simply celibacy (*brahmacarya*). For by means of celibacy alone does one find protection for oneself while existing.
Now, that which they call "silence" is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya);
for it is by means of celibacy alone that one, having discovered the Self, reflects upon it.

Now, that which they call "sattrāyaṇa" (the sacrificial session) is indeed celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Being thus, one finds protection (*trāṇa*) and preservation (*rakṣaṇa*) for oneself from the Supreme Self by means of the practice of celibacy; therefore, that which is called "sattrāyaṇa" is also truly celibacy.

Now, that which they call "mauna" (silence) is also celibacy. Being endowed with the practice of celibacy as the means, one understands the Self through the scriptures and the teacher, and thereafter reflects upon and meditates (*dhyāyati*) upon it.
Therefore, even the word *mauna* (silence) is indeed *brahmacarya* (the life of sacred study). //2//
Now,
that which they call "fasting unto death" is actually celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
for this Self does not perish, which one finds through celibacy.
Now, that which they call "the journey to the forest" (araṇyāyana) is in fact the life of sacred study (brahmacarya).
For there, in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here, are the two oceans called Ara and Ṇya;
there also is the lake Airammadīya.
That is the Aśvattha tree, the presser of Soma;
that is the unassailable city of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord.

Now, that which they call "the path of non-perishing" (anāśakāyana) is indeed celibacy (brahmacarya). For that Self which one finds through celibacy does not perish for one who possesses the means of celibacy; therefore, even the "path of non-perishing" is simply celibacy.
Furthermore, that which they call "the path of the forest" (araṇyāyana) is indeed celibacy.

Because it is praised by such great means for achieving the goals of man (puruṣārtha)— such as being called "araṇya" (forest) because one goes to the forest (*araṇya*), "arṇava" (ocean) because of its vastness, "brahmacarya" (chastity) because of practicing celibacy, "yajña" (sacrifice) because of knowledge, "iṣṭa" (offering) because of seeking, "sattrāyaṇa" (sacrificial session) because of protecting the virtuous, "mauna" (silence) because of contemplation, "anāśakāyana" (fasting unto death) because of not eating, and "araṇyāyana" (going to the forest) because of departing for the forest— therefore, brahmacarya is the supreme auxiliary cause and means for attaining knowledge. Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that it must be protected with effort by one who knows Brahman.

For there, in that world of Brahman, there are indeed two famous oceans, Ara and Ṇya—likened to seas or lakes—located in the third heaven from here, counting from this world as the first, with the earth and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) making up the first two.
In that third heaven...

In that very place is the lake named Airammadīya; "aira" refers to food made from *air* (barley), and "manda" is a thick gruel made thereof, so it is full of that. It is called "Airammadīya" because it produces intoxication—meaning joy—for those who partake of it. In that same place is the tree named Aśvattha, known as Somasavana; "soma" means nectar (*amṛta*), so it is either "that which flows [nectar]" or "the flow of nectar.

And in that very world of Brahmā is the city of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha named Aparājitā, which cannot be conquered by others who lack the means of celibate practice (*brahmacarya*) compared to those who possess such means.

And that which was specially measured out and constructed by the Lord Brahmā—that golden, i.e., made of gold, "Prabhuvimita" (the Pavilion Measured by the Lord)—is the completion of the sentence. //3//
Now, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)— to them alone belongs this world of Brahman;
for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds.

In that regard, those who find the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) by means of the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)— that world of Brahman which has been described as consisting of these two oceans called Ara and Ṇya— belonging to them alone is that world of Brahman; and for those knowers of Brahman who have attained their goal through the practice of celibacy, there is freedom of movement at will in all worlds.
The meaning is that this is not for others who are devoted to unchaste conduct and whose intellects are attached to external objects, even at any time.

Now, some might argue: "Just as someone worthy of high praise is extolled here with words such as 'You are Indra,' 'You are Yama,' and 'You are Varuṇa,' so too, by means of words like 'desired' (*iṣṭa*) and so forth, it is not merely the cessation of thirst for objects such as women that is worthy of praise; rather, since knowledge is the means to liberation, it is that very knowledge which is praised by these words. This is not so.
For those whose minds are carried away by thirst for external objects such as women and the like, the discriminative knowledge of the inner Self (pratyagātman) is impossible to attain;
this is established by hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts, such as: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self.

Thus, it is entirely appropriate to praise that [renunciation], since it must indeed be enjoined as the means for the cessation of thirst for objects such as women, which serves as an auxiliary cause for knowledge.
But is it not the case that, since celibacy is praised by means of sacrifices and so forth, it is understood that sacrifices and the like are means for attaining the goals of human life?
True, this is understood.

However, in this context, celibacy is not praised by means of sacrifices and so forth with the intention of establishing sacrifices as the means for attaining the world of Brahman; rather, it is done with reference to their well-known status as means for attaining the goals of human life.
Just as a king [is present] through Indra and others, yet it is not the case that the king's activity exists only where the activity of Indra and others exists—so it is here.

Are these oceans and so forth belonging to the world of Brahmā, and the enjoyments such as fathers born of mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), material—consisting of earth and water as they are seen here in this world, such as oceans, trees, cities, and golden pavilions—or are they merely mental conceptions (*mānasapratyaya*)? What follows from this? If they were gross, consisting of earth and water, their containment within the space of the heart (*hṛdyākāśa*) would be impossible.

Furthermore, it would contradict the Purāṇic statement: "In the world of Brahman, the body and other such things are composed of mind," as well as Vedic texts such as "free from sorrow and free from pride. Now, one might object that the Purāṇic Smṛti—which states, "The oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, sacrifices, Vedas, mantras, and so forth, having taken on embodied forms, wait upon Brahmā"—would be contradicted if they were merely mental.
No;
for it is impossible for those things whose forms are well-known to possess corporeality to travel there.
Therefore, apart from their well-known corporeal forms, the oceans and so forth must assume another form, taken up by the oceans themselves, which travels to the world of Brahmā.
In the case of mental construction (*kalpanā*), it is appropriate to conceive of the forms of men, women, and so forth, as they are commonly known, as being endowed with mental shapes;
for this is established by the possibility of a connection corresponding to a mental body.
Indeed, forms of men, women, and so forth, possessing mental shapes, are observed in dreams.
[Objection: But surely those [desires] are indeed unreal;
if that were so, the scriptural statement "these desires are real" would be contradicted. [Reply: No, because it is possible for mental cognition to possess reality.
For mental cognitions in the form of women, men, and so forth are seen in dreams.
[Objection: Surely those things seen in dreams are of the nature of impressions from the waking state, and women and such do not actually exist there in the dream.
[Reply: This that you say is far too little.

Even the objects of the waking state are produced solely from mental cognitions, because those waking objects consist of fire, water, and food, which are themselves produced through the power of true insight (*sadīkṣā*).
For it has been stated that "the worlds have their root in volition" (*saṃkalpa*) in the passage, "Heaven and earth were united in volition.
Furthermore, in all the Vedas, the origin, dissolution, and abiding of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) therein are described in such passages as, "As the spokes are fixed in the hub," and so forth.
Therefore, it is indeed accepted that mental and external objects stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, like a seed and its sprout.
Although external objects are themselves mental and mental objects are themselves external, they never become unreal with respect to their own nature.
[Objection: But surely, for one who has awakened, the objects seen in a dream become unreal?
This is indeed true;
however, that unreality is relative to waking awareness and not intrinsic.
Likewise, the unreality of objects perceived in the waking state is relative to dream-awareness and not intrinsic.

However, the mere appearance of specific forms is the cause of all false cognitions; thus, "modification is a mere verbal handle, a name, and unreal; only the three forms (earth, water, and fire) are real.

Even these are unreal in terms of their specific forms, yet real in themselves as being of the nature of pure Being (*sanmātra*). Prior to the awakening to the Self that is Existence, everything—even within one's own sphere—is indeed real, like the objects seen in a dream; thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, the forests and so forth, as well as the fathers and other objects of desire belonging to the world of Brahman, are purely mental.

The meaning is that because they are free from impurity—unlike the enjoyment of external objects—they are produced by the volitions of pure beings (*śuddhasattva*); thus, they are unsurpassed pleasures and are real for the Lords (*īśvara*).

Even when there is the awakening to the reality of the True Self, things such as snakes imagined upon a rope attain the very nature of the real Self; therefore, they are indeed real by virtue of being the True Self. //4//
Thus ends the fifth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Now, those channels of the heart— those of the minute, tawny-colored [subtle body]— stand filled with [fluids] that are white, blue, yellow, and red.
That sun is tawny; it is white, it is blue, it is yellow, it is red.

Now, for one who—endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and having abandoned the false thirst for external objects—worships Brahman, characterized by the qualities described above, residing within the lotus of the heart, his departure by means of the artery at the crown of the head must be explained; thus the section on the arteries (*nāḍī-khaṇḍa*) begins:
"Now, those which are these arteries connected to the heart, the lotus-shaped seat of the meditation on Brahman..."

Emerging from all sides from the lump of flesh that is the heart, like rays from the orb of the sun, these [channels] remain and exist filled with the essence of a subtle fluid (*aṇiman*) characterized by a specific color—namely, tawny (*piṅgala*); the meaning is that they persist having that very form.
Likewise, the phrase "filled with the essence" is to be supplied in every case for white, blue, yellow, and red.

Due to contact with the solar heat known as bile (pitta), which is produced by digestion, and with a small amount of phlegm (kapha), the solar heat becomes tawny; that same [heat] becomes blue due to a predominance of wind (vāta), and white due to a predominance of phlegm;
when there is equilibrium with phlegm, it is yellow.
Blood is red due to an abundance of blood;
or rather, the specific colors should be investigated from medical science as to how they come to be.
However, scripture says that these specific colors belong to that light of the sun itself which has entered into the channels (nāḍīs).
How so?
This sun is tawny in color; this very sun is white, this is blue, this is yellow, and this is red—the sun itself.
Just as a great highway stretches out and goes to both villages— this one and that one— so too do these rays of the sun go to both worlds— this one and that one.
They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels.
From these channels they extend out; they have entered into yonder sun.

Regarding how its connection with the internal channels (*nāḍīs*) occurs, he provides an illustration: "In that regard, just as in the world a great, wide path—a highway—that stretches across reaches both this nearby [village] and that distant, far-off one; just as the highway in the illustration enters both villages, even so these..."
The rays of the sun go to both worlds— that solar orb and this person— having entered into both,
just like a great highway.
How so?
From that solar orb, they extend out and become continuous.
They have crept—that is, gone and entered—into those internal channels (nāḍīs) of the aforementioned colors such as tawny (piṅgalā) and so forth.
From these channels, they extend out, having proceeded and become a continuous stream, reaching back to that [solar orb].
Because rays possess both genders, they are referred to by the pronoun "te" (they). //2//
Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream,
he has then entered into these channels (nāḍīs).
No evil whatsoever touches him,
for he is then endowed with splendor.
This being so, at that time— when this living self (jīva) is asleep, that is, in a state of slumber—
the qualification "completely withdrawn" is given because sleep is of two kinds;
it means that all the functions of the organs have been withdrawn.
Therefore, due to the absence of the turbidity produced by contact with external objects, he becomes perfectly clear and serene (*saṃprasanna*).
For this very reason, he does not cognize— that is to say, he does not experience— the dream-cognition, which is mental and appears in the form of external objects.

When he has thus fallen asleep within these aforementioned channels (nāḍīs) which are filled with the solar radiance, then, having entered through the channels acting as gateways, he has gone to the space of the heart—this is the meaning.

For there is no perception of dreams elsewhere than in the attainment of Being (sat); therefore, by implication, the locative case "in the channels" (nāḍīṣu) is transformed into an instrumental sense.
No one at all—no evil whatsoever in the form of merit or demerit—touches him who is united with Being, because at that time the Self abides in its own true nature.

For evil touches one who is distinguished by a body and senses by bestowing the effects of pleasure and pain; however, no evil at all dares to touch one who has attained Being and abides in his true nature, because such a one is not an object [of evil].
Indeed, one thing becomes an object for another, but there is no longer any state of being "another" for one who has attained Being, regardless of who it might be or from whatever source.

We have already stated in the sixth [chapter] that the falling away from one's own true nature—the soul's transition toward the states of waking and dreaming, and the perception of external objects—is caused by the burning of the seed of ignorance, desire, and karma by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman; this should be understood here as well.
When one has thus fallen asleep, one becomes completely endowed with and pervaded by the solar light situated within the channels (nāḍīs).
Therefore, at that time, his organs do not specifically project outward through the channels of the eyes and other senses for the enjoyment of external objects.
Consequently, it is logical that due to the cessation of the organs, he remains established in his own self and does not perceive dreams. //3//
Now,
when he has been reduced to weakness,
those sitting around him say, "Do you know me? Do you know me?"
As long as he has not departed from this body, so long does he know. (ChU 8.6.4)

This being so, when—at whatever time—Devadatta has been brought to a state of weakness (*abalimāna*), that is, a condition of physical frailty caused by disease or the like, or a state of emaciation caused by old age and the like; in other words, when he is about to die—then his relatives, sitting all around him on every side, say: "Do you recognize me, your son? Do you recognize me, your father? and so forth.
As long as he who is about to die has not yet departed from this body—that is, as long as he has not gone out—he perceives his sons and other relatives. //4//
Now, when he departs from this body,
he ascends upwards by means of these very rays.
He passes away either with the utterance "Om" or with the sound "Hod.
As quickly as one could direct the mind, he goes to the sun.
This, indeed, is the door to the world, the path for those who know, and the obstruction for those who do not know.
Now, when he departs from this body— this being a qualification of the action—

then he ascends upwards by means of these very rays as previously described, toward the world acquired according to his karma, if he is ignorant; but the other, the wise one, endowed with the aforementioned means, meditating on the Self with the syllable *oṃ*, either proceeds as previously stated, or indeed exactly so.
The meaning is that if he is a knower, he goes upward; otherwise, he goes horizontally.
"Is measured" (mīyate) means "is measured out" (pramīyate), which is to say, he goes.

That knower, when about to depart, reaches the sun in the time it takes for the mind to be cast forth—that is, in as much time as it would take for the mind to be projected; the sense is that he goes quickly, and not [in the manner previously described].
The intended meaning is "in that very amount of time.
For what purpose does he go to the sun? It is said: it is well known that the sun is indeed the gate to the world of Brahman; by means of that gate, the knower goes to the world of Brahman.
Therefore, for the wise, it is the "means of entry" (*prapadana*); one enters the world of Brahman through this gate, hence it is called the "means of entry."
It is called "cessation" (nirodha) because cessation occurs for the ignorant from this sun;

the meaning is that, being obstructed by the solar heat within the body itself, they do not depart at all through the channel at the crown of the head, as stated in the verse beginning with "the others in all directions. //5//
Concerning this, there is this verse:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; one of them extends out toward the crown of the head."
Going upwards by that [path], one attains immortality; the others lead to departure in various directions—yes, they lead to departure.
Regarding this matter as it has been stated, there is this verse, a mantra:
"One hundred and one"—that is, one hundred and one principal channels belong to the heart, which is a mass of flesh;
for the channels of the body are infinite in number.

Of these, one has issued forth from the head; going upwards by that [path], one attains immortality, which is the state of being immortal. The other channels are spread out in various directions—both horizontally and upwards—and serve as the gateways for movement within saṃsāra;
they do not lead to immortality. Rather, the meaning is that they exist solely for the purpose of departing according to one's karma.
The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the section. //6//
Thus ends the sixth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true— that is what must be sought after, that is what one must desire to understand.
"He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires"—thus indeed spoke Prajāpati.

Now, regarding that which was stated: "Now, this serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form; this is the Self," it has been said, "this is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman. In this context, what is this serene being? Or how is its attainment [to be understood]? And how is it to be sought out as distinct from this body? This is indeed a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) and not an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).
"In this way he should seek" means "he should desire to know";
for seeking and desiring to know have a visible purpose.
