And he will demonstrate that they have a visible purpose more than once with the words, "I see nothing here to enjoy."

Furthermore, since the removal of erroneous apprehension is seen as the visible fruit when the true nature of the Self—which is ordinarily perceived through the forms of others such as the body—is realized, it is appropriate that this injunction has the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*); however, an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) like those concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites is not possible here. //1//
Both the gods and the asuras became aware of this.
They said, "Come, let us search for that Self, by searching for which one obtains all worlds and all desires."
Indra, indeed, went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the Asuras.
Without communicating with one another, they both approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands.
The purpose of the narrative beginning with "Then both" has been stated.

It is said that both—the gods and the asuras, collectively referred to as "devāsurāḥ"—heard this speech of Prajāpati handed down through tradition as it came within the range of their own ears; they understood it.
Having understood this speech of Prajāpati, what did they do? That is now told: "They said," the gods spoke to one another.
And the Asuras in their own assembly said, "Alas! If you have permission, let us seek that Self which was spoken of by Prajāpati;

let us perform the search for that Self, having sought which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Having said this, Indra—the king himself among the gods—having set aside the other gods and all his enjoyments and possessions, [proceeded].
Virocana, the leader of the asuras, set out toward Prajāpati with his physical body alone;
this demonstrates that teachers must be approached with humility,
for [the pursuit of knowledge] is weightier than even sovereignty over the three worlds.
Since the two kings of the gods and the asuras, though worthy of the most precious enjoyments, had thus approached their teacher, they—

being unaware of each other and not communicating with one another, yet displaying mutual envy regarding the fruit of their knowledge— approached Prajāpati with fuel in hand, having come to him carrying loads of sacrificial wood.
The two of them lived as religious students for thirty-two years.
Prajāpati said to them: "Desiring what have you dwelt here?"

They both said, "That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolve is true—that is what must be sought, that is what one must desire to understand.
He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires—such is the word of the venerable ones they proclaim. Desiring that [Self], we have come here. (ChU 8.7.3)
Having gone there, the two of them lived as students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*), intent on service for thirty-two years.
Prajāpati, knowing their intention, said to them: "Desiring what? With what purpose in mind did you live here? Being thus addressed, they both replied:
"The learned ones declare that which is the Self (*ātman*) and so forth according to the words of the Blessed One; therefore, desiring to know that Self, we have lived here."

Although they had previously been filled with mutual envy before approaching Prajāpati, nevertheless, having abandoned the defects of passion, hatred, delusion, envy, and so forth due to the gravity of the purpose for which they had acquired knowledge, they lived the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati.
By this, the greatness of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*) was proclaimed. //3//
Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye, this is the Self," he said;
"this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
"Then, O Venerable Sir, as for this one who is perceived in water and this one who is perceived in a mirror—who among these is he?
"It is he indeed who is perceived within all these ends," he said.

Having perceived that those two were thus ascetic, purified of taints, and fit [for instruction], Prajāpati said to them: "This person who is seen in the eye by those whose vision has turned inward and whose passions have been subdued—this is the Self (Ātman) possessing qualities such as being free from evil, of which I spoke previously; through the knowledge of whom there is the attainment of all worlds and desires; this is the Immortal, called the 'Shining' (Bhā), and for that very reason it is 'Fearless' (Abhaya), and for that very reason it is 'Brahman,' the most ancient.
Now, having heard these words of Prajāpati, "The person is seen in the eye," the two of them grasped the person in the form of a reflection.
Having grasped this, they asked Prajāpati for the sake of firm conviction:

"Now, O Blessed One, regarding that which is perceived all around in water, and that which is perceived as the form of one's own reflection in a mirror, in a sword, and so forth—which among these is the one spoken of by your reverences? Or is it one and the same in all?"
Being thus questioned, Prajāpati said: "It is indeed this very one whom I spoke of as the seer in the eye.
Having kept this in mind, he said: "He is perceived within all these ends and in their midst.
But how is it appropriate for Prajāpati, being a teacher free from all defects, to permit such a contrary apprehension on the part of his disciple?
It is indeed true that it was not permitted.
How so?
Because Indra and Virocana had superimposed upon themselves the qualities of scholarship, greatness, and wisdom, and were thus renowned in the world in exactly that way.

Prajāpati thinks: "If these two were told by me, 'You two are deluded' or 'You have grasped the matter incorrectly,' then distress would arise in their minds; and from that mental dejection, there would be an obstruction to their enthusiasm for further questioning, listening, grasping, and retaining [the teaching]. Therefore, the disciples must be protected."
"Take it for now; I shall remove it by means of the analogy of the water in the cup.
[The opponent objects: "But surely it is not proper to speak such a falsehood as 'this very thing'? [The teacher replies:
"No falsehood has been spoken."
How so?

Prajāpati spoke of the Person in the eye as being more closely situated in the mind than the shadow-self grasped by the disciple, and as being within all, according to the scriptural text, "He who is within all" (*sarvāntara*).
He spoke of that very same one when he said, "This one indeed. Therefore, nothing false was spoken by Prajāpati.
And likewise, he has indeed stated this for the purpose of removing the erroneous apprehension regarding those two. //4//
"Having looked at yourselves in a bowl of water, tell me whatever you do not understand of the Self," he said.
The two of them looked into a vessel of water.
Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? They both replied, "Venerable Sir, we see our entire self here as a reflection, down to the very hairs and the nails. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.8.1)

"Look at yourselves in a water-filled saucer or similar vessel; then, regarding that self which you see there, tell me what you do not understand. Thus addressed, they both looked into the water-filled saucer and performed the act of looking.

When the two had done so, Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? Although they were told, "Tell me that," they looked into the water-jar and did not inform Prajāpati, saying, "This was not known by us. Since they had failed to report it—the very cause of their ignorance—Prajāpati again asked, "What do you see? What is the intention behind this?

It is said: [The objection is] that there was no doubt on their part that "this [distinction] is unknown to us both," for the conviction regarding the self in the shadow-self was indeed certain; as he will later state, "The two of them, with peaceful hearts, went forth.
For a state of peace in the heart is not possible when the intended object is not certain.
Therefore, they did not say, "This is unknown to us. Furthermore, since disciples who hold perverted views must not be neglected, he himself asked, "What do you see?
and will later say, "Well-adorned," and so forth, in order to remove their erroneous conviction.
The two said: "Venerable sir, we see this entire self of ours as it truly is, down to the very hairs and nails;
for just as we ourselves, O venerable sir, possess hair, nails, and so forth, even so do we see this reflection of ours in the water-bowl, complete with hair, nails, and the rest. //1//
Prajāpati said to them: "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a pan of water. So they, having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, looked into a pan of water.
Prajāpati said to them both: "What do you see? 8.8.2.
Prajāpati spoke to them again in order to remove their conviction that the reflection was the Self:

"Having become well-adorned, as you would at home, wearing fine garments and costly clothes, and being well-groomed with hair and nails clipped, look into a vessel of water so that the misconception regarding the reflection as the Self may be removed. By this, it is understood that just as the adventitious ornaments, fine garments, and the like produce a reflection in the water-vessel when connected to the body, so too did the body previously possess the capacity to produce a reflection.

Furthermore, certain parts of the body, such as hair and nails, which were previously intended to be permanent and uncut, possessed the quality of casting a shadow; however, when these are cut, no shadow of the hair or nails is seen. Therefore, just like the hair and nails, it is established that the body is also subject to coming into being and passing away. Thus, it is established that the body—which is the cause of the reflection seen in a water-jar or similar vessel—is not the Self. In the water-jar and so forth...
Because it casts a shadow, like ornaments and other things connected to the body;

not only this much, but by this [reasoning], whatever is considered one's own—such as pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and delusion—is to be understood as non-self because it is occasional, like nails and hair.
Thus, when Prajāpati had spoken the illustration of the fine ornaments and so forth for the purpose of removing all false attachments, having heard it accordingly...

Since even after performing [the experiment], their misconception of the reflection as the Self did not depart, it is understood that Indra and Virocana were obstructed by some personal defect such that their discriminative knowledge was blocked;
thus, with their convictions remaining as firm as before, he asked them, "What do you see? (2).

They both said, "Just as we two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed here, even so these two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed. "This is the Self," he said.
"This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.
With their hearts thus pacified, the two of them departed.

The two of them accepted it exactly as it was presented—"this is so"—just as before; they became even more firmly convinced of their misconception, thinking, "Just as we ourselves were previously distinguished by fine ornaments and the like, so too are these two shadow-selves.
While they were still seeking further particulars regarding that Self whose characteristic was described as "the Self free from evil," [that which is] this...

When it was directly pointed out that "the person is seen in the eye," and even when the illustration of the water-jar and the well-dressed ornament was given to remove misconceptions contrary to that, the misconception regarding the true nature of the Self did not go away.

Therefore, thinking that the capacity for discriminative knowledge was obstructed by some personal defect of his own, [Janaka] kept the Self exactly as he had conceived it in his mind and said: "This is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."
Prajāpati is as before;
however, he did not intend that [specific] Self.

For both [disciples] had been prepared by hearing the definition of the Self beginning with "That which is the Self," by the scriptural teaching of the Person in the eye, and by the logical reasoning concerning the water-vessel and so forth.

Thinking that, by repeatedly remembering all his words and through the destruction of their obstacles, discernment regarding the Self would arise spontaneously, and wishing to avoid causing mental distress to them during the instruction on celibacy, Prajāpati remained indifferent even as they departed with the conviction that they had already achieved their goal.

The meaning is that both Indra and Virocana were peaceful in heart, satisfied in heart, and possessed of the realization that their purpose was fulfilled; however, this was not merely tranquility, for if such tranquility had truly arisen in them, their misconception would have vanished, yet they instead departed and went away. //3//
Having looked at them both, Prajāpati said:
"If they depart without perceiving the Self and without knowing it, whichever of these two— whether gods or asuras— shall have this as their secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they will perish."
With his heart thus pacified, Virocana went to the Asuras and taught them this secret doctrine (upaniṣad): "In this world, the self alone is to be magnified; the self is to be served.
By magnifying the self and serving the self in this world, one attains both worlds—this one and the one beyond."

When Indra and Virocana had thus departed, the Teacher, fearing that those two kings— being attached to worldly enjoyments— might forget what had been taught, and desiring to remove their mental distress by means of direct instruction for that which is not perceptible to the senses,

observed them as they were traveling far away and thought: "This [teaching] also shall come within the range of their hearing, just like the statement beginning with 'The Self which is free from evil'."
Prajāpati said:

"Without perceiving the Self as described by its characteristics, without realizing it through direct personal experience, and having formed contrary convictions, these two, Indra and Virocana, are departing and going away.

Therefore, whichever of the two—whether gods or asuras—possess this *upaniṣad*, that is, this knowledge of the Self which has been grasped by them as their secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), they shall become possessed of such a realization."
The meaning is that they will become certain of this.
What will they do? They will be defeated; the meaning is that they will be fallen away from the path to the highest good (*śreyas*), excluded from it, and ruined.
Of the two kings of the gods and the asuras who were going to their own homes, he who was the king of the asuras, Virocana, went to the asuras with a peaceful heart.
Having gone to those Asuras, he spoke this Upaniṣad—the secret doctrine concerning the body as the Self—which his father had taught him: "The Self is merely the body.

Therefore, in this world, the body alone is the Self; it is to be magnified, worshipped, served, and attended upon. By magnifying and serving the body, which is the Self in this world, one attains both worlds—this one and the next.
"And also this world. The king's intention is that all worlds and all desires are included within these very two: this world and the next world. //4//
Therefore, even today, they say of one who does not give, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an asura!
For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the asuras.
They prepare the body of the deceased with alms-food, clothing, and ornaments; for they think, "By this we shall conquer the other world. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.8.5)

Therefore, that tradition continues even today; thus, in this world, the learned, feeling distressed, say of one who does not give—that is, who does not practice charity, who is of a non-distributive nature, who lacks faith—meaning devoid of faith regarding meritorious deeds—and who, according to his ability, does not sacrifice—that is, whose nature is not to perform sacrifices: "This man is truly asuric, for he possesses such a nature; alas! they say.
For this is the *upaniṣad* (secret doctrine) of the Asuras, characterized by lack of faith and so forth.

Being refined by that *upaniṣad*, they consecrate the corpse—the dead body—of the deceased through alms consisting of perfumes, garlands, food, and the like, through clothing such as garments and the like, through the manner of covering and so forth, and through ornaments made of banners, flags, and the like; it is by means of this that they consecrate it.
Thinking they will conquer that world which is to be reached after death, they imagine themselves to be winning it through the preparation of a corpse. //5//
Thus ends the eighth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Now,
Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this fear.

Just as this [self] becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, it becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and crippled when it is crippled.
Following the destruction of this very body, it perishes.
"I see no object of enjoyment here," he said. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.1)

Now, it is said that Indra, even before reaching the gods, while traveling and repeatedly recollecting the words of his teacher because he was endowed with divine qualities such as fortitude, perceived this fear about to be described— namely, the cause for his own apprehension.
A portion of the reasoning concerning the purpose of the illustration of the water-cup (udaśarāva) which Prajāpati had stated occurred to Maghavan’s mind.
And by what means did he perceive the fault in grasping the shadow-self?
How so?
Just as indeed, when this body is well-adorned, the shadow-self also becomes well-adorned; when it is well-clothed...

And when one is well-dressed and adorned, the reflection-self (chāyātman) also becomes well-adorned; just as when the bodily parts such as nails and hair are removed, the reflection-self also becomes well-adorned and devoid of those nails, hair, and so forth.

In exactly the same way, this reflection-self, because its status as a bodily part is equal [to the actual body], becomes blind when the eyes are lost in a blind person, and lame when the legs are lost in a lame person.
A *srāma* is said to be "one-eyed" because he has lost one eye due to blindness;
or, he is a *srāma* whose eyes or nose constantly discharge [pus]. A *parivṛkṇa* is one whose hand is severed or whose foot is severed.
When the body is wounded or mangled, the shadow-self likewise becomes so;
thus, following the destruction of this body, it perishes. //1//
With fuel in his hand, he returned once more.
Prajāpati said to him:
"O Maghavan, since you went forth as an ascetic together with Virocana with a tranquil heart, desiring what have you come back again?

He replied, "Just as indeed, O Venerable Sir, this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, this [self] becomes blind when this [body] is blind."
"In sickness he becomes sick; when the body is mangled, he becomes mangled. Following the destruction of this very body, he perishes.
I see nothing enjoyable in this. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.2)

"Therefore, I see no fruit of enjoyment here in this view of the self as a reflection, nor in this view of the self as the body. Having thus determined the defect in the view of the self as either the body's shadow or the body itself, he returned with fuel in his hand to dwell [with Prajāpati] as a religious student.
Prajāpati said to him: "O Maghavan, since you went away with a peaceful heart along with Virocana, desiring what have you come back?"
Even though he already knew, Prajāpati questioned him again in order to make Indra’s intention manifest, just as one might say, "Approach me with what you know.
And so, Indra made his own intention clear by saying, "As indeed this [body]...
and so forth; and Prajāpati approved, saying, "It is exactly so."
Now, since the report regarding the "Person in the Eye" was equal for both, why did Indra grasp the shadow of the body as the Self, while Virocana grasped the body itself?
Regarding this, it is considered as follows:

Just as in the case of Indra—who, while remembering Prajāpati’s words concerning the water-jar and so forth, had not yet reached the gods—there occurred, through his understanding of the teacher’s instruction, the grasping of the shadow-self and the perception of its defects.
It was not so for Virocana; rather, he perceived the body itself as the Self, nor did he perceive any defect in it.
Just like that, Indra’s and Virocana’s respective graspings of the shadow-self and the body depended on the degree of their defects that obstructed the capacity to receive true knowledge.

Because Indra had fewer defects, he accepted the literal meaning of the scriptural statement, "That which is seen," out of faith. The other [Virocana], however, set aside the body—which is the cause of the shadow—and grasped the figurative meaning of the scriptural statement as spoken by Prajāpati.
The word "this" [refers to the reflection] because of the preponderance of defects.

Just as, for instance, when two garments—one blue and one not blue—are seen in a mirror, if someone says, "That which is blue is of great value," it is the garment itself that is being referred to on account of its shadow, and not the shadow; such was the intention of Virocana.

For it has been demonstrated in another Vedic passage that the determination of the meaning of words depends solely on the virtues and defects of one's own mind, even when the hearing of the sound is identical: from the mere hearing of the syllable *da* in the words "Be self-controlled (*dāmyata*)," "Give (*datta*)," and "Be compassionate (*dayadhvam*)."
The signs as well become auxiliary factors that are entirely concordant with it. //2//
"It is just so, O Maghavan," he said.
"I shall explain this very same thing to you further."
"Stay for another thirty-two years.
He lived there for another thirty-two years.
Then he said to him:

"Precisely so, O Maghavan, has this been correctly understood by you; it is not the shadow-self," said Prajāpati. "That Self which was introduced by me—that very Self, though previously explained, I shall explain further to you.

For although what was explained once reached the range of comprehension for those free from defects, you did not grasp it; therefore, [I shall explain it again] because of some defect [on your part]."
"Since you possess the capacity to grasp what is connected [to this teaching], therefore dwell for another thirty-two years in order to destroy those remaining defects.
Having said this, he spoke to him who had lived accordingly and whose defects were destroyed. //3//
"He who moves about being honored in a dream— this is the Self," he said. Thus ends the ninth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.
With a peaceful heart, he departed.
But even before reaching the gods, he beheld this fear.
Therefore, even if this body becomes blind, he does not become blind; if it becomes lame, he does not become lame.
Indeed, he is not defiled by its defect.
That Self characterized by the qualities of being free from evil and so forth, which was explained in the passage beginning with "He who is in the eye," is this very one.
Who is he?
He is the one who, being honored—that is, being worshipped—by women and others while moving about in a dream, experiences various kinds of dream-enjoyments; this is the meaning.
"This is the Self," he said, and so on, as before.
Having been addressed thus, Indra departed with a peaceful heart.
But even before reaching the gods, as previously, he perceived fear in this Self as well.
How so?
Although this body runs blind, he who is the self in the dream state is not blind;
although this body is lame, he is not lame. Indeed, this self in the dream state is not defiled by the defects of this body. //1//
It is not killed by its being killed;
it does not become weary by its being worn out.
But they indeed strike him; they seem to overwhelm him;
he becomes as if he experiences what is unpleasant.
"Moreover, it seems as if it weeps, for I see no enjoyment in this."
With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him:
"Maghavan, since you have departed with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?"
He said:
"Therefore, venerable sir, even if this body becomes blind, he (the self) remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not lame.
Indeed, he is not affected by its defect."
It is not slain by its being slain; it does not waste away by its wasting away;
yet, as it were, they do slay it.
It is as if she were concealing herself;
it is as if she were experiencing something unpleasant;
she even seems to weep.
"I see no object of enjoyment here," [Yājñavalkya said].
"It is even so, O Maghavan," he replied,
"but I shall explain this very matter to you further."
"Stay for another thirty-two years.
He lived there for another thirty-two years,
and then he said to him:
Nor is he killed by the killing of this [body], nor is he weary by its weariness, just like the shadow-self; rather, he becomes the dream-self.

That which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter on the basis of scripture alone—namely, "He does not age with the aging of this [body]," and so forth—is here established by means of reasoning.
To begin with, he is not possessed of the defects of the body like the shadow-self, yet they do indeed kill him.

The word *eva* has the sense of *iva* (as if). It should be understood as "some [people] seem to kill him," because it is impossible for Prajāpati, who is being accepted as an authority, to be rendered a speaker of falsehood.
How could Indra, taking Prajāpati as his authority, render false this statement of Prajāpati that "this is the immortal"?
One might object: when Prajāpati spoke of the shadow-person, Indra pointed out the defect that "when this body perishes, he perishes"; would it not be the same here as well?
It is not so.
Why?
If one were to think, "This person who is seen in the eye [is the Self]," then how could he, having taken Prajāpati as his authority, go again with fuel in hand to hear [the teaching]?
Yet, he did indeed go.
Therefore, one considers that the Self consisting of shadow was not what Prajāpati spoke of.
And thus it has been explained: "The Seer is seen in the eye.
Likewise, [the reflection] seems to shrink away, as it were, and seems to flee away, as it were; and likewise, due to the death of a son or others, it becomes as if it experiences what is unpleasant.
Moreover, it seems to weep of its own accord. [Objection: But surely it does indeed experience what is unpleasant; how can it be said that it "seems" to experience it?
[Reply: It is said in response: because the statement regarding its being immortal and fearless would otherwise be untenable.
And because of another scriptural passage stating, "It is as if it meditates.
If it is argued that this contradicts direct perception, we say no; for, like the perception of the body as the self, such [perception] can be an error.
"Let it be for now whether one experiences what is unpleasant or not;
I see no enjoyment here.
The intention is that even in the knowledge of the self as being like a dream, one does not obtain a desired fruit. "It is exactly so according to your view"—this is the completion of the sentence.

Because it was intended that the Self possesses the qualities of immortality and fearlessness, Prajāpati— thinking that although he had stated it twice, [the student] did not comprehend it correctly due to logical reasons, and therefore even now there exists an obstacle for him as before— instructed him, saying, "Dwell for another thirty-two years in the life of a religious student (brahmacarya)" in order to destroy that obstacle.
To him who has dwelt thus and whose impurities have been destroyed, I said: [2-3-4]
Thus, in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the tenth section:
"When one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream— that is the Self," so he said.
"This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.
With his heart thus pacified, he departed.
However, even before reaching the gods, he perceived this fear.
Indeed, he does not at this time know himself thus: "This is I. Nor does he know these beings.
He has simply passed into destruction.
"I see no enjoyment here," he said.
With fuel in his hand, he returned.
Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you have gone forth with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back?
He replied: "Indeed, O Venerable One, this Self does not now know itself as 'this is I'."
"In that case, these beings do not exist;
one has simply gone to destruction.
I see nothing here to be enjoyed. Thus spoke [Nārada]. ChU 8.11.2.
Having said "But him indeed, my dear," and so forth as before, the passage beginning with "Now, when he is thus asleep" has been explained.

He who is the seer in the eye and who moves about being honored in the dream state—he, when asleep, unified and serene, does not perceive any dream; "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
This is precisely his intended meaning.
Even there, Maghavā perceived a fault.
How?
He said: "Indeed, even while in the state of deep sleep, this Self does not now—at this very time—truly know itself; it does not know itself in this way."
How?
"This is I" does not occur, nor do these beings occur,
as they do when one is awake or dreaming.
Therefore, "destruction itself as if it were destruction" is to be understood as before;
the intended meaning is that he becomes "gone away," as if he has perished.
For it is only when cognition exists that the existence of the cognizer is apprehended, not when cognition is absent.

And since no cognition is observed in one who is in deep sleep, the intention [of the opponent] is that the self is as if destroyed; however, one who desires to maintain the authority of the scriptural declarations that the self is immortal and fearless does not believe in its actual destruction. 1–2.
"Exactly so, Maghavan," he said.
"I shall explain this very same thing to you further."
"Indeed, it cannot be otherwise than this;
let me dwell for another five years.
And he dwelt for another five years.
They became one hundred and one. This is what they say:
"For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Prajāpati."
He said to him: "ChUp 8.11.3"

Having said, "It is exactly as before," [Indra replied]: "That very Self which I have described to you through these three stages—do not think that there is anything else other than this Self; rather, I shall explain this very same one. However, a small defect remains in you; dwell for another five years in order to exhaust it. Having been told this, he did accordingly. To him, Maghavan, whose defects such as impurity had been rubbed away, he spoke of the true nature of the Self—which is free from connection with the defects of the three states and characterized by freedom from sin and so forth.
Those amounted to one hundred and one years; they became fully completed.

That which the cultured people (*śiṣṭa*) in the world say—"Maghavān indeed dwelt as a religious student (*brahmacarya*) with Prajāpati for one hundred and one years"—is shown by this passage beginning with "thirty-two," etc.; thus, departing from the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), it is stated by the Śruti.

Thus, he praises self-knowledge, saying that it is indeed more weighty even than the status of Indra; for even by Indra himself, with great effort and the exertion of a hundred years plus one, this knowledge of the Self was attained. Therefore, there is no other human goal (puruṣārtha) higher than this. //3//
Thus ends the eleventh section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
"O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal; it is seized by death."
That is the substratum of this immortal, bodiless Self.
Indeed, the embodied one is seized by pleasure and pain.
For one who is embodied, there is no removal of pleasure and pain.
Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless.

"O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal, subject to the law of death. As for what you think— that the Self described by me as characterized by the eye, the support, and so forth, and characterized by serene clarity, simply perishes when it has entered [the body]—
listen to the reason for that."
This body is indeed mortal and perishable;
moreover, it is perpetually seized and swallowed by death.

When it is said that "it is mortal" in the sense that it dies only at some point, one does not experience such terror as when it is said that it is "already swallowed" and "perpetually pervaded by death. This distinction is stated for the purpose of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*).
"It has been seized by death.
How indeed can one who is detached from the identification with the body turn back?
Here, in the word "body" (śarīra), it is meant together with the senses and the mind.

That body of this serene being (*saṃprasāda*)—who is understood to have three stations, who is immortal, and who is devoid of the attributes of death, the physical body, the senses, and the mind—is as follows:

although his bodilessness is already established by the term "immortal" (*amṛta*), the further statement "of the bodiless one" (*aśarīrasya*) is intended to ensure that the Self does not possess parts or material form like wind and other such elements.
Or rather, for the Self who exists as the Seer, there has arisen a substratum produced through the sequence of fire, water, and earth.

"Adhiṣṭhāna" means that which, having entered in the form of the individual soul (jīva), presides over this [body] along with the gods. Since this locus of experience—produced by merit and demerit—is of such a nature, being eternally seized by death and characterized by pleasure and pain, one who is presided over by it becomes "possessed of a body" (saśarīra).

For the Self, whose true nature is bodiless, its state of being "possessed of a body" arises from the lack of discrimination, thinking "this very thing is I" and "I am this very body. It is precisely because of this that, being possessed of a body, it is "seized" or "devoured" by pleasure and pain.

This is well known: for one who is still embodied and who, regarding the conjunctions and disjunctions with external objects— which are the causes of pleasure and pain— thinks "these are mine," there is no removal, destruction,
or cessation of those two as they exist in a continuous stream.

Furthermore, when that [Self], which has its body of non-discriminative knowledge dissolved through the realization of its own bodiless nature by means of the cessation of the conceit of being the body, exists as such, pleasure and pain do not touch it.

The verb "touches" (spṛśati) is connected with each term individually; thus, there are two statements: "pleasure does not touch it" and "pain does not touch it," just as in the expression, "one does not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous."

For merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are indeed the effects of the body; however, bodilessness is one's true nature (*svarūpa*). Since merit and demerit are impossible there [in that state], the existence of their effects is even further removed. Therefore, pleasure and pain do not touch it. Now, if even pleasure does not touch the bodiless, then what Maghavan said—that "one situated in deep sleep has surely gone to destruction"—would apply here as well.

This is not a fault, because what is intended to be expressed is the negation of pleasure and pain—which are the effects of merit and demerit and are connected with the body—by the statement, "pleasure and pain do not touch the bodiless one.

For the word "touch" (*sparśa*) is seen to apply to things that come and go, as in "the touch of cold" or "the touch of heat," but it is not said that "there is a touching by fire" of its own heat and light, which constitute its very nature; likewise, [this applies] to bliss which constitutes the essential nature of Fire and the Sun.

There is no denial here even of that which is dear (*priya*), because of such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*) and "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*), and because it has been stated here as well that the Infinite alone (*bhūmā*) is happiness. [Objection: But if the Infinite and the dear are one, then it must be either imperceptible or eternally perceptible by its very nature; thus, it would be devoid of distinctions, and this is not what Indra desires.

For it has been said: "Indeed, he does not now know himself as 'I am this,' nor does he know these beings; he has gone to utter destruction. I see nothing here to enjoy. Therefore, that knowledge which Indra desired—by which one knows both the beings and the Self, and perceives no unpleasantness at all, and by which one attains all worlds and all desires—that is the truth Indra desired: "These beings are from me..."
"Other than me, all the worlds and all desires are distinct; I am their master"—this was not beneficial for Indra. And that which is beneficial for Indra must be spoken by Prajāpati.

Prajāpati intended that what should be told to Indra as his benefit was that attainment which comes through realizing one's identity with all beings, worlds, and desires by virtue of being a bodiless self like space;
it was not, however, like a king’s attainment of a kingdom, as something distinct from oneself.
This being so, when there is the oneness of the Self, who could perceive whom? [One would think: "These beings, this 'I' am."

[Objection: But in this view, scriptural passages concerning sovereignty—such as "by women or by vehicles," "if he is desirous of the world of the fathers," and "he becomes onefold"—would be untenable. [Reply: No; for there is no contradiction, since it is possible for the Self of all to be connected with all fruits, just as clay attains the state of all jars, dishes, bowls, and so forth.
If it is objected that, since [the Self] is the self of all, there would also be a connection with suffering, we say no;
for there is no contradiction, as suffering itself is admitted to be of the nature of the Self.
Sufferings have their cause in the conceptualization of ignorance within the Self, just as the conceptualization of a snake and so forth has its cause in a rope.

When that [ignorance] is severed by the vision of the true nature of the unity of the body and the Self, the suspicion of a connection with suffering is no longer possible. However, regarding desires caused by the volitions of pure *sattva*, the connection with the body of the Lord (*īśvara*) is such that He alone is the enjoyer of those mental desires within all beings through the medium of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of all living entities; thus, the Supreme Self alone is the locus for all transactions produced by ignorance.
"There is no other" is the established conclusion of the Vedānta.
That "person who is seen in the eye" mentioned by Prajāpati is merely the reflection-person (chāyāpuruṣa);
and in the states of dreaming and deep sleep, it is indeed something else.
Some maintain that the Supreme Self is not [meant here], because its characteristics—such as being free from evil and so forth—are contradictory [to those of the reflected selves].
They state the purpose for teaching the selves consisting of shadow and the rest as follows:

if the Supreme Self were taught at the very beginning, since it is difficult to comprehend, there might be confusion upon hearing of such an extremely subtle reality in those whose minds are excessively attached to external objects. Therefore, [the Supreme Self is taught later].

Just as, it is said, one who wishes to show the subtle moon on the second day first points out a certain tree, saying, "Look, this is the moon," then another, and then yet another mountain peak situated near the moon, saying, "This is the moon," and only then does he see the moon; in the same way, that which was spoken by Prajāpati in three stages beginning with "That which is in the eye" is not the Supreme.
But in the fourth stage, having risen from the mortal body and attained bodilessness, one becomes of the nature of light.
That Supreme Person in whom one exists eating, playing, and rejoicing with women and so forth—that Supreme Person is said to be the Highest; thus they say.
True, this interpretation is indeed pleasant to hear.
However, the meaning of this text cannot be understood in this way.
How so?
Having introduced the statement, "The person is seen in the eye," the two disciples grasped it as referring to the reflection-self; thus, their grasp was contrary to the truth.

If Prajāpati had taught that the reflection alone was the Self seen in the eye, then his presentation of the water-jar for its removal, his question "What do you see?", and his instruction regarding fine adornment would all be purposeless. Furthermore, if he had indeed taught [the reflection] himself, he would have had to state the reason for the subsequent removal of that very notion.

One should also state oneself the cause for removing [the misconception] regarding the grasping of the self in the states of dream and deep sleep; however, that has not been stated. Therefore, we consider that the shadow-self was not what was taught by Prajāpati in the eye.
Furthermore, if the seer in the eye had been taught as being visible, then this [objection] would be appropriate.
But after saying, "This very one, indeed, to you," there is the teaching of the seer himself even in the context of the dream.
If it is argued that the seer is not taught [to exist] in the dream state, we say no;
for there is the teaching: "He is as if weeping, as if experiencing what is unpleasant.
Furthermore, there is no one other than the seer who moves about being honored in the dream state.
In this regard, it is established by reasoning and by other scriptural passages that "this person here is self-luminous.
Even though one possesses the intellect (*dhī*) during dream, nevertheless the intellect does not function as an instrument for the perception of dream-enjoyments.

Rather, like a painting on a canvas, the intellect is merely an object of sight based upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state; thus, there is no sublation of the self-luminosity of the Seer.
Furthermore:
while awake and dreaming, one knows both the elements and the self, thinking, "These are the elements" and "I am this.
Since such knowledge is actually present, a negation would be appropriate [only if it were absent], as in the passage beginning with "But truly, he does not [know this]," and so forth.
Thus, having stated that for the conscious self alone, while possessing a body caused by ignorance, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant,

it is logical that for that very same self, when it exists as bodiless and knowledge is present, there is a negation of those two states which were previously thought to occur in the state of being embodied: "Verily, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is bodiless."

Furthermore, it is established in another scriptural text that the single Self moves unattached between the states of dreaming and waking, like a great fish. As for the claim that the "serene one" (saṃprasāda), having risen from the body, rejoices in women and other objects— that which is designated as the locus where he rejoices is a different, supreme Person (uttama puruṣa) distinct from the serene one— that too is incorrect.
Because in the fourth section as well, it says, "It is indeed this very one.
If he had intended someone other than that, Prajāpati would not have said, "It is indeed this very one," as before; otherwise, he would be speaking falsely.

Furthermore, after showing the entry of the Existent (Sat), the creator of fire, water, food, and so forth, into the sprout of his own body which is a modification of himself, the instruction "That thou art" given to the one who has entered would result in being false.
If the Supreme Person were other than the serene being (saṃprasāda), then the instruction "In that [state], you will be free from fear of women and so forth" would have been appropriate.
Likewise, if the Bhūman were other than the individual soul (jīva), he would not have concluded with "All this is indeed the Self," after having taught "I am indeed the Bhūman" and so on;
for there is also another scriptural passage stating, "There is no seer other than He."

Furthermore, the application of the word "Self" (ātman) to the Supreme in all the Vedas would not have occurred if the inner Self were not the supreme Self of all living beings; therefore, it is established that the Self under discussion is one and the same.
Nor does the transmigratory state belong to the Self, because transmigration is superimposed upon the Self through ignorance (avidyā).

For it is not the case that snakes, silver, impurities, and so forth—which are superimposed through false cognition upon a rope, mother-of-pearl, the sky, and so on—actually belong to those [objects].
By this, it is explained that for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain.
And as for the established statement, "he is surely a knower of the unpleasant," it is proven that he is *not* merely a knower of the unpleasant.

This being the case, in all these various formulations, Prajāpati’s statement— "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman"— must indeed be true, whether it be the word of Prajāpati himself or the word of the Śruti appearing in the form of Prajāpati. It is not proper to render this false through the intellect of fallacious reasoning.
For there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than that.
If it is argued that the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of being the experiencer of unpleasantness such as suffering is experienced without error, we say no;
for its existence is established by way of direct perceptual experiences such as: "I am old though free from old age," "I have been born," "I am long-lived," "I am fair," "I am dark," or "I am dead."

If it is argued that all of this is indeed true, it is certainly so; yet it is difficult to comprehend, for even the King of the Gods (Indra), despite being shown the reasoning regarding non-destruction through the example of the water-cup and so forth, was utterly bewildered here by the thought, "He has entered into destruction.
Likewise, Virocana, though highly wise and a son of Prajāpati, came to hold the view that the self is merely the body.
Similarly, the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) sank into an ocean of fear regarding the destruction of the self, even while Indra was present.

Likewise, the Sāṃkhyas, although they have understood the seer to be distinct from the body and so forth, remain fixed in a vision of duality—which is the very domain of death—because they have abandoned the authority of the scriptures.

Similarly, others who follow the systems of Kaṇāda and others have set out to purify the substance of the self, which they believe is endowed with nine qualities, just as one purifies a cloth dyed with astringent dye using alkaline substances and the like.

Likewise, other ritualists, whose minds are captivated by external objects, even though they accept the Veda as authoritative, regard the oneness of the Self—the ultimate reality—as if it were destruction, like Indra; and like a water-wheel, they are incessantly engaged in the process of ascending and descending.
It wanders about;
what else can be said of other lowly creatures who, being devoid of discernment (*viveka*), have their minds naturally carried away by external objects?

Therefore, this [state] is for those wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsa*s, who have abandoned all external desires, who have no other refuge, who have transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramin*), and who are devoted to the realization of the Vedānta.

This work, which is to be experienced by those most worthy of worship and composed in four chapters by those following this tradition of Prajāpati, teaches in such a way that even today it remains exactly as it was and not otherwise. //1//
The wind is bodiless;
the cloud, lightning, and thunder— these are bodiless.
Just as these [rays], having risen from that space and having attained the highest light, manifest in their own true form.

In this regard, since the serene being (*saṃprasāda*), though bodiless, has attained a state of embodiedness through ignorance by becoming indistinguishable from the body, it must be explained how its manifestation in its own true form occurs after rising out of the body; therefore, an illustration is given:
"The wind is bodiless"—that is, it is bodiless because it lacks a body characterized by a head, hands, and so forth.
Furthermore, the cloud, lightning, and thunder— these are bodiless. This being so, when their purpose such as rain has been accomplished,
just as the word "from that" (amuṣmāt) refers to a region of space connected with the heavenly world, so too does the scripture, situated on earth, designate that celestial location.

These [elements], having attained a form equal to space as previously described, and being ungraspable in their own forms such as air and so forth, have reached the state called "space" (ākāśa), just as the serene being (saṃprasāda) has, in the state of ignorance, attained the very nature of the body as the self.
And those elements, being thus constituted, emerge from that region of space connected with yonder world for the purpose of accomplishing rain and other effects.
How?
At the end of the cold season, having reached the supreme, intense summer light of the sun— that is, having encountered the heat of the sun—

they are separated from their own forms by the solar heat; thus, the clouds, having abandoned their state of stillness, assume the form of winds such as the *purovāta* and so forth, while the earth and mountains take on the forms of elephants and other creatures, and the lightning likewise assumes its own flickering form as streaks of light and the like.
Even the thundercloud manifests by its own nature as the form of thunder and lightning; thus, with the arrival of the rainy season, they emerge in their respective forms. //2//
In this very way, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form;
it is the Supreme Person.
There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing with women, or with carriages, or with his kinsmen, not remembering this body into which he was born.
Just as a draft animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (prāṇa) yoked to this body.

Just as in this illustration where air and the other elements attain a state of equality with space and the rest, so too one who has attained identification with the body during the state of transmigratory existence— thinking "I am the son of such-and-such," "I am born," "I have grown old," "I shall die"— is enlightened by the instruction "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), just as Maghavan was by Prajāpati in the manner previously described, [realizing] that you do not possess the attributes of the body, senses, and so forth.

This serene being, the living self (*jīva*), having emerged from this body— just as wind and other elements emerge from space— and having realized the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, abandons the identification with the body;
this has been explained previously by the statement that it "manifests in its own form," which is the nature of pure Being (*sat*).

By whatever form that serene being (*saṃprasāda*) emerges after its previous state of delusion—that cause of error—it becomes a snake, just as a rope [mistakenly perceived] later emerges in its own true form as a rope once it has been illuminated. And thus, he is the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*), for he is both supreme and a person; he alone is the Supreme Person—the one who was manifest as the person in the eye and in the dream state, as well as unmanifest, merged, and serene in deep sleep.
"And the body by its own form.

This one, established in his own form, is the Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa) in relation to the perishable and the imperishable, the manifested and the unmanifested; for this has been defined in the Gītā.
He is that state of perfect serenity (saṃprasāda); in his own form, being established in himself as the Self of all, he moves about here and there, sometimes in the form of Indra and so forth.

Eating—that is, laughing or consuming various desired foods—somewhere with objects produced either by the mere mind through its own volition or belonging to the world of Brahmā; and sporting, that is, taking delight with women and others, by means of the mind alone; and not remembering this body, which is called *upajana* because it is born (*jāyate*) from the mutual union of a woman and a man, or because it is born in proximity to the self (*ātmasāmīpyena*) as a manifestation of the self. He does not remember this body.
For upon remembering that, there would indeed be suffering, because its very nature is suffering.
[Objection: But if one does not remember what has been experienced, then the liberated one would lack omniscience.

This is not a fault. For that which was produced by false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) and the like has its false cognition and so forth destroyed by *vidyā*; therefore, it was never truly experienced at all. Thus, there is no loss of omniscience due to the non-recollection of that [experience]. Indeed, what was experienced by one who is insane or possessed by a spirit need not be remembered even when the insanity or possession has ceased; likewise here, as well, that which is experienced by transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) who possess the defect of ignorance (*avidyā*) does not belong to the Self, which is bodiless and the soul of all.
It does not touch [them],
because the cause of ignorance is absent.

However, those desires which are experienced by those whose defects are severed and whose impurities are worn away— desires that are real but have falsehood as their covering— are manifested by knowledge.

Thus, they are described as being connected with that which is liberated and has become the Self of all; this is stated for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, it is rightly specified:
"those who [attain] these worlds of Brahman.
For wherever they may be, they exist indeed in the world of Brahman alone; thus, because Brahman is the Self of all, they are so called.

But how is it not contradictory that [the text says] "being one, he sees nothing else, knows nothing else; that is the Infinite (bhūman)" and also "seeing the desires belonging to the world of Brahman, he rejoices"?
For it would be as if one were to see in one very same moment and yet not see in that very same moment.
This is not a fault.
Because this has been resolved in another scriptural passage:
"Since the vision of the seer is never lost, he continues to see;
yet, because desires do not exist apart from the seer, he does not see."
Although that was stated regarding deep sleep, for the liberated one as well, the absence of a second is the same because of the oneness of all;

and it has already been said: "By what means and whom would he see? Yet, Prajāpati asked how this person, whose true nature is bodiless and characterized by the removal of evil and so forth, is seen in the eye.
In this regard, since it must be explained how [the self] is directly perceived in the eye, this [section] is commenced.

To the question, "What is the reason for seeing in the eye? he says: that is the illustration, such as a "yoke-ox" (*prayogya*) or one "beyond the yoke" (*prayogyapara*), which possesses the word "yoke.
It is called a "yoke-ox" (*prayogya*) because it is employed (*prayujyate*)—that is, a horse or a bullock.
Just as in the world a chariot or a cart is called "ācaraṇa" because one moves by means of it, and a horse or ox is yoked to that vehicle for the purpose of drawing it,

so too in this body— which stands in the place of a chariot— the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) is yoked; joined with the senses, the mind, and the intellect, the conscious self (*prajñātman*), whose nature is a conflation of the two powers of cognition and action, is appointed for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its own past actions.
"In what, upon my departure, shall I depart? Or in what, being established, shall I be established?
Thus [the self] is appointed to the operations of seeing, hearing, and movement by the Lord, like a prime minister by a king.
Of that [Lord] alone, however, the eye-faculty is but a single part, serving as the gateway for the perception of form. //3//

Now, where this eye is directed toward space, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing. And he who knows, "Let me smell this," he is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling.
Now, he who knows "I shall speak this" is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking.
And he who knows "I shall hear this" is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing. (ChU 8.12.4)

Now, where the space characterized by the black pupil (kṛṣṇatāra) is present—pervading, attached to, and following along with the cavity of the body—therein is that aforementioned bodiless Self, who is "of the eye" (cākṣuṣa), meaning he exists in the eye. For the purpose of seeing—that is, for the perception of form—the eye is his instrument; because he is conjoined with the body and other elements, he exists here in the eye for the sake of the Supreme Seer.

By means of the sign of vision, the Supreme— who is bodiless and uncomposed— is perceived. Prajāpati’s statement, "He is seen in the eye," is intended as an illustration for all the doors of the senses,
for He alone is indeed the perceiver of all objects.
In all the Vedic texts, the specific term "eyes" is used because they are the cause of clear perception;
as the Śruti says: "When one thinks, 'I have seen,' that becomes true.

Furthermore, he who within this body knows, "How may I smell this, whether it be fragrant or foul? May I perceive its odor?"—he is the Self, and the nose is for his sake, for the purpose of smelling, that is, for the perception of odors.
Now, he who knows, "I shall utter this speech," "I will speak"—that Self, for the sake of accomplishing the act of articulation, has the organ of speech as its instrument.
Now, he who knows, "I shall hear this"—that Self, for the sake of hearing, has the ear. //4//
Now,
he who knows, "I am thinking this," that is the Self;
the mind is its divine eye.
Verily, with this divine eye, the mind, he beholds these desires that are in the world of Brahman and rejoices in them.
Now, he who knows, "I shall think this"—knowing that the activity of thinking is not touched by the senses but is purely thinking—he is the Self; the mind is for the purpose of thinking.
Because of the application [of the term] everywhere in the form "he who knows is the Self," it is understood that knowing is his essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Just as when it is said, "He who illumines the east is the sun; he who illumines the south, the west, the north, and the zenith is the sun," it is understood that its essential nature is illumination.
The sense organs, such as the eye, exist for the purpose of accomplishing actions like seeing;
this is understood through the capacity of this self.
The self's status as the agent of cognition exists by its mere existence alone, and not through active exertion.
Just as the sun possesses the agency of illumination by its mere existence and not through any active exertion, so it is here:
the mind (*manas*) is the divine, non-material eye of this Self, uncommon to the other senses; it "sees" (*caṣṭe*), meaning it perceives, by means of this [mind], which is therefore called the "eye.
Furthermore, the [other] senses have objects belonging to the present time, and for that reason they are "non-divine."

The mind, however, is called the divine eye because it is the instrument for perceiving objects of the three periods of time; when its defects are suppressed, it becomes the instrument for perceiving all things—subtle, concealed, and so forth.

Indeed, that liberated one, having attained his true nature, being separated from the body, senses, and mind created by ignorance, and having reached the state of being the Self of all, is pure like space. Being the Lord of all with the mind as his limiting adjunct, he, through this very Lordly mind—which is eternally pervasive like the light of the sun—enjoys these desires.
He delights in beholding them by means of vision.

He specifies which desires these are: "those which exist in the world of Brahman like a hidden treasure of gold, covered over by the untruth of attachment to external objects, and obtainable through mere volition"—this is the meaning. //5//
The gods, indeed, worship this very Self;
therefore, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them.
"He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires. Thus spoke Prajāpati; thus spoke Prajāpati.
Because this Self was told to Indra by Prajāpati, therefore even today the gods worship that Self after having heard of it from him.
And through that worship, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them.
The intention is that the gods have obtained the fruit of that for which Indra lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) with Prajāpati for one hundred and one years.

It may be argued that this is appropriate for the gods because of their great fortune, but it is not possible now for humans because of their short lifespan and their more limited intelligence; to this objection, the following is said: "He attains all worlds and all desires—even one belonging to the present time.
Who is he?
"He who, like Indra and others, realizes and understands that Self"—thus indeed Prajāpati spoke in general terms.

Therefore, the meaning is that for all [disciples], the knowledge of the Self and the attainment of its fruit are exactly the same. The repetition [of the concluding statement] is for the purpose of marking the end of the section. //6//
Thus ends the twelfth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
From the dark I pass over to the variegated.
"From the variegated I pass to the dark;

shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I—being perfected in self—attain the uncreated world of Brahman, I attain it. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad Bhāṣya 8.13.1). This traditional recitation of the mantra beginning with "From the dark I pass to the variegated" is purifying, intended for silent recitation (*japa*), or for meditation (*dhyāna*).

The color is dark and profound; it is "dark" (śyāma) as if it were dark because the Brahman within the heart is extremely difficult to fathom. Having known that dark Brahman within the heart through meditation, I shall reach—that is, I shall go upward by means of my mind after the fall of the body—to that variegated (śabala) world of Brahman. It is called "variegated" because the world of Brahman is mixed with various desires such as those for forests and so forth. I shall attain that variegated world of Brahman.

The intention is this: "Since I am departing from the variegated world of Brahmā (*śabalo brahmalokaḥ*) for the sake of manifesting name and form, I resort to the dark one; I have entered the state of the heart. Therefore, the meaning is: "Having resorted to that very Self, which is the primordial nature and is variegated.
It is asked: "How does one resort to the variegated world of Brahmā? It is said: "Like a horse shaking off its own hairs by means of shaking."

Just as one becomes stainless by removing dust and other impurities from the hair through effort, so too, having shaken off evil and the mixture of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) by means of the knowledge of the Brahman within the heart, one becomes radiant— just as the moon, seized by Rāhu, is released from that eclipse and shines forth.
Likewise, having shaken off and abandoned the body, which is the locus of all misfortunes, one whose self is perfected here and now through meditation [attains liberation].
"Having accomplished what was to be done, I shall eternally attain the uncreated world of Brahman.
The repetition [of the mantra] is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the mantra. //1//
Thus ends the thirteenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form.
That which is between them is Brahman; that is the immortal; that is the Self.
I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati. May I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, the glory of the Kṣatriyas, and the glory of the Vaiśyas.
I have attained glory.
I am indeed that glory of glories;
may I not go to the white, toothless, toothless, soft [worm]; may I not go to the white, soft [worm].
"Space, indeed," and so forth, is for the purpose of providing a definition of Brahman for the sake of meditation.
"Space" is the name by which the Self is well-known in the Vedas,
because, like space, it is bodiless and subtle.

And that space (*ākāśa*) is the sustainer, the bearer, and the manifester of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which reside within its own self, constitute the seed of the world, and stand in the relation of foam to water. That Brahman is "within" (*antarā*) those two name-and-form—that is, it exists in the midst of them—or rather, it is that which is "between" (*antarā*) name-and-form, untouched by name-and-form. This Brahman is thus distinct in nature from name-and-form and untouched by them; nevertheless, it possesses the quality of being their sustainer.
The meaning is that Brahman is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

This very point is stated in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa; because pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is found to follow through everywhere, it is understood that the nature of everything is simply the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatā*), and thus a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatā*) is established. To the question "How is this understood?", he says: "That is the Self (*sa ātmā*)."

For the so-called Self is indeed well-known as the direct consciousness of all living beings, self-evident; by that very nature, it should be understood that the Self—bodiless, all-pervading like space—is Brahman.
And that Self, which is Brahman, is immortal, having the quality of being deathless.
Hereafter follows the mantra.
I enter—that is, I go to—the assembly hall, the abode, the mansion built by the Lord, of Prajāpati who has four faces.
Furthermore, I am glory; I am the Self named Glory belonging to the Brāhmaṇas.
For it is the Brāhmaṇas alone who especially worship Him; therefore, I become their glory.
Likewise, [I am the self] of kings and of vaiśyas;
since they too are indeed [my] subjects, I am their self as well.
Thus, I shall attain, and I desire to attain, that fame; for I am the self of those fames characterized by the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect.
To the question, "For what purpose do I resort to this?", it is said: It is white in color, like a ripe jujube fruit; it is red.

Likewise, it is *adatka*—meaning toothless (*adanta*), yet *adatka* in the sense of being a devourer (*bhakṣayitṛ*). It is that which destroys—that is, the destroyer and annihilator—of the luster, strength, vigor, wisdom, and merit of those who indulge in it. This refers to the female organ (*strīvyañjana*).
Whatever is characterized in this way—white, slimy, and slippery—may I not go toward it; may I not approach it.
The repetition [of the negative particle] is for the purpose of demonstrating that it is the cause of absolute misfortune. //1//
Thus ends the fourteenth section of the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
This very [knowledge] Brahmā told to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his offspring.

Having studied the Veda according to the rules from the family of a teacher, and having returned home with the remainder of his time after performing services for the teacher, he should dwell in a household, reciting his private study in a clean place, maintaining righteous conduct, withdrawing all his senses into himself, and not harming any living beings except at the prescribed sacred sites.
Indeed, conducting himself thus for as long as life lasts, he attains the world of Brahman;
and he does not return again, he does not return again.

Now, this very knowledge of the Self, together with its auxiliary means— namely, the meditations beginning with "Om is this syllable"— along with the text that expresses it, characterized as the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, was spoken by Brahmā, whether he be Hiraṇyagarbha or the Supreme Lord, through him to Prajāpati Kaśyapa.

He [Brahmā] imparted it to his son Manu, and Manu to the progeny; thus, the knowledge of the Upaniṣads, having come down through a succession of traditional transmission of the meaning of the Śruti, is still understood among the learned even today.
Just as the knowledge of the Self revealed here in the three chapters beginning with the sixth is understood along with its fruit, so it is not the case for ritual actions.

When it might be concluded that [the study of the Veda] has no purpose, in order to avoid the resulting charge of pointlessness, the meaningfulness of this ritual action—performed by the learned—is stated through its possession of a specific fruit: "Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher" means having completed the study along with its meaning; "according to rule" means being endowed with the restraints as prescribed in the Smṛtis.

Since every duty prescribed in the Smṛtis must be performed toward one's preceptor, he says the following in order to demonstrate the preeminence of service to the teacher: "Having performed whatever work for the teacher is to be done, with the remaining time that is free from such work, one should study the Veda.
The intention is that the Veda studied by one who observes such a discipline leads to the attainment of the fruits of ritual action and knowledge, but not otherwise.

The meaning is: having returned from the teacher’s house after completing the inquiry into Dharma, having duly taken a wife, and remaining in the household while established in the duties prescribed for the householder stage.

Even therein, in order to demonstrate the preeminence of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) among the duties prescribed for the householder, it is said: "In a pure, secluded place free from impurities and the like, sitting as long as necessary, one should study the Vedic recitation, both the obligatory and the additional."
Practicing the study of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures according to his ability, making his sons and disciples righteous and endowed with dharma, and restraining them through righteousness;

having established and withdrawn all the senses into the Brahman within his own heart—that is, in the *hārda*—and having renounced actions by the very mention of the senses; and practicing non-violence, meaning not causing injury or pain to others, and thus not afflicting any beings, whether stationary or moving.
Since even wandering for the sake of alms and so forth might cause suffering to others, he says: "except at sacred sites" (*anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ*).
A "sacred site" (*tīrtha*) refers to a domain permitted by the scriptures; the meaning is "other than that.
And this applies equally to all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*): except at sacred sites, there is indeed non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).

Others describe it thus: he who performs all this within the household itself is indeed authorized [to do so]; by conducting himself in the manner just described for as long as life lasts, for as long as one lives, he reaches the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) at the end of the body and does not return again to assume a body, because of the prohibition against returning once it has been attained.

By the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), having attained the world of the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahma-loka*), he remains right there for as long as that world of Brahman endures; the meaning is that until then, he does not return.
The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of marking the completion of the Upaniṣadic teaching. //1// //
Thus ends the fifteenth section of the eighth chapter in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
